principality-of-heitersheim.t: The seat of the Knights of Saint John's Grand Priory of Germany, whose grand priors ruled a tiny principality in the Breisgau.
principality-of-heitersheim.o: The Order of Saint John, the Knights Hospitaller, acquired Heitersheim near Freiburg in the 13th century, and from 1505 it was the residence of the order's Grand Prior of [[e:germany|Germany]]. In 1548 Emperor [[e:charles-v-holy-roman-emperor|Charles V]] raised the grand prior to a prince of the empire, making Heitersheim a small principality.
principality-of-heitersheim.r: The grand prior governed Heitersheim and a few neighbouring villages directly and oversaw the order's [[e:commandery|commanderies]] in [[e:germany|Germany]], which sent knights and revenues to Malta. The principality lay within the sphere of [[s:further-austria|Further Austria]], and the [[e:habsburg-dynasty|Habsburgs]] disputed its full independence. It remained Catholic.
principality-of-heitersheim.e: In 1806 Baden annexed Heitersheim, and the Grand Priory was dissolved. The priors' castle, the Malteserschloss, survives as a convent and museum.

principality-of-schaumburg-lippe.t: Tiny north German state at Bückeburg that survived from the Thirty Years' War to 1918, famed for a soldier-count's military academy.
principality-of-schaumburg-lippe.o: When the counts of Schaumburg died out in 1640, their lands were divided in 1647. Philip, a younger brother of the Count of Lippe, received a share including Bückeburg and Stadthagen, founding Schaumburg-Lippe, while the rest went to [[s:electorate-of-hesse|Hesse-Kassel]] and Brunswick-Lüneburg.
principality-of-schaumburg-lippe.r: Count William, in the 18th century, was a military reformer who built the island fortress of Wilhelmstein in the Steinhuder Meer and ran a school for officers where Gerhard von Scharnhorst trained. He also commanded allied forces in Portugal in 1762. The princely title came in 1807. The economy relied on farming and sandstone quarries, and the princes became wealthy landowners.
principality-of-schaumburg-lippe.e: Schaumburg-Lippe joined the [[s:german-confederation|German Confederation]] and in 1871 the [[s:german-empire|German Empire]] as one of its smallest states. Prince Adolf II abdicated in November 1918, and it continued as the [[s:free-state-of-schaumburg-lippe|Free State of Schaumburg-Lippe]].

principality-of-schwarzburg-rudolstadt.t: A small Thuringian principality ruled from the Heidecksburg above Rudolstadt, whose last prince was the last German monarch to abdicate in 1918.
principality-of-schwarzburg-rudolstadt.o: The counts of [[s:county-of-schwarzburg|Schwarzburg]] were among the oldest noble houses of Thuringia. After the death of Count Günther XLI in 1583 and a period of joint rule, the Treaty of Stadtilm of 1599 divided the County of Schwarzburg between brothers, creating the Rudolstadt and Sondershausen lines.
principality-of-schwarzburg-rudolstadt.r: The counts, raised to princes in 1710, ruled two separate blocks of territory, the Upper Lordship around Rudolstadt and part of the Lower Lordship in northern Thuringia, and gradually shook off [[e:saxons|Saxon]] overlordship. The Lutheran court rebuilt the Heidecksburg palace in Baroque style after a fire in 1735. Schiller first met Goethe in Rudolstadt in 1788.
principality-of-schwarzburg-rudolstadt.e: Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt joined the [[s:german-confederation|German Confederation]] and the [[s:german-empire|German Empire]]. Its last prince, Günther Victor, who had ruled both [[s:county-of-schwarzburg|Schwarzburg]] states since 1909, abdicated in November 1918, the last German monarch to do so. In 1920 it merged into the [[s:free-state-of-thuringia|Free State of Thuringia]].

phimai-regime.t: A short-lived Siamese breakaway regime on the Khorat plateau after Ayutthaya's fall, led by a prince of the old royal house.
phimai-regime.o: When the [[s:ayutthaya-kingdom|Ayutthaya Kingdom]] fell to the Burmese in 1767, its provincial governors and princes set up rival regimes. At Phimai, on the Khorat plateau, Prince Thepphiphit, a son of King Borommakot who had earlier been exiled to [[e:ceylon|Ceylon]], gathered followers and claimed authority as the legitimate heir.
phimai-regime.r: The regime controlled the north-eastern plateau around Phimai and Nakhon Ratchasima, a region with old [[e:khmer-empire|Khmer]] temples and Lao and Khmer populations. Its power rested on Thepphiphit's royal prestige and local nobles. It was one of five main contenders for the Siamese succession.
phimai-regime.e: In 1768 Taksin of the [[s:thonburi-kingdom|Thonburi Kingdom]] attacked Phimai and defeated its forces. Thepphiphit was captured and executed, and the plateau was brought under Thonburi rule.

principality-of-halberstadt.t: Former prince-bishopric in the Harz foreland turned into a Brandenburg-Prussian principality by the Peace of Westphalia.
principality-of-halberstadt.o: The Bishopric of Halberstadt, founded around 804, had become Lutheran during the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] and was ruled by administrators. At the [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] in 1648 it was secularised and given to [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]] as compensation for its claims to [[s:duchy-of-pomerania|Pomerania]], becoming the Principality of Halberstadt.
principality-of-halberstadt.r: The principality was governed by Brandenburg-Prussian officials through a provincial government, with the cathedral chapter kept as a Protestant institution. It was a fertile grain-growing region with a sizeable garrison. In the 18th century the poet Johann Wilhelm Ludwig Gleim lived there as cathedral secretary, gathering a circle of writers.
principality-of-halberstadt.e: After [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia's]] defeat in 1806, Halberstadt was given to the [[s:kingdom-of-westphalia|Kingdom of Westphalia]] in 1807. It returned to Prussia in 1815 and became part of the Province of Saxony; the town is now in Saxony-Anhalt.

pharsalus.t: Thessalian city of Phthiotis, long ruled by aristocratic families, whose plain saw Caesar's victory over Pompey in 48 BCE.
pharsalus.o: Pharsalus stood on a hill above the plain of the Enipeus in southern Thessaly, in the region Greek myth linked to Achilles's Phthia. It became a city in the Archaic period and one of the leading members of the [[s:thessalian-league|Thessalian League]] with [[s:larissa|Larissa]] and [[s:tyranny-of-pherae|Pherae]].
pharsalus.r: Pharsalus was dominated by aristocratic families such as the Echecratidae. In the 370s BCE Polydamas governed the city and was forced to submit to Jason of [[s:tyranny-of-pherae|Pherae]]. Daochus, a Pharsalian, served Philip II as tetrarch of Thessaly and set up a family monument at [[s:delphi|Delphi]].
pharsalus.e: Pharsalus passed under Macedonian rule, was freed by [[e:rome|Rome]] in 196 BCE and came under Roman control by 146 BCE. In 48 BCE [[e:julius-caesar|Julius Caesar]] defeated [[e:pompey|Pompey]] nearby at the Battle of Pharsalus.

principality-of-achaea.t: Most successful crusader state in Greece, a French chivalric society in the Peloponnese whose story is told in the Chronicle of the Morea.
principality-of-achaea.o: In 1205 William of Champlitte and Geoffrey of Villehardouin, crusaders of the [[e:fourth-crusade|Fourth Crusade]], conquered the western Peloponnese after defeating local [[e:greeks|Greeks]] at the Olive Grove of Koundouros. Geoffrey I took control after Champlitte left, and his family ruled for three generations under the nominal suzerainty of the [[s:latin-empire|Latin Empire]].
principality-of-achaea.r: The principality was a model feudal state, divided into twelve baronies, such as Karytaina, Akova and [[s:barony-of-patras|Patras]], whose lords sat in the prince's council. Its laws were codified as the Assizes of [[s:kingdom-of-romania|Romania]]. The court at Andravida and the port of Clarentza were famed for French culture, and the castle of Chlemoutsi guarded the coast. Greek archons kept their lands.
principality-of-achaea.e: Captured at Pelagonia in 1259, William II of Villehardouin ceded Mistras and Monemvasia to [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]], creating the base of the [[s:despotate-of-the-morea|Despotate of the Morea]]. Angevin, Navarrese and Zaccaria rulers followed. Thomas Palaiologos annexed the rest of the principality in 1430-1432.

principality-of-wales.t: The Welsh state built by the princes of Gwynedd and recognised by England in 1267, the high point of native Welsh political independence.
principality-of-wales.o: Llywelyn ap Iorwerth, Llywelyn the Great, made [[s:kingdom-of-gwynedd|Gwynedd]] dominant in Wales, and at Aberdyfi in 1216 the other Welsh rulers accepted his overlordship. His grandson Llywelyn ap Gruffudd took the title Prince of Wales, which Henry III recognised in the Treaty of Montgomery in 1267.
principality-of-wales.r: The principality was a feudal overlordship over lesser Welsh lords such as those of [[s:powys-fadog|Powys Fadog]] and [[s:powys-wenwynwyn|Powys Wenwynwyn]]. Its princes ruled from Gwynedd's courts, including Aber Garth Celyn, and used Welsh law, stone castles such as Dolwyddelan and a growing chancery.
principality-of-wales.e: Llywelyn's refusal to do homage to Edward I led to war in 1277, and a revolt begun by his brother Dafydd in 1282 ended in conquest. He was killed near Cilmeri in 1282, and his brother Dafydd executed in 1283. The Statute of Rhuddlan of 1284 annexed the principality to the [[s:kingdom-of-england|Kingdom of England]].

principality-of-koknese.t: A small Orthodox principality on the Daugava, vassal of Polotsk, swallowed by the crusading Bishopric of Riga in 1208.
principality-of-koknese.o: Koknese, called Kukenois by the Germans, was a fortified centre on the Daugava in what is now [[s:republic-of-latvia|Latvia]], inhabited by Latgalians and [[s:selonians|Selonians]]. By the late 12th century it was ruled by a prince of Rus' origin, Vyachko, as a tributary of the [[s:principality-of-polotsk|Principality of Polotsk]]. It is known almost entirely from the chronicle of Henry of [[s:livonian-confederation|Livonia]].
principality-of-koknese.r: The principality controlled a stretch of the Daugava trade route between Polotsk and the Baltic and collected tribute from the surrounding Baltic peoples. Its prince and his retinue were [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] Christians, while most of the population remained pagan. When German crusaders founded Riga in 1201, Koknese came under pressure from [[e:bishop|Bishop]] Albert.
principality-of-koknese.e: In 1207 Vyachko gave half his land to the [[e:bishop|bishop]] in return for protection. Quarrels with German knights followed, and in 1208 he burned his castle and fled to Rus'. The bishop built a stone castle on the site, and Vyachko died defending Tartu against the crusaders in 1224.

patna-state.t: A Chauhan Rajput state in western Odisha, once head of a cluster of eighteen hill forts, whose last Maharaja became Chief Minister of Orissa.
patna-state.o: Tradition holds that Ramai Deva, a Chauhan [[e:rajputs|Rajput]], founded the dynasty at Patnagarh in the mid-14th century and became overlord of the surrounding chiefs, a group known as the Athara Garhjat, or eighteen forts. A branch of the family later founded [[s:sambalpur-state|Sambalpur State]].
patna-state.r: [[e:patna|Patna]] was a large inland state of [[e:rice|rice]] fields and forest, home to Kondh, Binjhal and other communities. Its capital later moved to Bolangir. Under the [[e:maratha-empire|Marathas]] it was tributary to the [[e:bhonsles|Bhonsles]] of the [[s:nagpur-kingdom|Nagpur Kingdom]], and under the British it belonged to the Orissa Tributary States from 1905.
patna-state.e: [[e:patna|Patna]] merged into Orissa on 1 January 1948. Its last ruler, Rajendra Narayan Singh Deo, entered politics and served as Chief Minister of Orissa from 1967 to 1971. The area is now Bolangir district.

principality-of-rostov.t: An appanage principality based on the ancient town of Rostov on Lake Nero, gradually bought out by Moscow.
principality-of-rostov.o: Rostov is one of the oldest towns of north-eastern Rus', first mentioned in 862 in the land of the Finnic Merya, and was long the seat of a [[e:bishop|bishop]]. In 1207 Vsevolod the Big Nest gave it to his eldest son Konstantin, and his descendants ruled it as a principality within the [[s:vladimir-suzdal|Vladimir-Suzdal]] lands.
principality-of-rostov.r: Rostov was a religious and commercial centre with a long tradition of chronicle writing. Its prince Vasilko Konstantinovich was captured and killed by the [[e:mongols|Mongols]] after the Battle of the Sit in 1238. Later the principality was split between two lines, each ruling half the town, and it became a minor power between [[e:moscow|Moscow]] and Tver.
principality-of-rostov.e: [[e:moscow|Moscow's]] influence grew through the 14th century, and the Rostov princes sold the first half of their rights to Moscow in the 15th century. In 1474 the last princes sold the remaining half to [[e:ivan-iii|Ivan III]]. The town remained a great church centre, and its kremlin was built by Metropolitan Jonah in the 17th century.

principality-of-hereti.t: A small Christian principality between Georgia and Caucasian Albania whose Queen Dinar is remembered for bringing it into the Georgian Orthodox church.
principality-of-hereti.o: Hereti lay along the Alazani and Iori rivers and around Shaki, a borderland between [[s:kingdom-of-iberia|Kartli]] and the old [[s:caucasian-albania|Caucasian Albania]]. In the 9th century, as Arab power waned, a local dynasty with ties to the former [[s:mihranid-principality-of-albania|Mihranid Principality of Albania]] established its own rule, sometimes called the kings of the Rans.
principality-of-hereti.r: Its population mixed Georgians, [[e:armenians|Armenians]] and Caucasian [[e:albanians|Albanians]], and its church long followed the anti-Chalcedonian Armenian tradition. In the 10th century Queen [[e:dinar|Dinar]], of Georgian Bagratid descent, converted the principality to Georgian Orthodoxy. Its rulers fought the [[s:emirate-of-tbilisi|Emirate of Tbilisi]] and competed with [[s:principality-of-kakheti|Kakheti]], controlling farmland and routes to the Caspian.
principality-of-hereti.e: Hereti was absorbed by the [[s:principality-of-kakheti|Principality of Kakheti]] in the late 10th century, and around 1010 the two formed the [[s:kingdom-of-kakheti-hereti|Kingdom of Kakheti-Hereti]]. The name survived as a province of the Georgian kingdom.

principality-of-brandenburg-bayreuth.t: The Franconian margraviate of the Hohenzollerns, ruled from Kulmbach and Bayreuth and made a rococo showcase by Margravine Wilhelmine.
principality-of-brandenburg-bayreuth.o: When the Hohenzollern rulers of the [[s:burgraviate-of-nuremberg|Burgraviate of Nuremberg]] divided their Franconian lands in 1398, the territory 'above the mountains' around Kulmbach and the Plassenburg went to John III. After the family gained the [[s:margraviate-of-brandenburg|Margraviate of Brandenburg]] in 1415, its Franconian principalities were usually ruled by younger sons with the title of margrave.
principality-of-brandenburg-bayreuth.r: Margrave Albert Alcibiades devastated Franconia in his wars of the 1550s. The territory was Lutheran, and the court moved from Kulmbach to Bayreuth in the early 17th century. Margravine Wilhelmine, sister of Frederick the Great, and her husband Frederick made Bayreuth a cultural centre, building the Margravial Opera House and founding the university at Erlangen in 1743.
principality-of-brandenburg-bayreuth.e: In 1769 Bayreuth passed to Charles Alexander, margrave of the [[s:principality-of-brandenburg-ansbach|Principality of Brandenburg-Ansbach]], who in 1791 ceded both principalities to the [[s:kingdom-of-prussia|Kingdom of Prussia]]. [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]] gave Bayreuth to the [[s:kingdom-of-bavaria|Kingdom of Bavaria]] in 1810. Richard Wagner later built his festival [[e:theatre|theatre]] in the town.

pre-islamic-mecca.t: The sanctuary town of the Kaaba, governed by the clans of Quraysh, whose trade and pilgrimage made it the birthplace of Islam.
pre-islamic-mecca.o: Arab tradition credits Qusayy ibn Kilab with gathering the [[e:quraysh|Quraysh]] clans in [[e:mecca|Mecca]] in the 5th century and taking control of the Kaaba, a shrine already visited by pilgrims from across western [[e:arabia|Arabia]]. He distributed the hereditary offices of the sanctuary: guarding the Kaaba, giving water and food to pilgrims and holding the war banner.
pre-islamic-mecca.r: [[e:mecca|Mecca]] had no king. Clans such as Hashim, Makhzum, Umayya and Abd al-Dar shared power through an assembly of elders. The town lived on the pilgrimage, the sacred months that protected trade, nearby fairs such as Ukaz and caravans to [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]] and [[s:republic-of-yemen|Yemen]]. The Kaaba housed images of many deities, Hubal chief among them, and Allah was recognised as a high god.
pre-islamic-mecca.e: Muhammad, of the clan of Hashim, began preaching around 610, met growing opposition and left for [[e:medina|Medina]] in 622. After years of war, [[e:mecca|Mecca]] surrendered to the [[s:islamic-state-of-medina|Islamic state of Medina]] in 630; the idols of the Kaaba were destroyed and the town became the holiest city of [[e:islam|Islam]].

phitsanulok-regime.t: A breakaway regime in northern Siam led by the governor of Phitsanulok, one of the rivals Taksin had to overcome after Ayutthaya's fall.
phitsanulok-regime.o: After the Burmese sack of the [[s:ayutthaya-kingdom|Ayutthaya Kingdom]] in 1767, the governor of Phitsanulok, a Thai noble named Rueang, declared himself ruler of the northern provinces of the central plain, an area that included the old cities of [[s:sukhothai-kingdom|Sukhothai]] and Phichit. He took royal style as Chao Phitsanulok.
phitsanulok-regime.r: The regime controlled the upper Chao Phraya and Nan river region, a rich [[e:rice|rice]]-growing area with strong defensive positions. It repelled an early attack by Taksin in 1768, during which Taksin was wounded. Little else is known of its administration, which probably continued the provincial structures of [[s:ayutthaya-kingdom|Ayutthaya]].
phitsanulok-regime.e: Chao Phitsanulok died in 1768, soon after crowning himself, and his territory was seized by the neighbouring [[s:sawangkhaburi-regime|Sawangkhaburi regime]] of Chao Phra Fang. Taksin of the [[s:thonburi-kingdom|Thonburi Kingdom]] conquered the whole north in 1770.

portuguese-mombasa.t: Portugal's main stronghold on the Swahili coast, centred on Fort Jesus, which fell to Oman after a siege of nearly three years.
portuguese-mombasa.o: After decades of hostility with [[s:mombasa|Mombasa]], the Portuguese occupied the island in 1593, built Fort Jesus to an Italian design and installed the ruler of [[s:malindi|Malindi]] as sultan. The fort became the headquarters of Portuguese power north of [[s:portuguese-mozambique|Mozambique]], guarding the routes to [[e:india|India]].
portuguese-mombasa.r: A Portuguese captain commanded the fort and collected customs, while a client [[e:swahili|Swahili]] sultan governed the town. Relations were tense: in 1631 [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Yusuf ibn al-Hasan, raised as a Catholic in [[e:goa|Goa]] as Dom Jeronimo Chingulia, returned to [[e:islam|Islam]], massacred the Portuguese garrison and briefly held the fort before abandoning it. Catholic missions had little lasting success.
portuguese-mombasa.e: The [[s:omani-empire|Omani Empire]], after expelling the Portuguese from [[e:muscat|Muscat]], besieged Fort Jesus from 1696 until it fell in December 1698. Portugal briefly regained it in 1728 to 1729, but [[s:mombasa|Mombasa]] passed to Omani governors and then the [[s:mazrui-sultanate|Mazrui Sultanate]]. Fort Jesus is a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

provisional-government-of-schleswig-hols.t: Rebel German government set up in Kiel in 1848 to free Schleswig and Holstein from Denmark, which fought the First Schleswig War and lost.
provisional-government-of-schleswig-hols.o: In March 1848, as revolutions spread across [[e:europe|Europe]], [[e:denmark|Denmark's]] new liberal government moved to tie Schleswig more closely to the kingdom. German nationalists in the duchies responded by forming a provisional government at [[e:kiel|Kiel]] on 24 March, led by Wilhelm Hartwig Beseler and Prince Frederick of Noer, claiming both duchies for the [[s:german-confederation|German Confederation]].
provisional-government-of-schleswig-hols.r: The government raised a Schleswig-Holstein army and received support from [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] and the [[s:german-confederation|German Confederation]], whose troops fought the Danes in 1848-1849. It governed from [[e:kiel|Kiel]] with the backing of the German-speaking estates, while Danish-minded inhabitants of northern Schleswig opposed it. Great-power pressure forced Prussia to make peace with [[e:denmark|Denmark]] in 1850.
provisional-government-of-schleswig-hols.e: Fighting alone, the Schleswig-Holstein army was defeated at Isted (Idstedt) in July 1850. Under pressure from [[e:austria|Austria]] and [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]], the government dissolved in early 1851, and Danish rule was restored. The [[e:london|London]] Protocol of 1852 confirmed the settlement, but the dispute reignited in the war of 1864.

pashalik-of-vidin.t: Rebel domain of Osman Pazvantoğlu on the Danube, who defied the Ottoman sultan and let loose raiders across Bulgaria and Wallachia.
pashalik-of-vidin.o: Osman Pazvantoğlu, a [[e:janissaries|janissary]] from Vidin, opposed [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Selim III's military reforms and seized control of Vidin around 1794. He gathered disbanded janissaries and kardzhali bandits, and in 1798 defeated a large Ottoman army sent to besiege the town. Unable to remove him, the sultan pardoned him and appointed him pasha of Vidin.
pashalik-of-vidin.r: Pazvantoğlu ruled as a warlord with his own army and treasury, and conducted his own diplomacy with [[e:russia|Russia]] and [[e:france|France]]. His bands raided much of [[s:bulgaria|Bulgaria]] and crossed into [[s:principality-of-wallachia|Wallachia]], burning Craiova in 1800. He backed the [[e:janissaries|janissary]] dahije who seized power in the Pashalik of [[e:belgrade|Belgrade]], whose abuses helped provoke the Serbian uprising of 1804.
pashalik-of-vidin.e: Pazvantoğlu died in 1807, and his successors soon returned Vidin to Ottoman control. His career showed the weakness of central authority under Selim III; Bulgarian memory recalls the kardzhali years as a time of terror.

principality-of-leiningen.t: A Palatinate county ruled by the Leiningen family from the Haardt hills, raised to a principality in 1779 before being swept away by the French.
principality-of-leiningen.o: Count Emich I of Leiningen appears around 1128, with castles in the Haardt hills of the [[s:electoral-palatinate|Palatinate]]. The original line died out in 1220, and the lands passed through a sister to the Saarbrücken family, who took the Leiningen name. The family split in 1317 into Leiningen-Hardenburg and Leiningen-Dagsburg.
principality-of-leiningen.r: The counts ruled scattered territories in the [[s:electoral-palatinate|Palatinate]] and Alsace, with castles at Hardenburg and Altleiningen. They were often in rivalry with the Electoral Palatinate. The Hardenburg line moved its residence to Dürkheim in the 18th century and was raised to princely rank in 1779.
principality-of-leiningen.e: French revolutionary forces annexed the left bank of the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] in the 1790s. In 1803 the princes received former church lands at Amorbach in Franconia, but these were mediatised in 1806 and divided between Baden, Bavaria and Hesse. Queen Victoria's half-brother Carl was a prince of Leiningen.

principality-of-yuryev-polsky.t: A small appanage of the Vladimir-Suzdal lands, best known for the richly carved Cathedral of Saint George.
principality-of-yuryev-polsky.o: Yuri Dolgoruky founded Yuryev-Polsky in 1152 in the open fields, the polye, between Vladimir and Pereslavl-Zalessky. When Vsevolod the Big Nest's sons divided his lands, [[e:sviatoslav-i-of-kiev|Sviatoslav]] Vsevolodovich received Yuryev in 1212 and it became a separate [[e:appanage|appanage]].
principality-of-yuryev-polsky.r: It was a small agricultural principality whose rulers were closely tied to Vladimir. [[e:sviatoslav-i-of-kiev|Sviatoslav]] built the Cathedral of Saint George between 1230 and 1234, whose walls are covered with carved stone reliefs of saints, beasts and plants. The town was sacked by the [[e:mongols|Mongols]] in 1238.
principality-of-yuryev-polsky.e: [[e:sviatoslav-i-of-kiev|Sviatoslav's]] descendants held the principality as a minor [[e:appanage|appanage]]. It came under the control of the [[s:grand-duchy-of-moscow|Grand Duchy of Moscow]] in the first half of the 14th century, and by around 1340 its separate princely rule had ended.

provisional-government-of-lithuania-1941.t: Lithuanian government formed during the June Uprising of 1941, which hoped to restore independence but was dissolved by the Germans after six weeks.
provisional-government-of-lithuania-1941.o: When [[e:germany|Germany]] invaded the [[s:soviet-union|Soviet Union]] on 22 June 1941, the Lithuanian Activist Front launched the June Uprising against Soviet rule. On 23 June it proclaimed restored independence on Kaunas radio and formed a Provisional Government. Its intended head, Kazys Škirpa, was held in Berlin, so Juozas Ambrazevičius served as acting prime minister.
provisional-government-of-lithuania-1941.r: The government tried to reverse Soviet nationalisation and re-establish Lithuanian institutions, but the Germans did not recognise it. It also issued anti-Jewish regulations while killings of [[e:jews|Jews]] by German units and Lithuanian collaborators began, a record that remains deeply controversial.
provisional-government-of-lithuania-1941.e: The Germans set up their own civil administration within [[s:reichskommissariat-ostland|Reichskommissariat Ostland]], and on 5 August 1941 the Provisional Government dissolved itself rather than become a German instrument. [[s:republic-of-lithuania|Lithuania]] remained under German occupation until 1944 and then became the [[s:lithuanian-soviet-socialist-republic|Lithuanian Soviet Socialist Republic]] again.

principality-of-mstislavl.t: An appanage of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania in eastern Belarus, ruled by descendants of Algirdas until 1529.
principality-of-mstislavl.o: Mstislavl, on the Sozh, was a town of the old [[e:smolensk|Smolensk]] lands. After the [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Grand Duchy of Lithuania]] took it in the mid 14th century, it was given as an [[e:appanage|appanage]] to sons of Algirdas, first Karigaila and later Lingvenis, whose descendants ruled it for over a century.
principality-of-mstislavl.r: Mstislavl was a frontier principality facing [[e:smolensk|Smolensk]] and [[e:moscow|Moscow]], with a largely [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] Ruthenian population. Lingvenis, who ruled from about 1390 to 1431, also served as a commander in Novgorod and fought at Grunwald. His line, and later the Mstislavsky family through marriage, held the land as [[e:vassal|vassals]] of the grand duke.
principality-of-mstislavl.e: In 1526 Prince Fyodor Mstislavsky fled to [[e:moscow|Moscow]], where his family became leading boyars. Mstislavl reverted to the grand duke, and in 1529 it lost its separate status, later becoming the Mstislavl Voivodeship.

principality-of-novosil.t: One of the Upper Oka principalities, founded by a son of Mikhail of Chernigov and caught between Lithuania and Moscow.
principality-of-novosil.o: After Mikhail of [[e:chernigov|Chernigov]] was killed at Batu's camp in 1246, his lands were divided among his sons. Semyon Mikhailovich received Glukhov and Novosil on the upper Oka, and Novosil became the senior seat of a group of small principalities known as the Upper Oka principalities.
principality-of-novosil.r: These were frontier lands, open to raids from the steppe and the [[s:golden-horde|Golden Horde]]. Novosil itself was ruined in the 14th century, and the princes moved their seat to Odoyev, so the line became known as the Odoyevsky. Related branches ruled Belyov and Vorotynsk. They usually served the [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Grand Duchy of Lithuania]] while bargaining with [[e:moscow|Moscow]].
principality-of-novosil.e: In the late 15th century the Upper Oka princes went over to [[e:ivan-iii|Ivan III]], and the peace of 1494 between [[e:moscow|Moscow]] and [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Lithuania]] confirmed their lands as part of the [[s:grand-duchy-of-moscow|Grand Duchy of Moscow]]. The Odoyevsky and Vorotynsky princes became prominent Russian nobles.

provisional-military-dictatorship-of-mug.t: A short-lived regime of Russian settlers in the Mughan steppe of south-eastern Azerbaijan, which resisted the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic in 1918-1919.
provisional-military-dictatorship-of-mug.o: The Mughan steppe and Lankaran area had many Russian settler villages, including Molokans and Old Believers, established in the 19th century. When the Russian administration collapsed in 1918, local settlers and former Russian officers formed their own armed government at Lankaran rather than accept the new Azerbaijani state.
provisional-military-dictatorship-of-mug.r: The regime was run by Russian officers and settler councils as a military administration, aligned with the anti-Bolshevik White movement of the [[s:russian-state|Russian State]] and receiving some British and White support. It controlled the Russian villages and fought local Talysh and Azerbaijani forces loyal to the [[s:azerbaijan-democratic-republic|Azerbaijan Democratic Republic]]. Little is known of its internal administration beyond military rule.
provisional-military-dictatorship-of-mug.e: In spring 1919 a regional congress of Mughan settlers turned against the military leadership, and the Bolsheviks took power, proclaiming the [[s:mughan-soviet-republic|Mughan Soviet Republic]]. The region was soon brought under Azerbaijani control.
provisional-military-dictatorship-of-mug.re: Russian Orthodox Christianity; Molokan and Old Believer communities

principality-of-anhalt-kothen.t: One of the Anhalt principalities of central Germany, home of the Fruitbearing Society and of the court where Johann Sebastian Bach wrote much of his instrumental music.
principality-of-anhalt-kothen.o: [[s:principality-of-anhalt|Anhalt]] was partitioned in 1603 among the sons of Prince Joachim Ernst, and Köthen fell to Ludwig, who founded the line of Anhalt-Köthen. Ludwig was a learned prince who in 1617 co-founded the Fruitbearing Society (Fruchtbringende Gesellschaft), the first society devoted to refining the German language.
principality-of-anhalt-kothen.r: The principality was a small Calvinist state in the Saale-Elbe region, living from agriculture. Its court is best known for Prince Leopold, a music lover who employed Johann Sebastian Bach as Kapellmeister from 1717 to 1723, when the [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]] Concertos and much chamber music were composed. In 1665 the line of [[s:principality-of-anhalt-plotzkau|Anhalt-Plötzkau]] inherited Köthen, continuing it under a new branch.
principality-of-anhalt-kothen.e: Köthen became a duchy in 1807 under [[e:napoleon|Napoleon's]] patronage and joined the [[s:german-confederation|German Confederation]]. When its last duke died without heirs in 1847, the territory passed to [[s:principality-of-anhalt-dessau|Anhalt-Dessau]] and [[s:principality-of-anhalt-bernburg|Anhalt-Bernburg]], and was absorbed into the united [[s:duchy-of-anhalt|Duchy of Anhalt]] by 1863.

principality-of-masserano.t: A tiny papal fief in northern Piedmont ruled by the Ferrero-Fieschi family until it was sold to the kings of Sardinia in 1767.
principality-of-masserano.o: Masserano and Crevacuore, small towns in the hills between Biella and the Sesia valley, belonged to the Fieschi family and then to the Ferrero, who took the Fieschi name. In 1598 [[e:papacy|Pope]] Clement VIII raised them to a principality held as a fief of the [[s:vatican-city|Holy See]], giving the family sovereign status.
principality-of-masserano.r: The Ferrero-Fieschi princes governed a few thousand subjects, minted coins and kept a small court, while often serving foreign rulers as soldiers and diplomats, especially [[e:spain|Spain]]. Surrounded by the [[s:duchy-of-savoy|Duchy of Savoy]], the state survived through papal protection and its rulers' connections abroad. Little else is recorded of its government.
principality-of-masserano.e: The House of [[s:duchy-of-savoy|Savoy]], now kings of the [[s:kingdom-of-sardinia|Kingdom of Sardinia]], long sought to absorb the enclave. In 1767 the prince ceded his [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]] to Charles Emmanuel III, ending the principality.

praisos.t: East Cretan city of the Eteocretans, a pre-Greek people whose language survives in a few undeciphered inscriptions.
praisos.o: Praisos stood on hills in the interior of eastern [[e:crete|Crete]]. [[e:herodotus|Herodotus]] and Strabo say its people were Eteocretans, 'true Cretans' descended from the island's pre-Greek inhabitants, and the settlement continued from the end of the [[e:bronze-age|Bronze Age]] into the Iron Age.
praisos.r: Inscriptions from Praisos, written in the Greek alphabet between the 6th and 3rd centuries BCE, record a non-[[e:greek-language|Greek language]] that remains undeciphered. The city controlled the sanctuary of Diktaean Zeus for a time and quarrelled with [[s:itanos|Itanos]]. It had harbours on both coasts of eastern [[e:crete|Crete]].
praisos.e: Praisos was destroyed by its neighbour [[s:hierapytna|Hierapytna]] c. 145 BCE, which took over its land. Its inscriptions are the main evidence for the Eteocretan language.
praisos.re: Cretan religion; cult of Diktaean Zeus

principality-of-hatuqwai.t: A small princely Circassian tribe of the western Caucasus foothills, known mainly from 18th- and 19th-century Russian and travellers' accounts.
principality-of-hatuqwai.o: The Hatuqwai were one of the smaller aristocratic Adyghe tribes of [[s:circassia|Circassia]], living between the Belaya and Laba rivers near the [[s:principality-of-temirgoy|Temirgoy]]. Little is known of their early history; they appear as a distinct community in sources of the 18th century.
principality-of-hatuqwai.r: Like other princely Circassian groups, they were ruled by princes and nobles over free peasants and serfs, following the Adyghe code of conduct and living by farming, [[e:horse-breeding|horse breeding]] and livestock. They usually acted in alliance with the neighbouring [[s:principality-of-temirgoy|Temirgoy]] and shared in the wider Circassian struggle against [[e:russia|Russia]].
principality-of-hatuqwai.e: The [[s:russian-empire|Russian Empire]] conquered their lands in the final campaigns of the Russo-Circassian War, completed in 1864. Almost all Hatuqwai were expelled to the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]], where their descendants were absorbed into the Circassian diaspora.

provisional-government-of-saskatchewan.t: The government declared by Louis Riel at Batoche in 1885, whose defeat ended the North-West Resistance and led to Riel's execution.
provisional-government-of-saskatchewan.o: Métis families who had moved west from Red River to the South Saskatchewan River after 1870 feared losing their river lots to surveys, while Cree nations faced hunger after the buffalo vanished. In 1884 they invited Louis Riel back from Montana. When Ottawa failed to respond to petitions, Riel proclaimed a provisional government at Batoche in March 1885.
provisional-government-of-saskatchewan.r: Its council was called the Exovedate, a name Riel coined meaning 'from the flock', and it mixed politics with Riel's religious ideas. Gabriel Dumont led its military. Métis fighters defeated the North-West Mounted Police at Duck Lake on 26 March, while Cree warriors from Big Bear's and Poundmaker's bands fought separately at Frog Lake, Battleford and Cut Knife.
provisional-government-of-saskatchewan.e: General Frederick Middleton's North-West Field Force won at Batoche in May 1885. Riel surrendered and was hanged in Regina that November, and eight Cree and Assiniboine men were hanged at Battleford. The execution deeply divided English and French [[s:canada|Canada]].

principality-of-starodub.t: A small appanage on the Klyazma whose princely line produced the Pozharsky family, including the liberator of Moscow in 1612.
principality-of-starodub.o: Starodub on the Klyazma, north-east of Vladimir, became the seat of Ivan Vsevolodovich, youngest son of Vsevolod the Big Nest. He is usually said to have received it from his brother Yaroslav in 1238, after the Mongol invasion, rather than in 1218.
principality-of-starodub.r: Starodub was a small forest principality within the [[s:vladimir-suzdal|Vladimir-Suzdal]] lands and later a minor player between [[e:moscow|Moscow]] and the [[s:golden-horde|Golden Horde]]. Its prince Fyodor Ivanovich was killed at the Horde in 1330. The family divided its land into tiny estates held by branches such as the Pozharsky, Ryapolovsky, Gagarin and Romodanovsky princes.
principality-of-starodub.e: By the mid 15th century the Starodub princes had become servitors of the [[s:grand-duchy-of-moscow|Grand Duchy of Moscow]], and their land was merged into Muscovite territory. Their descendant Prince Dmitry Pozharsky led the militia that freed [[e:moscow|Moscow]] from Polish occupation in 1612.

principality-of-boisbelle.t: A sovereign enclave in Berry, exempt from royal taxes, where Henry IV's minister Sully built the planned town of Henrichemont.
principality-of-boisbelle.o: Boisbelle was a lordship in Berry whose holders had long claimed [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]], a privilege tolerated by the French crown. In 1597 Maximilien de Béthune, later duke of Sully, Henry IV's chief minister, bought it and confirmed its status as a principality.
principality-of-boisbelle.r: Sully founded the town of Henrichemont in 1608, named after the king, on a regular grid around a central square, hoping to attract Protestant settlers and artisans. Its inhabitants paid no royal taxes, which drew some settlers, though the town never grew as planned. The Béthune family ruled the enclave for over 150 years.
principality-of-boisbelle.e: In 1766 the Duke of Sully's descendants sold the principality to Louis XV, ending its [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]], and it became part of the [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]].
ru: Maximilien de Béthune, Duke of Sully

province-of-senegambia.t: Britain's first crown colony in Africa, created after the capture of French Saint-Louis and lost again during the American War of Independence.
province-of-senegambia.o: British forces captured the French post of Saint-Louis in 1758 during the Seven Years War. The Treaty of [[e:paris|Paris]] of 1763 left it in British hands, and in 1765 Parliament created the Province of [[e:senegambia|Senegambia]], joining Saint-Louis with the British post of Fort James on the [[e:the-gambia|Gambia]] river. It was the first British crown colony on the African continent.
province-of-senegambia.r: A governor at Saint-Louis ruled a small garrison, merchants and the town's Afro-French population. The colony existed mainly to control the gum arabic trade of the [[e:senegal|Senegal]] river, valuable for textile dyeing, and to profit from the [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trade]]. The first governor, Charles O'Hara, quarrelled with traders and local rulers, and disease took a heavy toll on the garrison.
province-of-senegambia.e: [[e:france|France]] recaptured Saint-Louis in 1779 during the American War of Independence. The [[e:treaty-of-versailles|Treaty of Versailles]] of 1783 restored [[e:senegal|Senegal]] to France as [[s:french-senegal|French Senegal]] and left [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] the [[e:the-gambia|Gambia]], which later became the [[s:gambia-colony-and-protectorate|Gambia Colony and Protectorate]].

principality-of-bari.t: A short-lived Lombard principality carved out of Norman Apulia by a local strongman before Roger II brought it to heel.
principality-of-bari.o: In the weak reign of Duke William II of the [[s:duchy-of-apulia-and-calabria|Duchy of Apulia and Calabria]], the citizen Grimoald Alferanites took power in Bari in 1119 and called himself prince. Bari, the old seat of Byzantine government in [[e:italy|Italy]], had since 1087 housed the relics of Saint Nicholas, which made it a major pilgrimage centre.
principality-of-bari.r: Little is known of Grimoald's government beyond his alliances with [[e:venice|Venice]] and with other rebellious Apulian barons. He relied on Bari's port, its merchant community and the prestige of the Basilica of San Nicola. He submitted to Roger II of [[e:sicily|Sicily]] in 1129 when Roger took over Apulia.
principality-of-bari.e: Grimoald joined a baronial revolt against Roger II, who captured Bari in 1132 and sent him as a prisoner to [[e:sicily|Sicily]]. Bari was absorbed into the [[s:kingdom-of-sicily|Kingdom of Sicily]].

punadra-state.t: A minor chiefship of the Mahi Kantha country in northern Gujarat, one of its many small hereditary estates.
punadra-state.o: Punadra was one of the petty estates of the Mahi Kantha region, held by a local chiefly family from around 1600. Its origins are poorly documented.
punadra-state.r: Its ruler held a few villages, paid tribute through the [[e:gaekwads|Gaekwads]] of [[s:baroda-state|Baroda]] and was supervised by the British Mahi Kantha Agency. Standard references preserve few details of its history.
punadra-state.e: Punadra was merged into [[s:bombay-presidency|Bombay Province]] in 1948 and became part of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] in 1960.

ptolemaic-kingdom-of-cyrene.t: Cyrenaica as a separate Ptolemaic kingdom, created for a quarrelling royal brother and finally bequeathed to Rome.
ptolemaic-kingdom-of-cyrene.o: In 163 BCE [[e:rome|Rome]] settled a quarrel between the brothers Ptolemy VI and Ptolemy VIII by giving the younger [[e:cyrenaica|Cyrenaica]] as a separate kingdom, detached from the [[s:ptolemaic-empire|Ptolemaic Empire]]. Ptolemy VIII, nicknamed Physcon, ruled from [[s:republic-of-cyrene|Cyrene]] but constantly sought more, including [[e:cyprus|Cyprus]].
ptolemaic-kingdom-of-cyrene.r: After an assassination attempt in 155 BCE, Ptolemy VIII published a will, preserved on a stone at [[s:republic-of-cyrene|Cyrene]], leaving his kingdom to [[e:rome|Rome]] if he died without heirs. In 145 BCE he became king of [[e:egypt|Egypt]] and Cyrene was reunited with it. Around 116 BCE the kingdom was separated again for his son Ptolemy Apion. The Greek cities of the Pentapolis kept their councils, and the region exported grain, horses and the last of its silphium.
ptolemaic-kingdom-of-cyrene.e: Ptolemy Apion died in 96 BCE and bequeathed [[e:cyrenaica|Cyrenaica]] to [[e:rome|Rome]]. The Senate left the cities free at first, then organised the province of [[s:roman-cyrenaica|Roman Cyrenaica]] in 74 BCE, ending three centuries of Ptolemaic involvement in the region.

principality-of-hohenlohe-schillingsfurs.t: Franconian principality of a Catholic Hohenlohe branch, whose family later produced a German chancellor.
principality-of-hohenlohe-schillingsfurs.o: The [[s:county-of-hohenlohe|Hohenlohe]] family ruled lands in north-eastern Württemberg and western Franconia from the Middle Ages and divided into many lines. The Catholic Waldenburg branch included Schillingsfürst, on a hill near Rothenburg, and in 1744 its head was raised to the rank of prince of the Empire.
principality-of-hohenlohe-schillingsfurs.r: The principality was small, Catholic and rural, governed from a baroque palace at Schillingsfürst, which still houses a falconry. It belonged to the Franconian Circle and shared the [[s:county-of-hohenlohe|Hohenlohe]] family's collective vote. Its princes served the emperors in court and army posts.
principality-of-hohenlohe-schillingsfurs.e: In 1806 the principality was mediatised and placed under the [[s:kingdom-of-bavaria|Kingdom of Bavaria]]. The family remained prominent: Chlodwig zu Hohenlohe-Schillingsfürst was Bavarian prime minister and German chancellor from 1894 to 1900.

principality-of-lichtenberg.t: Detached Saar-area exclave of Saxe-Coburg, given at Vienna and sold to Prussia after political unrest.
principality-of-lichtenberg.o: The [[e:congress-of-vienna|Congress of Vienna]] promised the Duke of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld territory for his services against [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]]. In 1816 he received a district around St. Wendel on the upper Nahe and Blies, far from Coburg, which was named the Principality of Lichtenberg in 1819 after the castle near Kusel.
principality-of-lichtenberg.r: The principality had about 25,000 inhabitants, Catholic and Protestant, living from farming and small crafts. It was governed by Coburg officials who were unpopular, and the region was touched by the radical democratic movement around the Hambach Festival of 1832. Unrest in St. Wendel in 1832 required troops to restore order.
principality-of-lichtenberg.e: Duke Ernest I found the distant territory hard to govern and sold it to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] in 1834 for an annual payment. It became the district of St. Wendel in the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] Province and is now part of Saarland.

principality-of-catalonia.t: The union of Catalan counties under the House of Barcelona, a land of parliaments, merchant cities and its own laws within the Crown of Aragon.
principality-of-catalonia.o: Catalonia grew out of the counties of the [[s:marca-hispanica|Marca Hispanica]], gradually gathered under the [[s:county-of-barcelona|County of Barcelona]]. In 1162 Alfonso II inherited both Barcelona and the [[s:kingdom-of-aragon|Kingdom of Aragon]], and the Catalan counties became one constituent of the [[s:crown-of-aragon|Crown of Aragon]]. The name Principality became usual in the 14th century.
principality-of-catalonia.r: Catalonia was governed under the Usatges of Barcelona and its Corts, whose standing committee, the Generalitat, was created in 1359. Barcelona's merchants traded across the [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]] under the Consulate of the Sea. Catalan literature flourished with Ramon Llull and Ausiàs March, while the [[e:black-death|Black Death]] and civil war of 1462-1472 brought decline.
principality-of-catalonia.e: The Reapers' War of 1640 led to the loss of Roussillon to [[e:france|France]] in 1659. Siding with the [[s:county-of-habsburg|Habsburg]] claimant in the [[e:war-of-the-spanish-succession|War of the Spanish Succession]], Barcelona fell in 1714, and the Nueva Planta decree of 1716 abolished Catalonia's institutions.

principality-of-wallachia.t: Romanian principality between the Carpathians and the Danube, home of Mircea the Elder and Vlad the Impaler, which united with Moldavia to form Romania.
principality-of-wallachia.o: Romanian voivodeships such as the [[s:voivodeship-of-litovoi|Voivodeship of Litovoi]] and the [[s:voivodeship-of-seneslau|Voivodeship of Seneslau]] were united under Basarab I in the early 14th century; tradition dates the founding to about 1310. In 1330 Basarab defeated Charles I of [[e:hungary|Hungary]] at Posada, securing independence.
principality-of-wallachia.r: The voivode (prince) ruled with boyars, and the throne was elective within the ruling family, which bred constant rivalry. Mircea the Elder (1386–1418) fought the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] at Rovine, and Vlad III fought them in 1462. From the 15th century Wallachia paid tribute to the Ottomans but kept its own rulers and [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] church. Michael the Brave briefly united Wallachia, [[s:principality-of-transylvania|Transylvania]] and [[s:principality-of-moldavia|Moldavia]] in 1600. From 1716 to 1821 the Ottomans appointed Phanariot Greek princes.
principality-of-wallachia.e: After the Treaty of Adrianople in 1829 Wallachia came under Russian protection. In 1859 both it and the [[s:principality-of-moldavia|Principality of Moldavia]] elected Alexandru Ioan Cuza as prince, creating the [[s:united-principalities|United Principalities]], which became [[s:kingdom-of-romania|Romania]].

perak-sultanate.t: A Malay sultanate founded by a son of Malacca's last sultan, grown rich on tin, and still reigning as a state of Malaysia.
perak-sultanate.o: After [[e:malacca|Malacca]] fell to Portugal in 1511, [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Mahmud Shah's eldest son, Raja Muzaffar, was invited by the people of the Perak River valley to be their ruler. He was installed around 1528 as Sultan Muzaffar Shah I, founding a dynasty that still reigns.
perak-sultanate.r: Perak's wealth came from [[e:tin|tin]], mined in the Kinta and Larut valleys. In the 17th century it fell under the [[s:aceh-sultanate|Aceh Sultanate]] and later signed tin contracts with the [[e:dutch|Dutch]]. Its succession system rotated the throne among branches of the royal family, and the court settled at Kuala Kangsar.
perak-sultanate.e: Disputes over succession and violent rivalry among Chinese [[e:tin|tin]] miners led to the Pangkor Treaty of 1874, which brought a British Resident. The killing of the Resident J. W. W. Birch in 1875 led to the Perak War. Perak joined the [[s:federated-malay-states|Federated Malay States]] in 1895 and [[s:malaysia|Malaysia]] in 1963. [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Nazrin Shah reigns today.

principality-of-erfurt.t: Thuringian city-state that Napoleon kept as his personal domain, scene of his 1808 congress with Tsar Alexander I.
principality-of-erfurt.o: Erfurt, long ruled by the [[s:electorate-of-mainz|Electorate of Mainz]], passed to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] in 1802. After defeating Prussia at Jena in October 1806, [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]] did not give Erfurt to any of his allies but kept it as a domain reserved to himself, the Principality of Erfurt, administered by French governors.
principality-of-erfurt.r: Erfurt was governed directly by French officials and garrisoned by French troops, with the Petersberg citadel as its stronghold. From September to October 1808 [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]] held the Congress of Erfurt there, meeting [[e:tsar|Tsar]] [[e:alexander-i-of-russia|Alexander I]] to renew their alliance and receiving Goethe in a famous audience. The city lived from trade, crafts and garden produce.
principality-of-erfurt.e: After the defeat at Leipzig, Erfurt was besieged by Prussian troops and its French garrison surrendered in 1814. The [[e:congress-of-vienna|Congress of Vienna]] returned the city to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] in 1815, as part of the Province of Saxony.

principality-of-the-hevelli.t: A Slavic principality on the Havel centred on Brandenburg, whose last prince bequeathed his land to Albert the Bear and so began the March of Brandenburg.
principality-of-the-hevelli.o: The Hevelli, also called Stodorani, were West Slavic settlers of the Havel lands west of modern Berlin from the 7th or 8th century. Their chief stronghold was Brenna, the later [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]] an der Havel. In 928 to 929 the East Frankish king Henry the Fowler captured it in winter across the frozen marshes.
principality-of-the-hevelli.r: The Hevelli were governed by princes from Brenna, controlling river crossings and fortified settlements on the Havel and Spree. German rule after 929 was lost in the Great Slav Rising of 983, and the Hevelli joined, and later stood apart from, the [[s:lutician-federation|Lutician Federation]]. The last prince, Pribislav-Henry, became a Christian and ruled as a German ally.
principality-of-the-hevelli.e: Pribislav-Henry named Albert the Bear his heir; on his death in 1150 Albert took [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]], securing it in 1157 after a fight with the Slavic prince Jaxa of Köpenick. The Hevelli lands became the core of the [[s:margraviate-of-brandenburg|Margraviate of Brandenburg]].

provisional-central-government-of-vietna.t: A transitional French-backed Vietnamese government of 1948 to 1949, set up to prepare Bao Dai's return as head of state.
provisional-central-government-of-vietna.o: As [[e:france|France]] sought a non-communist alternative to Ho Chi Minh, it negotiated with former emperor Bao Dai. In 1948 General Nguyen [[s:early-ly-dynasty|Van Xuan]], president of the government of [[s:french-cochinchina|Cochinchina]], formed the Provisional Central Government of [[s:socialist-republic-of-vietnam|Vietnam]], and the Ha Long Bay agreement of June 1948 recognised in principle the independence and unity of [[e:vietnam|Vietnam]] within the [[s:french-fourth-republic|French Union]].
provisional-central-government-of-vietna.r: The government had little real power: [[e:france|France]] retained control of the army, finances and foreign relations, and the [[e:viet-minh|Viet Minh]] held much of the countryside. It merged the separate administrations in the north, centre and south, including the [[s:autonomous-republic-of-cochinchina|Autonomous Republic of Cochinchina]], into a single framework.
provisional-central-government-of-vietna.e: The Elysee Accords of March 1949 between Bao Dai and President Vincent Auriol created the [[s:state-of-vietnam|State of Vietnam]], with Bao Dai as head of state, replacing the provisional government that year.

pathari-state.t: A small Muslim-ruled state of the Bhopal Agency in central India.
pathari-state.o: Pathari became a separate holding in the late 18th century under a Muslim family related to the Afghan nobility of the [[s:bhopal-state|Bhopal]] region.
pathari-state.r: Its Nawab ruled a few villages under the supervision of the [[s:bhopal-state|Bhopal]] Agency. Little is recorded of its internal history.
pathari-state.e: After accession to [[e:india|India]] Pathari was merged into [[s:madhya-bharat|Madhya Bharat]] in 1948; its lands are now in Madhya Pradesh.

patina.t: Patina, a Neo-Hittite kingdom of the Amuq plain whose founder called it Palistin, a name that may link it to the Philistines.
patina.o: After the [[e:late-bronze-age-collapse|Late Bronze Age collapse]], a kingdom arose in the Amuq plain around Antakya, the former [[s:kingdom-of-mukish|Kingdom of Mukish]]. Inscriptions of King Taita, found in the temple of the storm god at [[e:aleppo|Aleppo]], call it Palistin, and its capital was Kunulua, at Tell Tayinat.
patina.r: Its kings wrote Luwian hieroglyphic inscriptions and built palaces and temples in Syrian-Hittite style; a temple at Tell Tayinat yielded an Assyrian treaty tablet. [[e:assyrian-empire|Assyrians]] called the land Pattin or Unqi. It lived from the fertile plain and the route to the [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]].
patina.e: Patina paid tribute to Ashurnasirpal II and Shalmaneser III of the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]]. After King Tutammu rebelled, Tiglath-Pileser III captured Kunulua in 738 BCE and made the land an Assyrian province.

province-of-new-york.t: The English colony created from Dutch New Netherland in 1664, whose port grew into the commercial heart of British North America.
province-of-new-york.o: In 1664 an English fleet under Richard Nicolls seized [[e:new-amsterdam|New Amsterdam]], which Charles II had granted to his brother James, Duke of York. The colony was renamed after James, who ruled it as proprietor through governors under the Duke's Laws of 1665. The [[e:dutch|Dutch]] briefly recaptured it in 1673 to 1674.
province-of-new-york.r: When James became king in 1685, [[e:new-york|New York]] became a royal province, and in 1688 it was folded into the [[s:dominion-of-new-england|Dominion of New England]]. Its collapse triggered Leisler's Rebellion of 1689 to 1691. A large landholding elite owned Hudson Valley manors, and New York City grew as a trading port with many enslaved Africans. The Zenger trial of 1735 advanced press freedom, and the Albany Congress of 1754 met there. Alliance with the [[s:iroquois-confederacy|Iroquois Confederacy]] shaped frontier policy.
province-of-new-york.e: [[e:new-york|New York]] City hosted the Stamp Act Congress in 1765. In July 1776 the provincial congress endorsed independence and New York became a state of the [[s:united-states|United States]], though British forces occupied New York City until 1783.

provisional-government-of-milan.t: The government formed by the Milanese after the Five Days of 1848 drove out the Austrians, which merged Lombardy with Piedmont before Radetzky returned.
provisional-government-of-milan.o: From 18 to 22 March 1848 the people of [[s:duchy-of-milan|Milan]] fought the Five Days, barricade battles that forced Marshal Radetzky's Austrian garrison to leave the city. A provisional government headed by the mayor Gabrio Casati took power, while the democrat Carlo Cattaneo led the council of war during the fighting.
provisional-government-of-milan.r: The provisional government governed [[e:lombardy|Lombardy]] and called on Charles Albert of the [[s:kingdom-of-sardinia|Kingdom of Sardinia]], who declared war on [[e:austria|Austria]]. Moderates led by Casati favoured union with Piedmont, while republicans such as Cattaneo and Giuseppe Mazzini wanted to delay the question. A plebiscite in May and June approved fusion with Piedmont.
provisional-government-of-milan.e: After the Piedmontese defeat at Custoza in July 1848, Radetzky reoccupied [[s:duchy-of-milan|Milan]] on 6 August, and [[e:lombardy|Lombardy]] returned to the [[s:kingdom-of-lombardy-venetia|Kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia]].

pyu-city-states.t: A network of walled brick cities in the dry zone of Myanmar that brought Buddhism, writing and urban life to the Irrawaddy valley for over a thousand years.
pyu-city-states.o: From about the 2nd century BCE the Pyu, a Tibeto-Burman-speaking people, built large walled cities in the dry zone of central [[s:myanmar|Myanmar]], among them [[s:beikthano|Beikthano]], [[s:halin|Halin]], Maingmaw and later [[s:sri-ksetra-kingdom|Sri Ksetra]]. Their growth was tied to irrigated [[e:rice|rice]] farming and trade routes linking [[e:india|India]] and [[e:china|China]].
pyu-city-states.r: Each city was ruled by its own dynasty, and [[s:sri-ksetra-kingdom|Sri Ksetra]] became the leading centre by the 5th century. The Pyu wrote their own language in a script derived from Brahmi, and Chinese sources of the [[s:later-tang|Tang]] period describe a gentle Buddhist people with many monasteries, music and [[e:silver|silver]] coinage. Cylindrical stupas, urn burials and gold [[e:manuscript|manuscript]] leaves survive from their sites.
pyu-city-states.e: Raids by [[s:nanzhao|Nanzhao]] in the 830s, including the sack of [[s:halin|Halin]] in 832, broke Pyu power, and the cities declined as the Burmans settled the Kyaukse plain and built the [[s:pagan-kingdom|Pagan Kingdom]]. Pyu culture was absorbed into Burman society; three Pyu ancient cities became a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] in 2014.

prince-bishopric-of-bamberg.t: Franconian church state founded by Emperor Henry II, whose cathedral holds the Bamberg Horseman and whose bishops staged notorious witch trials.
prince-bishopric-of-bamberg.o: Emperor Henry II founded the diocese of Bamberg in 1007 and endowed it richly; he and his wife Kunigunde are buried in its cathedral. The [[e:bishop|bishops]] gathered lands in Upper Franconia, and after the extinction of the counts of Andechs-Meranien in 1248 they consolidated a territory and ruled it as imperial princes.
prince-bishopric-of-bamberg.r: The cathedral chapter elected the prince-[[e:bishop|bishops]]. The Romanesque-Gothic cathedral, with the Bamberg Horseman and the tomb of [[e:papacy|Pope]] Clement II, symbolises the see's standing. Under Johann Georg II Fuchs von Dornheim the territory suffered one of the worst witch persecutions in [[e:germany|Germany]] between 1626 and 1631. In the baroque era Lothar Franz von Schönborn built the New Residence.
prince-bishopric-of-bamberg.e: The prince-bishopric was secularised in 1802 and annexed by Bavaria, ending more than eight centuries of episcopal rule. Bamberg became an archdiocese in 1817, and its largely intact old town is a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].
ru: Johann Georg II Fuchs von Dornheim

prince-bishopric-of-sion.t: A prince-bishopric in the Valais, Switzerland, whose bishops held the county granted in 999 until the people of the Upper Valais took power from them.
prince-bishopric-of-sion.o: Sion, in the Rhône valley, had been a bishopric since the 6th century. In 999 King Rudolf III of [[s:duchy-of-burgundy|Burgundy]] granted the [[e:bishop|bishop]] the county of Valais, making him a temporal lord. When [[e:burgundy|Burgundy]] passed to the Empire in 1032, the bishops became imperial princes.
prince-bishopric-of-sion.r: The [[e:bishop|bishops]] faced the counts of [[s:county-of-savoy|Savoy]], who held the lower Valais, and the growing power of the German-speaking communes (Zenden) of the upper valley. Cardinal Matthäus Schiner, bishop from 1499, was a leading diplomat of the Swiss in the [[e:italian-wars|Italian Wars]]. The [[s:province-of-carolina|Carolina]] document claimed [[e:charlemagne|Charlemagne]] had granted the county.
prince-bishopric-of-sion.e: The seven Zenden gradually reduced the [[e:bishop|bishop]]'s power and in 1613 to 1634 forced bishops to renounce temporal [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]], making the Valais a republic allied with the [[s:old-swiss-confederacy|Swiss Confederacy]]. The Valais became a Swiss canton in 1815, and the bishops of Sion remain spiritual heads.

perinthus.t: Samian colony on the Sea of Marmara that, with Byzantium, defeated Philip II's siege of 340 BCE.
perinthus.o: Colonists from [[s:samos|Samos]] founded Perinthus c. 602 BCE on a promontory on the north shore of the Propontis, in Thrace. They soon fought off attacks by Megarian settlers from neighbouring colonies.
perinthus.r: Perinthus traded with the Thracian interior and along the Propontis route to [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]]. It resisted the Persian general Megabazus c. 512 BCE but was conquered. Later it paid tribute in the [[s:delian-league|Delian League]]. In 340 BCE Philip II besieged the city with towers and rams, but Persian [[e:satrapy|satraps]] and [[e:byzantine-empire|Byzantium]] helped it hold out.
perinthus.e: Perinthus kept its independence under Hellenistic kings and the [[s:odrysian-kingdom|Odrysian Kingdom]]'s influence. When [[e:rome|Rome]] made Thrace a province in 46 CE, it became the provincial capital, later renamed [[s:heraclea-lucania|Heraclea]]; it is modern Marmara Ereğlisi.

principality-of-samos.t: Autonomous Christian principality on the island of Samos under Ottoman suzerainty, created after the Greek War of Independence and united with Greece in 1912.
principality-of-samos.o: [[s:samos|Samos]] fought in the [[e:greek-war-of-independence|Greek War of Independence]], but the [[e:london|London]] Protocol of 1830 left it outside the new Greek state. As a compromise the Ottoman [[e:sultan|Sultan]] made it an autonomous principality, established in 1834, with a Christian prince appointed by the Porte and paying an annual tribute. Its first prince was Stefanos Vogoridis.
principality-of-samos.r: The prince, usually a Phanariot Greek, governed with an elected assembly and his own administration, flag and later postage stamps, from Vathy. Samians paid low taxes and enjoyed religious freedom. The economy rested on wine, especially muscat, tobacco and shipping. Politics were often turbulent, with clashes between princes and local factions.
principality-of-samos.e: During the First Balkan War, the Samian leader Themistoklis Sofoulis drove out the last Ottoman garrison and the assembly declared union with [[e:greece|Greece]] in November 1912. Greek troops landed in March 1913, and in 1914 the great powers confirmed its union with the [[s:kingdom-of-greece|Kingdom of Greece]].

palace-state-of-phaistos.t: Minoan palace centre of the Mesara plain in southern Crete, famous for its grand staircases and the enigmatic Phaistos Disc.
palace-state-of-phaistos.o: [[s:phaistos|Phaistos]] stands on a ridge above the Mesara, the largest plain of [[e:crete|Crete]], which had been settled since the Neolithic. Around 1950 BCE its first palace was built around a paved central court, and Phaistos became the leading power of southern Crete. After destructions in the 18th century BCE the palace was rebuilt on a grander scale.
palace-state-of-phaistos.r: [[s:phaistos|Phaistos]] controlled the agricultural wealth of the Mesara and probably the nearby port of Kommos, which traded with [[e:egypt|Egypt]] and the [[e:levant|Levant]]. Its archives of clay sealings and Linear A tablets reveal a developed palace bureaucracy. Finds include fine Kamares ware pottery and the stamped clay Phaistos Disc, whose script is still undeciphered. The nearby villa of Ayia Triada was closely linked to it.
palace-state-of-phaistos.e: The palace was destroyed c. 1450 BCE and its role passed largely to Ayia Triada and to [[s:palace-state-of-knossos|Knossos]], which came to dominate [[e:crete|Crete]] under Mycenaean rulers. [[s:phaistos|Phaistos]] later revived as a Greek city-state, described separately as Phaistos. The site was excavated by Italian archaeologists from 1900.

pequot-nation.t: The leading power of 17th-century eastern Connecticut, whose defeat in the Pequot War of 1636 to 1638 opened southern New England to English expansion.
pequot-nation.o: The Pequot lived along the Thames and Mystic rivers in what is now south-eastern Connecticut. By the early 17th century they had become the dominant people of the region, collecting tribute from neighbours and controlling the production and trade of wampum shell [[e:bead|beads]], which the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] of [[s:new-netherland|New Netherland]] bought in exchange for cloth and metal goods.
pequot-nation.r: Grand sachems such as Tatobem and his son Sassacus ruled through councils of lesser sachems and fortified villages. Their wealth from the wampum trade, and their alliance with the [[e:dutch|Dutch]], made them targets: the Dutch killed Tatobem in 1634, and rival sachem Uncas broke away to lead the Mohegan. English settlement in the Connecticut valley from 1633 brought rising tension.
pequot-nation.e: In 1637 English forces under John Mason, with Mohegan and Narragansett allies, burned the fortified village at Mystic, killing around 400 to 700 people. The Treaty of Hartford in 1638 dissolved the nation. Survivors later regained reservations at Mashantucket and Lantern Hill.

province-of-north-carolina.t: The British colony between Virginia and South Carolina, a land of small farms and naval stores, where the Regulator revolt foreshadowed the Revolution.
province-of-north-carolina.o: The northern settlements of the [[s:province-of-carolina|Province of Carolina]], around Albemarle Sound, had long been governed separately, and in 1712 the proprietors gave them their own governor, Edward Hyde. The colony was then fighting the [[s:tuscarora-nation|Tuscarora]] War. In 1729 the Crown bought out seven of the eight proprietors, and North Carolina became a royal province.
province-of-north-carolina.r: Without a good deep-water port, the colony grew more slowly than its neighbours, with small farms, tobacco, and naval stores of tar, pitch and turpentine from the longleaf pine forests. Scots-Irish and German settlers filled the backcountry. Governor William Tryon built an expensive palace at New Bern, the capital from the 1760s, and crushed the Regulator movement of backcountry farmers protesting corrupt officials at the Battle of Alamance in 1771.
province-of-north-carolina.e: Governor Josiah Martin fled in 1775. In April 1776 the Halifax Resolves made North [[s:province-of-carolina|Carolina]] the first colony to instruct its delegates to vote for independence, and it became a state of the [[s:united-states|United States]].
