principality-of-uglich.t: An appanage principality on the upper Volga, split off from Rostov and bought by Ivan Kalita of Moscow.
principality-of-uglich.o: Uglich on the upper [[e:volga|Volga]] belonged to the Rostov lands. In 1218 Konstantin Vsevolodovich of Rostov gave it to his son Vladimir, who became the first prince of a separate Uglich line.
principality-of-uglich.r: The principality was small, with its wealth drawn from [[e:volga|Volga]] trade and farming. It was sacked by the [[e:mongols|Mongols]] in 1238. Its prince Roman Vladimirovich, who died in 1285, was later venerated as a saint for his charity to the poor. Like other small [[e:appanage|appanages]] of the north-east, Uglich depended on the grand princes and the [[s:golden-horde|Golden Horde]].
principality-of-uglich.e: After its line declined, the principality was acquired by Ivan I Kalita of the [[s:grand-duchy-of-moscow|Grand Duchy of Moscow]] around 1328, one of his famous purchases of land. Uglich later became the scene of the death of Tsarevich Dmitry in 1591.

principality-of-soyo.t: A Kongo coastal province at the mouth of the Congo River that broke away to become an independent Catholic principality and defeated Portugal in 1670.
principality-of-soyo.o: [[e:soyo|Soyo]] was a province of the [[e:kingdom-of-kongo|Kingdom of Kongo]], ruled by a count ([[e:mani|Mani]] Soyo) from Mbanza Soyo, close to the river mouth. Its control of the port of Mpinda and direct trade with the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] made it rich, and in 1641 Count Daniel da Silva asserted independence from the Kongo king.
principality-of-soyo.r: [[e:soyo|Soyo's]] counts, later styled princes, ruled as Catholic monarchs, hosting Italian Capuchin missionaries and celebrating the feast of St James. Trade in slaves, [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and [[e:copper|copper]] with [[e:dutch|Dutch]] and English merchants funded a strong army. In 1670 Soyo defeated a Portuguese invasion at the Battle of Kitombo, and it later intervened in the [[e:kingdom-of-kongo|Kongo]] civil wars.
principality-of-soyo.e: [[e:soyo|Soyo]] remained autonomous through the 18th and 19th centuries, though its power waned with the end of the [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trade]]. It was incorporated into [[s:portuguese-angola|Portuguese Angola]] after the Berlin Conference of 1884–85. The town of Soyo is now an Angolan oil centre.

prince-bishopric-of-meissen.t: An Ottonian bishopric among the Sorbs of the middle Elbe whose territory was gradually absorbed by the Wettin rulers of Saxony.
prince-bishopric-of-meissen.o: [[e:otto-i|Otto I]] founded the bishopric of Meissen in 968 as part of his reorganisation of the eastern frontier under Magdeburg. It served the conversion of the [[s:sorbs|Sorbs]] and the Slavic lands between the Saale and the Bóbr. The [[e:bishop|bishops]] shared the castle hill of Meissen with the margraves of Meissen.
prince-bishopric-of-meissen.r: The [[e:bishop|bishops]] held scattered lands around Stolpen, Wurzen and Mügeln and governed a diocese that reached into Lusatia. The Gothic cathedral of Meissen, begun around 1260, rose beside the margraves' Albrechtsburg. Benno of Meissen, bishop in the late 11th century, was canonised in 1523; his relics were moved to Munich during the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]].
prince-bishopric-of-meissen.e: The Wettin dukes and [[e:prince-elector|electors]] steadily controlled the see. After Saxony became Lutheran, [[e:bishop|Bishop]] Johann IX von Haugwitz resigned in 1581 and the territory was annexed to the [[s:electorate-of-saxony|Electorate of Saxony]]. A Catholic remnant in Upper Lusatia continued at Bautzen and became the modern Diocese of Dresden-Meissen.

partabgarh-state.t: A Sisodia Rajput state in southern Rajasthan, an offshoot of Mewar, known for its distinctive Thewa jewellery of gold worked onto glass.
partabgarh-state.o: The rulers descended from a branch of the Sisodia dynasty of [[s:udaipur-state|Mewar]] that settled in the Kanthal region; tradition dates their rule to the early 15th century. The early capital was Deolia, and Maharawat Pratap Singh founded the new capital of Pratapgarh in 1698.
partabgarh-state.r: Partabgarh was a hilly state with a large Bhil and Mina population. It came under Mughal and then [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] domination, paying tribute to Holkar of [[s:indore-state|Indore State]], and signed a treaty with the British in 1818. Local goldsmiths developed Thewa, a technique of fusing gold filigree onto coloured glass.
partabgarh-state.e: Partabgarh joined the [[s:united-state-of-rajasthan|United State of Rajasthan]] in 1948. Pratapgarh became a separate district of Rajasthan in 2008.

principality-of-kostroma.t: A short-lived Volga appanage whose only prince, Vasily, rose to become grand prince of Vladimir.
principality-of-kostroma.o: Kostroma on the [[e:volga|Volga]] was a town of the [[s:vladimir-suzdal|Vladimir-Suzdal]] lands. In 1246, after the death of Yaroslav Vsevolodovich, his youngest son Vasily received Kostroma as his own [[e:appanage|appanage]].
principality-of-kostroma.r: Vasily of Kostroma was an active prince who fought the Lithuanians and the Novgorodians. In 1272 he became grand prince of Vladimir with the approval of the [[s:golden-horde|Golden Horde]], ruling from Kostroma rather than moving to Vladimir. The principality was a small [[e:volga|Volga]] land with little else recorded.
principality-of-kostroma.e: Vasily died in 1276 without sons, and Kostroma passed back to the grand princes of Vladimir. It later became part of the [[s:grand-duchy-of-moscow|Grand Duchy of Moscow]]. The Ipatiev Monastery near the town later played a part in the election of Michael [[e:russian-empire|Romanov]] in 1613.

palatinate-sulzbach.t: Small Wittelsbach duchy in the Upper Palatinate, a centre of religious tolerance and Hebrew printing whose line inherited the Palatinate and Bavaria.
palatinate-sulzbach.o: Sulzbach was split from [[s:palatinate-neuburg|Palatinate-Neuburg]] in 1614 as an [[e:appanage|appanage]] for Augustus, and in 1656 his son Christian August gained full [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]] over it as a duchy. Christian August converted to [[e:catholicism|Catholicism]] in 1655 but kept his Protestant subjects' rights.
palatinate-sulzbach.r: Christian August introduced the simultaneum, letting Catholics and Lutherans share churches, and allowed [[e:jews|Jews]] to settle. Sulzbach became a centre of learning: the Christian Kabbalist Christian Knorr von Rosenroth served at court, and [[e:hebrew|Hebrew]] [[e:printing-press|printing]] presses flourished from 1669. The duchy's economy relied on iron ore and smelting in the [[s:upper-palatinate|Upper Palatinate]].
palatinate-sulzbach.e: Charles Theodore of Sulzbach inherited the [[s:electoral-palatinate|Electoral Palatinate]] in 1742, merging Sulzbach into it. In 1777 he also inherited the [[s:electorate-of-bavaria|Electorate of Bavaria]], and the Sulzbach line thus united the Wittelsbach lands.

prince-bishopric-of-eichstatt.t: A Franconian church principality on the Altmühl, founded on the see of Saint Willibald, that became a showcase of Catholic Baroque.
prince-bishopric-of-eichstatt.o: Saint Boniface made his kinsman Willibald the first [[e:bishop|bishop]] of Eichstätt in the 740s. For centuries the bishops held little secular land, but in 1305 they inherited much of the lordship of the extinct counts of Hirschberg, laying the foundation of a territorial principality along the Altmühl valley between Franconia and Bavaria.
prince-bishopric-of-eichstatt.r: The prince-[[e:bishop|bishop]], elected by the cathedral chapter, governed from Eichstätt and the hilltop Willibaldsburg, where Johann Conrad von Gemmingen laid out the garden recorded in the Hortus Eystettensis of 1613. The territory belonged to the Franconian Circle and lived from farming, forests and limestone quarrying. It remained Catholic, and after the Swedish sack of 1634 the city was rebuilt in Baroque style by architects such as Gabriel de Gabrieli.
prince-bishopric-of-eichstatt.e: In 1802 the prince-bishopric was secularised. Its lands went to Bavaria, then largely to Ferdinand of Tuscany's [[s:electorate-of-salzburg|Electorate of Salzburg]], before passing to the [[s:kingdom-of-bavaria|Kingdom of Bavaria]] in 1805. The diocese survives, and Eichstätt is home to [[e:germany|Germany's]] only Catholic university.

province-of-west-florida.t: A British Gulf Coast colony stretching from Pensacola to the Mississippi, lost to Spanish forces during the American Revolution.
province-of-west-florida.o: Created by the Royal Proclamation of 1763 from territory [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] gained under the Treaty of [[e:paris|Paris]]: the western part of [[s:spanish-florida|Spanish Florida]] plus French lands east of the [[e:mississippi-river|Mississippi]] around Mobile. Pensacola became the capital, and in 1764 the northern boundary was pushed up to the latitude of the Yazoo River.
province-of-west-florida.r: West Florida had an elected assembly alongside royal governors such as George Johnstone and Peter Chester. Settlers came from the older colonies and [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] to farm along the [[e:mississippi-river|Mississippi]] near [[s:natchez-chiefdom|Natchez]] and Baton Rouge, while Pensacola and Mobile lived on the deerskin trade with the [[s:muscogee-confederacy|Muscogee Confederacy]], [[s:choctaw-nation|Choctaw Nation]] and [[s:chickasaw-nation|Chickasaw Nation]]. Like [[s:province-of-east-florida|East Florida]], it stayed loyal to the Crown after 1776.
province-of-west-florida.e: [[e:spain|Spain]] entered the war in 1779, and Bernardo de Gálvez, governor of [[s:spanish-louisiana|Spanish Louisiana]], took Baton Rouge, Mobile and finally Pensacola in 1781. The 1783 peace confirmed Spanish possession; disputes over the region's border later fed the [[s:republic-of-west-florida|Republic of West Florida]].

pahlavi-iran.t: The last Iranian monarchy, under Reza Shah and his son Mohammad Reza Shah, which pursued rapid modernisation until overthrown by the revolution of 1979.
pahlavi-iran.o: Reza Khan, an officer of the Persian [[e:cossacks|Cossack]] [[e:brigade|Brigade]], seized power in a coup in 1921 and became prime minister in 1923. In 1925 the Majlis deposed the last ruler of [[s:qajar-iran|Qajar Iran]], and Reza Khan was crowned Reza Shah Pahlavi.
pahlavi-iran.r: Reza Shah built a centralised state with a [[e:conscription|conscript]] army, the Trans-Iranian Railway (completed 1938), the University of Tehran and secular law, banned the women's veil in 1936 and asked foreign states to call the country [[e:iran|Iran]] from 1935. The Anglo-Soviet invasion of 1941 forced his abdication in favour of his son Mohammad Reza Shah. Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh nationalised oil in 1951 but was overthrown in a 1953 coup backed by the CIA and MI6. The shah's White Revolution of 1963 brought land reform and women's suffrage, while the SAVAK secret police suppressed opponents.
pahlavi-iran.e: [[e:inflation|Inflation]], repression and religious opposition led by Ayatollah Khomeini produced mass protests in 1978. The shah left [[e:iran|Iran]] in January 1979, and the [[s:islamic-republic-of-iran|Islamic Republic of Iran]] was proclaimed that April.

cr.a: Original emblem: Government of Iran (1970s) Vectorization and manual modifications by Shfarshid

phaltan-state.t: The Deccan fief of the Nimbalkar family, one of the oldest Maratha houses, into which Shivaji married and which survived as a princely state until 1948.
phaltan-state.o: The Nimbalkars claim to have held Phaltan since the late 13th century, and they are counted among the oldest [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] families. In the 16th and 17th centuries they served the [[s:bijapur-sultanate|Bijapur Sultanate]] as military chiefs.
phaltan-state.r: Saibai Nimbalkar of Phaltan became the first wife of [[e:shivaji|Shivaji]], linking the family to the founder of the [[s:maratha-empire|Maratha Empire]]. Phaltan later held its lands under the Satara rulers and the [[e:peshwa|Peshwas]]. After 1818 it came under British protection as one of the Satara [[e:jagir|jagirs]] and then the [[e:deccan|Deccan]] States Agency.
phaltan-state.e: Phaltan merged into Bombay State in 1948. Its last ruler, Malojirao Nimbalkar, went on to serve as a minister in Bombay. The town is now in Satara district, Maharashtra.

principality-of-minsk.t: A small principality of the Polotsk lands whose town grew into the capital of modern Belarus.
principality-of-minsk.o: Minsk first appears in the chronicle in 1067, when the sons of Yaroslav the Wise sacked it during their war with Vseslav of Polotsk and defeated him on the Nemiga river. After Vseslav died in 1101 his son Gleb received Minsk, which became a separate principality.
principality-of-minsk.r: Gleb Vseslavich made Minsk a power in its own right and fought Kiev and Vladimir Monomakh until he was captured and died in Kiev in 1119. Afterwards the principality was a minor [[e:appanage|appanage]] of the Polotsk dynasty. Little is known of its later rulers or institutions, and it lived in the shadow of Polotsk and the growing [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Grand Duchy of Lithuania]].
principality-of-minsk.e: By the early 14th century Minsk was dependent on [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Lithuania]], and around 1326 a Prince Vasily of Minsk appears as a [[e:vassal|vassal]] of Gediminas. It was absorbed into the [[e:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Grand Duchy of Lithuania]].

paramara-dynasty.t: The Malwa dynasty of the scholar-king Bhoja, whose capital Dhar became a byword for learning and the patronage of poets.
paramara-dynasty.o: The Paramaras emerged in [[e:malwa|Malwa]] in the 9th century, probably as feudatories of the [[s:rashtrakuta-dynasty|Rashtrakuta dynasty]] or the [[s:gurjara-pratihara|Gurjara-Pratihara]]. Later legend said their ancestor sprang from a sacrificial fire on Mount Abu. Siyaka, also called Harsha, made the dynasty independent and sacked the Rashtrakuta capital Manyakheta in 972.
paramara-dynasty.r: Vakpati Munja was a poet and patron who fought the [[s:western-chalukya-empire|Western Chalukya Empire]] and was captured and executed by Tailapa II. Bhoja, ruling from about 1010 to 1055, was celebrated as a polymath credited with works on poetics, architecture and medicine; he made Dhar a centre of learning, built the Bhojpur Shiva temple and was remembered in countless legends. The Paramaras also built the Udayeshvara temple at Udaipur in [[e:malwa|Malwa]].
paramara-dynasty.e: After Bhoja's defeat by the [[s:chaulukya-dynasty|Chaulukya dynasty]] and the [[s:kalachuris-of-tripuri|Kalachuris of Tripuri]], the kingdom weakened. The [[s:delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]] attacked repeatedly, and in 1305 an army of [[e:alauddin-khalji|Alauddin Khalji]] conquered [[e:malwa|Malwa]], ending Paramara rule.

prince-bishopric-of-chur.t: Alpine church state ruled by the bishops of Chur, one of the oldest sees north of the Alps, whose temporal power was broken by the leagues of Graubünden.
prince-bishopric-of-chur.o: A [[e:bishop|bishop]] of Chur is recorded in 451, making it one of the oldest dioceses north of the [[e:alps|Alps]]. Carolingian and Ottonian kings granted the bishops immunities, tolls and lands in Rhaetia, controlling routes to the Alpine passes. In 1170 Emperor [[e:frederick-barbarossa|Frederick Barbarossa]] raised the bishop to the rank of an imperial prince, giving the church a recognised secular principality.
prince-bishopric-of-chur.r: The [[e:bishop|bishops]] governed estates in the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] valley, the Engadine and the Vinschgau from their court in Chur, with officials in castles along the pass roads. Romansh, German and [[e:kingdom-of-the-lombards|Lombard]] dialects were all spoken in their lands. To resist episcopal power, the subjects formed the [[s:league-of-gods-house|League of God's House]] in 1367, which later joined the [[s:grey-league|Grey League]] and the [[s:league-of-the-ten-jurisdictions|League of the Ten Jurisdictions]] in the [[s:three-leagues|Three Leagues]].
prince-bishopric-of-chur.e: The Ilanz Articles of 1524 and 1526 stripped the [[e:bishop|bishop]] of most secular authority and handed it to the communes of the [[s:three-leagues|Three Leagues]]. The bishops kept a few rights and the title of prince until 1803, and the Catholic diocese of Chur continues today.

patrae.t: Achaean city at the mouth of the Gulf of Corinth, a founder of the Achaean League and forerunner of modern Patras.
patrae.o: Patrae was formed, according to Pausanias, by uniting the villages of Aroe, Antheia and Mesatis on the coast of western Achaea. It was one of the twelve Achaean cities and controlled the narrows at the entrance to the Gulf of [[s:corinth|Corinth]].
patrae.r: Patrae was a modest farming and trading town in the Classical period. In 280 BCE it joined [[s:dyme|Dyme]], Tritaea and Pharae in reviving the [[s:achaean-league|Achaean League]]. In 279 BCE the Patraeans were the only Achaeans to send troops against the invading [[e:gauls|Gauls]], suffering heavy losses. The city had a sanctuary of Artemis Laphria.
patrae.e: Patrae passed under [[e:rome|Rome]] in 146 BCE. Augustus made it a Roman colony c. 14 BCE, and it became the chief port of the region, growing into the modern city of [[s:barony-of-patras|Patras]].
patrae.re: Greek religion; cult of Artemis Laphria

phulra-state.t: A tiny Tanoli chiefship in the Hazara hills, a neighbour and kinsman of Amb State.
phulra-state.o: Phulra was established in the early 19th century, around 1828, by a branch of the Tanoli chiefs of [[s:amb-state|Tanawal]] who also ruled Amb State, during the period of [[e:sikhism|Sikh]] expansion into [[e:hazara|Hazara]].
phulra-state.r: Under British rule it was a very small autonomous holding on the North-West Frontier, governed by a Khan over a Muslim population speaking Hindko. Little else of its history is recorded.
phulra-state.e: Phulra acceded to [[s:islamic-republic-of-pakistan|Pakistan]] after 1947 and was abolished and merged into the North-West Frontier Province in 1950; its area is now in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

principality-of-calenberg.t: A Guelph principality between the Deister and the Leine that grew into the Electorate of Hanover and the dynasty of Britain's Georgian kings.
principality-of-calenberg.o: The Guelph lands of the old [[s:duchy-of-brunswick-luneburg|Duchy of Brunswick-Lüneburg]] were repeatedly divided. In 1432 the territory between the Deister and the Leine, named after Calenberg castle, became a separate principality under William the Victorious, split off from the [[s:principality-of-wolfenbuttel|Principality of Wolfenbüttel]].
principality-of-calenberg.r: Calenberg was ruled from Calenberg castle and other residences, and from 1636 from Hanover. Duchess Elisabeth, regent in the 1540s, introduced [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]]. The principality absorbed Göttingen in 1495 and later Grubenhagen. Duke John Frederick brought Leibniz to Hanover as librarian in 1676, and Ernest Augustus built a more centralised state.
principality-of-calenberg.e: In 1692 Emperor Leopold I made Ernest Augustus an elector, and Calenberg became the core of the [[s:electorate-of-hanover|Electorate of Hanover]], which absorbed the [[s:principality-of-luneburg|Principality of Lüneburg]] in 1705. His son George became King of [[s:kingdom-of-great-britain|Great Britain]] in 1714.

provisional-government-of-oregon.t: A self-made government formed by American and Canadian settlers in the Willamette Valley while Britain and the United States both claimed Oregon.
provisional-government-of-oregon.o: Under an 1818 agreement, [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] and the [[s:united-states|United States]] jointly occupied the Oregon Country, but neither governed it. Settlers, missionaries and retired Hudson's Bay Company employees in the Willamette Valley needed law for property and estates. At Champoeg on 2 May 1843 they voted narrowly to create a provisional government, and wagon trains on the Oregon Trail soon swelled their numbers.
provisional-government-of-oregon.r: The government's Organic Laws provided for a legislature, courts and land claims of up to 640 acres. A three-man executive committee was replaced in 1845 by a single governor, George Abernethy, at Oregon City. It levied voluntary taxes, banned [[e:slavery|slavery]] but also passed laws excluding black settlers, and raised militia for the Cayuse War after the Whitman killings of 1847.
provisional-government-of-oregon.e: The Oregon Treaty of 1846 gave the area south of the 49th parallel to the [[s:united-states|United States]]. Congress created Oregon Territory in 1848, and the provisional government ended when Governor Joseph Lane arrived in March 1849.

province-of-georgia.t: The last of Britain's thirteen mainland colonies, founded by James Oglethorpe as a buffer against Spanish Florida and an experiment without slavery.
province-of-georgia.o: In 1732 George II granted a charter to a board of Trustees led by James Oglethorpe for the land between the [[e:savannah|Savannah]] and Altamaha rivers. Oglethorpe founded Savannah in 1733, with the help of the Yamacraw leader Tomochichi. The colony was meant to shield the [[s:province-of-south-carolina|Province of South Carolina]] from [[s:spanish-florida|Spanish Florida]] and to offer a new start to the poor.
province-of-georgia.r: The Trustees banned [[e:slavery|slavery]], limited landholdings and forbade hard liquor, and they recruited Protestant Salzburgers, Scottish Highlanders and others. Oglethorpe defeated a Spanish invasion at Bloody Marsh in 1742. Settlers, envious of Carolina's [[e:rice|rice]] wealth, pressed for slavery, which was allowed in 1751. The Trustees surrendered the charter, and [[s:georgia|Georgia]] became a royal province in 1752, with rice plantations spreading along the coast under governor James Wright.
province-of-georgia.e: Patriots took control in 1776 and [[s:georgia|Georgia]] became a state of the [[s:united-states|United States]], though British forces reoccupied [[e:savannah|Savannah]] from 1778 to 1782 and restored royal government there. [[e:georgia|Georgia]] adopted its first state constitution in 1777.

principality-of-berat.t: Albanian lordship of the Muzaka family around Berat and the Myzeqe plain, a leading noble realm of late medieval Albania.
principality-of-berat.o: The Muzaka were powerful Albanian nobles of the Myzeqe plain. Around 1335 Andrea II Muzaka received the Byzantine title of despot for fighting the Angevins, and the family built a lordship in the area. Berat itself was taken by the [[s:serbian-empire|Serbian Empire]] in the 1340s and only came firmly into Muzaka hands around 1372.
principality-of-berat.r: The Muzaka ruled from the fortress of Berat over Albanian peasants and herders, balancing [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]], the [[e:serbs|Serbs]], [[e:venice|Venice]] and the Balšić lords of Zeta. They joined coalitions against the Balšići and against the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]]; Theodore II Muzaka died fighting at Kosovo in 1389 according to tradition.
principality-of-berat.e: Ottoman pressure grew after their victory at Savra in 1385. The [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] took Berat in 1417, and the Muzaka lands became part of the Sanjak of [[s:albania|Albania]]. The family later took part in Skanderbeg's resistance.

prince-bishopric-of-brixen.t: An Alpine prince-bishopric on the Brenner route, set up by emperors to guard the road to Italy, whose bishops ruled parts of Tyrol for nearly 800 years.
prince-bishopric-of-brixen.o: The bishopric moved from Säben to Brixen (Bressanone) around 990. In 1027 Emperor Conrad II granted [[e:bishop|Bishop]] Hartwig the counties of the Inn and Eisack valleys, and in 1091 the Puster valley followed, so that loyal bishops would hold the passes on the imperial road to [[e:rome|Rome]].
prince-bishopric-of-brixen.r: The [[e:bishop|bishops]] entrusted their counties to advocates, chiefly the counts of Tyrol, who gradually absorbed most of their power. The bishopric retained Brixen, Bruneck and scattered lands. Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa, bishop from 1450, clashed bitterly with Duke Sigismund of Tyrol and was imprisoned in 1460.
prince-bishopric-of-brixen.e: The prince-bishopric was secularised in 1803 and annexed by [[e:austria|Austria]], then passed to Bavaria from 1805 to 1814, and back to Austria. After the [[e:first-world-war|First World War]] Brixen became part of [[e:italy|Italy]], and in 1964 the see moved to Bolzano, becoming the Diocese of Bolzano-Brixen.

phocaea.t: Ionian city whose daring sailors founded Massalia and explored the western Mediterranean as far as Tartessos in Spain.
phocaea.o: Phocaea, the northernmost Ionian city, was founded on a peninsula north of the Hermus c. 1000 BCE by settlers said to have come from Phocis. Its rocky territory pushed the Phocaeans to the sea, and from the 7th century BCE they sailed long distances in fast fifty-oared ships.
phocaea.r: [[e:herodotus|Herodotus]] credits Phocaeans with opening the Adriatic, Tyrrhenian and Iberian seas. They founded [[s:lampsacus|Lampsacus]], [[s:massalia|Massalia]] c. 600 BCE, Alalia on [[s:corsican-republic|Corsica]] and [[s:emporion|Emporion]] in [[e:spain|Spain]], and won the friendship of King Arganthonius of [[s:tartessos|Tartessos]]. When Harpagus besieged the city c. 545 BCE, most citizens sailed west; those at Alalia fought [[e:carthage|Carthaginians]] and Etruscans c. 540 BCE.
phocaea.e: Phocaea recovered and provided Dionysius, commander of the Greek fleet at Lade in 494 BCE. In 132 BCE it backed Aristonicus against [[e:rome|Rome]] and was spared destruction only through Massalia's appeal, then joined the province of [[e:asia|Asia]].

principality-of-mozhaysk.t: A western appanage of Moscow whose prince Ivan helped capture and blind Grand Prince Vasily II during Moscow's civil war.
principality-of-mozhaysk.o: Mozhaysk, on the Moskva river west of [[e:moscow|Moscow]], was taken from [[e:smolensk|Smolensk]] in 1303. In his will of 1389 Dmitry Donskoy left it, with Vereya and Beloozero, to his son Andrei, who ruled it as an [[e:appanage|appanage]] within the [[s:grand-duchy-of-moscow|Grand Duchy of Moscow]].
principality-of-mozhaysk.r: The principality guarded [[e:moscow|Moscow's]] approach from [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Lithuania]] and [[e:smolensk|Smolensk]]. During the long civil war over the Moscow throne, Andrei's son Ivan of Mozhaysk joined Dmitry Shemyaka, and in 1446 he helped seize Vasily II at the Trinity Monastery, after which Vasily was blinded.
principality-of-mozhaysk.e: When Vasily II regained power, he sent an army against Mozhaysk in 1454. Ivan fled to the [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Grand Duchy of Lithuania]], and Mozhaysk was absorbed into [[e:moscow|Moscow's]] lands, while Vereya continued for a time under Ivan's brother Mikhail.

principality-of-sedan.t: A Protestant sovereign principality on the Meuse, ruled by the La Marck and La Tour d'Auvergne families, which sheltered Huguenots and French rebels.
principality-of-sedan.o: In 1424 Everard de la Marck acquired the lordship of Sedan on the Meuse, at the frontier between [[e:france|France]], [[s:county-of-luxembourg|Luxembourg]] and [[s:prince-bishopric-of-liege|Liège]]. His descendants built a great fortress there and claimed [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]], owing allegiance to neither the French king nor the emperor.
principality-of-sedan.r: Robert II de la Marck and his successors were also dukes of [[s:duchy-of-bouillon|Bouillon]]. The princes adopted [[e:calvinism|Calvinism]], and Sedan became a Huguenot refuge with a Protestant academy founded in 1602. In 1591 the heiress Charlotte de la Marck married Henri de La Tour d'[[s:county-of-auvergne|Auvergne]], father of Marshal [[s:viscounty-of-turenne|Turenne]], who was born at Sedan in 1611. Sedan's cloth industry later flourished.
principality-of-sedan.e: Frédéric-Maurice de La Tour d'[[s:county-of-auvergne|Auvergne]] joined the conspiracy of Cinq-Mars against Richelieu, and to save his life ceded Sedan to Louis XIII in 1642. The principality was absorbed into the [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]].
ru: Henri de La Tour d'Auvergne, Duke of Bouillon

principality-of-pronsk.t: An appanage principality of the Ryazan land whose princes repeatedly challenged the grand princes of Ryazan.
principality-of-pronsk.o: Pronsk, on the Pronya river south of [[s:grand-principality-of-ryazan|Ryazan]], was a fortified frontier town facing the steppe. In the 1180s it became the seat of a separate branch of the Ryazan princely house, and for three centuries its rulers held it as an [[e:appanage|appanage]] of the Grand Principality of Ryazan.
principality-of-pronsk.r: Pronsk princes often fought their [[s:grand-principality-of-ryazan|Ryazan]] cousins for the senior throne, sometimes with the help of the [[s:golden-horde|Golden Horde]] or [[e:moscow|Moscow]]. In 1408 Ivan Vladimirovich of Pronsk briefly drove out the Ryazan grand prince with [[e:tatars|Tatar]] support. Like other border lands, Pronsk suffered heavily from steppe raids and was sacked by the [[e:mongols|Mongols]] in 1237.
principality-of-pronsk.e: In the 15th century Pronsk was gradually reabsorbed into [[s:grand-principality-of-ryazan|Ryazan]], and by the 1480s its princes had lost their independent role. The territory followed Ryazan into the [[s:grand-duchy-of-moscow|Grand Duchy of Moscow]] in 1521, while the Pronsky princely family served in the Russian nobility.

principality-of-birkenfeld.t: Hunsrück exclave of the Grand Duchy of Oldenburg, ruled from the North Sea coast for more than a century.
principality-of-birkenfeld.o: At the [[e:congress-of-vienna|Congress of Vienna]], the Grand Duke of [[s:county-of-oldenburg|Oldenburg]] was awarded territory on the left bank of the [[e:rhine|Rhine]]. In 1817 he received a district of the former French Saar [[e:departement|department]] around Birkenfeld in the Hunsrück, which became the Principality of Birkenfeld, an exclave hundreds of kilometres from Oldenburg.
principality-of-birkenfeld.r: The principality was governed by a regional government in Birkenfeld under Oldenburg's laws and had its own provincial council. Its people were mostly Protestant farmers, with gemstone cutting and agate working around Idar and Oberstein as a distinctive industry. After 1918 it formed a part of the [[s:free-state-of-oldenburg|Free State of Oldenburg]].
principality-of-birkenfeld.e: Under the Greater [[s:free-and-hanseatic-city-of-hamburg|Hamburg]] Act of 1937, [[s:county-of-oldenburg|Oldenburg]] ceded Birkenfeld to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]], which made it a district of the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] Province. It is now part of Rhineland-Palatinate.

paser-sultanate.t: A Malay-Dayak sultanate in the southeast of East Kalimantan, ruled from Paser Belengkong until the Dutch took control in 1906.
paser-sultanate.o: Paser lay on the Kendilo River in southeast [[e:borneo|Borneo]], between the [[s:banjar-sultanate|Banjar Sultanate]] and [[s:kutai-kartanegara-sultanate|Kutai Kartanegara]]. Local tradition traces its royal house to Putri Petung, a princess born from a bamboo stem, who married a prince from [[e:java|Java]]. Its rulers adopted [[e:islam|Islam]] in the 16th century, and the register dates the sultanate from 1516.
paser-sultanate.r: Paser drew on [[e:rice|rice]] farming and forest products such as rattan and resin, and traded with Banjarmasin and with Bugis merchants, many of whom settled on its coast in the 18th century and gained influence at court. It acknowledged Banjar overlordship at times.
paser-sultanate.e: The [[e:dutch|Dutch]] made treaties with Paser in the 19th century and annexed it into their administration in 1906, leaving the sultan as a figurehead. Its lands became Paser Regency, and the old palace at Paser Belengkong is now a museum.

praeneste.t: Latin hill city east of Rome, famous for its princely tombs, its bronze cistae and the oracle of Fortuna Primigenia.
praeneste.o: Praeneste, modern Palestrina, occupied a spur of the Monti Prenestini commanding the routes from Latium to Campania. In the 7th century BCE its rulers were buried in the Bernardini and Barberini tombs with gold, [[e:silver|silver]] and [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] from the eastern [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]], among the richest burials in [[e:italy|Italy]].
praeneste.r: Praeneste was a powerful and often independent member of the [[s:latin-league|Latin League]]. Its workshops produced engraved bronze cistae, cylindrical boxes for toiletries such as the Ficoroni cista. The sanctuary of Fortuna Primigenia, where oracles were drawn by lot, was later rebuilt on a vast terraced scale in the 2nd century BCE. Local [[e:latin|Latin]] had distinct features noted by Roman writers.
praeneste.e: Praeneste fought [[e:rome|Rome]] in the [[e:latin|Latin]] War and lost land in 338 BCE, but remained a separate allied city until it gained citizenship after the Social War. It sheltered Gaius Marius the Younger in 82 BCE; Sulla took it, executed its men and planted a colony.

plataea.t: Small Boeotian city that defied Thebes, stood with Athens at Marathon and gave its name to the battle that ended the Persian invasion of Greece in 479 BCE.
plataea.o: [[e:battle-of-plataea|Plataea]] lay on the northern slopes of Mount Cithaeron, on the border between Boeotia and Attica. When [[s:thebes|Thebes]] pressed it to join the [[s:boeotian-league|Boeotian League]] in the late 6th century BCE, the Plataeans turned to [[s:athens|Athens]], traditionally in 519 BCE. That alliance shaped the rest of their history: alone among the [[e:greeks|Greeks]], they sent their whole levy to fight beside the Athenians at Marathon in 490 BCE.
plataea.r: A modest farming community governed by its own citizen assembly, [[e:battle-of-plataea|Plataea]] mattered far beyond its size. In 479 BCE the allied Greek army under the Spartan Pausanias defeated the Persian general Mardonius on its territory, and the city was charged with tending the graves of the fallen and hosting a festival of freedom, the Eleutheria. Its people spoke the Boeotian dialect and kept close cultural ties with [[s:athens|Athens]].
plataea.e: Theban aggression began the [[e:peloponnesian-war|Peloponnesian War]] at [[e:battle-of-plataea|Plataea]] in 431 BCE; after a famous siege the city surrendered to [[s:sparta|Sparta]] and was razed in 427 BCE. Restored in 386 BCE, it was destroyed again by [[s:thebes|Thebes]] in 373 BCE and rebuilt under Philip II and Alexander. It then belonged to the [[s:boeotian-league|Boeotian League]] until Roman conquest in 146 BCE.

peoples-republic-of-korea.t: A government proclaimed by Korean leaders in Seoul in September 1945, after liberation from Japan, and rejected by the American occupation.
peoples-republic-of-korea.o: On [[e:japan|Japan's]] surrender the moderate leftist Lyuh Woon-hyung formed the Committee for the Preparation of Korean Independence, which organised local committees to keep order. On 6 September 1945, two days before American troops landed, a national assembly in Seoul proclaimed the People's Republic of [[e:korea|Korea]].
peoples-republic-of-korea.r: Its cabinet named prominent figures, including Syngman Rhee as chairman, often without their consent, and leftists dominated. People's committees across the country ran local affairs, organised land and labour programmes and took over Japanese property in many areas.
peoples-republic-of-korea.e: The [[s:united-states-army-military-government-in-korea|United States Army Military Government in Korea]] refused to recognise it, declared in October 1945 that it had no authority and later suppressed its committees in the south; it faded by early 1946. In the north, its committees were absorbed into the Soviet-backed administration.

panchala.t: A powerful Vedic kingdom east of the Kurus, between the Ganges and the Yamuna, later one of the sixteen mahajanapadas of early Buddhist texts.
panchala.o: Formed in the Later Vedic period from an alliance of several clans, among them the Krivis, the Panchalas settled east of the Kuru lands. Vedic texts pair Kuru and Panchala as the heart of the Vedic world, and Panchala kings such as Keshin Dalbhya appear in the Brahmanas as patrons of sacrifice and ritual learning.
panchala.r: The Panchala king Pravahana Jaivali appears in the Upanishads instructing [[e:brahmins|Brahmins]] on the doctrine of rebirth, a sign of the court's intellectual standing. The [[e:ganges-plain|Ganges]] divided the kingdom into a northern half with its capital at Ahichchhatra and a southern half centred on Kampilya. Iron tools and [[e:rice|rice]] and barley farming supported a growing population in Painted Grey Ware settlements. The Mahabharata makes Draupadi a Panchala princess.
panchala.e: By the 6th century BCE Panchala had become a sangha governed by leading clans. It was absorbed by the [[s:nanda-empire|Nanda Empire]] in the 4th century BCE and passed to the [[e:maurya-empire|Mauryas]]. Local kings of the Mitra line later issued coins at Ahichchhatra in the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE.

pogesanians.t: Prussian people between the Elbląg and Pasłęk rivers, whose land saw the founding of Elbing and fierce fighting in the Great Prussian Uprising.
pogesanians.o: Pogesania lay along the Vistula Lagoon east of the Elbląg river, in modern northern [[e:poland|Poland]]. Its Prussian inhabitants lived near the old trading centre of Truso, a [[e:vikings|Viking]] Age emporium described by the traveller Wulfstan around 890, and they are known from Peter of Dusburg's chronicle.
pogesanians.r: Pogesanian society was led by nobles holding hillforts, with farming, fishing and the amber trade as mainstays. They kept the Prussian gods and customs, including cremation of the dead, which Wulfstan described in detail.
pogesanians.e: The Teutonic Order and the Hanseatic settlers of [[s:free-and-hanseatic-city-of-lubeck|Lübeck]] founded Elbing on their land in 1237. In the Great Prussian Uprising from 1260 the Pogesanians, led by Auktume, attacked Elbing and other castles, but they were subdued by 1274. Their territory became part of the Order's state.

principality-of-serpukhov.t: An appanage of the Moscow princes south of the capital, ruled by Vladimir the Bold, hero of the Battle of Kulikovo.
principality-of-serpukhov.o: Serpukhov on the Oka guarded [[e:moscow|Moscow's]] southern approaches against the steppe. In 1341 Ivan I Kalita's will took effect, and his youngest son Andrei received Serpukhov and surrounding lands, including Borovsk, as an [[e:appanage|appanage]] within the [[s:grand-duchy-of-moscow|Grand Duchy of Moscow]].
principality-of-serpukhov.r: Andrei's son Vladimir the Bold, cousin of Dmitry Donskoy, was [[e:moscow|Moscow's]] leading general. At Kulikovo in 1380 he and the commander Dmitry Bobrok led the ambush regiment whose attack decided the battle. He built the Serpukhov kremlin and founded monasteries, and his principality served as a buffer against [[e:tatars|Tatar]] and Lithuanian raids.
principality-of-serpukhov.e: During [[e:moscow|Moscow's]] civil war Vladimir's grandson Vasily Yaroslavich supported Vasily II, but in 1456 the grand prince had him arrested and annexed Serpukhov. Vasily died in prison, and the [[e:appanage|appanage]] ended.

principality-of-lippe.t: Small Westphalian principality at Detmold that survived as a German state into the 20th century and played a part in Hitler's rise.
principality-of-lippe.o: The lords of Lippe held lands around Detmold and Lemgo from the 12th century, becoming counts in 1528. Though granted princely rank in 1720, they did not use the title until Count Leopold I accepted it in 1789, when the [[s:county-of-lippe|County of Lippe]]-Detmold became the Principality of Lippe.
principality-of-lippe.r: Princess Pauline, regent from 1802 to 1820, kept Lippe independent by joining the [[s:confederation-of-the-rhine|Confederation of the Rhine]] and introduced social reforms, including a nursery school. Lippe was rural and Calvinist, and many men worked seasonally as brickmakers elsewhere. A disputed succession between 1895 and 1905, involving [[e:kaiser|Kaiser]] William II's brother-in-law, was settled by arbitration in favour of the Biesterfeld line.
principality-of-lippe.e: Lippe joined the [[s:german-empire|German Empire]] in 1871. Prince Leopold IV abdicated in November 1918, and the state continued as the [[s:free-state-of-lippe|Free State of Lippe]] until 1947.

principality-of-nassau-diez.t: Nassau territory on the Lahn whose counts, as hereditary stadtholders of Friesland, became the House of Orange-Nassau that rules the Netherlands today.
principality-of-nassau-diez.o: Nassau-Diez arose in the 1606 partition of the lands of John VI of [[s:county-of-nassau-dillenburg|Nassau-Dillenburg]], when Ernst Casimir received Diez on the Lahn. Ernst Casimir served the [[s:dutch-republic|Dutch Republic]] as a general and became stadtholder of [[s:lordship-of-frisia|Friesland]] and Groningen, beginning his line's long connection with the northern [[s:kingdom-of-the-netherlands|Netherlands]].
principality-of-nassau-diez.r: The German lands were small and governed from Diez and later the Oranienstein palace, while the counts spent their careers in the [[s:dutch-republic|Dutch Republic]], where they held the Frisian stadtholdership hereditarily. They were raised to princes of the Empire in 1654. John William Friso inherited part of William III's [[s:principality-of-orange|Orange]] claims in 1702, and his son William IV united all Nassau-Ottonian lands by 1743.
principality-of-nassau-diez.e: William IV became stadtholder of all the [[s:dutch-republic|United Provinces]] in 1747. In 1806 [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]] confiscated the German lands, which went to the [[s:grand-duchy-of-berg|Grand Duchy of Berg]], and after 1815 they passed to the [[s:duchy-of-nassau|Duchy of Nassau]] and [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]]. William IV's grandson became King William I of the [[s:kingdom-of-the-netherlands|Netherlands]].

provisional-government-of-western-thrace.t: Short-lived Muslim-led state in Western Thrace in 1913, set up by Ottoman officers to keep the region from Bulgaria after the Second Balkan War.
provisional-government-of-western-thrace.o: [[s:bulgaria|Bulgaria]] took Western Thrace in the First Balkan War. When the Second Balkan War broke out in 1913, the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] retook [[e:edirne|Edirne]], and Ottoman officers led by Süleyman Askerî, together with local Turkish and Pomak irregulars, drove Bulgarian forces from the region. In late August 1913 they proclaimed an independent government at Gümülcine, today Komotini.
provisional-government-of-western-thrace.r: The government had a president, ministers, a flag, stamps and an army of a few thousand irregulars, drawing on the region's Muslim majority. It was effectively run by Ottoman officers acting unofficially, and no foreign power recognised it. It lasted about two months.
provisional-government-of-western-thrace.e: By the Treaty of [[e:constantinople|Constantinople]] in September 1913 the Ottoman government recognised Bulgarian possession of Western Thrace and withdrew support, and Bulgarian troops took over in October. The region passed to [[e:greece|Greece]] after the [[e:first-world-war|First World War]], where its Muslim minority remains.

prince-bishopric-of-merseburg.t: An Ottonian bishopric on the Saale whose bishop Thietmar wrote a famous chronicle, later absorbed into Saxony after the Reformation.
prince-bishopric-of-merseburg.o: [[e:otto-i|Otto I]] founded the bishopric of Merseburg in 968 to fulfil a vow made before the [[e:battle-of-lechfeld|Battle of Lechfeld]], as a suffragan of Magdeburg. It was dissolved in 981, its lands divided among neighbours, but Henry II restored it in 1004. The [[e:bishop|bishops]] built a cathedral beside the royal palace at Merseburg.
prince-bishopric-of-merseburg.r: [[e:bishop|Bishop]] Thietmar of Merseburg, from 1009 to 1018, wrote a chronicle that is a key source on the Ottonian empire, the [[e:slavs|Slavs]] and early [[e:poland|Poland]]. The bishops ruled a small territory along the Saale. The cathedral library preserves the Merseburg Charms, the only surviving [[e:old-high-german|Old High German]] pagan spells.
prince-bishopric-of-merseburg.e: Merseburg came under the influence of the Wettin rulers of Saxony. After the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]], a [[e:saxons|Saxon]] prince became administrator in 1561, and from 1565 the see was effectively a Saxon possession. From 1656 to 1738 it formed the [[s:duchy-of-saxe-merseburg|Duchy of Saxe-Merseburg]], before reverting to the electorate and passing to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] in 1815.

paris-commune.t: The revolutionary government that ruled Paris for ten weeks in 1871, and whose bloody suppression became a lasting symbol for the socialist left.
paris-commune.o: After [[e:france|France's]] defeat by [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] and the long siege of [[e:paris|Paris]], the government of Adolphe Thiers tried to remove the National Guard's [[e:field-artillery|cannons]] from Montmartre on 18 March 1871. Parisians resisted, the government withdrew to [[e:versailles|Versailles]], and elections on 26 March created the Commune.
paris-commune.r: The Commune's council, a mix of Jacobins, socialists and followers of Proudhon and Blanqui, separated church and state, abolished night work in bakeries, let workers take over abandoned workshops and postponed rents. Women such as Louise Michel played prominent roles. The Communards also pulled down the Vendôme Column.
paris-commune.e: Government troops entered [[e:paris|Paris]] on 21 May, and during the 'Bloody Week' that followed thousands of Communards were killed, many by summary execution; the Communards shot hostages and burned the Tuileries. Thousands more were tried and deported to [[s:new-caledonia|New Caledonia]]. The [[s:french-third-republic|French Third Republic]] survived.

principality-of-polotsk.t: The oldest principality of the Belarusian lands, a Dvina trading power that kept its own dynasty and long resisted Kiev.
principality-of-polotsk.o: Polotsk on the Western Dvina was a Krivich town ruled in the 10th century by the Scandinavian Rogvolod, until Vladimir I killed him and married his daughter Rogneda. Around 987 Vladimir gave Polotsk to their son Izyaslav, whose descendants held it as a separate dynasty.
principality-of-polotsk.r: Polotsk controlled the Dvina route to the Baltic and traded with Riga and [[s:gotland|Gotland]]. Its princes often fought the rest of Rus', and Vseslav, called the Sorcerer, who ruled for over fifty years, even held Kiev briefly in 1068. The Cathedral of Saint Sophia and the abbess Euphrosyne of Polotsk made it a religious centre.
principality-of-polotsk.e: By the 12th century the land split into smaller principalities, including Minsk and Vitebsk, and German crusaders took its Livonian tributaries. Polotsk came under the [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Grand Duchy of Lithuania]] in the early 14th century, and its separate princely rule ended in 1392 when Vytautas installed his own governors.

principality-of-abkhazia.t: A principality on the Black Sea coast ruled by the Shervashidze family, between Georgian, Ottoman and Russian power, until Russia abolished it in 1864.
principality-of-abkhazia.o: As the [[s:kingdom-of-georgia|Kingdom of Georgia]] broke up in the 1460s, the Shervashidze, or Chachba, family who governed the Abkhaz coast as eristavis under the Dadiani of [[s:principality-of-mingrelia|Mingrelia]] made themselves independent princes with their seat at Sukhumi and later Lykhny. Family tradition traced the line to the [[s:shirvanshah-state|Shirvanshahs]], a claim that cannot be verified.
principality-of-abkhazia.r: The princes ruled a society of nobles and peasants living by livestock, farming and coastal trade, including a [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trade]] with Ottoman ports. From the 16th century Ottoman influence grew: the coast came under Ottoman garrisons, and many Abkhaz nobles adopted [[e:islam|Islam]]. Keleshbey Chachba strengthened the principality but was assassinated in 1808.
principality-of-abkhazia.e: His son Giorgi accepted a Russian [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] in 1810. The [[s:russian-empire|Russian Empire]] abolished the principality in 1864, and after revolts many Abkhaz were deported to the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]] in the exodus called the Mahajirstvo.

patdi-state.t: A small state on the edge of the Little Rann of Kutch, unusual for being ruled by a Kanbi (Patidar) family of Desais rather than Rajputs.
patdi-state.o: Patdi emerged in the 18th century when a family of Kanbi Desais, holders of revenue rights in the region, established themselves as hereditary rulers of the town and surrounding villages.
patdi-state.r: The Desai of Patdi governed a small, dry territory near the salt flats of the Little Rann, where salt production was important. It was a minor state under British political supervision, and little else of its history is recorded.
patdi-state.e: After independence Patdi was absorbed into the Indian administration in 1948; it now lies in Surendranagar district of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]].

pontianak-sultanate.t: Arab-founded Malay sultanate at the mouth of the Kapuas river in West Borneo, origin of the city of Pontianak.
pontianak-sultanate.o: Syarif Abdurrahman Alkadrie, son of a Hadhrami Arab cleric who had settled in Mempawah, built a trading settlement at the junction of the Kapuas and Landak rivers in 1771. With Bugis support he made it a thriving port and was proclaimed sultan in 1778, founding a dynasty of Arab descent.
pontianak-sultanate.r: Pontianak controlled the trade of the Kapuas basin, exporting gold, diamonds, rattan and forest products. The [[s:dutch-east-india-company-territories|Dutch East India Company]] recognised the sultan in 1779 in return for a share of trade. The Kadriah palace and the [[e:jami|Jami]] mosque of [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Syarif Abdurrahman survive in the city.
pontianak-sultanate.e: During the Japanese occupation [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Syarif Muhammad Alkadrie and much of the West Bornean elite were executed in the Mandor killings. Sultan Hamid II, who designed the Garuda Pancasila emblem, led West Kalimantan within the [[s:united-states-of-indonesia|United States of Indonesia]], but was arrested in 1950 and the sultanate was absorbed into [[s:indonesia|Indonesia]].

principality-of-badakhshan.t: A mountain principality of the Pamirs and upper Amu Darya, ruled by mirs from Faizabad until the Afghan Emirate absorbed it.
principality-of-badakhshan.o: Badakhshan, famed since antiquity for its lapis lazuli and rubies, was ruled in the 16th and early 17th centuries by Timurid and [[e:uzbeks|Uzbek]] governors. Around 1657 a local dynasty of mirs of the Yarid family, claiming saintly descent, established independent rule from Faizabad on the Kokcha River.
principality-of-badakhshan.r: The mirs ruled a mountainous land of Tajik farmers and herders, including [[e:ismailism|Ismaili]] communities in the Pamirs and [[e:sunni-islam|Sunni]] Muslims in the lowlands. Revenue came from mines, trade routes to [[s:kingdom-of-shule|Kashgar]] and [[s:chitral-state|Chitral]], and tribute from [[e:vassal|vassal]] valleys such as Shughnan and Wakhan. The state was frequently raided by the [[s:kataghan-khanate|Kataghan Khanate]] and the [[s:durrani-empire|Durrani Empire]].
principality-of-badakhshan.e: In 1859 the [[s:emirate-of-afghanistan|Emirate of Afghanistan]] made Badakhshan a [[e:vassal|vassal]], and around 1881 Abdur Rahman Khan annexed it fully. The Anglo-Russian boundary settlements of the 1890s divided the region along the Panj River between [[s:islamic-emirate-of-afghanistan-2021-present|Afghanistan]] and the Russian [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] of [[e:bukhara|Bukhara]].

principality-of-dombes.t: A small sovereign principality north of Lyon, with its own parliament and mint at Trévoux, held by royal relatives until it was sold to Louis XV.
principality-of-dombes.o: The Dombes, a plateau of ponds east of the Saône, belonged to the lords of Beaujeu and then the dukes of [[s:ile-bourbon|Bourbon]]. After the confiscation of the Constable of [[e:house-of-bourbon|Bourbon's]] lands in 1523 it was held by the crown, then restored in 1560 to the Bourbon-Montpensier family, who ruled it as a sovereign principality outside the [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]].
principality-of-dombes.r: The princes kept a parliament at Trévoux, minted coin and taxed separately, though in practice the land was closely tied to [[e:france|France]]. Anne Marie Louise d'Orléans, La Grande Mademoiselle, held it and in 1681 ceded it to the Duke of [[s:county-of-maine|Maine]], [[e:louis-xiv|Louis XIV's]] legitimised son. [[e:jesuits|Jesuits]] at Trévoux published the Journal de Trévoux and the Dictionnaire de Trévoux.
principality-of-dombes.e: In 1762 the Duke of Maine's son, the Count of Eu, exchanged the principality with Louis XV for lands in [[e:france|France]], and it became part of the kingdom.

prince-bishopric-of-warmia.t: A church principality in Prussia, ruled by its bishops for over 500 years, where Nicolaus Copernicus worked as a canon.
prince-bishopric-of-warmia.o: In 1243 the papal legate William of Modena divided conquered [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] into four dioceses, one of them Warmia. Its [[e:bishop|bishop]] received a third of the diocese as his own territory, while the rest went to the Teutonic Order. The bishops made Lidzbark their residence and the cathedral chapter settled at Frombork.
prince-bishopric-of-warmia.r: The [[e:bishop|bishops]] ruled as territorial princes, with their own castles, towns and officials, and Warmia was settled by German colonists alongside Old Prussians and later [[e:poles|Poles]]. Lucas Watzenrode, bishop from 1489, brought his nephew Nicolaus Copernicus to serve the chapter, and Copernicus wrote his work on the heavens at Frombork. Bishop Stanislaus Hosius made it a stronghold of the Counter-[[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]].
prince-bishopric-of-warmia.e: After the Second Peace of Thorn in 1466 Warmia came under the protection of the Polish Crown, keeping wide self-government as part of [[s:royal-prussia|Royal Prussia]]. The [[e:first-partition-of-poland|First Partition of Poland]] in 1772 gave it to the [[s:kingdom-of-prussia|Kingdom of Prussia]], which took over the [[e:bishop|bishops]]' lands. The last bishop-prince, the poet Ignacy Krasicki, kept only his spiritual office.

pajang-sultanate.t: A short-lived inland Javanese sultanate under Hadiwijaya that moved power from the coast to the interior between Demak and Mataram.
pajang-sultanate.o: Hadiwijaya, also known as Jaka Tingkir, was a son-in-law of [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Trenggana of [[s:demak-sultanate|Demak]] and ruler of Pajang, near modern [[s:surakarta-sunanate|Surakarta]]. In the succession war after Trenggana's death he defeated Arya Penangsang with the help of Ki Ageng Pemanahan and his son Sutawijaya, and took the title sultan, the register dating his rule from 1568.
pajang-sultanate.r: Pajang moved the centre of Javanese power from the north coast to the [[e:rice|rice]] lands of the interior. Hadiwijaya received the homage of the East Javanese lords at [[s:giri-kedaton|Giri Kedaton]] and rewarded Ki Ageng Pemanahan with the land of [[s:mataram-sultanate|Mataram]].
pajang-sultanate.e: Sutawijaya grew powerful at [[s:mataram-sultanate|Mataram]] and defied Pajang. After Hadiwijaya died in 1582, Arya Pangiri of [[s:demak-sultanate|Demak]] seized the throne, but in 1586 Sutawijaya, allied with Hadiwijaya's son Pangeran Benawa, deposed him. Pajang became a dependency of the Mataram Sultanate.

principality-of-vyazma.t: A small appanage of the Smolensk lands on the road to Moscow, taken by Lithuania in 1403.
principality-of-vyazma.o: Vyazma, on the upper Vyazma river east of [[e:smolensk|Smolensk]], is first mentioned in the 13th century as a town of the [[s:principality-of-smolensk|Principality of Smolensk]]. In the mid 13th century it became a separate [[e:appanage|appanage]] held by a junior line of the Smolensk princes, the ancestors of the Vyazemsky family.
principality-of-vyazma.r: Its importance came from its position on the main route between [[e:smolensk|Smolensk]] and [[e:moscow|Moscow]], which made it a trading post and a frontier fortress. Little is known of its individual rulers or institutions, and it was usually subordinate to Smolensk.
principality-of-vyazma.e: Vytautas of the [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Grand Duchy of Lithuania]] took Vyazma in 1403 in the course of his conquest of the [[e:smolensk|Smolensk]] lands, and its princes became Lithuanian [[e:vassal|vassals]]. The [[s:grand-duchy-of-moscow|Grand Duchy of Moscow]] captured it in 1494, and the Vyazemsky princes entered Russian service.

province-of-freedom.t: A short-lived settlement of freed Black Londoners on the Sierra Leone peninsula, the first attempt at what became Freetown.
province-of-freedom.o: The Province of Freedom grew out of the campaign by Granville Sharp and the Committee for the Relief of the Black Poor to resettle impoverished Black people in [[e:london|London]], many of them Loyalists from the American War of Independence. About 400 settlers sailed in 1787 and landed in May on land obtained from local Koya Temne rulers, where they founded Granville Town.
province-of-freedom.r: Sharp designed it as a self-governing community with elected leaders, including Richard Weaver, and a frankpledge system of mutual responsibility. In practice the settlers suffered from disease, poor harvests and the rainy season, and many died or left to work for slave traders on nearby Bunce Island. Relations with neighbouring Temne chiefs were uneasy.
province-of-freedom.e: In 1789 a Temne ruler known as King Jimmy burned Granville Town after a dispute. The survivors regrouped, and the [[e:sierra-leone|Sierra Leone]] Company took over the project, founding the [[s:sierra-leone-colony-and-protectorate|Sierra Leone Colony and Protectorate]] at Freetown in 1792.

priene.t: Small Ionian city near Mount Mycale, home of the sage Bias and later rebuilt as the best-preserved example of a Hellenistic grid-planned town.
priene.o: Priene was one of the twelve Ionian cities, founded by tradition by settlers from [[s:athens|Athens]] and [[s:thebes|Thebes]] c. 1000 BCE. Its original site near the Maeander has never been found. The [[s:ionian-league|Panionion]], the common sanctuary of the Ionian League on Mount Mycale, lay in its territory, giving Priene a role in Ionian affairs out of proportion to its size.
priene.r: In the 6th century BCE Bias of Priene, counted among the Seven Sages, advised the Ionians to emigrate to [[e:sardinia|Sardinia]] rather than submit to [[e:persia|Persia]]. Priene fell to the [[s:kingdom-of-lydia|Kingdom of Lydia]] and then the [[s:achaemenid-empire|Achaemenid Empire]], sent 12 ships to the Battle of Lade in 494 BCE and later paid tribute in the [[s:delian-league|Delian League]].
priene.e: In the mid-4th century BCE the city was rebuilt on a terrace of Mycale with a strict grid; Alexander dedicated its temple of Athena Polias. It passed to [[e:rome|Rome]] in 133 BCE. As the Maeander silted its harbour, Priene declined, leaving its ruins remarkably intact.
priene.re: Greek religion; cult of Athena Polias

provisional-government-of-the-french-rep.t: The government that restored the Republic after liberation, gave French women the vote and built the post-war welfare state.
provisional-government-of-the-french-rep.o: In June 1944 the French Committee of National Liberation in [[e:algiers|Algiers]] renamed itself the Provisional Government of the [[s:french-fifth-republic|French Republic]], led by [[e:charles-de-gaulle|Charles de Gaulle]]. After [[e:paris|Paris]] was liberated in August 1944, it moved to the capital and declared that [[s:vichy-france|Vichy France]] had never been legitimate.
provisional-government-of-the-french-rep.r: The government included Gaullists, communists, socialists and Christian democrats from the Resistance. Women voted for the first time in 1945. It nationalised Renault, [[e:coal|coal]], electricity and major banks, created the social security system and the Monnet Plan for reconstruction, and oversaw the trials of collaborators. [[e:france|France]] gained a seat on the UN Security Council and an occupation zone in [[e:germany|Germany]].
provisional-government-of-the-french-rep.e: [[e:charles-de-gaulle|De Gaulle]] resigned in January 1946 over disputes about the constitution, and Félix Gouin and Georges Bidault led the government. After a first draft was rejected, voters approved a new constitution in October 1946, founding the [[s:french-fourth-republic|French Fourth Republic]].

pakualaman.t: Small Javanese princely house carved out of Yogyakarta in 1812, whose ruler today serves as the region's vice-governor.
pakualaman.o: During [[s:british-java|British Java]], Prince Natakusuma, a brother of the sultan of the [[s:yogyakarta-sultanate|Yogyakarta Sultanate]], sided with the British, who stormed the Yogyakarta kraton in 1812. As a reward Raffles granted him an apanage and the title Paku Alam I, creating an autonomous princely house modelled on [[s:mangkunegaran|Mangkunegaran]].
pakualaman.r: The Paku Alam ruled from the Puro Pakualaman in [[s:yogyakarta-sultanate|Yogyakarta]] and a coastal district at Adikarto, holding a status below the sultan. The court was a centre of Javanese literature and arts, and the family produced Ki Hajar Dewantara, founder of the Taman Siswa school movement and pioneer of Indonesian national education.
pakualaman.e: Paku Alam VIII supported the [[s:indonesia|Republic of Indonesia]], and when [[s:yogyakarta-sultanate|Yogyakarta]] became a Special Region in 1950 its rulers became vice-governors alongside the sultan, an arrangement confirmed in 2012. Paku Alam X holds the post today.

principality-of-serbia.t: Autonomous and then independent Serbian principality of the 19th century, built by the rival Obrenović and Karađorđević dynasties on the way to a modern kingdom.
principality-of-serbia.o: After the collapse of [[s:revolutionary-serbia|Revolutionary Serbia]] in 1813, Miloš Obrenović launched the Second Serbian Uprising at Takovo in 1815. Combining fighting with negotiation, he won recognition as supreme prince in 1817, and an Ottoman decree of 1830 made [[s:serbia|Serbia]] an autonomous hereditary principality paying tribute, with Ottoman garrisons only in a few fortresses.
principality-of-serbia.r: Miloš ruled autocratically, but the Sretenje Constitution of 1835 and the Ottoman-imposed constitution of 1838 set up a council that curbed him. Power swung between Obrenović princes and Alexander Karađorđević, who reigned from 1842 to 1858. Michael Obrenović modernised the army and secured the departure of the last Ottoman garrisons in 1867. Peasant smallholders raised pigs for export to [[e:austria|Austria]].
principality-of-serbia.e: [[s:serbia|Serbia]] fought the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] in 1876 to 1878, and the Congress of Berlin in 1878 recognised its independence and added Niš and Pirot. In 1882 Prince [[s:duchy-of-milan|Milan]] Obrenović proclaimed the [[s:kingdom-of-serbia|Kingdom of Serbia]].

parthenopean-republic.t: The Neapolitan republic of 1799, whose idealistic leaders were crushed by Cardinal Ruffo's peasant army and executed in their hundreds.
parthenopean-republic.o: After the [[s:kingdom-of-naples|Kingdom of Naples]] attacked the French in [[e:rome|Rome]] in late 1798 and was defeated, King Ferdinand IV fled to [[e:sicily|Sicily]]. French troops under General Championnet fought their way into Naples, and in January 1799 local patriots proclaimed a republic named after [[s:neapolis|Parthenope]], the ancient Greek name for the city.
parthenopean-republic.r: The republic was led by intellectuals and liberal nobles such as Carlo Lauberg and the jurist Francesco Mario Pagano, who drafted a constitution. Eleonora Fonseca Pimentel edited its newspaper, the Monitore Napoletano. It tried to abolish feudalism, but had little support among the poor and peasants, and depended on French troops, who withdrew in May.
parthenopean-republic.e: Cardinal Fabrizio Ruffo's Sanfedisti army retook Naples in June 1799. The surrender terms were broken with Nelson's backing, and over a hundred republicans, including Pagano, Pimentel and Admiral Francesco Caracciolo, were executed.

portuguese-cape-verde.t: Atlantic island colony that became a key hub of the early slave trade and birthplace of a Creole society, until independence in 1975.
portuguese-cape-verde.o: The uninhabited [[e:cape-verde|Cape Verde]] islands were reached by navigators in Portuguese service between 1456 and 1462. Settlement began on [[s:spanish-jamaica|Santiago]] under the Genoese captain Antonio de Noli, and Ribeira Grande, today's Cidade Velha, became one of the first European towns in the tropics.
portuguese-cape-verde.r: Ribeira Grande served as an [[e:entrepot|entrepot]] for enslaved Africans shipped to the [[e:americas|Americas]], and the islands grew [[e:cotton|cotton]] and bred horses and [[e:cattle|cattle]]. Portuguese settlers and enslaved Africans formed a [[e:criollo-people|Creole]] society with its own language, Kriolu, and music. The capital moved to Praia in 1770. Repeated droughts caused famines that killed tens of thousands.
portuguese-cape-verde.e: In the 20th century Cape Verdeans joined Amilcar Cabral's PAIGC, which fought for the independence of [[s:portuguese-guinea|Portuguese Guinea]] and the islands. After the 1974 revolution in Portugal, [[e:cape-verde|Cape Verde]] became independent on 5 July 1975.

province-of-south-australia.t: Australia's planned free colony, founded on Wakefield's theories of systematic settlement and later a pioneer of democratic reforms.
province-of-south-australia.o: Inspired by Edward Gibbon Wakefield's ideas, the South Australian Colonisation Commission sold land to fund free emigration, so that the new colony would receive no convicts. The first settlers arrived in 1836 and Governor John Hindmarsh proclaimed the province at Holdfast Bay on 28 December. Colonel William Light chose and laid out the site of Adelaide.
province-of-south-australia.r: Early financial crisis forced Governor George Grey to impose austerity in the 1840s, but [[e:copper|copper]] finds at Kapunda and Burra and wheat farming brought prosperity. Many Lutheran settlers came from [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]], and religious dissenters gave the colony a reputation for tolerance. It introduced the secret ballot and adult male suffrage in 1856, the Torrens title system of land registration in 1858, and votes for women in 1894.
province-of-south-australia.e: South [[s:commonwealth-of-australia|Australia]] also administered the Northern Territory from 1863 to 1911, building the Overland [[e:telegraph|Telegraph]] from Adelaide to Darwin in 1872. It joined the federation and became a state of the Commonwealth of [[e:australia|Australia]] in 1901.

pan-pan.t: A small Indianised kingdom on the Malay Peninsula that sent envoys to China in the 5th to 7th centuries and was known for its Brahmins and Buddhist monks.
pan-pan.o: Pan Pan appears in Chinese dynastic histories from 424, when it began sending tribute missions to the [[s:liu-song|Liu Song]] court. Its location is uncertain: most scholars place it on the east coast of the [[e:malay-peninsula|Malay Peninsula]], perhaps around the Bay of Bandon near [[e:surat|Surat]] Thani, though [[s:kelantan-sultanate|Kelantan]] and [[s:terengganu-sultanate|Terengganu]] have also been proposed.
pan-pan.r: Chinese sources describe a kingdom where many [[e:brahmins|Brahmins]] from [[e:india|India]] lived and were honoured by the king, and where there were Buddhist monasteries and monks who studied the scriptures. Like other peninsular ports, it profited from trade crossing the isthmus between the Bay of [[e:bengal|Bengal]] and the [[e:south-china-sea|South China Sea]], offering aromatics and other local goods.
pan-pan.e: Missions from Pan Pan stop being recorded after the 7th century, and it was probably absorbed into larger networks such as [[e:srivijaya|Srivijaya]] or the states that became [[s:tambralinga|Tambralinga]]. Its main interest today lies in what it shows of early Indian religious influence on the peninsula.

panama-canal-zone.t: Strip of land across Panama governed by the United States for 76 years, where the Panama Canal was built and run.
panama-canal-zone.o: The Hay-Bunau-Varilla Treaty of November 1903 granted the [[s:united-states|United States]], in perpetuity, rights over a zone about ten miles wide across the isthmus, as if it were sovereign. American construction began in 1904; William Gorgas's campaign against mosquitoes conquered yellow fever, and George Washington Goethals completed the canal, which opened in August 1914.
panama-canal-zone.r: The zone was run by a governor, who also headed the canal company, and was administered from Balboa Heights. American civilians, known as Zonians, lived in subsidised towns, while the many West Indian workers were paid on a separate [[e:silver|silver]] roll and lived under segregation. US military bases, including Southern Command, made the zone a strategic hub. Panamanians resented the foreign enclave, and the flag riots of January 1964 left over twenty dead.
panama-canal-zone.e: The Torrijos-Carter Treaties of 1977 abolished the Canal Zone on 1 October 1979, returning most of its territory to the [[s:republic-of-panama|Republic of Panama]]. A joint commission ran the canal until Panama took full control on 31 December 1999.

principality-of-oettingen-spielberg.t: A Catholic line of the counts of Oettingen in the Ries, which inherited much of the family's lands in 1731 and became princely in 1734.
principality-of-oettingen-spielberg.o: The counts of [[s:county-of-oettingen|Oettingen]] ruled the Ries crater basin from the 12th century. In 1522 the house split into the Oettingen-Oettingen line, which became Lutheran, and the Catholic [[s:principality-of-oettingen-wallerstein|Oettingen-Wallerstein]] line. A Catholic branch formed at Spielberg in the 17th century inherited much of the Oettingen-Oettingen lands in 1731 and received princely rank in 1734.
principality-of-oettingen-spielberg.r: The princes ruled from [[s:county-of-oettingen|Oettingen]], a town long divided along its main street between Catholic and Lutheran halves, a legacy of the dynasty's split. The territory lived from farming in the fertile Ries and belonged to the Swabian Circle.
principality-of-oettingen-spielberg.e: In 1806 the principality was mediatised and placed under the [[s:kingdom-of-bavaria|Kingdom of Bavaria]]. The princely family of Oettingen-Spielberg still owns the residence palace at [[s:county-of-oettingen|Oettingen]] in [[s:duchy-of-bavaria|Bayern]].

proto-kingdom-of-thinis.t: The kingdom of Thinis and Abydos, whose Dynasty 0 rulers left the earliest Egyptian writing and went on to unite Egypt.
proto-kingdom-of-thinis.o: Thinis, near [[s:abydos|Abydos]] in [[e:upper-egypt|Upper Egypt]], became the seat of a line of rulers in the late 4th millennium BCE. Their burials in Cemetery U at Abydos grew steadily richer, and by c. 3200 BCE the Thinite chiefs had absorbed the [[s:proto-kingdom-of-naqada|Proto-kingdom of Naqada]] and extended their reach over the [[s:proto-kingdom-of-nekhen|Proto-kingdom of Nekhen]].
proto-kingdom-of-thinis.r: Tomb U-j at [[s:abydos|Abydos]], built around 3320 BCE, contained hundreds of imported Levantine wine jars and small bone labels carrying some of the earliest known Egyptian writing. Kings now wrote their names inside a serekh, a palace façade topped by the Horus falcon. These rulers, known today as Dynasty 0, ran an economy of grain, wine and prestige goods and pushed their trade into the Delta.
proto-kingdom-of-thinis.e: The Thinite line culminated in Narmer, who around 3100 BCE ruled both Upper and [[e:lower-egypt|Lower Egypt]] and is usually counted as the founder of [[s:early-dynastic-egypt|Early Dynastic Egypt]]. [[s:abydos|Abydos]] remained the burial ground of the [[e:old-babylonian-empire|First Dynasty]] kings and later became the great cult centre of Osiris.

province-of-canada.t: The British colony that united Upper and Lower Canada in 1841, won responsible government, and ended in deadlock that produced Confederation.
province-of-canada.o: Following the rebellions of 1837 and 1838 and Lord Durham's report, the Act of Union of 1840 merged [[s:upper-canada|Upper Canada]] and [[s:lower-canada|Lower Canada]] into a single province, proclaimed in February 1841. The two halves, known as [[s:canada|Canada]] West and [[e:canada|Canada]] East, received equal seats in the assembly despite Canada East's larger population.
province-of-canada.r: The capital moved between Kingston, Montreal, Toronto and [[s:province-of-quebec|Quebec]] City until Queen [[s:colony-of-victoria|Victoria]] chose Ottawa in 1857. Reformers Robert Baldwin and Louis-Hippolyte LaFontaine achieved responsible government in 1848, confirmed when Lord Elgin signed the Rebellion Losses Bill despite riots that burned Montreal's parliament in 1849. Canals, the Grand Trunk Railway and the Reciprocity Treaty of 1854 with the [[s:united-states|United States]] boosted trade.
province-of-canada.e: By the 1860s sectional rivalry made stable government impossible. John A. Macdonald, George-Étienne Cartier and George Brown formed the Great Coalition of 1864 to pursue federation, and in 1867 the province was split into Ontario and [[s:province-of-quebec|Quebec]] within the new [[s:canada|Canada]].

principality-of-grubenhagen.t: Small Guelph principality in the western Harz and around Einbeck, famous for its beer, whose line died out in 1596.
principality-of-grubenhagen.o: When the sons of Albert I of Brunswick divided their inheritance around 1291, Henry I the Admirable received Grubenhagen, named after a castle near Einbeck, with lands in the western Harz around Osterode and Herzberg. This became a separate Guelph principality.
principality-of-grubenhagen.r: The principality was small, divided at times among co-rulers. Its towns included Einbeck, whose beer was exported across northern [[e:europe|Europe]], and Osterode. [[e:silver|Silver]] mining in the Harz around Clausthal brought income. Philip I introduced the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] in the 1530s. Herzberg castle served as the main residence.
principality-of-grubenhagen.e: When Philip II died without heirs in 1596, Henry Julius of the [[s:principality-of-wolfenbuttel|Principality of Wolfenbüttel]] seized Grubenhagen, but in 1617 an imperial court awarded it to the [[s:principality-of-luneburg|Principality of Lüneburg]]. It later formed part of the [[s:electorate-of-hanover|Electorate of Hanover]] and is now in Lower Saxony.

palenque.t: The Classic Maya kingdom of B'aakal in the Chiapas foothills, whose elegant architecture and the tomb of K'inich Janaab Pakal made it one of the best known Maya cities.
palenque.o: Palenque, anciently Lakamha', lies on a ridge above the Gulf lowlands of [[e:chiapas|Chiapas]]. Its kings counted their dynasty from K'uk' B'ahlam I, who took power in 431 CE, and the city grew as the seat of the B'aakal kingdom.
palenque.r: Palenque was sacked twice by the [[s:kingdom-of-kaan|Kingdom of Kaan]], in 599 and 611, but recovered under K'inich Janaab Pakal, who reigned from 615 to 683. He built the Palace with its tower and the Temple of the Inscriptions, where his tomb with its carved sarcophagus lid was found in 1952. His son K'inich Kan B'ahlam II built the Cross Group. Palenque was notable for women rulers, its stucco art and long texts.
palenque.e: [[s:tonina|Toniná]] captured the king K'an Joy Chitam II in 711, and Palenque declined through the 8th century. The last recorded ruler acceded in 799, and the city was abandoned soon after.

prince-bishopric-of-freising.t: The Bavarian church state of Saint Corbinian, a small principality on the Isar with scattered estates reaching into Austria and Carniola.
prince-bishopric-of-freising.o: The diocese goes back to Saint Corbinian, who worked at Freising around 720, and was formally organised by Saint Boniface in 739. Over the following centuries the [[e:bishop|bishops]] gathered estates across Bavaria, [[e:austria|Austria]], Tyrol and Carniola. Their territory as an imperial principality took shape around the city and the county of Werdenfels, bought in 1294.
prince-bishopric-of-freising.r: The [[e:bishop|bishop]], elected by the cathedral chapter, ruled as a prince of the [[s:holy-roman-empire|Holy Roman Empire]], but his small core lands were surrounded by Bavaria and he depended heavily on the Wittelsbach dukes, several of whose sons held the see. Freising's cathedral hill was a centre of learning, and the nearby abbey of Weihenstephan brewed beer. The territory remained Catholic.
prince-bishopric-of-freising.e: In 1802 and 1803 the prince-bishopric was secularised and its lands passed to the [[s:electorate-of-bavaria|Electorate of Bavaria]], while estates in [[e:austria|Austria]] went to the [[e:habsburg-dynasty|Habsburgs]]. The see moved to Munich in 1821 as the Archdiocese of Munich and Freising.
