prince-bishopric-of-minden.t: Weser valley church state founded after Charlemagne's Saxon wars and secularised into a Brandenburg principality in 1648.
prince-bishopric-of-minden.o: The diocese of Minden was founded around 800 after [[e:charlemagne|Charlemagne's]] conquest of the [[s:saxons|Saxons]], on a crossing of the Weser. Its [[e:bishop|bishops]] gained counties and immunities from the Ottonian and Salian kings. After Henry the Lion fell in 1180 they ruled a territory along the Weser as imperial princes, though Minden itself grew increasingly self-governing.
prince-bishopric-of-minden.r: The cathedral chapter elected the [[e:bishop|bishops]], who often lived at Petershagen because of friction with Minden's citizens. Their land was small, rural and hemmed in by neighbours such as the counties of Schaumburg, [[s:county-of-ravensberg|Ravensberg]] and Hoya. The city of Minden adopted [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]] in 1530, and in the later 16th century the see was held by Lutheran princes of the houses of Brunswick-Lüneburg and Schaumburg.
prince-bishopric-of-minden.e: At the [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] in 1648 the see was secularised as the [[s:principality-of-minden|Principality of Minden]] and given to [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]]. It remained Prussian, apart from the Napoleonic period, and the town is now in North Rhine-Westphalia.

plaisance.t: France's fortified fishing colony on the south coast of Newfoundland, which raided English settlements before being ceded to Britain in 1713.
plaisance.o: French fishing crews had long used the sheltered harbour of Plaisance, now Placentia, on the Avalon Peninsula. French claims to the harbour date from the 1650s, but the colony is usually dated from 1662, when a garrison and the first resident governor arrived, making Plaisance the administrative centre of French [[s:dominion-of-newfoundland|Newfoundland]].
plaisance.r: Plaisance was a small military and fishing post with a few hundred residents and many more seasonal fishermen from Saint-Malo and the Basque coast. Its governors, such as Jacques-François de Brouillan, oversaw Fort Saint-Louis and the dry cod trade. In 1696 to 1697 Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville led raids from Plaisance that destroyed most English settlements on [[s:dominion-of-newfoundland|Newfoundland]], including St John's.
plaisance.e: By the [[e:treaty-of-utrecht|Treaty of Utrecht]] in 1713 [[e:france|France]] ceded [[s:dominion-of-newfoundland|Newfoundland]] to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]], keeping only fishing rights on part of the coast. Governor Philippe Pastour de Costebelle moved the settlers to Louisbourg on [[s:ile-royale|Ile Royale]], and Placentia became a British garrison town in the [[s:colony-of-newfoundland|Colony of Newfoundland]].

peoples-republic-of-zanzibar.t: The revolutionary state born in Zanzibar's violent overthrow of the sultan in January 1964, which lasted three months before union with Tanganyika.
peoples-republic-of-zanzibar.o: A month after the [[s:sultanate-of-zanzibar|Sultanate of Zanzibar]] became independent, on 12 January 1964 an uprising led by the Ugandan-born John Okello and supporters of the Afro-Shirazi Party overthrew [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Jamshid bin Abdullah and the Arab-dominated government. Abeid Karume of the Afro-Shirazi Party became president of the People's Republic of Zanzibar and Pemba.
peoples-republic-of-zanzibar.r: The revolution was accompanied by mass killings of [[e:arabs|Arabs]] and South Asians, with thousands dead, and the confiscation of property. A Revolutionary Council ruled by decree, and the new state turned to the Soviet bloc, [[e:china|China]] and East [[e:germany|Germany]] for support, raising Western fears of an African [[e:cuba|Cuba]].
peoples-republic-of-zanzibar.e: On 26 April 1964 Karume and Julius Nyerere joined [[s:sultanate-of-zanzibar|Zanzibar]] with [[s:tanganyika|Tanganyika]] to form the United Republic, later named [[s:tanzania|Tanzania]]. Zanzibar kept its own president and government within the union.

principality-of-bzhedugh.t: A princely Circassian tribe on the lower Kuban, one of the few Adyghe groups that largely remained in their homeland after 1864.
principality-of-bzhedugh.o: The Bzhedugh were one of the aristocratic Adyghe tribes of [[s:circassia|Circassia]], living along the left bank of the Kuban and the Psekups river near modern Krasnodar. They are recorded as a distinct princely community by the 16th and 17th centuries; their earlier history is not recorded separately.
principality-of-bzhedugh.r: Princes and nobles held power over free peasants and serfs. When the commoners of the [[s:shapsugs|Shapsugs]] and [[s:natukhaj|Natukhaj]] rebelled against their nobility, Bzhedugh princes backed the aristocrats and were defeated at Bziyuqo in 1796. The tribe lay close to Russian forts on the Kuban and often negotiated with [[e:russia|Russia]] while trading and fighting with it.
principality-of-bzhedugh.e: The Bzhedugh came under Russian control in the course of the Russo-Circassian War, which the [[s:russian-empire|Russian Empire]] completed in 1864. More of them stayed than most Circassian groups, and they form a large part of the Adyghe population of Adygea today.

pakao.t: Mandinka district of the middle Casamance known as a centre of Muslim scholarship in a largely non-Muslim region.
pakao.o: Known mainly from oral tradition and colonial records. Pakao was settled by [[e:mandinka|Mandinka]] families along the north bank of the Casamance river, probably by the 16th century, at the edge of the [[e:kaabu-empire|Kaabu Empire's]] sphere.
pakao.r: Pakao was organised as a set of villages under chiefs, but stood out for its clerical lineages, who ran Quranic schools and spread [[e:islam|Islam]] among neighbouring peoples. It paid tribute to [[e:kaabu-empire|Kaabu]] and maintained ties with Gambian [[e:mandinka|Mandinka]] states.
pakao.e: In the second half of the 19th century Pakao was caught up in the wars of [[e:fula|Fula]] and [[e:mandinka|Mandinka]] Muslim leaders and then came under French rule, becoming part of [[s:french-senegal|French Senegal]] by the 1880s.

provisional-government-of-hawaii.t: The government set up by American and European businessmen after the overthrow of Queen Liliʻuokalani in 1893, created to secure annexation by the United States.
provisional-government-of-hawaii.o: In January 1893 Queen Liliʻuokalani proposed a new constitution to restore royal power. A Committee of Safety led by Lorrin A. Thurston, made up mostly of American [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] interests, seized government buildings on 17 January, while the US minister John L. Stevens landed marines from USS [[e:boston|Boston]]. The queen yielded under protest to the superior force of the [[s:united-states|United States]], and the committee proclaimed a provisional government.
provisional-government-of-hawaii.r: Sanford B. Dole headed an executive council, with an advisory council of the overthrow's supporters, and ruled without elections, requiring officials to swear loyalty. Its single goal was annexation, and it quickly sent a treaty to Washington. It kept the [[s:kingdom-of-hawaii|Kingdom of Hawaii]]'s laws and bureaucracy largely in place.
provisional-government-of-hawaii.e: President Grover Cleveland withdrew the treaty and, after the Blount Report found American complicity, asked for the queen's restoration. Dole refused. To secure itself until annexation became possible, the government proclaimed the [[s:republic-of-hawaii|Republic of Hawaii]] on 4 July 1894. The [[s:united-states|United States]] formally apologised for the overthrow in 1993.

paeligni.t: Sabellic people of the Abruzzo mountains whose town Corfinium became the rebel capital of the Social War and whose Sulmo was Ovid's birthplace.
paeligni.o: The Paeligni lived in the upland basin of the Aterno and Gizio rivers in central Abruzzo, surrounded by the [[s:marsi|Marsi]], [[s:vestini|Vestini]] and [[s:samnite-league|Samnites]], from the early 1st millennium BCE. Ancient writers counted them among the Sabellian peoples descended from the [[s:sabines|Sabines]], and they spoke a dialect close to Oscan.
paeligni.r: Their main towns were Corfinium, Sulmo and Superaequum, small hill communities that formed a league. Inscriptions in the Paelignian dialect, many in [[e:latin|Latin]] letters, record local gods and priestesses. They kept sheep and controlled routes through the Apennines between [[e:rome|Rome]] and the Adriatic.
paeligni.e: The Paeligni made peace and an alliance with [[e:rome|Rome]] in 304 BCE, together with the [[s:marsi|Marsi]] and [[s:marrucini|Marrucini]]. In 91 BCE they joined the Italian revolt, and Corfinium was renamed [[s:italia-social-war-confederation|Italia]] as the capital of the rebel confederation. After the Social War they received citizenship; the poet Ovid was born at Sulmo in 43 BCE.

patriarchate-of-aquileia.t: A church principality in Friuli whose patriarchs ruled as imperial princes for over three centuries and whose parliament was among Europe's earliest.
patriarchate-of-aquileia.o: During the Investiture Controversy, Emperor Henry IV rewarded Patriarch Sigehard of Aquileia for his loyalty by granting him the county of Friuli in 1077, soon followed by [[s:histria|Istria]] and Carniola. The patriarchs thus became temporal princes of the [[s:holy-roman-empire|Holy Roman Empire]], heirs to one of the oldest bishoprics in the [[e:latin|Latin]] West.
patriarchate-of-aquileia.r: Patriarchs, usually German nobles in the early centuries and later Italians or Frenchmen, ruled from Aquileia, Cividale and from the 13th century mainly Udine. The Parliament of Friuli, bringing together clergy, nobles and towns, voted taxes and troops. The principality was constantly squeezed by the counts of Gorizia, the [[s:duchy-of-austria|Duchy of Austria]] and the [[s:republic-of-venice|Republic of Venice]]; Patriarch Bertrand was murdered by Friulian nobles in 1350.
patriarchate-of-aquileia.e: [[e:venice|Venice]] conquered Friuli in 1420, ending the patriarchs' temporal rule; a settlement in 1445 left them only a few towns. The patriarchate continued as a church office until 1751, when [[e:papacy|Pope]] Benedict XIV divided it into the archdioceses of Udine and Gorizia.

picentes.t: Italic people of the central Adriatic coast, said to have followed a woodpecker to their new land, whose warrior culture lasted until Rome conquered them in 268 BCE.
picentes.o: The Picentes lived in Picenum, the coastal strip and hills of the modern Marche and northern Abruzzo, from the early 1st millennium BCE. Roman tradition said they descended from [[s:sabines|Sabines]] who left home in a 'sacred spring' migration, guided by a woodpecker (picus), the bird of Mars. Archaeologists call their culture the Picene culture.
picentes.r: Picene society was dominated by warrior elites buried with helmets, weapons, [[e:chariot|chariots]] and amber from the Baltic. Their South Picene inscriptions, in a Sabellic language written in a distinctive alphabet, appear on stone stelae, and the Novilara stele in the north bears a still undeciphered text. Asculum was their main centre, and they traded across the Adriatic and with Etruria.
picentes.e: The Picentes allied with [[e:rome|Rome]] in 299 BCE but revolted in 269 BCE and were conquered in 268 BCE; part of the population was moved to the Gulf of [[s:principality-of-salerno|Salerno]]. Asculum became an allied city, and its massacre of [[e:roman-empire|Romans]] in 91 BCE began the Social War. Picenum became part of Augustus's Regio V.

pacajes.t: An Aymara kingdom on the southern shore of Lake Titicaca whose territory included Tiwanaku and later became a key Spanish province.
pacajes.o: The Pacajes, or Pakasa, formed one of the Aymara kingdoms that emerged around Lake Titicaca after Tiwanaku's collapse, occupying the high plain south of the lake in modern [[s:republic-of-bolivia|Bolivia]] from the 12th century. Their capital was Caquiaviri.
pacajes.r: Like other Aymara kingdoms, Pacajes was divided into two halves, Urcosuyu and Umasuyu, each with its own lords. Its economy was based on herding llamas and alpacas and farming tubers such as [[e:potato|potatoes]], freeze-dried into chuño. Pacajes lords built chullpa burial towers and kept colonies in warmer valleys to the east.
pacajes.e: Pacajes was absorbed into the [[s:inca-empire|Inca Empire]] in the mid-15th century. Under Spanish rule it became a province of the [[s:royal-audiencia-of-charcas|Royal Audiencia of Charcas]], and its people supplied labour for the [[e:potosi|Potosí]] mines under the [[e:mita|mita]]. Caquiaviri retains a notable colonial church.

prince-archbishopric-of-salzburg.t: Alpine church state that grew rich on salt and gold, built a baroque capital, expelled its Protestants in 1731 and employed the young Mozart.
prince-archbishopric-of-salzburg.o: Saint Rupert founded a church and monastery at the Roman town of Iuvavum around 696, and Salzburg became an archbishopric in 798. Its archbishops gained lands and immunities over the centuries, and by the early 13th century, around 1213, they were recognised as princes ruling a territory largely independent of the [[s:duchy-of-bavaria|Duchy of Bavaria]].
prince-archbishopric-of-salzburg.r: The archbishop, elected by the cathedral chapter, governed a land whose wealth came from salt at Hallein and gold and [[e:silver|silver]] mines in the Gastein valley. Wolf Dietrich von Raitenau and Markus Sittikus rebuilt Salzburg in Italian baroque style, and [[e:paris|Paris]] Lodron kept it out of the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years War]]. In 1731 Leopold Anton von Firmian expelled about 20,000 Protestants. Mozart was born there in 1756 and served Archbishop Hieronymus von Colloredo.
prince-archbishopric-of-salzburg.e: The see was secularised in 1803 as the [[s:electorate-of-salzburg|Electorate of Salzburg]] for Ferdinand of [[s:grand-duchy-of-tuscany|Tuscany]], then passed to [[e:austria|Austria]] in 1805 and to Bavaria in 1810. In 1816 most of it was returned to Austria, of which it is now a federal state.

cr.a: Roke (map), Hanno Sandvik (addition of colours, based on Putzger Historischer Weltatlas, 103rd ed., 2005)

prince-bishopric-of-liege.t: A church principality on the Meuse that lasted eight centuries, grew rich on coal and arms making, and balanced its bishops against assertive townspeople.
prince-bishopric-of-liege.o: [[e:bishop|Bishop]] Notger (972–1008) gathered secular rights from the Ottonian emperors, including the county of Huy in 985, and turned the see of Liège into a territorial principality of the [[s:holy-roman-empire|Holy Roman Empire]]. He rebuilt the city and its schools, and Liège became one of the leading intellectual centres of the empire.
prince-bishopric-of-liege.r: The prince-[[e:bishop|bishops]] shared power with the cathedral chapter and towns; the Peace of Fexhe of 1316 required the consent of the estates for major decisions. Liège mined [[e:coal|coal]] from the 12th century and became famous for metalwork and weapons. Charles the Bold sacked the city in 1468. Erard de la Marck rebuilt it in the early 16th century, and the principality kept a careful neutrality.
prince-bishopric-of-liege.e: The [[s:republic-of-liege|Liège Revolution]] of 1789 drove out the prince-[[e:bishop|bishop]] and created the Republic of Liège; Austrian troops restored him in 1791. French armies annexed the principality in 1795, and its lands were later divided between [[s:kingdom-of-belgium|Belgium]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-the-netherlands|Netherlands]].

principality-of-salm.t: A Vosges principality of the Salm family around the abbey town of Senones, which voted to join France in 1793.
principality-of-salm.o: The counts of Salm, a branch of the Wild- and Rhinegraves, held lands in the Vosges around [[s:senones|Senones]] and Badonviller. In 1623 Philip Otto of Salm was made a prince of the [[s:holy-roman-empire|Holy Roman Empire]], and the territory became a principality.
principality-of-salm.r: The principality was a small mountain land of forests, ironworks and later textile workshops. Its life centred on [[s:senones|Senones]] and its Benedictine abbey, whose abbot Dom Augustin Calmet was a celebrated scholar. In 1751 the territory was reorganised and Senones became the princes' residence, with a modest court.
principality-of-salm.e: Surrounded by Revolutionary [[e:france|France]] and cut off by its [[e:naval-blockade|blockade]], the inhabitants voted to join France, and the [[s:french-first-republic|French First Republic]] annexed the principality in 1793. The [[s:principality-of-salm-1802|Salm-Salm]] princes received compensation in [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Westphalia]].

pahra-state.t: One of the Chaube jagirs near Kalinjar in Bundelkhand, created by the British in 1812.
pahra-state.o: Pahra was one of the estates granted in 1812 to members of the Chaube family, [[e:brahmins|Brahmin]] governors of Kalinjar fort, when they surrendered the fortress to the British.
pahra-state.r: It was a minor holding of a few villages under the [[e:bundelkhand|Bundelkhand]] Agency. Little else is recorded.
pahra-state.e: After independence Pahra was merged into [[s:vindhya-pradesh|Vindhya Pradesh]] with the other [[e:bundelkhand|Bundelkhand]] states and absorbed by 1950.

panna-state.t: The Bundela kingdom of Chhatrasal in Bundelkhand, famous for its diamond mines and as a holy centre of the Pranami faith.
panna-state.o: Chhatrasal, a Bundela [[e:rajputs|Rajput]], rebelled against Mughal rule from the 1670s and built an independent kingdom with its capital at Panna. With [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] help under [[e:baji-rao-i|Baji Rao I]] he defeated a Mughal invasion in 1729; on his death his realm was divided among his heirs and the [[e:peshwa|Peshwa]].
panna-state.r: The Maharajas of Panna ruled the eastern share of Chhatrasal's kingdom. The state was known for its diamond mines, which gave it revenue for centuries. Chhatrasal's guru Prannath made Panna a sacred centre of the Pranami sect. Under British paramountcy it was a salute state of the [[e:bundelkhand|Bundelkhand]] Agency.
panna-state.e: Panna joined [[s:vindhya-pradesh|Vindhya Pradesh]] in 1948 and Madhya Pradesh in 1956. The diamond mines at Majhgawan and Panna National Park lie in its former territory.

pellendones.t: A Celtiberian people of the upper Douro around the Picos de Urbión, living in the high country north of Numantia.
pellendones.o: The Pellendones lived around the sources of the Douro in northern Soria and southern La Rioja from about the 4th century BCE. Pliny counts them among the [[s:celtiberians|Celtiberians]], and some ancient geographers placed Numantia in their territory rather than that of the [[s:arevaci|Arevaci]].
pellendones.r: They were a highland people of hillforts and herding, with towns such as Visontium and Augustobriga named by Ptolemy. Their society was probably organised in clans under local elites like that of their Celtiberian neighbours, but no details are recorded.
pellendones.e: They were drawn into the Celtiberian wars against [[e:rome|Rome]] and came under Roman control after the fall of Numantia in 133 BCE, becoming part of [[s:hispania-citerior|Hispania Citerior]].

province-of-new-jersey.t: The English colony between the Hudson and Delaware rivers, granted in 1664, split in two for a generation and reunited under the Crown in 1702.
province-of-new-jersey.o: After seizing [[s:new-netherland|New Netherland]] in 1664, James, Duke of York, granted the land between the Hudson and Delaware to Lord John Berkeley and Sir George Carteret, naming it after Carteret's home island of [[s:bailiwick-of-jersey|Jersey]]. Their Concession and Agreement of 1665 promised religious freedom and an elected assembly, drawing settlers to Elizabethtown and other towns.
province-of-new-jersey.r: Disputes over land and quitrents led to division into [[s:east-jersey|East Jersey]] and [[s:west-jersey|West Jersey]], which existed from 1674 until the proprietors surrendered government to the Crown in 1702. The reunited royal colony shared its governor with the [[s:province-of-new-york|Province of New York]] until 1738, and its capital alternated between Perth Amboy and Burlington. Diverse Puritan, Quaker, [[e:dutch|Dutch]] and Scottish settlers farmed grain, and the colleges that became Princeton and Rutgers were founded in 1746 and 1766.
province-of-new-jersey.e: Royal governor William Franklin, son of Benjamin Franklin, was arrested in 1776. On 2 July 1776 New [[s:bailiwick-of-jersey|Jersey]] adopted a state constitution, and it became a state of the [[s:united-states|United States]].

panduvamshis-of-dakshina-kosala.t: A dynasty of Chhattisgarh ruling from Sirpur, whose brick Lakshmana temple and Buddhist monasteries are among the treasures of early medieval India.
panduvamshis-of-dakshina-kosala.o: The Panduvamshis, claiming descent from the lunar line, rose in Dakshina [[s:kingdom-of-kosala|Kosala]], the upper Mahanadi valley of modern Chhattisgarh, in the 6th century. Under Tivaradeva they united the region and made Shripura, modern Sirpur, their capital, displacing earlier local rulers.
panduvamshis-of-dakshina-kosala.r: The kings were mostly Vaishnava but tolerant of Shaivism and [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]]. Mahashivagupta Balarjuna, who ruled for about sixty years in the 7th century, was a Shaiva who also endowed Buddhist monasteries; his mother Vasata built the Lakshmana temple at Sirpur, one of the finest early brick temples in [[e:india|India]]. Excavations at Sirpur have revealed monasteries, markets and temples of a thriving city, which Xuanzang described.
panduvamshis-of-dakshina-kosala.e: After Balarjuna the dynasty declined in the 8th century. Its line, known as the Somavamshis, moved east into Odisha, where it later ruled as the [[s:somavamshi-dynasty|Somavamshi dynasty]], while Dakshina [[s:kingdom-of-kosala|Kosala]] passed to other rulers.

principality-of-anhalt-dessau.t: The leading Anhalt principality, famed for the Old Dessauer's drill reforms and the Dessau-Wörlitz Garden Realm of the Enlightenment.
principality-of-anhalt-dessau.o: Anhalt-Dessau was created in the 1603 partition of [[s:principality-of-anhalt|Anhalt]], with Prince John George I receiving Dessau on the Mulde near its junction with the Elbe. The line was Calvinist and closely tied to the [[s:margraviate-of-brandenburg|Electorate of Brandenburg]] by marriage.
principality-of-anhalt-dessau.r: Leopold I, the Old Dessauer, was a Prussian field marshal who introduced the iron ramrod and cadenced marching. His grandson Leopold III Friedrich Franz was a model [[e:age-of-enlightenment|Enlightenment]] ruler who laid out the landscape gardens of Wörlitz, built schools and founded the Philanthropinum, a progressive school, in 1774. The principality became a duchy in 1807.
principality-of-anhalt-dessau.e: Anhalt-Dessau inherited [[s:principality-of-anhalt-kothen|Anhalt-Köthen]] in 1847 and [[s:principality-of-anhalt-bernburg|Anhalt-Bernburg]] in 1863, after which Duke Leopold IV Friedrich ruled a united [[s:duchy-of-anhalt|Duchy of Anhalt]] from Dessau. The Garden Realm is now a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

principality-of-orange.t: A tiny sovereign principality in the Rhône valley whose title passed to the house of Nassau and gave the Dutch royal family its name.
principality-of-orange.o: Orange was a Roman colony and later a county within the [[s:kingdom-of-arles|Kingdom of Arles]]; the troubadour Raimbaut d'Orange ruled part of it in the 12th century. In 1163 Emperor [[e:frederick-barbarossa|Frederick Barbarossa]] raised it to a principality, and it passed in 1173 to Bertrand of Baux, whose family ruled it for over two centuries.
principality-of-orange.r: The principality was a small enclave inside [[s:county-of-provence|Provence]] and the [[s:comtat-venaissin|Comtat Venaissin]], with Roman monuments, a university founded in 1365 and its own courts. It passed to the Chalon family in 1393. René of Chalon left it to his cousin William of [[s:county-of-nassau|Nassau]] in 1544, and under William the Silent Orange became a refuge for Protestants.
principality-of-orange.e: [[e:louis-xiv|Louis XIV]] occupied Orange several times and destroyed its fortifications. After the death of William III of [[e:england|England]] in 1702, [[e:france|France]] took it, and the [[e:treaty-of-utrecht|Treaty of Utrecht]] in 1713 recognised its annexation. The princes of Orange-Nassau kept the title, which the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] royal house still bears.

pataudi-state.t: A small Pathan Nawabi state near Delhi, famous in the 20th century for its two cricket-captain Nawabs.
pataudi-state.o: Faiz Talab Khan, a Pathan of the Barech tribe, served the British in the war against the [[e:maratha-empire|Marathas]], and in 1804 the British granted him the district of Pataudi south-west of [[e:delhi|Delhi]] as a hereditary state.
pataudi-state.r: Pataudi was a small, non-salute state of the [[e:punjab|Punjab]], ruled by a Nawab over a mainly [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] farming population. Nawab Iftikhar Ali Khan Pataudi played Test cricket for [[e:england|England]] and later captained [[e:india|India]], and his son Mansoor Ali Khan Pataudi became India's youngest Test captain.
pataudi-state.e: Pataudi acceded to [[e:india|India]] and in 1948 was merged into East [[e:punjab|Punjab]]; the town is now in Gurugram district of Haryana. The family's title was abolished with all princely privileges in 1971.

principality-of-blankenburg.t: Harz principality of a Brunswick prince whose daughter became mother of Empress Maria Theresa.
principality-of-blankenburg.o: The County of Blankenburg in the Harz had passed to the dukes of [[s:principality-of-wolfenbuttel|Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel]] in 1599. Duke Anthony Ulrich gave it to his younger son Louis Rudolph, and in 1707 Emperor Joseph I raised it to a principality, giving Louis Rudolph a seat among the princes of the Empire.
principality-of-blankenburg.r: Louis Rudolph ruled the small Lutheran territory from Blankenburg Castle, which he rebuilt, with a court [[e:theatre|theatre]] and gardens. The principality's prestige came from [[e:diplomatic-marriage|dynastic marriages]]: his daughter Elisabeth Christine married the future Emperor Charles VI and became mother of Maria Theresa, while another daughter married the son of [[e:peter-the-great|Peter the Great]].
principality-of-blankenburg.e: In 1731 Louis Rudolph inherited the Principality of [[s:principality-of-wolfenbuttel|Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel]], and Blankenburg was reunited with it. It remained a Brunswick possession and became part of the [[s:duchy-of-brunswick|Duchy of Brunswick]].

portuguese-angola.t: Portugal's West African colony centred on Luanda, for three centuries the largest source of enslaved Africans shipped to Brazil.
portuguese-angola.o: In 1575 Paulo Dias de Novais arrived on the coast with a royal charter to conquer the [[s:kingdom-of-ndongo|Kingdom of Ndongo]], founding Luanda the following year. The colony grew from a coastal base through wars with Ndongo, alliances with Imbangala bands and the founding of Benguela in 1617, always driven by the demand for slaves in [[s:new-republic-brazil|Brazil]].
portuguese-angola.r: Governors in Luanda relied on forts along the Kwanza, African auxiliaries and trading fairs to obtain captives, and Luanda's merchants were closely tied to [[s:new-republic-brazil|Brazil]]. The [[e:dutch|Dutch]] occupied Luanda from 1641 until [[e:salvador|Salvador]] Correia de Sa recaptured it in 1648. After the end of the [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trade]] in the 19th century, Portugal pushed inland, and 20th-century settlers developed [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]], diamonds and later oil.
portuguese-angola.e: Nationalist revolt began in 1961, with the MPLA, FNLA and UNITA fighting Portugal. After the [[e:carnation-revolution|Carnation Revolution]] of 1974, Portugal withdrew, and [[e:angola|Angola]] became independent on 11 November 1975 amid a civil war between the movements.

peucetians.t: Iapygian people of central Apulia around modern Bari, whose towns such as Rubi became centres of Greek-influenced art and vase collecting.
peucetians.o: The Peucetians occupied central Apulia between the [[s:daunians|Daunians]] to the north and the [[s:messapians|Messapians]] to the south, from the early 1st millennium BCE. Greek writers explained their name through Peucetius, a son of the Arcadian Lycaon, but their culture developed from local Iron Age communities related to their Iapygian neighbours.
peucetians.r: They lived in separate fortified towns, among them Caelia, Azetium, Rubi (Ruvo di Puglia) and the site of Monte Sannace, without a known central government. Their geometric painted pottery gave way, from the 5th century BCE, to strong Greek influence: the elite of Rubi buried their dead with Athenian and Apulian red-figure vases, many from [[s:taras|Taras]]. They grew cereals and olives and traded through coastal landings.
peucetians.e: The Peucetian towns came under Roman control around the end of the 4th and start of the 3rd centuries BCE during [[e:rome|Rome's]] expansion into Apulia. They were later absorbed into Roman Apulia and became municipia. Collections of vases from Ruvo, such as the Jatta collection, preserve much of their material culture.

palatinate-neuburg.t: The 'Young Palatinate' on the Danube, created after the Landshut War, whose dukes inherited Jülich and Berg and then the Palatine electorate.
palatinate-neuburg.o: The [[s:free-imperial-city-of-cologne|Cologne]] arbitration of 1505 that ended the War of the Landshut Succession created a new principality from parts of the [[s:duchy-of-bavaria-landshut|Duchy of Bavaria-Landshut]] for Otto Henry and Philip, the young sons of Rupert of the [[s:electoral-palatinate|Palatinate]]. Known as the Young Palatinate, it had Neuburg on the [[e:danube|Danube]] as its capital.
palatinate-neuburg.r: Otto Henry introduced [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]] in 1542 and rebuilt Neuburg castle in [[e:renaissance|Renaissance]] style before becoming Elector Palatine. Wolfgang William converted to [[e:catholicism|Catholicism]] in 1613 to strengthen his claim in the Jülich succession and won Jülich and Berg, ruling from Düsseldorf. His son Philip William became Elector Palatine in 1685, after which the Neuburg dukes ruled from Düsseldorf, Heidelberg and Mannheim.
palatinate-neuburg.e: When Elector Charles Philip, the last of the Neuburg line, died in 1742, his lands passed to Charles Theodore of [[s:palatinate-sulzbach|Palatinate-Sulzbach]], who in 1777 also inherited Bavaria. Neuburg was absorbed into the Wittelsbach lands of Bavaria.

principality-of-hohenzollern-sigmaringen.t: The Catholic Swabian branch of the Hohenzollerns, ruling from Sigmaringen castle on the Danube, which later gave Romania its kings.
principality-of-hohenzollern-sigmaringen.o: When Count Charles I of the [[s:county-of-hohenzollern|County of Hohenzollern]] died in 1576, his lands were divided among his sons. Charles II received Sigmaringen and Veringen on the upper [[e:danube|Danube]], founding the Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen line, and the counts were raised to princes in 1623.
principality-of-hohenzollern-sigmaringen.r: The princes ruled a small Catholic territory from Sigmaringen's castle on a rock above the [[e:danube|Danube]], under strong [[s:county-of-habsburg|Habsburg]] influence since parts of their lands were Austrian fiefs. Thanks partly to Princess Amalie Zephyrine, a friend of Joséphine de Beauharnais, the principality survived the mediatisation of 1806, joined the [[s:confederation-of-the-rhine|Confederation of the Rhine]] and even gained territory.
principality-of-hohenzollern-sigmaringen.e: After the revolution of 1848, Prince Charles Anthony ceded his [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]] to his Prussian cousins in 1849, and in 1850 the principality became part of [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]]. His son Carol became prince and later king of [[s:kingdom-of-romania|Romania]], and another son's candidacy for the Spanish throne helped trigger the [[e:franco-prussian-war|Franco-Prussian War]] of 1870.

province-of-carolina.t: The proprietary colony of eight English lords, whose planned feudal constitution by John Locke gave way to a plantation society centred on Charles Town.
province-of-carolina.o: In 1663 Charles II granted the land between [[e:virginia|Virginia]] and [[s:spanish-florida|Spanish Florida]] to eight Lords Proprietors, among them Anthony Ashley Cooper and the Earl of Clarendon. Settlers from Virginia had already reached the Albemarle Sound region in the north, and in 1670 an expedition largely from [[s:barbados|Barbados]] founded Charles Town, which moved to its present site in 1680.
province-of-carolina.r: The Fundamental Constitutions of 1669, drafted by Ashley Cooper and his secretary John Locke, proposed a hereditary nobility but were never fully applied. Planters from [[s:barbados|Barbados]] brought the slave plantation system, and a large trade in deerskins and in enslaved Native people grew. [[e:rice|Rice]] became the leading crop in the south from the 1690s, while the distant northern settlements had their own deputy governor and assembly.
province-of-carolina.e: The [[s:tuscarora-nation|Tuscarora]] War of 1711 exposed the weakness of the divided colony, and in 1712 the proprietors gave the two parts separate governors, creating the [[s:province-of-north-carolina|Province of North Carolina]] and the [[s:province-of-south-carolina|Province of South Carolina]].

paldeo-state.t: One of the Chaube jagirs near Kalinjar in Bundelkhand, granted by the British in 1812.
paldeo-state.o: Paldeo was among the small estates given in 1812 to members of the Chaube family, [[e:brahmins|Brahmin]] governors of Kalinjar fort, when they surrendered the fort to the British.
paldeo-state.r: It was a minor holding of a few villages under the [[e:bundelkhand|Bundelkhand]] Agency. Few details of its later history are recorded.
paldeo-state.e: After independence Paldeo was merged into [[s:vindhya-pradesh|Vindhya Pradesh]] with the other [[e:bundelkhand|Bundelkhand]] states and absorbed by 1950.

paratarajas.t: An obscure dynasty of Balochistan, known almost only from its coins, which ruled on the borderlands of Iran and India.
paratarajas.o: The Paratarajas, kings of the Paratas or Paradas, ruled in what is now Balochistan from around the 2nd century. They are known mainly from coins with legends in Brahmi and Kharoshthi that name a sequence of kings and their fathers, and they appear to have been connected to the [[s:indo-parthian-kingdom|Indo-Parthian Kingdom]].
paratarajas.r: Their [[e:silver|silver]] and [[e:copper|copper]] coins show the king's bust on one side and a swastika on the other, with titles that call the ruler Paratarajas. Kings such as Yolamira and Arjuna are known only by name. The state probably controlled routes between the [[e:indus|Indus]] valley and south-eastern [[e:iran|Iran]].
paratarajas.e: The Paratarajas likely came under the [[s:sasanian-empire|Sasanian Empire]] in the 3rd century; the Paikuli inscription of the Sasanian king Narseh mentions a ruler of the Paradan among his [[e:vassal|vassals]]. Their coinage ends around 300.

province-of-south-carolina.t: The richest colony in British North America, whose rice and indigo plantations around Charles Town depended on an enslaved African majority.
province-of-south-carolina.o: The southern settlements of the [[s:province-of-carolina|Province of Carolina]], centred on Charles Town, received a separate governor in 1712. After the Yamasee War of 1715 to 1717 nearly destroyed the colony, settlers overthrew proprietary rule in 1719 and asked for royal government, which the Crown formalised in 1729.
province-of-south-carolina.r: [[e:rice|Rice]] grown in tidal swamps, and from the 1740s [[e:indigo|indigo]], developed by Eliza Lucas Pinckney, made the planter elite of the Lowcountry the wealthiest in British America. Enslaved Africans formed the majority of the population, and the Gullah language and culture took shape on the coastal plantations. The Stono Rebellion of 1739 led to harsh new slave laws. Charles Town was a lively port with [[e:theatre|theatres]], libraries and the deerskin trade with the Cherokee and Muscogee.
province-of-south-carolina.e: The last royal governor, Lord William Campbell, fled in 1775. In March 1776 South [[s:province-of-carolina|Carolina]] adopted its own constitution, and in June its defenders repulsed a British fleet at Sullivan's Island. It became a state of the [[s:united-states|United States]].

principality-of-salerno.t: Lombard principality of southern Italy, home of the famous medical school of Salerno, conquered by Robert Guiscard in 1077.
principality-of-salerno.o: A long civil war in the [[s:duchy-of-benevento|Principality of Benevento]] ended in 849 with a formal partition: Siconulf became prince of Salerno, ruling the western half including the coast of Campania, Lucania and parts of Calabria, while Radelchis kept Benevento.
principality-of-salerno.r: Salerno was a prosperous coastal city with links to [[s:republic-of-amalfi|Amalfi]] and the Byzantine world. The Schola Medica Salernitana, the first great medical school of medieval [[e:europe|Europe]], flourished there from the 10th century, drawing on Greek, [[e:latin|Latin]] and Arabic learning. Under Guaimar IV (1027–1052) the principality reached its height, controlling Amalfi, Sorrento and [[s:principality-of-capua|Capua]], and he invested the Norman leaders with Apulia.
principality-of-salerno.e: After Guaimar IV was murdered in 1052, Norman power grew rapidly. Robert Guiscard, who had married Sichelgaita, sister of Prince Gisulf II, besieged Salerno and took it in 1077, making it his capital. The principality became part of the Norman [[s:duchy-of-apulia-and-calabria|Duchy of Apulia]].

polemonid-pontus.t: Polemonid Pontus, a Roman client kingdom on the Black Sea ruled by Polemon I, his queen Pythodorida and their son.
polemonid-pontus.o: In 37 BCE [[e:mark-antony|Mark Antony]] made Polemon, son of the orator Zeno of Laodicea, king of part of the former [[s:kingdom-of-pontus|Kingdom of Pontus]]. Polemon kept his throne after Actium by switching to Augustus and was also made king of the [[s:bosporan-kingdom|Bosporan Kingdom]].
polemonid-pontus.r: The kingdom covered the eastern Pontic coast and inland valleys, including [[s:trapezus|Trapezus]] and Zela. After Polemon was killed c. 8 BCE, his widow Pythodorida, a granddaughter of [[e:mark-antony|Mark Antony]], ruled in her own name for many years. Strabo, a native of the region, praised her government.
polemonid-pontus.e: Caligula gave the kingdom to her grandson Polemon II in 38 CE. Nero deposed him in 62 CE and annexed [[s:kingdom-of-pontus|Pontus]] to the [[s:roman-empire|Roman Empire]].

principality-of-hungary.t: Hungarian state of the Árpád dynasty in the Carpathian basin, from the conquest of 895 to Stephen's coronation as king in 1000.
principality-of-hungary.o: After Pecheneg attacks drove them from Etelköz, the [[s:hungarian-tribal-federation|Hungarian tribal federation]] under Árpád crossed the Carpathians in 895. By the first years of the 10th century they held the whole basin, and in 907 they destroyed a Bavarian army at Pressburg, securing the conquest.
principality-of-hungary.r: For half a century Hungarian horsemen raided [[e:europe|Europe]] from Saxony to [[e:spain|Spain]] and [[e:constantinople|Constantinople]], until [[e:otto-i|Otto I]] defeated them at the Lechfeld in 955. The grand princes then centralised power: Taksony and especially Géza, ruling from Esztergom, curbed tribal chiefs and invited Western missionaries. Géza was baptised and married his son Vajk to Gisela of Bavaria.
principality-of-hungary.e: Géza's son Vajk, baptised Stephen, defeated the pagan Koppány and was crowned king on Christmas Day 1000 (or 1 January 1001) with a crown from [[e:papacy|Pope]] Sylvester II, founding the [[s:kingdom-of-hungary-1000-1301|Kingdom of Hungary]] (1000-1301).

prince-bishopric-of-geneva.t: The temporal lordship of the bishops of Geneva, whose loss to the citizens and the Reformation turned the city into the 'Protestant Rome' of Calvin.
prince-bishopric-of-geneva.o: [[s:republic-of-geneva|Geneva]] had been a bishopric since the 4th century. In 1124 the Treaty of Seyssel between [[e:bishop|Bishop]] Humbert de Grammont and the Count of Geneva confirmed the bishop's lordship over the city, and [[e:frederick-barbarossa|Frederick Barbarossa]] recognised him as an imperial prince in 1162.
prince-bishopric-of-geneva.r: The [[e:bishop|bishops]] ruled the city through officials, while the counts of [[s:republic-of-geneva|Geneva]] and later the dukes of [[s:county-of-savoy|Savoy]] held the vidomnat, an important judicial office. Citizens gained a charter of liberties from Bishop Adhémar Fabri in 1387. Geneva's fairs made it a major trading centre in the 15th century. Savoy princes increasingly held the bishopric itself.
prince-bishopric-of-geneva.e: [[s:republic-of-geneva|Geneva]] allied with [[s:canton-of-fribourg|Fribourg]] and Bern in 1526, and in 1533 [[e:bishop|Bishop]] Pierre de La Baume left the city. In 1535 to 1536 it adopted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] and became an independent republic. John Calvin arrived in 1536. Geneva joined [[s:swiss-confederation|Switzerland]] in 1815.

pallava-dynasty.t: The dynasty of Kanchipuram that created the rock-cut temples of Mamallapuram and spread South Indian script and art across Southeast Asia.
pallava-dynasty.o: The Pallavas first appear in the 3rd and 4th centuries in Prakrit charters from Andhra and the Kanchipuram region, as the [[s:satavahana-dynasty|Satavahana dynasty]] and the [[s:ikshvaku-dynasty|Ikshvaku dynasty]] declined. [[e:samudragupta|Samudragupta]] defeated a Vishnugopa of Kanchi in the 4th century. The dynasty became a major power after Simhavishnu expelled the [[s:kalabhra-dynasty|Kalabhra dynasty]] from the Kaveri delta in the late 6th century.
pallava-dynasty.r: Mahendravarman I, a playwright who wrote the satire Mattavilasa, built South [[e:india|India's]] first rock-cut temples and, according to tradition, turned from Jainism to Shaivism. His son Narasimhavarman I took Vatapi in 642, killing Pulakeshin II of the [[s:chalukyas-of-badami|Chalukyas of Badami]], and gave his name to the port of Mamallapuram, with its monolithic rathas. Narasimhavarman II built the Shore Temple and the Kailasanatha temple at Kanchipuram, a great centre of [[e:sanskrit|Sanskrit]] learning.
pallava-dynasty.e: Weakened by wars with the Chalukyas, [[s:rashtrakuta-dynasty|Rashtrakutas]] and [[s:later-pandyan-empire|Pandyas]], the Pallavas lost their kingdom when Aparajita was defeated by Aditya I of the [[s:chola-empire|Chola Empire]] around 897. Pallava Grantha script became the ancestor of many Southeast Asian alphabets.

province-of-maine.t: A proprietary colony granted to Sir Ferdinando Gorges in what is now southern Maine, absorbed by Massachusetts in the 1650s.
province-of-maine.o: In 1622 the Council for New [[e:england|England]] granted Sir Ferdinando Gorges and John Mason the land between the Merrimack and Kennebec rivers. When they divided it in 1629, Gorges took the eastern part. Fishing stations and small settlements grew along the coast at Kittery, York and Saco, and in 1639 a royal charter made Gorges proprietor of the Province of [[s:county-of-maine|Maine]].
province-of-maine.r: Gorges never crossed the Atlantic, ruling through deputies such as his cousin Thomas Gorges. He planned an Anglican, manorial society and in 1641 chartered York as Gorgeana, the first English city in America. In practice settlers lived from fishing, [[e:timber|timber]] and fur trading and quarrelled with the rival Lygonia grant to the north. After Gorges died in 1647, the towns organised their own government.
province-of-maine.e: [[s:massachusetts-bay-colony|Massachusetts Bay Colony]] claimed that its charter covered the region and absorbed the towns between 1652 and 1658, organising them as Yorkshire County. [[s:province-of-massachusetts-bay|Massachusetts]] bought the Gorges heirs' claim in 1677, and [[s:county-of-maine|Maine]] remained part of Massachusetts until statehood in 1820.

pal-lahara-state.t: A small, hilly princely state in northern Odisha, one of the Orissa Tributary States until 1948.
pal-lahara-state.o: Tradition dates the ruling family to around 1500, but its origins are not reliably known.
pal-lahara-state.r: Pal Lahara was a thinly populated state of forest and hills, with Bhuyan and other Adivasi communities. It became one of the Orissa Tributary Mahals under British supervision after 1803. Its history is poorly recorded.
pal-lahara-state.e: Pal Lahara merged into Orissa on 1 January 1948 and is now in Angul district.

principality-of-capua.t: Lombard principality of northern Campania that broke away from Benevento and later became the first Norman principality in southern Italy.
principality-of-capua.o: In the civil wars of the [[e:kingdom-of-the-lombards|Lombard]] south in the 840s, Landulf I, gastald of [[s:capua|Capua]], made his town practically independent of both Benevento and [[s:principality-of-salerno|Salerno]]. Arab raiders destroyed old Capua in 841, and in 856 his family founded a new Capua on the site of Casilinum by the Volturno. Its rulers took the title of prince by the early 10th century.
principality-of-capua.r: [[s:capua|Capua]] was ruled by quarrelsome branches of Landulf's family, who controlled northern Campania and much of the Liri valley. Pandulf Ironhead (died 981) briefly united Capua, Benevento and Spoleto under imperial patronage. Pandulf IV, called the Wolf of the Abruzzi, despoiled Monte Cassino and, like his rivals, hired Norman [[e:mercenary|mercenaries]], helping the Normans gain a foothold in Campania.
principality-of-capua.e: The Norman [[e:richard-i-of-england|Richard I]] of [[s:county-of-aversa|Aversa]] took [[s:capua|Capua]] in 1058, and his family ruled it as princes for nearly eighty years. After Robert II of Capua resisted Roger II, the principality was absorbed into the [[s:kingdom-of-sicily|Kingdom of Sicily]] in 1135.

principality-of-isenburg.t: Hessian principality of the Isenburg-Birstein line that rose to sovereignty under Napoleon only to be mediatised at Vienna.
principality-of-isenburg.o: The counts of [[s:county-of-isenburg-budingen|Isenburg]] had held lands in the Wetterau and around Büdingen since the Middle Ages, divided into many lines. The Birstein branch was raised to princely rank in 1744 under Wolfgang Ernst I, ruling from Birstein Castle in the Vogelsberg foothills.
principality-of-isenburg.r: The territory was small and agrarian, with Offenbach am Main as its most important town, where Huguenot settlers had built crafts and trade. Prince Charles joined the [[s:confederation-of-the-rhine|Confederation of the Rhine]] in 1806, gaining full [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]] and absorbing the lands of other [[s:county-of-isenburg-budingen|Isenburg]] lines, and supplied a regiment to [[e:napoleon|Napoleon's]] army.
principality-of-isenburg.e: After [[e:napoleon|Napoleon's]] fall [[s:county-of-isenburg-budingen|Isenburg]] was occupied by the allies, and the [[e:congress-of-vienna|Congress of Vienna]] mediatised it. In 1816 its lands were divided between the [[s:grand-duchy-of-hesse|Grand Duchy of Hesse]] and the [[s:electorate-of-hesse|Electorate of Hesse]], the princes keeping their estates.

prince-abbey-of-fulda.t: Abbey founded by a disciple of Saint Boniface, a centre of Carolingian learning, and later a baroque prince-bishopric in eastern Hesse.
prince-abbey-of-fulda.o: Sturm, a disciple of Saint Boniface, founded the monastery at Fulda in 744, and Boniface was buried there in 754. Under Abbot Hrabanus Maurus in the 9th century it became one of the great centres of learning in the Frankish realm. Its abbots gathered vast estates and were recognised as imperial princes by 1220.
prince-abbey-of-fulda.r: The prince-abbots ruled a sizeable territory in the Rhön and the Fulda valley, with the support of a powerful noble chapter. Abbot Balthasar von Dernbach led a fierce Counter-[[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] in the late 16th century. The baroque cathedral by Johann Dientzenhofer and the abbots' palace reshaped the town, and in 1752 the abbey was raised to a prince-bishopric.
prince-abbey-of-fulda.e: Secularised in 1802, Fulda went to William Frederick of [[s:principality-of-nassau-diez|Nassau-Orange]], then to French control and the [[s:grand-duchy-of-frankfurt|Grand Duchy of Frankfurt]]. In 1816 it passed to the [[s:electorate-of-hesse|Electorate of Hesse]]. The diocese of Fulda continues today.

piedras-negras.t: A Classic Maya kingdom on the Usumacinta whose stelae enabled Tatiana Proskouriakoff to prove in 1960 that Maya inscriptions record real history.
piedras-negras.o: Piedras Negras, anciently Yo'k'ib', occupied the Guatemalan bank of the Usumacinta, upstream from [[s:yaxchilan|Yaxchilan]]. Its kings appear in inscriptions from the 5th century, around 460 CE, and the city fought long wars with Yaxchilan over the river valley.
piedras-negras.r: From 628 its rulers raised a series of stelae marking accessions, showing a king seated in a niche above a ladder. Analysing these sequences, Proskouriakoff demonstrated that the glyphs named rulers and dated events in their lives. The kingdom was often allied with the [[s:kingdom-of-kaan|Kingdom of Kaan]] and built sweat baths, palaces and a fine carved throne.
piedras-negras.e: In 808 [[s:yaxchilan|Yaxchilan]] captured K'inich Yat Ahk II, the last known king, and the city declined swiftly, being abandoned by the early 9th century. Excavations in the 1930s and 1990s revealed much of its layout.

phocian-league.t: Federation of the towns of Phocis in central Greece, which seized Delphi and fought the Third Sacred War against Thebes and Philip II.
phocian-league.o: The Phocians lived in the valley of the Cephissus and around Mount Parnassus, in some twenty small towns such as Elateia. By the 6th century BCE they formed a federation with a common council house, the Phokikon. Their long wars with the Thessalians included famous stratagems with chalk-whitened warriors.
phocian-league.r: Phocis guarded the path around [[e:battle-of-thermopylae|Thermopylae]] and fought in 480 BCE before submitting to [[e:persia|Persia]]. In 356 BCE, fined by the Amphictyony, the Phocians under Philomelus seized [[s:delphi|Delphi]] and used its treasure to hire [[e:mercenary|mercenaries]]. Onomarchus twice defeated Philip II in 353 BCE but was killed at the Battle of the Crocus Field in 352 BCE.
phocian-league.e: In 346 BCE Phalaecus surrendered to Philip II. The Phocian towns were broken into villages, Phocis lost its vote in the Amphictyony and owed annual indemnities to [[s:delphi|Delphi]]. It later revived as a league.

principality-of-khachen.t: An Armenian principality in the highlands of Karabakh that survived Arab, Seljuk and Mongol overlords for nearly eight centuries and built the monastery of Gandzasar.
principality-of-khachen.o: Khachen emerged in the 9th century in the mountains of Artsakh, in the former lands of the [[s:mihranid-principality-of-albania|Mihranid Principality of Albania]]. Its early prince Sahl Smbatean became famous for capturing the rebel leader Babak in 837 and handing him to the [[e:abbasid-caliphate|Abbasids]]. The principality took its name from the fortress of Khachen.
principality-of-khachen.r: Princes ruled from mountain fortresses such as Khokhanaberd over Armenian villages, vineyards and monasteries. The greatest, Hasan-Jalal Dawla, prince from 1214, built the monastery of Gandzasar, seat of the Catholicos of [[s:caucasian-albania|Aghvank]]. Khachen served as a [[e:vassal|vassal]] of [[s:zakarid-armenia|Zakarid Armenia]], the [[e:mongols|Mongols]] and the [[s:ilkhanate|Ilkhanate]], keeping local autonomy through skilful diplomacy and [[e:diplomatic-marriage|dynastic marriages]].
principality-of-khachen.e: After Hasan-Jalal's execution by the [[e:mongols|Mongols]] in 1261, Khachen fragmented among branches of his house. Under the [[s:safavid-empire|Safavid Empire]] in the early 17th century its lands were reorganised into the [[s:melikdoms-of-karabakh|Melikdoms of Karabakh]], ruled by descendants of the Hasan-Jalalyan family.

prince-bishopric-of-worms.t: A small prince-bishopric on the upper Rhine whose bishops lost their city of Worms and ruled a few scattered lands from Ladenburg.
prince-bishopric-of-worms.o: [[s:free-imperial-city-of-worms|Worms]] had been a bishopric since Roman times. [[e:bishop|Bishop]] Burchard of Worms, who issued a famous collection of canon law around 1020, gained wide rights over the city. In 1156 [[e:frederick-barbarossa|Frederick Barbarossa]] confirmed the bishop's possessions, and the bishops became princes of a small territory.
prince-bishopric-of-worms.r: The [[e:bishop|bishops]] lost control of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-worms|Worms]] itself, which became a free imperial city; the Concordat of Worms in 1122 and Luther's appearance at the Diet of Worms in 1521 took place there. The bishops ruled scattered lands, sharing Ladenburg with the [[s:electoral-palatinate|Electoral Palatinate]]. The see was often held together with [[e:mainz|Mainz]].
prince-bishopric-of-worms.e: [[e:france|France]] annexed the left-bank lands in the 1790s, and in 1803 the remaining territories were secularised and given to [[s:grand-duchy-of-hesse|Hesse-Darmstadt]] and Baden. The diocese itself was dissolved in 1801 and later merged into the diocese of [[e:mainz|Mainz]].

principality-of-bryansk.t: A forest principality on the Desna that inherited the senior role in the Chernigov lands after the Mongol sack, before falling to Lithuania.
principality-of-bryansk.o: Bryansk on the Desna was a town of the [[s:principality-of-chernigov|Principality of Chernigov]]. After the [[e:mongols|Mongols]] destroyed [[e:chernigov|Chernigov]] in 1239 and Prince Mikhail was killed in 1246, his son Roman Mikhailovich made Bryansk his seat, and it became the leading principality of the old Chernigov lands.
principality-of-bryansk.r: Protected by thick forests, Bryansk recovered more quickly than the open lands to the south. Roman Mikhailovich, who ruled until the 1280s, fought off Lithuanian raids and allied by marriage with the princes of [[s:kingdom-of-galicia-volhynia|Galicia-Volhynia]]. From the early 14th century princes of the [[e:smolensk|Smolensk]] line held the town, and it was torn by disputes between pro-Lithuanian and pro-Horde factions.
principality-of-bryansk.e: Around 1356 Algirdas of the [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Grand Duchy of Lithuania]] took Bryansk and later gave it to his son Dmitry. It remained Lithuanian until the [[s:grand-duchy-of-moscow|Grand Duchy of Moscow]] took it in 1500.

principality-of-schwarzburg-sondershause.t: A Thuringian principality of the house of Schwarzburg, ruled from Sondershausen and Arnstadt, where the young Bach held his first organ post.
principality-of-schwarzburg-sondershause.o: The Treaty of Stadtilm of 1599 split the [[s:county-of-schwarzburg|Schwarzburg]] lands, and Count John Günther I's line received Sondershausen and Arnstadt, forming Schwarzburg-Sondershausen alongside the [[s:principality-of-schwarzburg-rudolstadt|Principality of Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt]].
principality-of-schwarzburg-sondershause.r: The counts became princes in 1697 and ruled a Lutheran territory in two parts, the Lower Lordship around Sondershausen and the Upper Lordship around Arnstadt. Arnstadt gave Johann Sebastian Bach his first post as organist in 1703. The princes kept a court orchestra, and in the 19th century Sondershausen became known for its public concerts and music school.
principality-of-schwarzburg-sondershause.e: The principality joined the [[s:german-empire|German Empire]] in 1871. When Prince Karl Günther died childless in 1909, Günther Victor of Rudolstadt inherited it in personal union. He abdicated in November 1918, and in 1920 the state merged into the [[s:free-state-of-thuringia|Free State of Thuringia]].

principality-of-reuss-schleiz.t: Branch of the Reuss family in Thuringia that eventually reunited the Younger Line of Reuss under its rule.
principality-of-reuss-schleiz.o: Reuss-Schleiz was created in the 1647 division of the Younger Line of the House of Reuss, centred on the town of Schleiz. The counts, descended from the medieval Vögte of Weida, Gera and Plauen, held small territories in eastern Thuringia.
principality-of-reuss-schleiz.r: The territory was small and agrarian, with textile crafts, and its counts, all named Heinrich, ruled through a Lutheran church and a small court at Schleiz. The Schleiz line was raised to princely rank in 1806, joined the [[s:confederation-of-the-rhine|Confederation of the Rhine]] and then the [[s:german-confederation|German Confederation]], and shared the inheritance of Reuss-Gera when that line died out in 1802.
principality-of-reuss-schleiz.e: In 1848, after the abdication of the Prince of [[s:principality-of-reuss-ebersdorf|Reuss-Lobenstein-Ebersdorf]], the Schleiz line united all lands of the Younger Line as the Principality of [[s:principality-of-reuss-gera|Reuss Younger Line]], with Gera as capital. That state survived until 1918 and became part of the [[s:peoples-state-of-reuss|People's State of Reuss]].

pushyabhuti-dynasty.t: The dynasty of Harsha, who ruled much of northern India from Kannauj in the 7th century and was described by the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang.
pushyabhuti-dynasty.o: The Pushyabhutis ruled [[s:thanesar-state|Thanesar]], north of [[e:delhi|Delhi]], from around 500. Prabhakaravardhana made them a regional power in the late 6th century. After his death his elder son Rajyavardhana was murdered by Shashanka of the [[s:gauda-kingdom|Gauda Kingdom]], and in 606 his younger brother Harsha took the throne, also inheriting the kingdom of the [[s:maukharis|Maukharis]] at Kannauj.
pushyabhuti-dynasty.r: Harsha campaigned across northern [[e:india|India]], though Pulakeshin II of the [[s:chalukyas-of-badami|Chalukyas of Badami]] stopped him at the Narmada. He governed through [[e:vassal|vassal]] kings, toured his realm and held great religious assemblies at Kannauj and Prayag. A patron of [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]] and of Shaiva and Sun cults, he wrote three [[e:sanskrit|Sanskrit]] plays, and his court poet Banabhatta composed the Harshacharita. Harsha exchanged embassies with [[e:tang-dynasty|Tang China]].
pushyabhuti-dynasty.e: Harsha died in 647 without an heir, and his empire collapsed at once. A minister seized Kannauj, and northern [[e:india|India]] broke into rival states until the [[s:gurjara-pratihara|Gurjara-Pratihara]] rose in the 8th century.

principality-of-samarkand.t: The leading Sogdian city-state, ruled by ikhshids whose merchants ran Silk Road trade networks from Byzantium to China.
principality-of-samarkand.o: [[e:samarkand|Samarkand]], ancient Maracanda, had been the chief city of Sogdiana since Achaemenid times. After the fall of the [[s:hephthalite-empire|Hephthalite Empire]] it emerged in the 6th century as the foremost of the Sogdian principalities under rulers with the title ikhshid, recognising the overlordship of the [[s:western-turkic-khaganate|Western Turkic Khaganate]].
principality-of-samarkand.r: The ikhshids presided over a merchant aristocracy rather than an absolute monarchy. Sogdian traders dominated [[e:caravan-trade|caravan commerce]] across [[e:asia|Asia]], with communities in [[e:china|China]] and [[s:mongolia|Mongolia]]. The famous murals of Afrasiab, painted for the ruler Varkhuman around 660, show embassies from China, [[e:korea|Korea]] and the Turks. Religion was a local [[e:zoroastrianism|Zoroastrianism]] with [[e:fire-temple|fire temples]] and ossuary burial, alongside [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]], [[e:manichaeism|Manichaeism]] and [[e:christianity|Christianity]].
principality-of-samarkand.e: Qutayba ibn Muslim took [[e:samarkand|Samarkand]] for the [[s:umayyad-caliphate|Umayyad Caliphate]] in 712, and the ikhshid Ghurak ruled as a [[e:vassal|vassal]] while also courting the [[s:turgesh-khaganate|Turgesh Khaganate]]. After the Abbasid takeover around 750 the ikhshids lost power, and the city passed to the [[s:samanid-empire|Samanid Empire]] in the 9th century.

principality-of-benevento-1806-1815.t: A papal enclave in southern Italy that Napoleon turned into a sovereign principality for his foreign minister Talleyrand.
principality-of-benevento-1806-1815.o: Benevento, a small city surrounded by the [[s:kingdom-of-naples|Kingdom of Naples]], had belonged to the [[s:papal-states|Papal States]] since the 11th century. In 1806 [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]] seized it and made Charles-Maurice de Talleyrand, his foreign minister, sovereign Prince of Benevento.
principality-of-benevento-1806-1815.r: Talleyrand never visited his principality. He ruled through a governor, Louis de Beer, who introduced French-style administration and the [[e:napoleonic-code|Napoleonic Code]], abolished feudal privileges and improved roads and finances. The small state continued to depend on the [[s:kingdom-of-naples-1806-1815|Napoleonic Kingdom of Naples]] (1806–1815) around it.
principality-of-benevento-1806-1815.e: With [[e:napoleon|Napoleon's]] fall, Talleyrand gave up the title, and the [[e:congress-of-vienna|Congress of Vienna]] returned Benevento to the [[s:papal-states|Papal States]] in 1815. It remained papal until 1860.

provisional-government-of-cuba.t: The second US occupation of Cuba, from 1906 to 1909, invoked under the Platt Amendment after a revolt against President Estrada Palma.
provisional-government-of-cuba.o: Tomás Estrada Palma's disputed re-election in 1906 provoked a Liberal revolt in August. Estrada Palma asked for US help and then resigned, leaving [[e:cuba|Cuba]] without a government. Under the Platt Amendment, Theodore Roosevelt sent Secretary of War William Howard Taft, who proclaimed a provisional government in September 1906.
provisional-government-of-cuba.r: Taft was soon replaced by Charles Magoon, who governed until 1909 while preserving [[e:cuba|Cuba's]] flag and laws. Magoon used government jobs and contracts to buy peace among Cuban factions, built roads and public works, created a permanent army and drafted new electoral laws. Critics accused his administration of waste and of draining the surplus left by Estrada Palma.
provisional-government-of-cuba.e: Elections in 1908 were won by the Liberal José Miguel Gómez, who took office on 28 January 1909, restoring the [[s:republic-of-cuba-1902-1959|Republic of Cuba]] (1902-1959). The occupation confirmed US influence over Cuban politics for decades.

pella.t: Pella, a Canaanite town in the Jordan Valley known to the Egyptians as Pihilu, whose rulers wrote to the pharaoh in the Amarna age.
pella.o: Pihilu stood at Tabaqat Fahl, beside a perennial spring above the [[s:hashemite-kingdom-of-jordan|Jordan]] Valley, inhabited since the Neolithic. In the Middle [[e:bronze-age|Bronze Age]] it became a walled town, named in Egyptian execration texts, and controlled farmland and the route from the valley into the [[s:emirate-of-transjordan|Transjordan]] highlands.
pella.r: University of Sydney excavations since 1979 have uncovered fortifications, a [[e:late-bronze-age|Late Bronze Age]] governor's residence and a temple. In the 14th century BCE its ruler Mut-Bahlu wrote to the [[s:egyptian-empire-new-kingdom|Egyptian Empire New Kingdom]] in the [[e:amarna-letters|Amarna letters]], and Akkadian tablets have been found at the site.
pella.e: The Canaanite town declined with Egyptian power in the 12th century BCE. Pella revived in the [[e:hellenistic-period|Hellenistic period]] and became one of the cities of the [[s:decapolis-levant|Decapolis (Levant)]].

pale-of-calais.t: England's last foothold in mainland France, a fortified port and wool staple held for two centuries after Edward III's siege of 1346–1347.
pale-of-calais.o: After his victory at Crécy, Edward III besieged Calais for eleven months and took it in 1347; the story of the six [[e:burghers|burghers]] who offered their lives is famous. The English expelled much of the population and settled the town with English colonists, adding a surrounding district of marsh and forts, the Pale.
pale-of-calais.r: Calais was garrisoned by the largest standing force of the English crown. From 1363 it hosted the Staple, through which [[e:england|England's]] raw wool exports passed, and the Merchants of the Staple funded its defence. From 1536 it sent members to the English Parliament. It was a base for English armies in [[e:france|France]] for two centuries.
pale-of-calais.e: In January 1558, during a war in alliance with [[e:spain|Spain]], Francis, duke of Guise, captured Calais in a surprise winter attack. Mary I reportedly said that Calais would be found written on her heart. The Pale became part of the [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]].

patria-vieja.t: Chile's first period of self-government, from the junta of 1810 to the royalist victory at Rancagua in 1814.
patria-vieja.o: On 18 September 1810, a date still celebrated as Chile's national day, a cabildo in [[s:spanish-jamaica|Santiago]] created a governing junta led by the elderly Mateo de Toro Zambrano, ruling in the name of the captive Ferdinand VII. It replaced the governor of the [[s:captaincy-general-of-chile|Captaincy General of Chile]].
patria-vieja.r: The junta opened ports to free trade and convened the First National Congress in 1811. José Miguel Carrera seized power in a series of coups and introduced a provisional constitution, the first national flag and the newspaper Aurora de [[s:republic-of-chile|Chile]], edited by Camilo Henríquez. Divisions between the Carreras and Bernardo O'Higgins weakened the patriots as the [[e:viceroy-of-india|viceroy]] of [[e:peru|Peru]], José Fernando de Abascal, sent troops in 1813.
patria-vieja.e: The Treaty of Lircay in 1814 briefly halted the war. Royalist forces then defeated O'Higgins at Rancagua in October 1814, and the patriots fled to Mendoza. The [[e:reconquista|Reconquista]] lasted until Chacabuco in 1817.

pashalik-of-scutari.t: Semi-independent Ottoman province of the Bushati family in northern Albania, whose pashas waged their own wars and defied the sultan for decades.
pashalik-of-scutari.o: Mehmed Pasha Bushati, from a powerful Shkodër family, was appointed governor of the sanjak of Scutari in 1757 and made the post hereditary in practice. The Bushatis used the weakness of central Ottoman government in the later 18th century to build an autonomous domain over northern [[s:albania|Albania]] and parts of [[s:montenegro|Montenegro]] and Kosovo.
pashalik-of-scutari.r: The pashas ruled through Albanian clan chiefs and their own armies, collecting taxes and trading with [[e:venice|Venice]] and [[s:republic-of-ragusa|Ragusa]]. Mehmed built the Lead Mosque at Shkodër in 1773. Kara Mahmud Pasha Bushati expanded the domain, negotiated directly with [[e:austria|Austria]] and fought the Ottoman government, but was killed fighting the Montenegrins at Krusi in 1796. Catholic and Muslim [[e:albanians|Albanians]] coexisted.
pashalik-of-scutari.e: Mustafa Pasha Bushati, the last ruler, joined Bosnian notables against the reforms of Mahmud II. In 1831 the grand [[e:vizier|vizier]] Reşid Mehmed Pasha defeated him and forced his surrender at Rozafa castle, restoring direct Ottoman rule over Shkodër.

peoples-republic-of-kampuchea.t: The Vietnamese-backed Cambodian state established after the overthrow of the Khmer Rouge in 1979, isolated internationally for a decade.
peoples-republic-of-kampuchea.o: After [[s:socialist-republic-of-vietnam|Vietnam]] invaded [[s:democratic-kampuchea|Democratic Kampuchea]], its forces took Phnom Penh on 7 January 1979, and the People's Republic of [[s:kingdom-of-cambodia|Kampuchea]] was proclaimed, led by the Kampuchean United Front for National Salvation, a group of former [[e:khmer-empire|Khmer]] Rouge cadres who had defected to [[e:vietnam|Vietnam]], including Heng Samrin and Hun Sen.
peoples-republic-of-kampuchea.r: The PRK was a one-party state under the Kampuchean People's Revolutionary Party, with Vietnamese troops and advisers. It reopened schools, markets, pagodas and Phnom Penh itself, and gathered evidence of [[e:khmer-empire|Khmer]] Rouge crimes at Tuol Sleng. It faced famine in 1979 to 1980 and a [[e:guerrilla-warfare|guerrilla]] war from a coalition of the Khmer Rouge, royalists and republicans, which held [[e:cambodia|Cambodia's]] UN seat.
peoples-republic-of-kampuchea.e: As Soviet aid declined, [[s:socialist-republic-of-vietnam|Vietnam]] prepared to withdraw its troops, completed in 1989. That year the state was renamed the [[s:state-of-cambodia|State of Cambodia]], dropping some socialist features to prepare for a negotiated settlement.
