principality-of-murom.t: An old principality on the Oka, home of the legend of Peter and Fevronia, later absorbed into Moscow's growing realm.
principality-of-murom.o: Murom, named after the Finnic Muroma tribe, is mentioned in the Primary Chronicle under 862. Vladimir I's son Gleb, later venerated as a saint, held it in the early 11th century. It became the seat of the descendants of Yaroslav Sviatoslavich of [[e:chernigov|Chernigov]], and around 1127 split from the neighbouring [[s:grand-principality-of-ryazan|Grand Principality of Ryazan]] to form a separate principality.
principality-of-murom.r: Murom was a frontier town on the Oka, close to [[s:volga-bulgaria|Volga Bulgaria]] and the forest peoples, and lived from trade and farming. Its princes were usually overshadowed by [[s:vladimir-suzdal|Vladimir-Suzdal]]. The tale of Prince Peter and the peasant healer Fevronia, venerated as patrons of marriage, is set here, as is the epic hero Ilya Muromets.
principality-of-murom.e: The [[e:mongols|Mongols]] sacked Murom in 1239, and it declined into a minor dependent principality. In 1392 Vasily I of the [[s:grand-duchy-of-moscow|Grand Duchy of Moscow]] bought from the [[s:golden-horde|Golden Horde]] the right to rule Murom along with Nizhny Novgorod, ending its independence.

prince-bishopric-of-schwerin.t: Small Mecklenburg church state founded during the conversion of the Obotrites and absorbed by the dukes of Mecklenburg after the Reformation.
prince-bishopric-of-schwerin.o: The bishopric was set up by Henry the Lion during the conquest of the Slavic [[s:obotrite-confederation|Obotrites]], with the Cistercian monk Berno as its first [[e:bishop|bishop]] and its seat moved to [[s:county-of-schwerin|Schwerin]] around 1160. After [[e:prince-henry-the-navigator|Henry's]] fall in 1180 the bishops held their estates as imperial princes, a status the dukes of [[s:lordship-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg]] constantly disputed.
prince-bishopric-of-schwerin.r: The territory was small, consisting chiefly of lands around Bützow, where the [[e:bishop|bishops]] resided, and Warin. It grew through German settlement in former Slavic lands. In the 16th century the see was held by princes of the [[s:lordship-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg]] house, such as Ulrich of Mecklenburg, and became Lutheran, so the bishopric functioned in practice as a Mecklenburg [[e:appanage|appanage]].
prince-bishopric-of-schwerin.e: The [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] in 1648 secularised it as the Principality of [[s:county-of-schwerin|Schwerin]] and awarded it to the [[s:duchy-of-mecklenburg-schwerin|Duchy of Mecklenburg-Schwerin]] as compensation for [[s:swedish-wismar|Wismar]], which went to [[e:sweden|Sweden]]. It is now part of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

protectorate-of-northern-nigeria.t: The British protectorate built on the conquest of the Sokoto Caliphate, where Frederick Lugard developed the system of indirect rule through the emirs.
protectorate-of-northern-nigeria.o: On 1 January 1900 [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] took over the northern lands of the [[s:royal-niger-company-territories|Royal Niger Company]] and proclaimed the [[e:northern-nigeria-protectorate|Protectorate of Northern Nigeria]], with [[e:frederick-lugard|Frederick Lugard]] as high commissioner. Its capital was first Lokoja and from 1902 Zungeru. Between 1900 and 1903 British-led troops conquered the [[e:emirate|emirates]], taking [[e:kano|Kano]] and [[e:sokoto-caliphate|Sokoto]] in 1903.
protectorate-of-northern-nigeria.r: With few officials and little money, [[e:frederick-lugard|Lugard]] governed through the [[e:emir|emirs]] who accepted British authority, keeping their courts, taxes and officials under the supervision of British residents. This [[e:indirect-rule|indirect rule]], set out in his Political Memoranda, became a model for British [[e:africa|Africa]]. Christian missions were restricted in Muslim areas, and Western schooling spread slowly. A revolt at Satiru in 1906 was crushed.
protectorate-of-northern-nigeria.e: [[e:frederick-lugard|Lugard]] returned as governor of both [[e:protectorate|protectorates]] in 1912 and merged them on 1 January 1914 into [[s:colonial-nigeria|Colonial Nigeria]]. The north remained a separate administrative region, and the legacy of separate development shaped Nigerian politics.

principality-of-nassau-siegen.t: Iron-mining Nassau principality in the Siegerland, divided for a century between Catholic and Protestant branches of the house.
principality-of-nassau-siegen.o: After the death of Count John VI of [[s:county-of-nassau-dillenburg|Nassau-Dillenburg]] in 1606, his lands were divided and his son John VII received Siegen. Siegen was the birthplace of Peter Paul Rubens in 1577, when his parents lived there in exile.
principality-of-nassau-siegen.r: The Siegerland's iron ore and forges made it relatively prosperous. The house split confessionally: John VIII converted to [[e:catholicism|Catholicism]] and his line held part of the land while the Reformed line held the rest, so Siegen had two castles, the Upper and Lower. Johan Maurits of Nassau-Siegen, governor of [[s:dutch-brazil|Dutch Brazil]], belonged to the Reformed branch. Counts became princes in 1652 and 1664.
principality-of-nassau-siegen.e: The Reformed line died out in 1734 and the Catholic line in 1743, and the territory passed to Prince William IV of Orange-Nassau as part of [[s:principality-of-nassau-diez|Nassau-Diez]]. It later went to the [[s:grand-duchy-of-berg|Grand Duchy of Berg]] and in 1815 to the [[s:kingdom-of-prussia|Kingdom of Prussia]].

principality-of-thurn-and-taxis.t: Swabian territory acquired by the family that ran the Imperial Post, giving them a vote among the princes of the Empire.
principality-of-thurn-and-taxis.o: The Taxis family of [[e:kingdom-of-the-lombards|Lombard]] origin had run the imperial postal service since around 1500 and became hereditary postmasters general, raised to princes in 1695. To gain a seat in the Council of Princes they needed land, so in 1785 they bought the county of Friedberg-Scheer on the [[e:danube|Danube]], raised in 1786 to a princely county.
principality-of-thurn-and-taxis.r: The Swabian territory was a small Catholic rural district; the family's wealth and power came from the Imperial Post, which carried letters across the Empire and the [[s:kingdom-of-the-netherlands|Netherlands]]. The princes lived in [[s:free-imperial-city-of-regensburg|Regensburg]], where they represented the emperor as principal commissioner at the Perpetual [[e:imperial-diet|Imperial Diet]], and from 1812 resided in the former St Emmeram Abbey.
principality-of-thurn-and-taxis.e: In 1806 the territory was mediatised under the [[s:kingdom-of-wurttemberg|Kingdom of Württemberg]]. The family kept its postal business in many German states until selling it to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] in 1867 and remains among the largest landowners in [[e:germany|Germany]].

principality-of-gjirokaster.t: Albanian lordship of the Zenebishi family in southern Albania, one of the last Christian powers in Epirus before the Ottoman conquest.
principality-of-gjirokaster.o: Gjon Zenebishi, an Albanian chieftain whose clan had moved into Epirus during the 14th-century Albanian migrations, took the fortress of Gjirokastër (Argyrokastron) around 1386. He extended his rule over the Drino valley and parts of Chameria, and the Byzantine court recognised him with the title of sebastokrator.
principality-of-gjirokaster.r: The lordship was a clan-based military domain built around the hilltop citadel of Gjirokastër and its villages. Gjon fought the Italian rulers of the [[s:despotate-of-epirus|Despotate of Epirus]] at Ioannina, capturing Esau de' Buondelmonti in 1399, and courted [[e:venice|Venice]], which controlled nearby [[s:corcyra|Corfu]]. Society rested on Albanian pastoral clans and an [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] Greek and Albanian peasantry.
principality-of-gjirokaster.e: Repeated Ottoman campaigns under [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Mehmed I wore the lordship down, and Gjirokastër fell in 1418, the year Gjon died. His son Depa fled to Venetian territory and later led a failed rising in 1434. The town became the centre of an Ottoman sanjak.

principality-of-tmutarakan.t: A remote outpost of Kievan Rus' on the Taman peninsula, controlling the strait between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.
principality-of-tmutarakan.o: Tmutarakan grew out of the [[e:khazar-khaganate|Khazar]] town of Tamatarkha, on the site of ancient Hermonassa. After [[e:sviatoslav-i-of-kiev|Sviatoslav I]] broke Khazar power in the 960s, the Rus' took control, and around 988 Vladimir I gave the town to his son Mstislav as his own principality.
principality-of-tmutarakan.r: Its population of [[e:greeks|Greeks]], [[e:khazar-khaganate|Khazars]], [[s:alans|Alans]], Kasogs and [[e:slavs|Slavs]] lived by trade between the steppe, the [[e:caucasus|Caucasus]] and [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]]. Mstislav defeated the Kasog prince Rededya in single combat in 1022, and in 1024 beat his brother Yaroslav at Listven, dividing Rus' along the [[e:dnieper|Dnieper]]. The Tmutarakan Stone records Prince Gleb measuring the frozen strait in 1068.
principality-of-tmutarakan.e: Tmutarakan served as a refuge for exiled princes such as Oleg Sviatoslavich, who left it in 1094 to fight for [[e:chernigov|Chernigov]]. Cut off by the Cumans, it disappears from Rus' history afterwards, probably passing to Byzantine control. Its location was rediscovered in the 18th century.

prince-provostry-of-ellwangen.t: A Benedictine abbey on the Jagst that was converted in 1460 into a provostry of noble canons whose princes ruled a sizeable Swabian territory.
prince-provostry-of-ellwangen.o: Ellwangen abbey was founded around 764 by Hariolf, later [[e:bishop|bishop]] of Langres, and received Carolingian protection. It built up lands along the Jagst, and its abbots held princely rank from the 13th century. In 1460 [[e:papacy|Pope]] Pius II converted the abbey into a secular collegiate foundation headed by a prince-provost.
prince-provostry-of-ellwangen.r: The prince-provost, often a [[e:bishop|bishop]] elsewhere as well, governed a considerable territory around Ellwangen with his own courts and officials and sat among the ecclesiastical princes of the [[e:imperial-diet|Imperial Diet]]. The castle above the town was his residence. Witch trials between 1611 and 1618 were among the most severe in [[e:germany|Germany]], claiming several hundred victims.
prince-provostry-of-ellwangen.e: In 1802 and 1803 the provostry was secularised and annexed by Württemberg, which for some years made Ellwangen the seat of the government of its new Catholic lands. The castle and the Romanesque collegiate basilica survive.

puruha.t: A highland people of central Ecuador around Chimborazo who were absorbed by the Incas and later by the Spanish, but whose identity survives today.
puruha.o: The Puruhá occupied the highland basin around the volcano Chimborazo, in the modern provinces of Chimborazo and Bolívar, from around 800. Archaeology shows a sequence of local pottery traditions, with the Puruhá phase often linked to tombs found near Riobamba.
puruha.r: Little is known of their political organisation beyond a series of chiefdoms under local lords. They farmed [[e:maize|maize]], [[e:potato|potatoes]] and quinoa on the volcanic slopes and herded llamas. Their tombs contained [[e:copper|copper]] ornaments and distinctive pottery, including vessels with modelled human faces. Later chroniclers claimed that Puruhá lords allied by marriage with Quito, but these accounts are doubtful.
puruha.e: The Puruhá were brought under [[e:inca-empire|Inca]] rule around 1470 during the campaigns of Túpac Inca Yupanqui. After the Spanish conquest, Riobamba was founded in their territory in 1534. Their descendants, Kichwa-speaking communities of Chimborazo, keep a strong indigenous identity.

prince-abbey-of-corvey.t: The leading Carolingian abbey of Saxony, a base for missions to the north and home of the chronicler Widukind, whose westwork is a World Heritage Site.
prince-abbey-of-corvey.o: Corvey was founded in 822 on the Weser near Höxter by monks from Corbie in Picardy, led by Adalard and Wala, cousins of [[e:charlemagne|Charlemagne]], with the support of [[e:louis-the-pious|Louis the Pious]]. It was intended to anchor [[e:christianity|Christianity]] in newly conquered Saxony, and in 836 it received the relics of Saint Vitus from Saint-Denis.
prince-abbey-of-corvey.r: Corvey sent Ansgar on his mission to [[e:denmark|Denmark]] and [[e:sweden|Sweden]], and its school produced Widukind of Corvey, whose Deeds of the [[s:saxons|Saxons]] is a chief source for the Ottonian kings. The abbots were princes of the Empire ruling a small territory around Höxter. Its Carolingian westwork, completed in 885, is one of the few surviving from the period.
prince-abbey-of-corvey.e: Corvey shrank after the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years' War]]. In 1792 it was raised to a prince-bishopric, but in 1803 it was secularised and given to the Prince of Orange-Nassau-Fulda, then passed to [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Westphalia]] and [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]]. The poet Hoffmann von Fallersleben, author of the German national anthem, later worked in its library.

philistine-pentapolis.t: The Philistine Pentapolis, five city-states of the southern Levant coast founded by Aegean newcomers, whose name lives on in Palestine.
philistine-pentapolis.o: Around 1175 BCE [[e:ramesses-iii|Ramesses III]] of the [[s:egyptian-empire-new-kingdom|Egyptian Empire New Kingdom]] repelled the [[e:sea-peoples|Sea Peoples]], including the Peleset. Groups of these newcomers settled in [[s:gaza|Gaza]], [[s:ashkelon|Ashkelon]], [[s:ashdod|Ashdod]], [[s:ekron|Ekron]] and [[s:gath|Gath]], bringing Aegean-style pottery, cooking habits and pork-eating to the southern coast of [[e:canaan|Canaan]].
philistine-pentapolis.r: Each city was ruled by its own lord, called seren in the Bible, and they acted together in war. The Philistines adopted the local Semitic language and gods such as Dagon, and became Israel's main rivals in the stories of Samson, Saul and David.
philistine-pentapolis.e: From the 8th century BCE the cities were [[e:vassal|vassals]] of the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]]. [[e:nebuchadnezzar-ii|Nebuchadnezzar II]] of the [[s:chaldean-empire|Chaldean Empire]] destroyed [[s:ashkelon|Ashkelon]] and [[s:ekron|Ekron]] in 604 BCE and deported their people, ending a separate Philistine identity. [[e:greeks|Greeks]] and [[e:roman-empire|Romans]] called the region Palaestina after them.

principality-of-anhalt-zerbst.t: Small Anhalt principality on the Elbe best remembered as the birthplace dynasty of Catherine the Great of Russia.
principality-of-anhalt-zerbst.o: Rudolf, a son of Joachim Ernst, received Zerbst in the 1603 partition of [[s:principality-of-anhalt|Anhalt]]. The town, north of the Elbe, had been a prosperous brewing centre known for its beer, and the line included the lordship of Jever in Frisia, inherited in 1667.
principality-of-anhalt-zerbst.r: The principality was Lutheran in its later period and modestly governed from a baroque palace in Zerbst. Its most famous member was Sophie Auguste Friederike, daughter of Prince Christian August, who married the future Peter III and became Empress [[e:catherine-the-great|Catherine II]] of [[e:russia|Russia]]. Her brother Friedrich August, the last prince, lived mostly abroad and hired out soldiers to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] during the American Revolutionary War.
principality-of-anhalt-zerbst.e: Friedrich August died without heirs in 1793. The principality was divided among the other [[s:principality-of-anhalt|Anhalt]] lines, Dessau, Bernburg and Köthen, while Jever passed to [[e:catherine-the-great|Catherine the Great]] and so to [[e:russia|Russia]].

principality-of-arianiti.t: Lands of the Albanian lord Gjergj Arianiti, who led an early revolt against the Ottomans and became Skanderbeg's ally and father-in-law.
principality-of-arianiti.o: The Arianiti were an old noble family of central [[s:albania|Albania]], holding lands along the Shkumbin valley and around Elbasan. In 1432 Gjergj Arianiti, who had been a hostage at the Ottoman court, led a rising against the new Ottoman land registers and defeated several Ottoman armies in the mountains between 1432 and 1436.
principality-of-arianiti.r: Little is known of how the lands were governed: they were a mountain lordship of fortified villages and clan levies rather than a state with fixed institutions, and no clear capital is recorded. Gjergj built ties through marriage, wedding his daughter Donika to Skanderbeg in 1451, and negotiated with [[e:venice|Venice]], Naples and the [[e:papacy|papacy]].
principality-of-arianiti.e: Gjergj Arianiti joined the [[s:league-of-lezhe|League of Lezhë]] in 1444, though he later quarrelled with Skanderbeg. He died in 1462, and the family's lands fell to the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] in the following years. His descendants, the Arianiti Comneni, settled in [[e:italy|Italy]].

patiala-state.t: The largest of the Sikh Phulkian states of the Punjab, whose maharajas were among the most prominent princes of British India.
patiala-state.o: Ala Singh, a Sidhu Jat chief descended from Phul, built up his authority in the [[e:malwa|Malwa]] region of [[e:punjab|Punjab]] from the 1720s and founded the fort of Patiala in 1763. He survived by balancing between the [[e:sikhism|Sikh]] misls and [[e:ahmad-shah-abdali|Ahmad Shah Durrani]], from whom his grandson Amar Singh received the title Raja-i-Rajgan.
patiala-state.r: In 1809 Patiala and the other Cis-[[e:sutlej-river|Sutlej]] states placed themselves under British protection against [[e:ranjit-singh|Ranjit Singh]]. The rulers supported the British in the Anglo-[[e:sikhism|Sikh]] wars and in 1857, gaining land and honours. Bhupinder Singh (1900–38) was famed for his jewels, cricket patronage and role as Chancellor of the Chamber of Princes. The state had a Sikh ruling house, mixed Sikh, [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] and Muslim subjects, and a large army.
patiala-state.e: Yadavindra Singh acceded to [[e:india|India]] in 1947. In 1948 Patiala became the core of the [[s:patiala-and-east-punjab-states-union|Patiala and East Punjab States Union]], with him as Rajpramukh, which was merged into [[e:punjab|Punjab]] in 1956.

prince-bishopric-of-lausanne.t: A Swiss prince-bishopric on Lake Geneva whose bishops ruled Lausanne and its surroundings until Bern conquered Vaud and introduced the Reformation.
prince-bishopric-of-lausanne.o: The [[e:bishop|bishops]] of the Avenches area moved their seat to Lausanne around 600. In 1011 King Rudolf III of [[s:duchy-of-burgundy|Burgundy]] granted Bishop Henry the county of Vaud, establishing the bishop as a temporal lord. After 1032 the bishops became princes of the [[s:holy-roman-empire|Holy Roman Empire]].
prince-bishopric-of-lausanne.r: The prince-[[e:bishop|bishops]] ruled Lausanne and estates such as Lavaux, famous for vineyards, while the counts of [[s:county-of-savoy|Savoy]] dominated the rest of Vaud. The Gothic cathedral of Lausanne was consecrated in 1275 in the presence of [[e:papacy|Pope]] Gregory X and King Rudolf I. The townspeople gradually won rights of self-government.
prince-bishopric-of-lausanne.e: In 1536 Bern conquered Vaud from [[s:county-of-savoy|Savoy]], took Lausanne and expelled the [[e:bishop|bishop]], introducing the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] after the Lausanne Disputation in which Calvin and Farel spoke. Vaud remained Bernese until 1798 and became a Swiss canton in 1803.

prince-abbey-of-kempten.t: Benedictine abbey in the Allgäu whose prince-abbots ruled a sizeable territory and rebuilt Kempten in baroque splendour after the Thirty Years War.
prince-abbey-of-kempten.o: The Benedictine abbey of Kempten was founded in the mid 8th century near the old Roman town of Cambodunum and enjoyed the patronage of [[e:charlemagne|Charlemagne's]] wife Hildegard. It gathered estates throughout the Allgäu, and from 1213 its abbots were recognised as princes of the Empire, ruling a secular territory.
prince-abbey-of-kempten.r: The prince-abbots, drawn from the nobility, governed farmers and small towns in the Allgäu through officials and a strong territorial administration. They clashed constantly with the neighbouring [[s:free-imperial-city-of-kempten|Free Imperial City of Kempten]], which bought its freedom from the abbey in 1525, the year their own peasants rose in the Peasants' War. After the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years War]] Abbot Roman Giel von Gielsberg built the Residenz and the Basilica of St. Lorenz.
prince-abbey-of-kempten.e: The abbey was secularised in 1803 and annexed by Bavaria, which merged the abbey town with the Protestant imperial city into a single Kempten. The baroque Residenz and basilica survive.

principality-of-jersika.t: An Orthodox principality of the Latgalians on the Daugava, ruled by King Visvaldis until the crusaders of Riga absorbed it.
principality-of-jersika.o: Jersika was a hill fort on the Daugava in eastern [[s:republic-of-latvia|Latvia]] and the centre of a Latgalian principality linked to the [[s:principality-of-polotsk|Principality of Polotsk]]. By about 1200 it was ruled by a prince the German sources call Vissewalde, known in Latvian as Visvaldis, who was probably of mixed Latgalian and Rus' descent.
principality-of-jersika.r: Jersika controlled trade on the Daugava and ruled over Latgalians and [[s:selonians|Selonians]], some of whom were [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] Christians with churches. Henry of [[s:livonian-confederation|Livonia]] calls Visvaldis a king. He allied with the Lithuanians against the German crusaders who had founded Riga.
principality-of-jersika.e: In 1209 [[e:bishop|Bishop]] Albert of Riga stormed and burned Jersika, captured Visvaldis's wife and forced him to become a [[e:vassal|vassal]], receiving part of his land back as a fief. The rest of his territory passed gradually to Riga and the [[s:livonian-order|Livonian Order]], and the principality had disappeared by about 1239.

principality-of-ratzeburg.t: Secularised bishopric east of Lübeck that became a detached province of Mecklenburg-Strelitz for more than two centuries.
principality-of-ratzeburg.o: The Bishopric of Ratzeburg, founded in the 12th century under Henry the Lion, had become Lutheran in the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]]. At the [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] in 1648 it was secularised and given to the dukes of [[s:lordship-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg]] as the [[s:prince-bishopric-of-ratzeburg|Principality of Ratzeburg]], though the town of Ratzeburg itself belonged to Saxe-Lauenburg.
principality-of-ratzeburg.r: The principality was a rural area of villages and farms governed from Schönberg. It had no estates of its own, so its peasants were largely free of the noble domination typical of [[s:lordship-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg]]. Under the Treaty of [[s:free-and-hanseatic-city-of-hamburg|Hamburg]] in 1701 it was assigned to the new [[s:duchy-of-mecklenburg-strelitz|Duchy of Mecklenburg-Strelitz]], from which it was separated by [[s:duchy-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg-Schwerin]].
principality-of-ratzeburg.e: Ratzeburg remained part of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, raised to a grand duchy in 1815, until the monarchy ended in 1918, then belonged to the [[s:free-state-of-mecklenburg-strelitz|Free State of Mecklenburg-Strelitz]]. Today the area forms part of the district of Nordwestmecklenburg.

principality-of-serbia-early-medieval.t: The first Serbian state, ruled by the Vlastimirović dynasty in the inland Balkans and converted to Christianity in the 870s.
principality-of-serbia-early-medieval.o: [[e:serbs|Serbs]] settled in the western [[e:balkans|Balkans]] in the 7th century. Constantine VII names Višeslav as an early prince, usually dated to around 780, but the state becomes clear under Vlastimir, who united Serbian tribes in the 830s and repelled an invasion by the Bulgarian khan Presian around 839–842.
principality-of-serbia-early-medieval.r: The ruling prince (knez) shared power with relatives who held districts, and dynastic quarrels were frequent. The principality lay between [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] and the [[s:first-bulgarian-empire|First Bulgarian Empire]], often acting as a client of one against the other. Under Mutimir the [[e:serbs|Serbs]] adopted [[e:christianity|Christianity]] in the 870s, through Byzantine missions.
principality-of-serbia-early-medieval.e: Simeon I of [[s:bulgaria|Bulgaria]] conquered [[s:serbia|Serbia]] in 924. Prince Časlav restored it with Byzantine help from the late 920s, but after his death in the mid-10th century the state fragmented and [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] took [[e:ras|Ras]] around 970. Later Serbian states emerged in [[s:duklja|Duklja]] and [[s:grand-principality-of-serbia|Raška]].

principality-of-anhalt-bernburg.t: Anhalt principality ruled from a castle above the Saale at Bernburg, whose line outlasted every other branch of the 1603 partition except Dessau.
principality-of-anhalt-bernburg.o: When the [[s:principality-of-anhalt|Principality of Anhalt]] was divided in 1603 among the heirs of Joachim Ernst, Christian I received Bernburg. Christian was a leading Calvinist politician who directed the policy of the Protestant Union and the Elector Palatine before the defeat at the White Mountain in 1620.
principality-of-anhalt-bernburg.r: The state was small and agrarian, with [[e:silver|silver]] and [[e:copper|copper]] mining in its Harz exclave around Ballenstedt and Harzgerode. The ruling line was Calvinist. Branch lines split off, including Anhalt-Bernburg-Schaumburg-Hoym. Bernburg was raised to a duchy in 1806, with the court later moving partly to Ballenstedt.
principality-of-anhalt-bernburg.e: The last duke, Alexander Karl, died childless in 1863, and his lands passed to [[s:principality-of-anhalt-dessau|Anhalt-Dessau]], which thus united all the [[s:principality-of-anhalt|Anhalt]] territories into the [[s:duchy-of-anhalt|Duchy of Anhalt]]. Bernburg remained a district town within Anhalt.

pala-empire.t: The last great Buddhist empire of India, ruling Bengal and Bihar for four centuries and sponsoring the monastic universities of Nalanda and Vikramashila.
pala-empire.o: After a century of disorder in [[e:bengal|Bengal]], which later texts call matsyanyaya, the law of the fish, local chiefs chose Gopala as king around 750. His son Dharmapala expanded the kingdom across Bihar and installed his own candidate, Chakrayudha of the [[s:ayudha-dynasty|Ayudha dynasty]], on the throne of Kannauj.
pala-empire.r: The Palas fought the [[s:gurjara-pratihara|Gurjara-Pratihara]] and the [[s:rashtrakuta-dynasty|Rashtrakuta dynasty]] for control of Kannauj. They were [[e:mahayana-buddhism|Mahayana]] and Vajrayana Buddhists who also endowed [[e:brahmins|Brahmins]]. Dharmapala founded Vikramashila and the Somapura monastery at Paharpur, and Devapala supported Nalanda, which attracted scholars from [[e:southeast-asia|Southeast Asia]]. Pala bronze and stone sculpture influenced the art of [[s:tibet-1912-1951|Tibet]], [[s:kingdom-of-nepal|Nepal]] and [[e:java|Java]], and the monk Atisha, trained in Pala monasteries, helped revive [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]] in [[e:tibet|Tibet]].
pala-empire.e: After a decline in the 10th century, Mahipala I revived the empire, and Ramapala suppressed the Kaivarta revolt in north [[e:bengal|Bengal]]. The Palas lost Bengal to the [[s:sena-dynasty|Sena dynasty]] in the 12th century, and the last king, Madanapala, died around 1161.

principality-of-galich-mersky.t: An appanage around Galich in the north-east of Rus', whose princes later fought Moscow in its great dynastic civil war.
principality-of-galich-mersky.o: Galich, on Lake Galich in the old lands of the Finnic Merya, was a town of the [[s:vladimir-suzdal|Vladimir-Suzdal]] region known for its salt springs. In 1246 it became the [[e:appanage|appanage]] of Konstantin, son of Grand Prince Yaroslav Vsevolodovich, and his descendants held it for over a century.
principality-of-galich-mersky.r: The principality was a remote northern land of forests and salt workings, with little recorded about its government. Its princes were minor figures in the struggles of the grand princes of Vladimir and the [[s:golden-horde|Golden Horde]], and Galich often served as a refuge from the turmoil further south.
principality-of-galich-mersky.e: In 1363 Dmitry Donskoy of the [[s:grand-duchy-of-moscow|Grand Duchy of Moscow]] expelled its last independent prince and annexed Galich. It was later granted to Donskoy's son Yuri, whose line fought Vasily II for the throne of [[e:moscow|Moscow]] in the civil war of the 1420s to 1450s.

pashalik-of-yanina.t: Virtually independent domain of Ali Pasha of Tepelena, who ruled Epirus and much of mainland Greece from Ioannina and dealt with European powers as an equal.
pashalik-of-yanina.o: Ali Pasha, an Albanian notable from Tepelena, rose through brigandage and Ottoman service, becoming governor of Trikala and then, in the late 1780s, pasha of Ioannina. By force, alliances and intrigue he extended his authority over Epirus, southern [[s:albania|Albania]], Thessaly and parts of the Peloponnese, controlling the main routes of the western [[e:balkans|Balkans]].
pashalik-of-yanina.r: Ali ruled from his fortress palace in Ioannina through a personal network of officials and Albanian troops, with Greek secretaries and merchants prominent at court. Ioannina became a centre of Greek learning and trade. He negotiated with [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]] and [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]], entertained Lord Byron in 1809, crushed the Souliotes and acquired Parga in 1819.
pashalik-of-yanina.e: [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Mahmud II declared Ali a rebel in 1820 and besieged Ioannina; Ali was killed in January 1822. The long campaign tied down Ottoman forces just as the [[e:greek-war-of-independence|Greek War of Independence]] broke out in 1821, helping the revolt survive.

perusia.t: Etruscan hill city above the upper Tiber, known for its gates, its family tombs and a famous siege by Octavian in 41–40 BCE.
perusia.o: Perusia, Etruscan Persna, modern [[s:commune-of-perugia|Perugia]], grew on a group of hills west of the [[e:tiber-river|Tiber]], near the border with the [[s:umbrians|Umbrians]]. It developed into a city later than the coastal centres, gaining importance from the 6th century BCE and especially in the 4th and 3rd centuries BCE, when its great walls and gates were built.
perusia.r: Perusia controlled river routes and farmland on the upper [[e:tiber-river|Tiber]] and mixed with Umbrian neighbours. Its aristocratic families buried their dead in chamber tombs with carved urns, the finest being the Hypogeum of the Volumni. The Cippus of [[s:commune-of-perugia|Perugia]], a stone boundary text of about 130 words, is one of the longest Etruscan inscriptions, and the Arco Etrusco gate still stands.
perusia.e: Perusia joined other Etruscan cities against [[e:rome|Rome]], made truces in 310 and 294 BCE and became a Roman ally after the wars of the early 3rd century. In the Perusine War Octavian besieged Lucius Antonius there in 41–40 BCE; the city was taken and burned. Augustus rebuilt it as Augusta Perusia.

peru-bolivian-confederation.t: Andrés de Santa Cruz's union of Peru and Bolivia, which threatened the balance of power in South America and was destroyed by Chile in 1839.
peru-bolivian-confederation.o: In 1835 [[e:peru|Peru's]] president Luis José de Orbegoso asked the Bolivian president Andrés de Santa Cruz for help against rebels. Santa Cruz invaded, defeated Agustín Gamarra and Felipe [[s:spanish-jamaica|Santiago]] Salaverry in 1835 and 1836, and divided Peru into the [[s:north-peruvian-republic|North Peruvian Republic]] and [[s:south-peruvian-republic|South Peruvian Republic]], which joined the [[s:republic-of-bolivia|Republic of Bolivia]] in a confederation.
peru-bolivian-confederation.r: The Pact of Tacna of 1837 made Santa Cruz Supreme Protector, with broad powers over foreign affairs and the army. He introduced legal codes modelled on [[e:napoleon|Napoleon's]] and promoted trade. [[s:republic-of-chile|Chile]], under the influence of Diego Portales, saw the confederation as a threat, and Chile and the [[s:argentine-confederation|Argentine Confederation]] of Rosas declared war in 1837. Peruvian exiles and many in Lima resented Bolivian dominance.
peru-bolivian-confederation.e: A Chilean army under Manuel Bulnes, joined by Peruvian exiles, defeated Santa Cruz at Yungay on 20 January 1839. The confederation was dissolved, and Santa Cruz went into exile. [[e:peru|Peru]] and [[s:republic-of-bolivia|Bolivia]] were never united again, and [[s:republic-of-chile|Chile]] emerged as the leading power on the Pacific coast.

principality-of-galicia.t: A rich principality on the upper Dniester, built around the salt trade and the town of Halych, whose boyars were famously powerful.
principality-of-galicia.o: In the 1080s three Rurikid brothers, Rurik, Volodar and Vasylko Rostislavich, took control of the towns of Peremyshl, Zvenyhorod and Terebovl in the far south-west of Rus'. Their heir Volodymyrko united these lands and in 1141 made Halych on the Dniester his capital, creating the Principality of [[s:kingdom-of-galicia-and-lodomeria|Galicia]].
principality-of-galicia.r: [[s:kingdom-of-galicia-and-lodomeria|Galicia]] prospered from salt mines, which supplied much of Rus', and from trade along the Dniester to the [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]] and with [[e:hungary|Hungary]] and [[e:poland|Poland]]. Its landholding boyars were unusually strong and repeatedly deposed or defied their princes. Yaroslav Osmomysl, who ruled from 1153 to 1187, was praised in the Lay of Igor's Campaign as a mighty ruler.
principality-of-galicia.e: The dynasty of Volodymyrko died out with Vladimir Yaroslavich in 1199. Roman Mstislavich of the [[s:principality-of-volhynia|Principality of Volhynia]] then took Halych and joined the two lands into the [[s:kingdom-of-galicia-volhynia|Kingdom of Galicia-Volhynia]], though [[e:hungary|Hungary]] and [[e:poland|Poland]] long contested [[s:kingdom-of-galicia-and-lodomeria|Galicia]].

principality-of-luneburg.t: Guelph principality of the Lüneburg Heath ruled from Celle, which embraced the Reformation early and merged into the Electorate of Hanover in 1705.
principality-of-luneburg.o: In 1269 the brothers Albert and John divided the [[s:duchy-of-brunswick-luneburg|Duchy of Brunswick-Lüneburg]], which their father Otto the Child had received in 1235. John received the northern lands around Lüneburg and Celle, founding the Principality of Lüneburg, while Albert took the [[s:principality-of-wolfenbuttel|Principality of Wolfenbüttel]].
principality-of-luneburg.r: The salt city of Lüneburg was wealthy and largely independent, and after the War of the Lüneburg Succession in 1371 to 1388 the dukes moved their residence to Celle. Duke Ernest the Confessor introduced the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] from 1527. The principality was rural, with heathland, sheep and forests. George William, the last duke of Celle, saw his daughter Sophia Dorothea marry the future George I of [[s:kingdom-of-great-britain|Great Britain]].
principality-of-luneburg.e: When George William died in 1705, Lüneburg passed to his nephew and son-in-law George Louis of [[s:principality-of-calenberg|Calenberg]] and was merged into the [[s:electorate-of-hanover|Electorate of Hanover]]. It later formed part of the [[s:kingdom-of-hanover|Kingdom of Hanover]] and is now in Lower Saxony.

polyrrhenia.t: Fortified hill city of western Crete, the leading power of the island's far west in the Hellenistic period.
polyrrhenia.o: Polyrrhenia stood on a steep hill south of the Gulf of Kissamos in western [[e:crete|Crete]]. Strabo says it was founded by Achaeans and Laconians, who united the scattered villages of the area. Its name, meaning rich in flocks, reflects its pastoral economy.
polyrrhenia.r: Polyrrhenia controlled the west of [[e:crete|Crete]], with harbours at Phalasarna and Kisamos at times under its influence. It had [[e:kosmoi|kosmoi]] magistrates like other Cretan cities. In the Lyttian War of 220 BCE it broke with [[s:knossos|Knossos]] and allied with Philip V of the [[s:antigonid-kingdom-of-macedonia|Antigonid Kingdom of Macedonia]]. Its walls and cisterns survive.
polyrrhenia.e: Polyrrhenia came under Roman rule in the conquest of [[e:crete|Crete]] in 69 to 67 BCE and continued as a town, later a Byzantine bishopric.

peoples-republic-of-china.t: The Communist state proclaimed by Mao Zedong in 1949, which has governed mainland China ever since and grown into the world's second-largest economy.
peoples-republic-of-china.o: The Chinese Communist Party, which had governed rural base areas since the [[s:chinese-soviet-republic|Chinese Soviet Republic]] of the 1930s, won the civil war against the [[s:nationalist-government|Nationalist government]]. On 1 October 1949 Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic in [[e:beijing|Beijing]], while the [[s:republic-of-china|Republic of China]] retreated to [[e:taiwan|Taiwan]].
peoples-republic-of-china.r: The party-state carried out land reform, fought in the Korean War and adopted Soviet-style planning. The Great Leap Forward of 1958 to 1962 caused a famine that killed tens of millions, and the Cultural Revolution from 1966 to 1976 brought political persecution and chaos. From 1978 Deng Xiaoping's reforms opened the economy to markets and foreign investment, while the party kept its monopoly of power, crushing the Tiananmen protests in 1989.
peoples-republic-of-china.e: The People's Republic regained [[e:hong-kong|Hong Kong]] in 1997 and [[e:macau|Macau]] in 1999, joined the World Trade Organization in 2001 and became a leading manufacturing and trading power. Under Xi Jinping, leader since 2012, central party control has been reinforced.
peoples-republic-of-china.re: State atheism, Chinese folk religion, Buddhism, Taoism

parisii.t: Gallic people of the middle Seine whose town Lutetia became Paris.
parisii.o: The [[s:parisii-britain|Parisii]] settled on the Seine in the 3rd century BCE and controlled river traffic across the [[e:paris|Paris]] basin. Caesar mentions that he held a council of Gaul at Lutetia in 53 BCE. The exact site of their oppidum is debated; excavations at Nanterre have revealed a large Gallic settlement.
parisii.r: They struck fine gold coins, among the most elegant in Gaul. Their wealth came from trade on the Seine, and Roman inscriptions later record a powerful [[e:guild|guild]] of boatmen.
parisii.e: In 52 BCE they joined the revolt; the Aulercan leader Camulogenus burned Lutetia and was defeated by Caesar's legate Labienus. Under [[e:rome|Rome]] Lutetia was rebuilt on the Montagne Sainte-Geneviève, and on the Île de la Cité the boatmen dedicated the Pillar of the Boatmen to Jupiter under Tiberius. In late antiquity the town took the name of the people, [[e:paris|Paris]].

principality-of-lampang.t: A northern Thai principality whose Chet Ton dynasty led the expulsion of the Burmese from Lan Na and later ruled Chiang Mai.
principality-of-lampang.o: In 1732 Nan Thip Chang, a hunter turned local leader, drove out a Burmese-backed governor from Lampang and was recognised as ruler. His descendants, known as the Chet Ton or Chao Chet Ton dynasty, governed Lampang under Burmese overlordship.
principality-of-lampang.r: Lampang was a [[e:rice|rice]]-growing principality on the Wang river with the revered Wat Phra That Lampang Luang. In the 1770s its ruler Kawila allied with the [[s:thonburi-kingdom|Thonburi Kingdom]] and helped drive the Burmese out of [[s:lan-na|Lan Na]]. Thereafter Lampang was a Siamese [[e:vassal|vassal]], and Kawila's family also governed [[s:kingdom-of-chiang-mai|Chiang Mai]] and Lamphun.
principality-of-lampang.e: Lampang kept its own princes during the 19th century, while British [[e:timber|timber]] firms logged teak in its forests. The provincial reforms of the [[s:rattanakosin-kingdom|Rattanakosin Kingdom]] brought it under direct administration from 1899, and Lampang is now a province of [[s:thailand|Thailand]].

pahang-sultanate.t: Largest state of the Malay Peninsula, held by the Bendahara family of Johor before becoming a sultanate in 1882.
pahang-sultanate.o: Pahang had been a dependency of [[s:johor-sultanate|Johor]] since the 17th century. Around 1770 it was granted as a hereditary fief to the [[e:johor|Johor]] Bendahara, Tun Abdul Majid, whose descendants ruled from Pekan as Raja Bendahara. The breakup of the Johor-Riau realm in the early 19th century left them effectively independent.
pahang-sultanate.r: Pahang was thinly populated, with [[e:rice|rice]] villages, gold workings and [[e:tin|tin]] along its long rivers and great forests inland. A civil war from 1857 to 1863 brought Wan Ahmad to power, and in 1882 he proclaimed himself [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Ahmad Muadzam Shah. Chiefs ruled their districts with wide autonomy.
pahang-sultanate.e: The British forced a resident on Pahang in 1888, provoking the Pahang uprising of 1891 to 1895 led by Dato Bahaman and Mat Kilau. Pahang then joined the [[s:federated-malay-states|Federated Malay States]] and later [[s:malaysia|Malaysia]]; [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Abdullah served as king from 2019 to 2024.

principality-of-armenia.t: Armenia under Arab rule, when native princes governed beside the caliph's governor at Dvin and the Bagratid family rose towards kingship.
principality-of-armenia.o: As Arab armies overran the Sasanian lands, the Armenian commander Theodore Rshtuni made a treaty with [[e:muawiya-i|Muawiya]] in 653 accepting Arab overlordship in return for autonomy and keeping Armenian troops. The province of Arminiya, which also took in [[s:georgia|Georgia]] and [[s:albania|Albania]], was established with its centre at Dvin.
principality-of-armenia.r: An Arab governor, the ostikan, sat at Dvin while a native presiding prince represented the Armenian nobility. Heavy taxes provoked revolts, notably in 774-775, which were crushed and weakened the Mamikonian house. Arab [[e:emir|emirs]] settled in towns, while monasteries preserved Armenian learning. The Bagratids grew rich through lands and trade.
principality-of-armenia.e: With the [[s:abbasid-caliphate|Abbasid Caliphate]] weakening, Ashot Bagratuni was named prince of princes in 862, and around 884 the [[e:caliphate|caliph]] sent him a crown, founding [[s:bagratid-armenia|Bagratid Armenia]]. The period had preserved the noble houses, the church and a sense of separate identity that made this revival of Armenian kingship possible.

prince-bishopric-of-verdun.t: One of the Three Bishoprics of Lorraine, a church principality on the Meuse that passed from the Empire to France between 1552 and 1648.
prince-bishopric-of-verdun.o: Verdun, where the Carolingian empire was divided in 843, was an ancient bishopric. In 997 Emperor Otto III granted [[e:bishop|Bishop]] Haimo the comital rights over the city and its district, making the bishops princes of the [[s:holy-roman-empire|Holy Roman Empire]].
prince-bishopric-of-verdun.r: The [[e:bishop|bishops]]' temporal lands were small and lay along the Meuse, and they faced constant pressure from the counts of Bar and the dukes of [[s:duchy-of-lorraine|Lorraine]]. The citizens of Verdun gained wide self-government and imperial-city status, limiting the bishops' power at home. The city was a trading centre, known for its sugared almonds.
prince-bishopric-of-verdun.e: Henry II of [[e:france|France]] occupied Verdun with Metz and Toul in 1552, and the [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] in 1648 confirmed French [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]] over the Three Bishoprics. Verdun became part of the [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]] and later a major fortress.

papal-states.t: The territories of central Italy ruled by the popes as temporal sovereigns for over a thousand years, from Pepin's donation to the capture of Rome in 1870.
papal-states.o: When the [[e:kingdom-of-the-lombards|Lombards]] threatened [[e:rome|Rome]], [[e:papacy|Pope]] Stephen II won the protection of the Frankish king [[e:pepin-the-short|Pepin the Short]] in 754. Pepin defeated the Lombards and in 756 gave the pope the lands of the former [[s:exarchate-of-ravenna|Exarchate of Ravenna]] together with the [[s:duchy-of-rome|Duchy of Rome]]. [[e:charlemagne|Charlemagne]] confirmed and extended the grant in 774.
papal-states.r: The pope ruled as an elected monarch through cardinals, [[e:legatus|legates]] and governors, but for centuries real control was weak, contested by Roman nobles and local lords. Innocent III expanded papal power, and Cardinal Albornoz reasserted it in the 1350s with the Egidian Constitutions. [[e:renaissance|Renaissance]] popes such as Alexander VI and Julius II fought to bring the Romagna under control and built the new St Peter's. Ferrara (1598) and [[s:duchy-of-urbino|Urbino]] (1631) were later absorbed.
papal-states.e: [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]] annexed the States in 1809; they were restored in 1815. In 1860 Romagna, the Marche and Umbria joined the [[s:kingdom-of-italy|Kingdom of Italy]], and on 20 September 1870 Italian troops entered [[e:rome|Rome]]. Pius IX refused to recognise the loss, and the dispute was settled by the Lateran Treaty of 1929, creating [[s:vatican-city|Vatican City]].

principality-of-bulgaria.t: Autonomous Bulgarian principality created after the Russo-Turkish War, which united with Eastern Rumelia and proclaimed full independence in 1908.
principality-of-bulgaria.o: [[e:russia|Russia's]] victory over the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] led to the Treaty of San Stefano in March 1878, which created a large [[s:bulgaria|Bulgaria]]. The Congress of Berlin reduced it to an autonomous principality between the [[e:danube|Danube]] and the Balkan mountains, under Ottoman suzerainty. In 1879 the Tarnovo Constitution was adopted and Alexander of Battenberg elected prince, with Sofia as capital.
principality-of-bulgaria.r: The liberal Tarnovo Constitution created a parliament elected by male suffrage, though princes and strong premiers often ruled forcefully. Unification with [[s:eastern-rumelia|Eastern Rumelia]] in 1885 was defended by victory over [[s:serbia|Serbia]] at Slivnitsa. Russian anger forced Alexander's abdication in 1886, and Ferdinand of Saxe-Coburg was chosen in 1887, while premier Stefan Stambolov built a modern state and army.
principality-of-bulgaria.e: On 5 October 1908, during the crisis over Bosnia, Ferdinand proclaimed full independence at Tarnovo and took the title of tsar, creating the [[s:kingdom-of-bulgaria|Kingdom of Bulgaria]]. The Tarnovo Constitution remained in force until 1947.

province-of-venezuela.t: The Spanish governorate of the Caribbean coast of South America, centred first on Coro and then Caracas, which grew rich on cacao.
province-of-venezuela.o: [[e:spain|Spain]] founded Coro in 1527, and from 1528 the province was leased to the Welser bankers as [[s:klein-venedig|Klein-Venedig]]. After the Welser lease ended in the 1540s, Spanish governors took over. Diego de Losada founded [[s:spanish-jamaica|Santiago]] de León de Caracas in 1567, and it became the capital in 1578.
province-of-venezuela.r: The province was governed by a governor and captain-general under the [[s:captaincy-general-of-santo-domingo|Audiencia of Santo Domingo]] and later of Santa Fe de Bogotá. Its economy grew on [[e:cacao|cacao]] plantations worked by enslaved Africans, and Caracas cacao was exported to [[s:new-spain|New Spain]] and [[e:europe|Europe]]. From 1728 the Guipuzcoan Company of Caracas held a trade monopoly, provoking the revolt of Juan Francisco de León in 1749. The [[e:criollo-people|Creole]] elite, known as mantuanos, dominated society.
province-of-venezuela.e: In 1777 Charles III united the province with Cumaná, Guayana, Maracaibo and the islands of Trinidad and Margarita to form the [[s:captaincy-general-of-venezuela|Captaincy General of Venezuela]]. The province's [[e:criollo-people|Creole]] elite later led the independence movement of 1810.

palembang-sultanate.t: Javanese-influenced Malay sultanate of south Sumatra that grew rich on pepper and Bangka tin until Dutch conquest in 1821.
palembang-sultanate.o: [[e:palembang|Palembang]] had long been ruled by princes of Javanese descent loyal to [[s:mataram-sultanate|Mataram]]. In 1659 the [[s:dutch-east-india-company-territories|Dutch East India Company]] burned the town after its envoys were killed, and the ruler Kimas Hindi broke with Mataram and proclaimed himself sultan with the title Abdurrahman, founding an independent sultanate on the Musi river.
palembang-sultanate.r: The court combined Javanese ceremony with Malay [[e:islam|Islam]]. [[e:palembang|Palembang]] sold [[e:pepper|pepper]] to the Company under monopoly contracts, and after [[e:tin|tin]] was found on Bangka around 1710 it became one of the richest states of the archipelago. [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Mahmud Badaruddin I built the Great Mosque and the brick kraton of Kuto Besak.
palembang-sultanate.e: [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Mahmud Badaruddin II resisted both the British during [[s:british-java|British Java]] and the returning [[e:dutch|Dutch]], defeating a Dutch fleet in 1819. A larger expedition took [[e:palembang|Palembang]] in 1821, the sultan was exiled to [[s:ternate-sultanate|Ternate]], and the sultanate was abolished in 1823. He is now an Indonesian national hero.

prince-bishopric-of-hildesheim.t: Lower Saxon church state famed for Bishop Bernward's Romanesque art, which lost most of its land in a 1519 feud and won it back in 1643.
prince-bishopric-of-hildesheim.o: [[e:louis-the-pious|Louis the Pious]] founded the diocese of Hildesheim in 815. Around 1000 [[e:bishop|Bishop]] Bernward made the city a centre of art, building St. Michael's Church and commissioning its bronze doors and column. The bishops built up a territory between the Leine and Oker, and by the 13th century, around 1235, they ruled as imperial princes.
prince-bishopric-of-hildesheim.r: The cathedral chapter and estates shared power with the [[e:bishop|bishops]]. In the Hildesheim Diocesan Feud of 1519 to 1523 the see lost most of its territory to the Guelph dukes, retaining only the Small Diocese. The city of Hildesheim turned Lutheran, while the bishops stayed Catholic; Wittelsbach princes such as Clemens August of Bavaria often held the see alongside [[s:free-imperial-city-of-cologne|Cologne]].
prince-bishopric-of-hildesheim.e: The lost lands were restored in 1643. The see was secularised in 1803 and given to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]], then belonged to the [[s:kingdom-of-westphalia|Kingdom of Westphalia]], and in 1815 to the [[s:kingdom-of-hanover|Kingdom of Hanover]]. Its cathedral and St. Michael's are a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

prince-bishopric-of-lubeck.t: The only prince-bishopric to survive the Reformation in Protestant hands, ruled from Eutin by Holstein-Gottorp princes until secularised in 1803.
prince-bishopric-of-lubeck.o: Henry the Lion moved the bishopric of [[s:county-of-oldenburg|Oldenburg]] in [[s:county-of-holstein|Holstein]] to the new town of [[s:free-and-hanseatic-city-of-lubeck|Lübeck]] in 1160, and the [[e:bishop|bishops]] gathered estates in eastern Holstein. After [[e:prince-henry-the-navigator|Henry's]] fall in 1180 they held these lands as imperial princes. Conflicts with the citizens of the Free and Hanseatic City of [[e:lubeck|Lübeck]] led them to govern from Eutin.
prince-bishopric-of-lubeck.r: The territory was a small rural principality of lakes and estates around Eutin. After the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] the cathedral chapter turned Lutheran and from 1586 elected princes of the house of [[s:duchy-of-holstein-gottorp|Holstein-Gottorp]], an arrangement the [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] protected. One of them, Adolf Frederick, became King of [[e:sweden|Sweden]] in 1751. Eutin grew into a small court town of the [[e:age-of-enlightenment|Enlightenment]], later called the Weimar of the North.
prince-bishopric-of-lubeck.e: In 1803 the see was secularised as the Principality of [[s:free-and-hanseatic-city-of-lubeck|Lübeck]] and joined to the [[s:duchy-of-oldenburg|Duchy of Oldenburg]], whose ruler had been its last prince-[[e:bishop|bishop]]. It stayed Oldenburg's exclave until the Greater [[s:free-and-hanseatic-city-of-hamburg|Hamburg]] Act of 1937 merged it into Prussian [[s:provisional-government-of-schleswig-holstein|Schleswig-Holstein]].

palace-state-of-zakros.t: The easternmost Minoan palace on Crete, a harbour centre for trade with Egypt and the Levant, found unplundered with its treasures in place.
palace-state-of-zakros.o: Zakros lies in a sheltered bay at the eastern tip of [[e:crete|Crete]], a natural harbour facing [[e:egypt|Egypt]], [[e:cyprus|Cyprus]] and the [[e:levant|Levant]]. A settlement existed in the Early Minoan period, and a palace was built c. 1900 BCE. The surviving palace, smaller than [[s:palace-state-of-knossos|Knossos]] or [[s:palace-state-of-phaistos|Phaistos]], dates mostly from the Neopalatial period after c. 1700 BCE.
palace-state-of-zakros.r: The palace followed the standard Minoan plan with a central court, storerooms, workshops, a lustral basin and a cistern room. It likely controlled trade in [[e:copper|copper]], [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and elephant tusks, some of which were found on site. Its treasury held stone ritual vessels, including a rock-crystal rhyton, and Linear A tablets show local record-keeping.
palace-state-of-zakros.e: Zakros was destroyed by fire c. 1450 BCE and abandoned so suddenly that it was never looted. It was not reoccupied as a palace. Nikolaos Platon excavated it from 1961, recovering one of the richest collections of Minoan objects found in place.

polans-east-slavs.t: The East Slavic tribe of the middle Dnieper whose town of Kiev became the capital of Kievan Rus'.
polans-east-slavs.o: The Polans, the people of the fields, settled the wooded steppe on the middle [[e:dnieper|Dnieper]]. The chronicle credits their legendary founder Kyi, with his brothers Shchek and Khoriv and his sister Lybid, with founding Kiev. For a time they paid tribute to the [[e:khazar-khaganate|Khazars]], said to have been one sword for every household.
polans-east-slavs.r: The chronicler, himself from Kiev, praises the Polans as gentle and well mannered compared with their neighbours, particularly the [[s:drevlians|Drevlians]]. They farmed the fertile soil, and Kiev's position on the [[e:dnieper|Dnieper]] made it a centre of trade between [[e:scandinavia|Scandinavia]], [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] and the steppe. In the mid 9th century Kiev was held by the Varangians Askold and Dir.
polans-east-slavs.e: In 882 Oleg of Novgorod killed Askold and Dir and made Kiev his capital, so the Polan lands became the core of [[s:kievan-rus|Kievan Rus']]. The tribal name faded as the people of the region came to be called the Rus'.

portuguese-india.t: Portugal's Estado da India, ruled from Goa for over four centuries and the hub of its maritime empire from East Africa to Macau.
portuguese-india.o: After [[e:vasco-da-gama|Vasco da Gama]] reached [[e:calicut|Calicut]] in 1498, Portugal appointed [[e:francisco-de-almeida|Francisco de Almeida]] as first [[e:viceroy-of-india|viceroy]] in 1505. [[e:afonso-de-albuquerque|Afonso de Albuquerque]] captured [[e:goa|Goa]] from the [[s:bijapur-sultanate|Bijapur Sultanate]] in 1510, making it the capital of the [[e:estado-da-india|Estado da India]], an empire of forts and ports including Daman, Diu, Bassein, Cochin, [[e:malacca|Malacca]] and [[s:kingdom-of-ormus|Hormuz]].
portuguese-india.r: The Estado controlled sea trade through the cartaz pass system and fortified posts rather than large territories. [[e:goa|Goa]] became a centre of Catholic missions, with Francis Xavier based there and the Goa [[e:portuguese-inquisition|Inquisition]] from 1560. Its churches, such as the Basilica of Bom Jesus, are a World Heritage Site. A Luso-Indian society emerged, and Konkani and Portuguese were both spoken.
portuguese-india.e: The [[e:dutch|Dutch]] and English took most Portuguese posts in the 17th century, and the [[e:maratha-empire|Marathas]] captured Bassein in 1739. [[e:goa|Goa]], Daman and Diu remained Portuguese until the [[s:republic-of-india|Republic of India]] annexed them by military action in December 1961.

providence-island-colony.t: Short-lived Puritan colony off the coast of Central America, a sister venture of New England that turned to privateering and slavery before Spain destroyed it.
providence-island-colony.o: The Providence Island Company, whose investors included the Earl of Warwick, John Pym and Lord Saye and Sele, settled the small island of Santa Catalina in 1630. It was meant as a godly Puritan colony in the [[e:caribbean|Caribbean]], planted with tobacco and [[e:cotton|cotton]], and its leaders hoped it would outshine [[s:massachusetts-bay-colony|Massachusetts Bay]].
providence-island-colony.r: The company governed from [[e:london|London]] through appointed governors and a council, with New Westminster as the main settlement. Crops failed to pay, so the colony turned to privateering against Spanish shipping and came to rely on enslaved Africans, who by 1641 outnumbered the English settlers. An enslaved revolt in 1638 was among the earliest in English America. Church life followed Puritan practice.
providence-island-colony.e: [[e:spain|Spain]] saw the island as a pirate base on its treasure routes and attacked it, failing in 1635 and 1640 before capturing it in May 1641. The settlers were deported and the enslaved people seized. The company's leaders went on to play prominent parts on the Parliamentary side in the English Civil War.

palatinate-mosbach.t: A minor Wittelsbach duchy on the Neckar and in the Odenwald, created when King Rupert's lands were divided in 1410.
palatinate-mosbach.o: When King Rupert, Elector Palatine, died in 1410, his lands were divided among his four sons. [[e:otto-i|Otto I]] received the territory around Mosbach on the Neckar and in the Odenwald, founding the Palatinate-Mosbach line, and in 1448 he also inherited Neumarkt in the [[s:upper-palatinate|Upper Palatinate]].
palatinate-mosbach.r: The Mosbach dukes ruled a modest territory of small towns, forests and farms from Mosbach and Neumarkt, closely tied to the senior electoral line at Heidelberg. Their lands were scattered and their revenues small. Otto II, the second and last duke, never married and left no heirs.
palatinate-mosbach.e: When Otto II died in 1499, Palatinate-Mosbach passed back to the [[s:electoral-palatinate|Electoral Palatinate]]. Mosbach remained Palatine until 1803, when it went to the princes of [[s:principality-of-leiningen|Leiningen]] and then to the [[s:grand-duchy-of-baden|Grand Duchy of Baden]].

principality-of-lucca-and-piombino.t: The Tuscan principality Napoleon created for his sister Elisa Bonaparte, who governed it as an energetic reforming ruler.
principality-of-lucca-and-piombino.o: In 1805 [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]] abolished the [[s:republic-of-lucca|Republic of Lucca]] and joined it to the [[s:principality-of-piombino|Principality of Piombino]], granting the new state to his sister Elisa and her husband Felice Baciocchi. [[s:duchy-of-massa-and-carrara|Massa and Carrara]] were added in 1806.
principality-of-lucca-and-piombino.r: Elisa, not her husband, held real power. She introduced the [[e:napoleonic-code|Napoleonic Code]], closed many convents, reorganised schools and finances, and promoted the Carrara marble industry, founding an academy and workshops that produced busts of the Bonaparte family for all [[e:europe|Europe]]. She patronised the violinist Niccolò Paganini at her court. In 1809 [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]] also made her Grand Duchess of [[s:grand-duchy-of-tuscany|Tuscany]], ruling from [[s:duchy-of-florence|Florence]].
principality-of-lucca-and-piombino.e: Elisa fled as [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]]'s empire collapsed in 1814. The [[e:congress-of-vienna|Congress of Vienna]] gave [[s:republic-of-lucca|Lucca]] to Maria Luisa of [[s:ile-bourbon|Bourbon]] as the [[s:duchy-of-lucca|Duchy of Lucca]], while [[s:principality-of-piombino|Piombino]] went to the [[s:grand-duchy-of-tuscany|Grand Duchy of Tuscany]].

provisional-government-of-the-republic-o.t: The first major Chinese collaborationist regime of the Sino-Japanese War, set up in Beijing in 1937 to govern occupied northern China.
provisional-government-of-the-republic-o.o: After the [[e:marco-polo|Marco Polo]] Bridge incident of July 1937, the Japanese North [[e:china|China]] Area Army occupied [[e:beijing|Beijing]] and Tianjin and pushed south. On 14 December 1937, the day after Nanjing fell, it installed the Provisional Government of the [[s:republic-of-china|Republic of China]] in Beijing, headed by the former Beiyang finance minister Wang Kemin.
provisional-government-of-the-republic-o.r: The regime claimed to govern [[e:hebei|Hebei]], Shandong, [[e:shanxi|Shanxi]] and parts of Henan under the old five-coloured flag of the [[s:beiyang-government|Beiyang government]], though Japanese advisers controlled policy and much of the countryside was held by Communist and Nationalist [[e:guerrilla-warfare|guerrillas]]. It founded the Xinmin Hui, a mass organisation promoting cooperation with [[e:japan|Japan]], and absorbed the [[s:east-hebei-autonomous-government|East Hebei Autonomous Government]] in 1938.
provisional-government-of-the-republic-o.e: In March 1940 it was merged into the [[s:wang-jingwei-regime|Wang Jingwei regime]] at Nanjing, continuing as the semi-autonomous North [[e:china|China]] Political Council until 1945. Wang Kemin was arrested after the war and died in prison in 1945.

provisional-government-of-national-defen.t: Rival Greek government set up in Thessaloniki in 1916 by Eleftherios Venizelos, which took Greece into the First World War on the Allied side.
provisional-government-of-national-defen.o: During the [[e:first-world-war|First World War]], King [[e:constantine-i|Constantine I]] insisted on neutrality while Prime Minister Eleftherios Venizelos wanted to join the Entente. After Venizelos was forced out, officers in Allied-held Thessaloniki launched the National Defence movement in August 1916. In September and October Venizelos formed a provisional government there with Admiral Pavlos Kountouriotis and General Panagiotis Danglis.
provisional-government-of-national-defen.r: The government, led by this triumvirate, controlled northern [[e:greece|Greece]], [[e:crete|Crete]] and most of the [[e:aegean|Aegean]] islands with Allied support, raised an army and declared war on [[s:bulgaria|Bulgaria]] and [[e:germany|Germany]]. Greece was split in two, the National Schism, while Allied pressure on [[s:athens|Athens]] led to the armed clash of December 1916, the Noemvriana.
provisional-government-of-national-defen.e: In June 1917 the [[e:allies|Allies]] forced [[e:constantine-i|Constantine I]] to leave the country. Venizelos returned to [[s:athens|Athens]] as prime minister of a united [[s:kingdom-of-greece|Kingdom of Greece]], which entered the war fully. The bitterness of the schism shaped Greek politics for decades.

pedi-kingdom.t: The Maroteng kingdom of the north-eastern Transvaal, which dominated its region and resisted Boer and British conquest until 1879.
pedi-kingdom.o: The Pedi Maroteng dynasty, of Sotho-Tswana origin, settled around the Steelpoort river in the 17th century. Under Thulare in the late 18th and early 19th centuries it became a paramountcy dominating many smaller chiefdoms of the region.
pedi-kingdom.r: The Pedi king ruled through royal kin and tributary chiefs, with initiation regiments forming the army. After defeat by [[e:mzilikazi|Mzilikazi's]] [[e:ndebele-kingdom|Ndebele]] in the 1820s, Sekwati rebuilt the kingdom on fortified hilltops. Pedi men worked as migrant labourers in the Cape and on the diamond fields, buying guns, and [[e:christianity|Christianity]] divided the court in the 1860s.
pedi-kingdom.e: Sekhukhune I defeated a [[s:south-african-republic|Transvaal]] [[e:boers|Boer]] army in 1876, but after [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] annexed the Transvaal, a British and Swazi force stormed the capital Tsate in 1879 and captured him. The kingdom became part of the Transvaal, though the Pedi royal house survives.

purepecha-empire.t: The second largest state of Mesoamerica at the Spanish arrival, centred on Lake Pátzcuaro in Michoacán, which defeated the Aztecs and worked copper and bronze.
purepecha-empire.o: The Purépecha (Tarascans) developed in the Lake Pátzcuaro basin of Michoacán. According to the Relación de Michoacán, the leader Tariacuri united the lake communities in the 14th century, and his heirs divided the realm among Pátzcuaro, Ihuatzio and Tzintzuntzan, later reunited under Tzintzuntzan.
purepecha-empire.r: The Purépecha state was highly centralised under a king (cazonci) who ruled through officials and governors, and it worshipped the fire god Curicaueri. Its people, speaking a language unrelated to others in [[e:mesoamerica|Mesoamerica]], were skilled in [[e:copper|copper]] and bronze metallurgy, featherwork and lacquer. Its capital had distinctive keyhole-shaped yácata temples. In 1478-79 it routed an Aztec army under [[e:axayacatl|Axayacatl]].
purepecha-empire.e: The last king, Tangaxuan II, submitted to the Spanish peacefully in 1522 but was burnt to death by Nuño de Guzmán in 1530. [[e:bishop|Bishop]] Vasco de Quiroga later organised the Purépecha communities, and their language is still spoken.

prince-bishopric-of-munster.t: The largest church state in the Holy Roman Empire, scene of the Anabaptist kingdom of 1534 and of the peace talks that ended the Thirty Years War.
prince-bishopric-of-munster.o: The Frisian missionary Liudger founded a monastery at Mimigernaford around 793 and became the first [[e:bishop|bishop]] of Münster in 805. The bishops acquired counties across [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Westphalia]], and after Henry the Lion fell in 1180 they ruled as imperial princes. Their lands later stretched from the Lippe to the Ems and beyond to the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] border.
prince-bishopric-of-munster.r: The cathedral chapter and estates kept a strong voice beside the [[e:bishop|bishop]]. In 1534 to 1535 radical Anabaptists under Jan van Leiden turned the city into a theocratic kingdom until Bishop Franz von Waldeck retook it after a siege. The territory remained firmly Catholic. Christoph Bernhard von [[e:galen|Galen]] waged wars against the [[s:dutch-republic|Dutch Republic]], and in the 18th century the minister Franz von [[s:principality-of-furstenberg|Fürstenberg]] reformed schools and founded the university.
prince-bishopric-of-munster.e: The [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] was negotiated partly in Münster in 1648. The see was secularised in 1802 to 1803 and divided, with the largest share going to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] and smaller parts to [[s:county-of-oldenburg|Oldenburg]], Salm and [[s:duchy-of-arenberg|Arenberg]]. Münster became capital of the Prussian Province of Westphalia.

principality-of-wolfenbuttel.t: Guelph principality ruled from Wolfenbüttel, home of the great Herzog August Library and the University of Helmstedt, and forerunner of the Duchy of Brunswick.
principality-of-wolfenbuttel.o: In the division of the [[s:duchy-of-brunswick-luneburg|Duchy of Brunswick-Lüneburg]] in 1269, Albert I the Tall received the southern lands around Brunswick. After further partitions the Wolfenbüttel line took shape in the 15th century, with its residence at the castle of Wolfenbüttel, as the city of Brunswick largely governed itself.
principality-of-wolfenbuttel.r: Henry the Younger was a fierce Catholic opponent of the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]], but his son Julius introduced [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]] in 1568 and founded the University of Helmstedt in 1576. Augustus the Younger built the Herzog August Library, one of the great libraries of [[e:europe|Europe]], where Lessing later served as librarian. The dukes subdued Brunswick in 1671 and moved their court there in 1753.
principality-of-wolfenbuttel.e: The principality was absorbed into the [[s:kingdom-of-westphalia|Kingdom of Westphalia]] in 1807. Restored in 1813, it became the [[s:duchy-of-brunswick|Duchy of Brunswick]] in 1815, which lasted until 1918. The territory is now in Lower Saxony.

principality-of-nassau-usingen.t: Walramian Nassau principality in the Taunus that moved its court to Biebrich on the Rhine and co-founded the Duchy of Nassau.
principality-of-nassau-usingen.o: Nassau-Usingen was created in 1659 when the lands of [[s:county-of-nassau-saarbrucken|Nassau-Saarbrücken]] were divided among the sons of Count William Louis, and Walrad received Usingen in the Taunus. Walrad, a general in [[e:dutch|Dutch]] and imperial service, was raised to prince in 1688.
principality-of-nassau-usingen.r: The territory was Lutheran and mostly rural, but it grew as other Walramian lines died out: Nassau-Usingen inherited [[s:county-of-nassau-saarbrucken|Nassau-Saarbrücken]] and Nassau-Idstein in the 18th century. Prince Charles moved the residence to Biebrich Palace on the [[e:rhine|Rhine]], near Wiesbaden, in 1744, and the spa town of Wiesbaden grew under the princes. After 1797 it lost its left-bank lands but gained [[e:mainz|Mainz]] territory in 1803.
principality-of-nassau-usingen.e: In 1806 Nassau-Usingen and [[s:county-of-nassau-weilburg|Nassau-Weilburg]] united as the [[s:duchy-of-nassau|Duchy of Nassau]] within the [[s:confederation-of-the-rhine|Confederation of the Rhine]], with Frederick Augustus of Usingen as duke. When he died without sons in 1816, the Usingen line ended and [[s:county-of-nassau|Nassau]] passed to the Weilburg line.

patiala-and-east-punjab-states-union.t: PEPSU, the union of the Sikh and other princely states of east Punjab, an Indian state from 1948 to 1956 with Patiala as its capital.
patiala-and-east-punjab-states-union.o: In 1948 eight [[e:princely-state|princely states]], [[s:patiala-state|Patiala State]], [[s:nabha-state|Nabha State]], [[s:jind-state|Jind State]], [[s:kapurthala-state|Kapurthala State]], [[s:faridkot-state|Faridkot State]], Malerkotla, Nalagarh and [[s:kalsia-state|Kalsia State]], were merged into the Patiala and East [[e:punjab|Punjab]] States Union, with Maharaja Yadavindra Singh of Patiala as Rajpramukh.
patiala-and-east-punjab-states-union.r: PEPSU became a Part B state in 1950. Its politics were unstable: after the 1952 elections an Akali-led coalition under Gian Singh Rarewala collapsed, and President's rule was imposed in 1953. It had a predominantly [[e:sikhism|Sikh]] rural population and fertile irrigated farmland.
patiala-and-east-punjab-states-union.e: Under the States Reorganisation Act PEPSU was merged into [[e:punjab|Punjab]] on 1 November 1956. Its lands were later divided between Punjab, Haryana and Himachal Pradesh in 1966.
