principality-of-vitebsk.t: A Dvina trading principality split off from Polotsk, which passed peacefully to Lithuania through the marriage of Algirdas.
principality-of-vitebsk.o: Vitebsk, on the Western Dvina, belonged to the [[s:principality-of-polotsk|Principality of Polotsk]]. After the death of Vseslav of Polotsk in 1101, his sons divided his lands, and Vitebsk became the seat of its own line of princes, though the details of its early rulers are poorly recorded.
principality-of-vitebsk.r: The town lived from trade along the Dvina between Riga and the Rus' interior, and its merchants were included in the trade treaty that [[e:smolensk|Smolensk]] made with Riga and [[s:gotland|Gotland]] in 1229. Rule passed among descendants of the Polotsk dynasty and sometimes to princes from Smolensk, while the influence of the [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Grand Duchy of Lithuania]] grew through the 13th century.
principality-of-vitebsk.e: Algirdas, son of Gediminas, married Maria, daughter of the last prince Yaroslav, and inherited Vitebsk in 1320. The principality became part of the [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Grand Duchy of Lithuania]] and an important base for Algirdas.

prince-bishopric-of-metz.t: The largest of the Three Bishoprics of Lorraine, an ecclesiastical principality of the Empire ruled from Vic-sur-Seille after Metz itself broke free.
prince-bishopric-of-metz.o: Metz had been a bishopric since Roman times and a Carolingian centre of liturgy and chant. In the late 10th century the Ottonian kings confirmed the [[e:bishop|bishops]]' secular lordship over the city and scattered lands in [[s:duchy-of-lorraine|Lorraine]], making them princes of the [[s:holy-roman-empire|Holy Roman Empire]].
prince-bishopric-of-metz.r: The [[e:bishop|bishops]]' territory was fragmented and lay largely around the Seille valley, with salt works at Vic and Marsal providing revenue. By the 13th century the citizens of Metz had won independence as the [[s:free-imperial-city-of-metz|Free Imperial City of Metz]], so the bishops ruled from Vic-sur-Seille. They often struggled with the dukes of [[s:duchy-of-lorraine|Lorraine]].
prince-bishopric-of-metz.e: In 1552 Henry II of [[e:france|France]] seized Metz, Toul and Verdun, and the [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] in 1648 confirmed French [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]] over the Three Bishoprics. The bishopric then became part of the [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]].

prince-bishopric-of-strasbourg.t: The Alsatian church principality whose bishops lost their cathedral city to its burghers in 1262 but kept a territory on both banks of the Rhine until 1803.
prince-bishopric-of-strasbourg.o: [[s:free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg|Strasbourg]] had been a bishopric since late Roman times. In 982 Emperor Otto II granted the [[e:bishop|bishop]] extensive rights over the city, and later Ottonian and Salian grants added counties and estates in Alsace and the Ortenau, making the bishops princes of the [[s:holy-roman-empire|Holy Roman Empire]].
prince-bishopric-of-strasbourg.r: The [[e:bishop|bishops]] began the great Romanesque cathedral under Bishop Werner in 1015. In 1262 the citizens defeated Bishop Walter of [[s:county-of-hohengeroldseck|Geroldseck]] at Hausbergen and the city became the [[s:free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg|Free Imperial City of Strasbourg]], so the bishops governed from Saverne. Their lands lay in scattered pieces across lower Alsace and the right bank of the [[e:rhine|Rhine]].
prince-bishopric-of-strasbourg.e: After [[e:louis-xiv|Louis XIV]] took [[s:free-imperial-city-of-strasbourg|Strasbourg]] in 1681 the left-bank lands came under French [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]], and a line of Rohan cardinals held the see. The Revolution abolished the [[e:bishop|bishops]]' rights in Alsace, and the right-bank remainder was secularised and given to Baden in 1803.

principality-of-hohenzollern-hechingen.t: The senior Swabian branch of the Hohenzollerns, ruling from Hechingen beneath the dynasty's ancestral castle.
principality-of-hohenzollern-hechingen.o: The 1576 division of the [[s:county-of-hohenzollern|County of Hohenzollern]] gave the eldest son, Eitel Frederick IV, the ancestral Hohenzollern castle and the town of Hechingen. The counts of Hohenzollern-Hechingen were raised to princes in 1623.
principality-of-hohenzollern-hechingen.r: Eitel Frederick IV built a [[e:renaissance|Renaissance]] residence in Hechingen and maintained a celebrated court chapel of musicians. The principality was Catholic, small and often in debt, and in the 18th century its princes fought long lawsuits with their peasants before the imperial courts. It joined the [[s:confederation-of-the-rhine|Confederation of the Rhine]] in 1806 and so survived mediatisation.
principality-of-hohenzollern-hechingen.e: After the 1848 revolution the last prince, Frederick William Constantine, abdicated in 1849 in favour of the King of [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]], and in 1850 Hechingen became part of Prussia. Frederick William IV rebuilt the ancestral castle in neo-Gothic style from 1850 to 1867.

principality-of-kozelsk.t: A tiny appanage of the Chernigov lands whose town held out against the Mongols for seven weeks in 1238.
principality-of-kozelsk.o: Kozelsk on the Zhizdra river, a tributary of the Oka, was a small town of the [[e:chernigov|Chernigov]] land, first mentioned in 1146. It became the seat of a separate [[e:appanage|appanage]] in the early 13th century under a junior branch of the Olgovichi princes.
principality-of-kozelsk.r: The principality was small and poor, but its fortified town became famous in 1238 when Batu's army, returning from the north, besieged it for seven weeks. The defenders, led in the name of the child prince Vasily, killed many attackers before the town fell and everyone was slaughtered. The [[e:mongols|Mongols]] reportedly called it the evil town.
principality-of-kozelsk.e: Rebuilt, Kozelsk passed under the [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Grand Duchy of Lithuania]] in the 14th century and its princes became Lithuanian [[e:vassal|vassals]]. In the wars of the late 15th century it changed sides, and the peace of 1494 confirmed it as part of the [[s:grand-duchy-of-moscow|Grand Duchy of Moscow]].

phlius.t: Small inland city of the north-eastern Peloponnese, renowned for its steadfast loyalty to Sparta and its long siege by Agesilaus.
phlius.o: Phlius occupied an upland valley south-west of [[s:corinth|Corinth]], at the head of the Asopus river. Dorian settlers from [[s:argos|Argos]] formed the city in the early Iron Age. It was a small agricultural state known for its wine.
phlius.r: Phlius was usually an oligarchy and a loyal member of the [[s:peloponnesian-league|Peloponnesian League]]. A democratic faction took power in the 380s BCE, and Agesilaus II of [[s:sparta|Sparta]] besieged the city from 381 to 379 BCE to restore the exiles. [[e:xenophon|Xenophon]] praised the Phliasians for their faithfulness to [[e:sparta|Sparta]] during Theban invasions in the 360s BCE. The dramatist Pratinas, credited with the satyr play, was a citizen.
phlius.e: Phlius joined the [[s:achaean-league|Achaean League]] in 229 BCE, after its tyrant stepped down, and passed under Roman control in 146 BCE.

paloncha-samasthan.t: A Telugu samasthan in the forests of the Godavari valley, one of the hereditary estates under the Nizams of Hyderabad.
paloncha-samasthan.o: Paloncha was a hereditary estate in the forested country north of the Godavari, near Bhadrachalam, held by a Telugu chiefly family. The register dates it to around 1700. Its founding is not well documented.
paloncha-samasthan.r: As a samasthan within [[s:hyderabad-state|Hyderabad State]], Paloncha paid tribute to the Nizam while its Raja governed internally. The territory was heavily forested, with Koya and other tribal communities. Few further details are recorded in standard works.
paloncha-samasthan.e: With the integration of Hyderabad into [[e:india|India]] in 1948 and the abolition of samasthans, Paloncha ceased to exist. The town of Palvancha lies in Bhadradri Kothagudem district of Telangana.

palatinate-simmern.t: A Wittelsbach line in the Hunsrück that produced the Calvinist Electors Palatine, beginning with Frederick III in 1559.
palatinate-simmern.o: The 1410 division of King Rupert's lands gave his son Stephen the territories of Simmern and Zweibrücken, to which his marriage added part of the [[s:county-of-sponheim|County of Sponheim]]. In 1453 Stephen's lands were split: Frederick I received Simmern, while Louis took [[s:palatinate-zweibrucken|Palatinate-Zweibrücken]].
palatinate-simmern.r: The Simmern dukes ruled a hilly territory in the Hunsrück around Simmern together with their share of [[s:county-of-sponheim|Sponheim]]. John II introduced the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]]. In 1559, when the senior electoral line died out, Duke Frederick III of Simmern became Elector Palatine and made the [[s:electoral-palatinate|Palatinate]] Calvinist, issuing the Heidelberg Catechism in 1563. Simmern itself then passed to a younger branch.
palatinate-simmern.e: Frederick III's descendants, including Frederick V, the Winter King, ruled the [[s:electoral-palatinate|Electoral Palatinate]] until 1685. The junior Simmern branch ended with Duke Richard's death in 1598, and the duchy returned to the electorate, though a later Simmern line was briefly revived in the 17th century.

poseidonia.t: Greek colony on the Gulf of Salerno, later called Paestum, with three of the best-preserved Doric temples anywhere.
poseidonia.o: Colonists from [[s:sybaris|Sybaris]] founded Poseidonia around 600 BCE on the plain near the mouth of the Sele river, giving Sybaris an outlet on the Tyrrhenian Sea. Named after Poseidon, the city was laid out on a grid and enclosed later by walls nearly 5 km long.
poseidonia.r: Poseidonia prospered from farming and trade with the Etruscans and native peoples. Its three Doric temples, the so-called Basilica of about 550 BCE, the Temple of Athena and the temple of about 460 BCE once called the Temple of Neptune, still stand. The sanctuary of Hera at the mouth of the Sele and the painted Tomb of the Diver of about 470 BCE are famous.
poseidonia.e: Around 410 BCE the [[s:lucanians|Lucanians]] took over the city, which became Paistom, and Greek and Lucanian customs blended. In 273 BCE [[e:rome|Rome]] founded the [[e:latin|Latin]] colony of Paestum there. Malaria and silting led to its abandonment in the Middle Ages, which helped preserve the temples.

principality-of-bidache.t: A tiny sovereign lordship on the edge of the Basque Country whose Gramont lords claimed independence from France until the Revolution.
principality-of-bidache.o: Bidache, on the Bidouze river between [[s:viscounty-of-bearn|Béarn]], [[e:kingdom-of-navarre|Navarre]] and the Labourd, belonged to the Gramont family. Exploiting its uncertain position on the frontier of Navarre and [[e:france|France]], the Gramonts asserted full [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]] over it, and the register dates the principality from 1570.
principality-of-bidache.r: The Gramonts ruled the small territory from their castle at Bidache, administering justice and taxation without royal interference, while serving the French kings at court and in war. Antoine III de Gramont was a marshal of [[e:france|France]] and diplomat under [[e:louis-xiv|Louis XIV]]. The lands were rural, with Gascon and Basque speakers.
principality-of-bidache.e: The Revolution abolished the Gramonts' privileges, and in 1790 Bidache was incorporated into [[e:france|France]] and the new [[e:departement|department]] of Basses-Pyrénées. The ruined castle remains.

principality-of-wales-under-owain-glyndw.t: The last attempt at an independent Welsh state, led by Owain Glyndwr, who was proclaimed Prince of Wales in 1400 and held parliaments at Machynlleth.
principality-of-wales-under-owain-glyndw.o: Owain Glyndwr, a descendant of the princes of [[s:powys-fadog|Powys Fadog]] and [[s:kingdom-of-deheubarth|Deheubarth]], was proclaimed Prince of Wales by his followers in September 1400 after a land dispute with Lord Grey of Ruthin. His revolt quickly spread across Wales, fed by anger at English rule and taxes.
principality-of-wales-under-owain-glyndw.r: By 1404 Glyndwr held most of Wales, took Harlech and Aberystwyth castles, and summoned parliaments at Machynlleth and Harlech. He allied with [[e:france|France]] and with English rebels, the Percys and Mortimers, and in the Pennal Letter proposed an independent Welsh church and two universities.
principality-of-wales-under-owain-glyndw.e: From 1405 English forces under [[e:prince-henry-the-navigator|Prince Henry]] recovered ground, retaking Aberystwyth and Harlech by 1409. Glyndwr vanished around 1415. He became a lasting symbol of Welsh national identity.

principality-of-upper-hungary.t: Ottoman-backed realm of the Kuruc rebel Imre Thököly in what is now eastern Slovakia, which collapsed with the Ottoman defeat at Vienna.
principality-of-upper-hungary.o: Imre Thököly, a Lutheran noble, led the Kuruc rebels of northern [[e:hungary|Hungary]] against [[s:county-of-habsburg|Habsburg]] persecution of Protestants from 1678. After a string of victories he captured Kassa and much of Upper Hungary, and in 1682 [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Mehmed IV recognised him as king of Upper Hungary in return for tribute; Thököly himself used the title of prince.
principality-of-upper-hungary.r: Thököly governed from Kassa through diets of the northern counties, protecting Lutheran and Calvinist worship and paying the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] an annual tribute. His power rested on Kuruc troops of minor nobles, peasants and haiduks. His marriage to Ilona Zrínyi, widow of [[e:francis-i|Francis I]] Rákóczi, brought him the great Rákóczi estates and the castle of Munkács.
principality-of-upper-hungary.e: Thököly supported the Ottoman siege of [[e:vienna|Vienna]] in 1683, and after its failure [[s:county-of-habsburg|Habsburg]] armies retook his towns. In 1685 the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] arrested him and Kassa fell. Ilona Zrínyi held Munkács until 1688. Thököly died in exile in Ottoman Izmit in 1705.

palace-state-of-malia.t: Minoan palace centre on Crete's north coast, one of the island's great Bronze Age palaces and the source of the famous gold bee pendant.
palace-state-of-malia.o: Malia grew from an Early Minoan settlement on a fertile coastal plain east of [[s:palace-state-of-knossos|Knossos]]. Around 1950 BCE, in the Protopalatial period, a monumental palace was built around a central court, making it one of the earliest palace centres on [[e:crete|Crete]] alongside Knossos and [[s:palace-state-of-phaistos|Phaistos]]. The palace was destroyed c. 1700 BCE, probably by earthquake, and rebuilt on a similar plan.
palace-state-of-malia.r: Its rulers are unknown, as Minoan scripts remain undeciphered, but the palace stored grain, oil and wine in large pithoi and organised craft production. The nearby Quartier Mu workshops produced seals, pottery and metalwork, and the Chrysolakkos burial complex yielded the gold pendant of two bees. Inscriptions in Cretan hieroglyphic and Linear A show an administrative system shared with other palaces.
palace-state-of-malia.e: Like most Cretan palaces, Malia was destroyed by fire c. 1450 BCE, in the wave of destructions that preceded Mycenaean dominance from [[s:palace-state-of-knossos|Knossos]]. It was not rebuilt as a palace, though limited settlement continued. Excavated from 1915 and by the French School at [[s:athens|Athens]] since 1922, it is among the best-preserved Minoan sites.

principality-of-mindelheim.t: Swabian lordship briefly made a principality of the Empire for the Duke of Marlborough as a reward for Blenheim.
principality-of-mindelheim.o: Mindelheim, a Swabian lordship belonging to the [[s:electorate-of-bavaria|Electorate of Bavaria]], was confiscated by Emperor Joseph I after the Bavarian elector's defeat at Blenheim in 1704. In 1705 it was granted to John Churchill, Duke of Marlborough, as a principality, making him a prince of the [[s:holy-roman-empire|Holy Roman Empire]].
principality-of-mindelheim.r: Marlborough never lived there and visited only briefly; the lordship was administered by agents who collected its revenues from the town of Mindelheim and surrounding villages. Its importance was symbolic, giving the English general rank among the German princes. The population remained Catholic under a Protestant absentee prince.
principality-of-mindelheim.e: At the peace of Rastatt and Baden in 1714 the Elector of Bavaria was restored to his lands, and Mindelheim returned to Bavaria. Marlborough kept the title of Prince of Mindelheim, and the episode is remembered in the town's history.

principality-of-kabarda.t: The most powerful Circassian principality, on the plains of the central North Caucasus, an early ally of Muscovy and a major regional power.
principality-of-kabarda.o: Kabarda formed in the 15th century when Circassian princes, traditionally descended from the semi-legendary Inal, settled the plains along the Terek, Malka and Baksan rivers. Its princes extended their power over neighbouring Ossetians, Ingush, Balkars and Abazins. Russian and Ottoman sources speak of Kabarda as a distinct country from the 16th century.
principality-of-kabarda.r: Kabarda was ruled by an aristocracy of princes and nobles who held peasants and serfs, with assemblies settling major questions. Prince Temryuk Idarov allied with [[e:ivan-iv-of-russia|Ivan IV of Russia]], who married his daughter Maria in 1561. Kabardians bred famous horses and set standards of etiquette admired across the region. Their forces defeated a Crimean army at Kanzhal in 1708.
principality-of-kabarda.e: Divided into Greater and Lesser Kabarda, it became a battleground between [[e:russia|Russia]] and the [[s:crimean-khanate|Crimean Khanate]]. Russian forts from 1763 and the campaigns of General Yermolov after 1818 broke its independence, and by 1825 it was annexed to the [[s:russian-empire|Russian Empire]].

prince-bishopric-of-wurzburg.t: Franconian church state whose bishops styled themselves Dukes of Franconia and built one of Europe's grandest baroque palaces, the Würzburg Residenz.
prince-bishopric-of-wurzburg.o: The diocese was founded in 742 by Saint Boniface, with Burkard as its first [[e:bishop|bishop]]. Royal grants gave the bishops wide lands on the Main, and in 1168 Emperor [[e:frederick-barbarossa|Frederick Barbarossa]] confirmed their judicial and ducal rights across eastern Franconia, the basis of their later title of Dukes of Franconia and of a territorial principality inside the [[s:holy-roman-empire|Holy Roman Empire]].
prince-bishopric-of-wurzburg.r: The prince-[[e:bishop|bishop]] was elected by the noble cathedral chapter and governed from the Marienberg fortress, later from the town below. Julius Echter von Mespelbrunn refounded the university in 1582, built the Juliusspital and drove a forceful Counter-[[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]]. The 17th century saw some of [[e:germany|Germany's]] worst witch trials. Under the Schönborn bishops Balthasar Neumann built the Residenz, decorated with Tiepolo's ceiling frescoes, and vineyards along the Main supported a wealthy wine trade.
prince-bishopric-of-wurzburg.e: Secularised in 1802 and given to Bavaria, the territory became the [[s:grand-duchy-of-wurzburg|Grand Duchy of Würzburg]] under Ferdinand of [[s:grand-duchy-of-tuscany|Tuscany]] from 1805 to 1814 before returning to the [[s:kingdom-of-bavaria|Kingdom of Bavaria]]. The diocese survives, and the Residenz is a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

principality-of-liechtenstein.t: Alpine principality between Switzerland and Austria, the only surviving state of the Holy Roman Empire's princely bench.
principality-of-liechtenstein.o: The Liechtenstein family, great landowners in [[s:margraviate-of-moravia|Moravia]] and [[e:austria|Austria]], needed land held directly from the emperor to gain a seat in the [[e:imperial-diet|Imperial Diet]]. They bought the lordship of [[s:lordship-of-schellenberg|Schellenberg]] in 1699 and the county of [[s:county-of-vaduz|Vaduz]] in 1712, and in 1719 Emperor Charles VI united them as the Principality of Liechtenstein.
principality-of-liechtenstein.r: For a century the princes lived in [[e:vienna|Vienna]] and governed through officials. Liechtenstein became sovereign through the [[s:confederation-of-the-rhine|Confederation of the Rhine]] in 1806 and was a member of the [[s:german-confederation|German Confederation]] until 1866. It abolished its army in 1868, adopted the constitution of 1921, and formed a [[e:customs-union|customs union]] with [[s:swiss-confederation|Switzerland]] in 1923, using the Swiss franc.
principality-of-liechtenstein.e: [[e:franz-joseph-i|Franz Joseph]] II moved to [[s:county-of-vaduz|Vaduz]] in 1938 and the country stayed neutral in the [[e:second-world-war|Second World War]]. It joined the [[e:united-nations|United Nations]] in 1990 and the European Economic Area in 1995. A 2003 referendum strengthened the powers of Prince Hans-Adam II.

peloponnesian-senate.t: Revolutionary governing body of the Peloponnese in the first year of the Greek War of Independence, dominated by the region's notables.
peloponnesian-senate.o: When the Greek revolt broke out in March 1821, Petros Mavromichalis formed the Messenian Senate at Kalamata. In May and June 1821 leading notables and clergy of the Peloponnese met at the monastery of Kaltezes and created the Peloponnesian Senate to direct the war and administer liberated territory, later based at Tripolitsa after its capture.
peloponnesian-senate.r: The senate was controlled by the Peloponnesian primates (kodjabashis), local landowners and tax-farmers who had held power under the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]], with Petrobey Mavromichalis as president. It organised supplies and taxes for the siege of Tripolitsa and quarrelled with Demetrios Ypsilantis, who claimed national leadership, and with military chiefs such as Theodoros Kolokotronis.
peloponnesian-senate.e: The First National Assembly at [[s:epidaurus|Epidaurus]] in January 1822 created a central Provisional Administration, the [[s:first-hellenic-republic|First Hellenic Republic]]. The regional senate was subordinated and soon dissolved, though the rivalry between notables and military leaders continued into the civil wars of 1823-1825.

peoples-democratic-republic-of-ethiopia.t: The civilian-styled communist state that succeeded the Derg in 1987, led by Mengistu Haile Mariam until rebels took Addis Ababa in 1991.
peoples-democratic-republic-of-ethiopia.o: A new constitution, approved by referendum in February 1987, turned the military government of the [[s:derg|Derg]] into the People's Democratic Republic of [[s:federal-democratic-republic-of-ethiopia|Ethiopia]] in September 1987. [[e:mengistu-haile-mariam|Mengistu Haile Mariam]] became president, and the Workers' Party of [[e:ethiopia|Ethiopia]] was proclaimed the leading force of state and society.
peoples-democratic-republic-of-ethiopia.r: The PDRE was a one-party Marxist-Leninist state on the Soviet model, with collective farms, forced villagisation and resettlement of northerners to the south and west. Its army, among [[e:africa|Africa's]] largest, was badly overstretched by wars with the Eritrean People's Liberation Front and the Tigrayan-led EPRDF, and suffered a heavy defeat at Afabet in 1988. Soviet aid dwindled as the Cold War ended.
peoples-democratic-republic-of-ethiopia.e: Rebels captured [[e:massawa|Massawa]] in 1990 and advanced on the capital. Mengistu fled to [[e:zimbabwe|Zimbabwe]] on 21 May 1991, and the EPRDF entered [[e:addis-ababa|Addis Ababa]] on 28 May, forming the [[s:transitional-government-of-ethiopia|Transitional Government of Ethiopia]], while the EPLF took Asmara.

pethapur-state.t: A small Vaghela Rajput state of northern Gujarat, its town long famous for carved wooden blocks used in textile printing.
pethapur-state.o: Pethapur was held by a family of Vaghela [[e:rajputs|Rajputs]], who claimed descent from the Vaghela rulers of medieval [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]]. The estate on the Sabarmati emerged as a separate holding around 1600.
pethapur-state.r: The Thakor ruled a small territory under the Mahi Kantha Agency in the British period, paying tribute through the [[e:gaekwads|Gaekwads]] of [[s:baroda-state|Baroda]]. The town became known for its craftsmen who carved the wooden blocks used in [[e:printing-press|printing]] cloth across western [[e:india|India]].
pethapur-state.e: Pethapur merged into [[s:bombay-presidency|Bombay Province]] in 1948 and became part of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] in 1960. It now lies in Gandhinagar district, close to the state capital.

prince-bishopric-of-regensburg.t: Small Danube church state of the bishops of Regensburg, who governed a great Bavarian diocese from a Gothic cathedral but ruled only a little land.
prince-bishopric-of-regensburg.o: Saint Boniface organised the diocese of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-regensburg|Regensburg]] in 739, building on an older [[e:bishop|bishop]]'s seat in the Roman city. Its bishops were overshadowed in the city by the Bavarian dukes and the abbey of St. Emmeram, but gathered scattered lordships such as Donaustauf, Wörth and Hohenburg, which they ruled as imperial princes from the 13th century.
prince-bishopric-of-regensburg.r: The prince-[[e:bishop|bishop]]'s secular territory was small and fragmented, while his diocese covered much of eastern Bavaria. The scholar Albertus Magnus served briefly as bishop in 1260 to 1262. The Gothic cathedral of St. Peter was built from 1273 over more than two centuries. The see remained Catholic, while the [[s:free-imperial-city-of-regensburg|Free Imperial City of Regensburg]] around it turned Lutheran, and many bishops came from the Wittelsbach house.
prince-bishopric-of-regensburg.e: In 1803 the prince-bishopric was merged into the Principality of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-regensburg|Regensburg]] under Karl Theodor von Dalberg, which passed to Bavaria in 1810. The diocese continues, and its cathedral choir is world famous.

principality-of-rostov-suzdal.t: The north-eastern principality of Yuri Dolgoruky, founder of Moscow, which laid the foundations of later Russian power.
principality-of-rostov-suzdal.o: The forest lands between the [[e:volga|Volga]] and the Oka, once home to the Finnic Merya, were colonised by [[e:slavs|Slavs]] from the 10th century and ruled from Rostov. Vladimir Monomakh gave them to his son Yuri, who around 1125 made Suzdal his seat, turning the region into an independent principality.
principality-of-rostov-suzdal.r: Yuri Dolgoruky, the Long-armed, founded or fortified towns such as Yuryev-Polsky, Pereslavl-Zalessky and Dmitrov, and [[e:moscow|Moscow]] is first mentioned in 1147 as the place of a feast he held. Slavic settlers moved here from the troubled south. Its white-stone churches, such as the one at Kideksha, mark the start of a distinct north-eastern architecture.
principality-of-rostov-suzdal.e: Yuri fought for years to win Kiev, finally becoming its grand prince in 1155, and died there in 1157. His son Andrei Bogolyubsky moved the capital to Vladimir, and the land became [[s:vladimir-suzdal|Vladimir-Suzdal]].

province-of-east-florida.t: A short-lived British colony on the Florida peninsula, governed from St. Augustine and loyal to the Crown throughout the American Revolution.
province-of-east-florida.o: [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] received [[s:spanish-florida|Spanish Florida]] from [[e:spain|Spain]] under the Treaty of [[e:paris|Paris]] of 1763, in exchange for returning Havana. The Proclamation of 1763 split the territory at the Apalachicola River, creating East Florida with its capital at the old Spanish town of St. Augustine. Almost the entire Spanish population left for [[e:cuba|Cuba]].
province-of-east-florida.r: Royal governors, first James Grant and later Patrick Tonyn, tried to attract settlers with land grants. The most ambitious scheme, Andrew Turnbull's New [[s:smyrna|Smyrna]] colony of Minorcans, [[e:greeks|Greeks]] and Italians, collapsed amid disease and hardship. Plantations produced [[e:indigo|indigo]], [[e:rice|rice]] and naval stores. The province did not join the rebellion of 1776 and became a refuge for thousands of Loyalists from [[s:georgia|Georgia]] and the Carolinas.
province-of-east-florida.e: The Treaty of [[e:paris|Paris]] of 1783 returned both Floridas to [[e:spain|Spain]]. Most British settlers and Loyalists departed for the [[s:bahamas|Bahamas]], [[s:colony-of-nova-scotia|Nova Scotia]] or [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]], and the territory became part of [[s:spanish-florida|Spanish Florida]] again until its cession to the [[s:united-states|United States]] in 1821.

principality-of-theodoro.t: An Orthodox Greek principality in the mountains of south-western Crimea, the last remnant of Byzantine rule there until 1475.
principality-of-theodoro.o: The south-western [[e:crimea|Crimea]], known as Gothia after the Goths who settled there in late antiquity, came under a local Greek-speaking dynasty in the 14th century. The fortress of Mangup, called Theodoro, became its capital. Its rulers may have been linked to the Gabras family of [[s:empire-of-trebizond|Trebizond]], though their origins are uncertain.
principality-of-theodoro.r: The principality was a mountain state of [[e:greeks|Greeks]], Goths, [[s:alans|Alans]] and others, living from vineyards, farming and trade. Prince Alexios I fought the Genoese of [[s:genoese-gazaria|Genoese Gazaria]] for the coast and built a port at Kalamita. Theodoro's princes married into the ruling families of [[s:empire-of-trebizond|Trebizond]] and [[s:principality-of-moldavia|Moldavia]]; Maria of Mangup became the wife of Stephen the Great.
principality-of-theodoro.e: In 1475 the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]], having taken [[s:genoese-gazaria|Caffa]], besieged Mangup for months. The fortress fell in December 1475 and the princely family was taken to [[e:istanbul|Istanbul]] and killed. The [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] ruled the area directly, and Crimean Gothic, once spoken there, died out.

principality-of-chernigov.t: One of the largest and most powerful principalities of Kievan Rus', ruled by the Olgovichi, rivals of Kiev for the throne.
principality-of-chernigov.o: [[e:chernigov|Chernigov]] on the Desna, in the old Severian lands, became a princely seat in 1024 when Mstislav of Tmutarakan made it his capital. Under the will of Yaroslav the Wise it passed in 1054 to his son [[e:sviatoslav-i-of-kiev|Sviatoslav]] II, and the Lyubech conference of 1097 confirmed it to Sviatoslav's sons, founding the Olgovichi dynasty.
principality-of-chernigov.r: The principality stretched from the [[e:dnieper|Dnieper]] to the upper Oka and was divided into [[e:appanage|appanages]] such as Novgorod-Seversky and Kursk. Its princes competed for Kiev and often allied with the Cumans. The Transfiguration Cathedral of the 1030s is among the oldest churches in [[e:ukraine|Ukraine]], and the Lay of Igor's Campaign celebrates one of its princes.
principality-of-chernigov.e: The [[e:mongols|Mongols]] sacked [[e:chernigov|Chernigov]] in 1239, and Prince Mikhail was executed at Batu's camp in 1246. The land broke into small principalities under Mongol overlordship and in the 14th century passed largely to the [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Grand Duchy of Lithuania]].

phayao-kingdom.t: A northern Thai principality on Kwan Phayao lake that allied with Lan Na and Sukhothai in the 13th century before being absorbed by Lan Na.
phayao-kingdom.o: Northern Thai chronicles say Phayao was founded in the late 11th century by Khun Chom Tham, a prince of the [[s:ngoenyang|Ngoenyang]] line, on the shores of the lake now called Kwan Phayao. Its early history rests on chronicle tradition.
phayao-kingdom.r: Phayao was a Tai muang of [[e:rice|rice]]-growing valleys whose rulers were linked by kinship to [[s:ngoenyang|Ngoenyang]] and Nan. Its best-known ruler, Ngam Mueang, was an ally of Mangrai of [[s:lan-na|Lan Na]] and Ram Khamhaeng of [[s:sukhothai-kingdom|Sukhothai]]; the three are said to have sworn friendship around 1287, an event commemorated by the Three Kings Monument in [[s:kingdom-of-chiang-mai|Chiang Mai]].
phayao-kingdom.e: After Ngam Mueang's death Phayao weakened, and [[s:lan-na|Lan Na]] annexed it in 1338 under King Kham Fu. It became a provincial town of Lan Na and later of Siam, and is now the centre of Phayao province in northern [[s:thailand|Thailand]].

protectorate-general-to-pacify-the-south.t: The Tang dynasty's southern frontier command in northern Vietnam, whose name Annan, 'the pacified south', long remained a Chinese name for the country.
protectorate-general-to-pacify-the-south.o: In 679 the [[e:tang-dynasty|Tang dynasty]] reorganised its territories in the Red River delta, earlier Jiaozhou, into the Annan duhufu, the [[e:protectorate|Protectorate]] General to Pacify the South, one of several frontier protectorates. Its seat lay at Songping, later fortified as Dai La on the site of present-day [[e:hanoi|Hanoi]].
protectorate-general-to-pacify-the-south.r: [[s:later-tang|Tang]] governors ruled through prefectures and counties, collecting tax in [[e:rice|rice]], salt and tribute goods and keeping garrisons against hill peoples and [[s:champa|Champa]]. [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]] flourished, and local elites learned Chinese letters. Heavy taxation provoked revolts, notably that of Mai Thuc Loan in 722 and Phung Hung in the 790s. Governor Zhang Boyi built the walls of Dai La in 767.
protectorate-general-to-pacify-the-south.e: In the 850s and 860s [[s:nanzhao|Nanzhao]] invaded and briefly occupied the [[e:protectorate|protectorate]]. The [[s:later-tang|Tang]] general [[e:gao|Gao]] Pian drove them out in 866 and the region was reorganised as the [[s:tinh-hai-circuit|Tinh Hai Circuit]]. The Annan name endured and was used by [[e:china|China]] and later by [[e:france|France]] for central [[s:socialist-republic-of-vietnam|Vietnam]].

paurava-kingdom.t: The Punjab kingdom of Porus, who fought Alexander the Great at the Battle of the Hydaspes in 326 BCE and kept his throne as an ally.
paurava-kingdom.o: The Paurava kingdom lay between the [[e:jhelum|Jhelum]] and the [[e:chenab|Chenab]] rivers in the [[e:punjab|Punjab]], in modern [[s:islamic-republic-of-pakistan|Pakistan]], and emerged after Achaemenid control of the region faded in the 4th century BCE. Its king, called Porus by the [[e:greeks|Greeks]], perhaps from the Vedic clan name Puru, was a rival of Ambhi of the [[s:kingdom-of-taxila|Kingdom of Taxila]].
paurava-kingdom.r: Greek historians describe a strong monarchy with an army of infantry, [[e:chariot|chariots]] and [[e:war-elephant|war elephants]]. At the Battle of the Hydaspes, the [[e:jhelum|Jhelum]], in 326 BCE, Porus faced Alexander with his elephants; Alexander crossed the river by surprise and won. Arrian reports that the wounded Porus, asked how he wished to be treated, answered: like a king. Little else is known of the kingdom's society.
paurava-kingdom.e: Alexander restored Porus and enlarged his territory as far as the [[e:beas|Beas]]. After Alexander's death Porus was murdered around 317 BCE by the Macedonian officer Eudemus, and his lands passed into the [[s:maurya-empire|Maurya Empire]]. The meeting of Porus and Alexander became a celebrated story in both Greek and Indian memory.

principality-of-stavelot-malmedy.t: Tiny ecclesiastical principality of the Ardennes, ruled for over a thousand years by the abbots of twin monasteries.
principality-of-stavelot-malmedy.o: Around 648 to 651 the missionary Remaclus founded twin abbeys at Stavelot and Malmedy in the Ardennes forest, on land granted by Sigebert III of [[s:austrasia|Austrasia]]. The two houses shared a single abbot, and the community became one of the leading monasteries of the region.
principality-of-stavelot-malmedy.r: In the [[s:holy-roman-empire|Holy Roman Empire]] the abbots became princes with a seat in the [[e:imperial-diet|Imperial Diet]], ruling a small territory between the [[s:prince-bishopric-of-liege|Prince-Bishopric of Liège]] and the [[s:county-of-luxembourg|Duchy of Luxembourg]]. Abbot Wibald in the 12th century was an adviser to emperors, and the abbey's workshops produced masterpieces of Mosan goldsmith work such as the Stavelot Triptych.
principality-of-stavelot-malmedy.e: Revolutionary [[e:france|France]] annexed the principality in 1795 and dissolved the abbeys. In 1815 Stavelot went to the [[s:kingdom-of-the-netherlands|Netherlands]], and later [[s:kingdom-of-belgium|Belgium]], while Malmedy passed to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]]. Malmedy was transferred to [[e:belgium|Belgium]] in 1920, reuniting the two towns.

parvagupta-dynasty.t: A short Kashmiri dynasty best remembered for Queen Didda, who dominated the kingdom for half a century.
parvagupta-dynasty.o: Parvagupta, a scribe and minister, seized the throne of [[e:kashmir|Kashmir]] in the turmoil that followed the [[s:utpala-dynasty|Utpala dynasty]], killing the young king. Kalhana's Rajatarangini, the main source, portrays him as an ambitious official from the scribal class, which is why the dynasty is also called the Divira dynasty.
parvagupta-dynasty.r: Parvagupta's son Kshemagupta married Didda, a princess of Lohara. After her husband's death in 958 she ruled as regent for her son and grandsons, removing rivals and ministers, and from 980 she reigned in her own name. Kalhana portrays her as ruthless and cunning but effective, and she built temples and monasteries. The period was one of court intrigue and heavy taxation.
parvagupta-dynasty.e: Before her death in 1003 Didda chose her nephew Sangramaraja as heir, and he founded the [[s:lohara-dynasty|Lohara dynasty]], ending the Parvagupta line.

principality-of-taron.t: An Armenian principality west of Lake Van, ruled by a branch of the Bagratids, that passed peacefully to Byzantium in the 960s.
principality-of-taron.o: Taron, the plain around Mush, had long been a Mamikonian land. In the early 9th century the Bagratid Bagrat, son of Ashot Msaker, secured it as his share of the family lands, and in 826 his branch became its hereditary princes under the [[s:abbasid-caliphate|Abbasid Caliphate]].
principality-of-taron.r: Taron was a fertile, well-watered district on routes between [[s:armenia|Armenia]] and [[e:mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], and its monastery of Surb Karapet at Glak was among the most revered in [[e:armenia|Armenia]]. Its princes balanced between the Arab [[e:emir|emirs]], the kings of [[s:bagratid-armenia|Bagratid Armenia]] and the [[s:byzantine-empire|Byzantine Empire]]; Constantine VII describes Prince Grigor visiting [[e:constantinople|Constantinople]] and receiving a palace and pension.
principality-of-taron.e: Around 966 Grigor's sons Ashot and Grigor surrendered Taron to the [[s:byzantine-empire|Byzantine Empire]] in return for court titles and estates. It became a Byzantine theme, the first of the Armenian principalities to be annexed.

principality-of-albania-medieval.t: Principality of the Thopia family centred on Durrës, a leading Albanian realm of the late 14th century that ended when Durrës passed to Venice.
principality-of-albania-medieval.o: Karl Thopia, an Albanian noble claiming Angevin descent through his mother, built up lands between the Mat and Shkumbin rivers. In 1368 he took Durrës from the Angevins, ending the [[s:kingdom-of-albania-medieval|Kingdom of Albania (medieval)]], and styled himself Prince of [[s:albania|Albania]].
principality-of-albania-medieval.r: Karl ruled from Durrës and the inland town of Elbasan, rivalling [[s:zeta-under-the-balsici|Zeta under the Balšići]] and the Muzaka of Berat. He founded the monastery of Shën Gjon Vladimir near Elbasan. Balša II seized Durrës in 1385, and Karl called in the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]], who killed Balša at Savra; Karl recovered the city soon after.
principality-of-albania-medieval.e: Karl died in 1388. His son Gjergj Thopia, weakened by Ottoman pressure, handed Durrës to [[e:venice|Venice]] in 1392, and he died soon after. The remaining Thopia lands later fell under Ottoman control.

powhatan-confederacy.t: The paramount chiefdom of Tsenacommacah in coastal Virginia, whose ruler Powhatan faced the English settlers of Jamestown.
powhatan-confederacy.o: In the late 16th century Wahunsenacah, known to the English as Powhatan, inherited six chiefdoms on the upper James and York rivers. Through conquest and pressure he expanded his rule to some 30 Algonquian-speaking peoples between the Potomac and the James, perhaps 15,000 people, governing from Werowocomoco on the York River.
powhatan-confederacy.r: Each subject people kept its own weroance, or chief, who paid tribute in corn, deerskins, [[e:copper|copper]] and pearls to the paramount ruler. Priests held great influence, and towns of bark-covered houses stood among fields of [[e:maize|maize]], beans and squash. When the English founded [[e:jamestown|Jamestown]] in 1607, Powhatan hoped to make them tributaries; relations swung between trade and war, and his daughter Pocahontas's marriage to John Rolfe in 1614 brought a brief peace.
powhatan-confederacy.e: His brother Opechancanough launched great attacks on the [[s:colony-of-virginia|Colony of Virginia]] in 1622 and 1644; captured and killed in 1646, he left the chiefdom tributary to [[e:virginia|Virginia]]. The Treaty of Middle Plantation in 1677, signed by Cockacoeske of the Pamunkey, ended it, though Pamunkey and Mattaponi reservations survive.

principality-of-volhynia.t: A western Rus' principality around Volodymyr whose prince Roman united it with Galicia in 1199.
principality-of-volhynia.o: [[e:volhynia|Volhynia]], between the Bug and the upper Pripyat, was an old land of Rus' with its centre at Volodymyr. In the mid 12th century it became the hereditary domain of the descendants of Iziaslav Mstislavich of Kiev, and from 1154 his son Mstislav Iziaslavich ruled it as a separate principality.
principality-of-volhynia.r: [[e:volhynia|Volhynia]] was a fertile land of towns such as Volodymyr, Lutsk and Berestia, trading with [[e:poland|Poland]] and the West. Its princes, the senior branch of Monomakh's family, were among the strongest in Rus' and frequently fought for Kiev. Roman Mstislavich, who succeeded in 1170, was an energetic warrior who fought the Lithuanians and Cumans.
principality-of-volhynia.e: In 1199 Roman Mstislavich took [[s:principality-of-galicia|Halych]] after its dynasty died out and joined the two lands into the [[s:kingdom-of-galicia-volhynia|Kingdom of Galicia-Volhynia]]. [[e:volhynia|Volhynia]] later passed to [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Lithuania]] as the [[s:duchy-of-volhynia|Duchy of Volhynia]].

prince-bishopric-of-havelberg.t: A bishopric founded by Otto I among the Slavs of the Havel, lost in the revolt of 983 and refounded as a small territory that Brandenburg absorbed.
prince-bishopric-of-havelberg.o: [[e:otto-i|Otto I]] founded the bishopric of Havelberg in 946 or 948 at a stronghold on the Havel, to convert the [[e:slavs|Slavs]] of the [[s:northern-march|Northern March]]. It became a suffragan of the [[s:archbishopric-of-magdeburg|Archbishopric of Magdeburg]] in 968. The Great Slav Rising of 983 destroyed it, and its [[e:bishop|bishops]] lived in exile for more than a century.
prince-bishopric-of-havelberg.r: After the Wendish [[e:crusade|Crusade]] of 1147, [[e:bishop|Bishop]] Anselm of Havelberg, a noted theologian and diplomat to [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]], restored the see, and the cathedral was consecrated in 1170. The bishops ruled a small territory around Havelberg and Wittstock, where they built their residence, but depended on the margraves of [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]].
prince-bishopric-of-havelberg.e: With the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] in [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]], the last Catholic [[e:bishop|bishop]] died in 1548, and the Hohenzollern [[e:prince-elector|electors]] installed their own family as administrators. The territory was absorbed into the [[s:margraviate-of-brandenburg|Margraviate of Brandenburg]] by 1598. The cathedral on the hill at Havelberg survives.

principality-of-brandenburg-ansbach.t: The Hohenzollern margraviate around Ansbach in Franconia, an early Lutheran state that was sold to Prussia by its last margrave in 1791.
principality-of-brandenburg-ansbach.o: The 1398 division of the lands of the [[s:burgraviate-of-nuremberg|Burgraviate of Nuremberg]] gave Frederick VI, later the first Hohenzollern elector of [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]], the territory 'below the mountains' around Ansbach. From the 15th century it was usually ruled by a younger Hohenzollern son as margrave.
principality-of-brandenburg-ansbach.r: Margrave Albert Achilles, who also became elector, made Ansbach a centre of Hohenzollern power, and George the Pious introduced [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]] in 1528. The principality was rich in farmland and governed through a strong bureaucracy. Ansbach's Baroque residence was built in the 18th century, and the margraves hired out soldiers to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] for the American War of Independence.
principality-of-brandenburg-ansbach.e: The last margrave, Charles Alexander, inherited the [[s:principality-of-brandenburg-bayreuth|Principality of Brandenburg-Bayreuth]] in 1769 and in 1791 handed both principalities to his Prussian cousins before retiring to [[e:england|England]]. [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] ceded Ansbach to the [[s:kingdom-of-bavaria|Kingdom of Bavaria]] in 1806.

principality-of-valona.t: Albanian coastal lordship around Vlorë and Kanina, founded by a governor of the Serbian Empire and lost to the Ottomans in 1417.
principality-of-valona.o: Stefan Dušan of the [[s:serbian-empire|Serbian Empire]] took Valona (Vlorë) and Kanina from [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] around 1345. His brother-in-law John Komnenos Asen governed them, and after Dušan's death in 1355 ruled as an independent despot.
principality-of-valona.r: Its rulers held the port of Valona, the fortress of Kanina and nearby lands, trading with [[e:venice|Venice]] and [[s:republic-of-ragusa|Ragusa]] and taxing traffic across the Strait of Otranto. After John's son Alexander, the city passed to Balša II of [[s:zeta-under-the-balsici|Zeta under the Balšići]] around 1372, and then through his widow Komita to her son-in-law Merksha Žarković and, after his death in 1414, to his widow Ruđina.
principality-of-valona.e: Ruđina had ruled only briefly when the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] captured Valona and Kanina in 1417. Valona became an Ottoman port and centre of the Sanjak of Avlonya.

principality-of-bukhara.t: The Sogdian city-state ruled by the Bukhar Khudahs, whose queen-regent Khatun faced the Arab conquest of Transoxiana.
principality-of-bukhara.o: [[e:bukhara|Bukhara]], in the Zarafshan delta west of [[e:samarkand|Samarkand]], was ruled from the 6th or 7th century by a dynasty bearing the title Bukhar Khudah, lord of Bukhara. Tradition, recorded by Narshakhi, links its foundation to settlers and princes from the Hephthalite and Turkic period.
principality-of-bukhara.r: The Bukhar Khudahs ruled from the citadel of [[e:bukhara|Bukhara]] over an oasis of farms and walled estates. Their [[e:silver|silver]] coins, imitating the Sasanian king Bahram V, circulated widely as 'Bukhar Khudah drachms' for centuries. The regent known as Khatun ruled in the late 7th century during the Arab raids, alternately paying tribute and fighting.
principality-of-bukhara.e: Qutayba ibn Muslim captured [[e:bukhara|Bukhara]] in 709 and installed the young Tughshada as a [[e:vassal|vassal]] Bukhar Khudah, building the first mosque. The dynasty kept a ceremonial role until its last members were killed around 782, and Bukhara later became the capital of the [[s:samanid-empire|Samanid Empire]].

prince-bishopric-of-halberstadt.t: Church principality in the northern Harz foreland, founded under Charlemagne and secularised to Brandenburg at the Peace of Westphalia.
prince-bishopric-of-halberstadt.o: The diocese of Halberstadt was founded about 804 under [[e:charlemagne|Charlemagne]] to christianise the eastern [[s:saxons|Saxons]]. Its [[e:bishop|bishops]] gathered counties and estates in the Harz foreland. After the fall of Henry the Lion in 1180 freed them from his ducal power, they ruled a consolidated territory as imperial princes.
prince-bishopric-of-halberstadt.r: The cathedral chapter elected the [[e:bishop|bishop]], who ruled from Halberstadt and towns such as Gröningen. Its Gothic cathedral and treasury are among the richest in [[e:germany|Germany]]. From the 16th century the see was held by princes of the houses of [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]] and Brunswick, including Albert of Brandenburg and Henry Julius of [[s:principality-of-wolfenbuttel|Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel]], and the territory became Lutheran. In the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years War]] its administrator, Christian of Brunswick, fought for the Protestant side.
prince-bishopric-of-halberstadt.e: At the [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] in 1648 the see was secularised and given to [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]] as the [[s:principality-of-halberstadt|Principality of Halberstadt]]. It remained Prussian, apart from the [[s:kingdom-of-westphalia|Kingdom of Westphalia]] interlude, and is now in Saxony-Anhalt.

principality-of-beloozero.t: A northern principality on the White Lake, gateway to the fur trade, whose last princes died at Kulikovo before Moscow took it over.
principality-of-beloozero.o: Beloozero, the White Lake, is mentioned in the Primary Chronicle under 862 as the seat of Rurik's brother Sineus, in the land of the Finnic Ves. Part of the Rostov lands, it became a separate [[e:appanage|appanage]] in 1238 for Gleb Vasilkovich, son of the Rostov prince killed by the [[e:mongols|Mongols]].
principality-of-beloozero.r: The principality was a remote, thinly settled land of forests and lakes on the routes to the north, where [[e:fur-trade|furs]], fish and salt were gathered. Its princes depended on Rostov, the grand princes of Vladimir and the [[s:golden-horde|Golden Horde]]. Prince Fyodor Romanovich and his son were killed fighting for Dmitry Donskoy at Kulikovo in 1380.
principality-of-beloozero.e: After their deaths [[e:moscow|Moscow]] took control, and in his will of 1389 Dmitry Donskoy left Beloozero to his son Andrei. In 1397 the monk Kirill founded the Kirillo-Belozersky Monastery nearby, which became one of [[e:russia|Russia's]] richest monasteries.

principality-of-nassau-hadamar.t: Small Nassau principality in the Westerwald that became a Catholic outpost of the house and left a baroque residence town.
principality-of-nassau-hadamar.o: Hadamar was created in the 1607 division of the lands of John VI of [[s:county-of-nassau-dillenburg|Nassau-Dillenburg]] and went to his son John Louis. John Louis converted to [[e:catholicism|Catholicism]] in 1629 and served the emperor as a diplomat at the [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]], for which he was made a prince of the Empire in 1650.
principality-of-nassau-hadamar.r: After its ruler's conversion Hadamar became a Catholic enclave among Protestant [[s:county-of-nassau|Nassau]] lands, with a [[e:jesuits|Jesuit]] college and Franciscan friars. John Louis rebuilt Hadamar as a planned residence town with a new palace. The economy was agrarian, with small-scale iron and wool working in the Westerwald hills.
principality-of-nassau-hadamar.e: The line died out with Prince Francis Alexander in 1711, and the territory was divided among the other Nassau-Ottonian lines, [[s:principality-of-nassau-diez|Nassau-Diez]], [[s:principality-of-nassau-siegen|Nassau-Siegen]] and [[s:county-of-nassau-dillenburg|Nassau-Dillenburg]]. Its lands later passed to the [[s:duchy-of-nassau|Duchy of Nassau]] and, in 1866, to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]].

prince-bishopric-of-ratzeburg.t: Small Lauenburg church state founded by Henry the Lion among the Polabian Slavs, secularised to Mecklenburg in 1648.
prince-bishopric-of-ratzeburg.o: Henry the Lion founded the bishopric of Ratzeburg in 1154 during the conquest and conversion of the Slavic Polabians, with Evermod as its first [[e:bishop|bishop]]. The bishops built the Romanesque brick cathedral on the island of Ratzeburg and acquired lands east of the lake. After [[e:prince-henry-the-navigator|Henry's]] fall they ruled these lands as an imperial principality.
prince-bishopric-of-ratzeburg.r: The territory, centred on Schönberg, was small and rural, settled by German farmers among the earlier Slavic population. The [[e:bishop|bishops]] were overshadowed by the dukes of Saxe-Lauenburg, who held Ratzeburg town, and by the dukes of [[s:lordship-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg]]. In the 16th century the cathedral chapter turned Lutheran, and Mecklenburg princes held the see as administrators.
prince-bishopric-of-ratzeburg.e: The [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] in 1648 secularised the see as the [[s:principality-of-ratzeburg|Principality of Ratzeburg]] and gave it to the [[s:duchy-of-mecklenburg|Duchy of Mecklenburg]]. From 1701 it belonged to the [[s:duchy-of-mecklenburg-strelitz|Duchy of Mecklenburg-Strelitz]] and is now part of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

palmyrene-empire.t: The breakaway realm of the caravan city of Palmyra, which under Queen Zenobia briefly ruled Rome's East from Egypt to Anatolia.
palmyrene-empire.o: After the Persian king [[e:shapur-i|Shapur I]] captured the emperor [[e:valerian|Valerian]] in 260, the Palmyrene noble Odaenathus defeated the retreating [[e:persians|Persians]] and crushed the usurpers in the East, earning from Gallienus the title corrector of the whole East. His murder in 267 left power to his widow Zenobia, regent for their young son Vaballathus.
palmyrene-empire.r: Palmyra had grown rich on caravan trade linking the [[e:euphrates|Euphrates]] and the Gulf with the [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]], and its elite blended [[e:aramaic|Aramaic]], Arab, Greek and Roman culture, worshipping Bel and other Semitic gods. Zenobia kept a learned court that included the rhetorician Longinus. In 270 her armies took [[e:egypt|Egypt]] and much of [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]], and in 272 Vaballathus was proclaimed Augustus, an open break with [[e:rome|Rome]].
palmyrene-empire.e: The emperor Aurelian defeated Zenobia's armies at Immae and [[s:emesene-dynasty|Emesa]] in 272, besieged Palmyra and captured her as she fled towards [[e:persia|Persia]]. When the city rebelled again in 273 it was sacked and never recovered its wealth. Zenobia was taken to [[e:rome|Rome]].

pagaruyung-kingdom.t: The royal seat of the Minangkabau of West Sumatra, founded by Adityawarman and destroyed in the Padri War of the 19th century.
pagaruyung-kingdom.o: In 1347 Adityawarman, a prince who had served [[e:majapahit-empire|Majapahit]], proclaimed himself king of [[s:melayu-kingdom|Malayu]] at [[s:dharmasraya|Dharmasraya]] and moved his court up into the Minangkabau highlands, near Pagaruyung in the Tanah Datar valley. He left more than twenty inscriptions in [[e:sanskrit|Sanskrit]] and [[e:old-malay|Old Malay]] and patronised Tantric [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]].
pagaruyung-kingdom.r: Later rulers converted to [[e:islam|Islam]] in the 16th century. Royal authority was shared among the Rajo Tigo Selo, three kings of the world, of custom and of religion, but real power lay with the village councils under matrilineal [[e:adat|adat]] law. Gold from highland mines made the court famous, and Minangkabau migrants carried its prestige to [[s:negeri-sembilan|Negeri Sembilan]].
pagaruyung-kingdom.e: During the Padri War, reformist Muslims killed much of the royal family around 1815. Surviving nobles invited the [[e:dutch|Dutch]], who intervened from 1821. In 1833 the Dutch arrested the regent [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Tangkal Alam Bagagar and exiled him to [[e:batavia|Batavia]], ending the kingdom. A replica palace stands at Pagaruyung today.

principality-of-svaneti.t: A princely domain in the high Caucasus valleys of Svaneti, home of the stone defence towers, ruled by the Dadeshkeliani family until Russia ended it in 1858.
principality-of-svaneti.o: Svaneti, the highest inhabited valleys of the [[e:caucasus|Caucasus]], had long been a duchy of [[s:georgia|Georgia]]. After the kingdom broke apart, the free communities of Upper Svaneti governed themselves, while Lower Svaneti and part of the upper valley came under the Dadeshkeliani princes by about 1600, nominally as [[e:vassal|vassals]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-imereti|Kingdom of Imereti]].
principality-of-svaneti.r: The Svans lived in villages of fortified stone towers, guarding treasures of medieval icons and [[e:manuscript|manuscripts]] in their churches. Society was organised around clans, blood feuds and village assemblies, with the princes taking dues from peasants. The princes competed with the Dadiani of [[s:principality-of-mingrelia|Mingrelia]] and preserved the distinct Svan language.
principality-of-svaneti.e: The Dadeshkeliani accepted a Russian [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] in 1833. In 1857 Prince Constantine Dadeshkeliani killed the Russian governor Gagarin during a dispute and was executed, and in 1858 the [[s:russian-empire|Russian Empire]] abolished the principality.

peoples-socialist-republic-of-albania.t: Enver Hoxha's communist Albania, the most isolated state in Europe, which broke in turn with Yugoslavia, the Soviet Union and China and banned all religion.
peoples-socialist-republic-of-albania.o: Enver Hoxha's Communist-led Partisans took power as German forces withdrew in November 1944 from the [[s:albanian-kingdom-1943-1944|Albanian Kingdom]] (1943-1944). After elections with a single list in December 1945, the monarchy was formally abolished and the People's [[s:albania|Republic of Albania]] proclaimed on 11 January 1946, with Hoxha as leader. Opponents were tried, executed or imprisoned.
peoples-socialist-republic-of-albania.r: The regime was strictly Stalinist: land was collectivised, industry nationalised and the Sigurimi secret police watched everyone. Hoxha broke with [[e:yugoslavia|Yugoslavia]] in 1948, the [[s:soviet-union|Soviet Union]] in 1961 and [[e:china|China]] in 1978, leaving [[s:albania|Albania]] almost alone. In 1967 it declared itself the world's first atheist state, closing all mosques and churches, and built hundreds of thousands of concrete bunkers. It was renamed the People's Socialist Republic in 1976.
peoples-socialist-republic-of-albania.e: After Hoxha died in 1985, Ramiz Alia allowed cautious change. Student protests and mass flight abroad in 1990 forced the legalisation of opposition parties, and after the first multi-party elections the country was renamed the [[s:albania|Republic of Albania]] in April 1991.

powys-fadog.t: The northern half of the Welsh kingdom of Powys, ruled by Madog ap Maredudd's descendants from Castell Dinas Bran above Llangollen.
powys-fadog.o: When Madog ap Maredudd, the last king of all [[s:kingdom-of-powys|Powys]], died in 1160, his kingdom split. The northern part passed to his son Gruffydd Maelor and then to Gruffydd's son Madog ap Gruffydd Maelor, after whom it was named Powys Fadog, covering Maelor, Ial, Edeirnion and Cynllaith.
powys-fadog.r: Its princes usually aligned with Gwynedd's [[s:principality-of-wales|Principality of Wales]] against the English crown. Madog ap Gruffydd founded the Cistercian abbey of Valle Crucis around 1201, and Gruffydd ap Madog built [[s:county-of-castell|Castell]] Dinas Bran around 1260.
powys-fadog.e: Powys Fadog's princes backed Llywelyn ap Gruffudd in his final war, and after his death in 1282 Edward I granted the lands to English lords. Its line survived as minor [[e:gentry|gentry]]; Owain Glyndwr, who led the [[s:principality-of-wales-under-owain-glyndwr|Principality of Wales under Owain Glyndwr]], descended from it.

portuguese-guinea.t: Portugal's colony on the Upper Guinea coast, which won independence as Guinea-Bissau after a liberation war led by Amilcar Cabral.
portuguese-guinea.o: Portuguese and Cape Verdean traders had been active in the rivers of the [[e:guinea|Guinea]] coast since the 15th century. In 1588 the town of Cacheu was founded as a fortified trading base, followed by Bissau in the late 17th century. For long the posts were governed from [[s:portuguese-cape-verde|Portuguese Cape Verde]].
portuguese-guinea.r: For centuries Portuguese control barely reached beyond a few trading towns, where Luso-African traders dealt in slaves and later [[e:groundnut|groundnuts]]. The colony was separated from [[e:cape-verde|Cape Verde]] in 1879, and military campaigns between 1912 and 1915 imposed control over the interior. Under the [[e:estado-novo-portugal|Estado Novo]] it was governed through chiefs and forced labour.
portuguese-guinea.e: From 1963 the PAIGC, led by Amilcar Cabral until his assassination in 1973, fought a [[e:guerrilla-warfare|guerrilla]] war that liberated much of the countryside. Independence was declared in 1973, and Portugal recognised [[e:guinea-bissau|Guinea-Bissau]] in 1974 after its revolution.
