principality-of-rugen.t: Slavic principality on the Baltic island of Rügen whose princes, once pagan Rani, became Danish vassals and founders of Stralsund before dying out in 1325.
principality-of-rugen.o: The Slavic [[s:rani|Rani]] ruled Rügen from the temple fortress of Arkona, sanctuary of the god Svantevit. In 1168 King Valdemar I of [[e:denmark|Denmark]] and [[e:bishop|Bishop]] Absalon stormed Arkona, destroyed the idol and forced the Rani to accept [[e:christianity|Christianity]] and Danish overlordship. The native princely house kept its rule as Danish [[e:vassal|vassals]], first under Prince Tetzlav and then under his brother Jaromar I.
principality-of-rugen.r: The princes held the island and a strip of the Pomeranian mainland, where Wizlaw I granted Stralsund town rights in 1234. They founded monasteries such as Bergen and Eldena and invited German settlers, so Low German gradually replaced the Slavic speech of the [[s:rani|Rani]]. The court combined Danish loyalty with growing ties to the German north, and Wizlaw III composed love songs as a minnesinger.
principality-of-rugen.e: Wizlaw III died without a son in 1325, and the principality passed by inheritance treaty to the [[s:duchy-of-pomerania-wolgast|Duchy of Pomerania-Wolgast]] after a war of succession against [[s:lordship-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg]]. Rügen stayed Pomeranian, then Swedish and Prussian, and is now part of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

pudukkottai-state.t: The only Tamil princely state under the Madras Presidency, ruled by the Thondaiman Rajas from 1686 to 1948.
pudukkottai-state.o: Pudukkottai was founded in 1686 by Raghunatha Raya Thondaiman, a chief who had served the [[s:ramnad-kingdom|Sethupathis of Ramnad]]. The Thondaimans established an independent principality between Thanjavur and Ramnad.
pudukkottai-state.r: The Rajas allied with the British in the Carnatic Wars and against Mysore, which secured them recognition and protection. The state was a seventeen-gun salute state. Its territory contained many early temples, including the rock-cut cave temples at Sittannavasal with notable paintings. Martanda Bhairava Thondaiman spent much of his reign abroad.
pudukkottai-state.e: Pudukkottai merged into [[s:madras-presidency|Madras Province]] in March 1948 and is now a district of Tamil Nadu.

principality-of-furstenberg.t: Black Forest state of the Fürstenberg family, heirs of the Zähringen, whose court at Donaueschingen stood beside the source of the Danube.
principality-of-furstenberg.o: When the Zähringen line died out in 1218, the counts of Urach inherited part of their lands in the Baar and the Black Forest. Count Henry took the name Fürstenberg, after a castle near Donaueschingen, around 1250, founding a comital house that ruled the upper [[e:danube|Danube]] and Kinzig valleys.
principality-of-furstenberg.r: The family split into several lines, and its counts served the [[e:habsburg-dynasty|Habsburgs]] as officers and diplomats. Branches were raised to princely rank in 1664 and 1716, and in 1744 the lands were reunited under Joseph Wilhelm Ernst, with Donaueschingen as residence. The territory produced [[e:timber|timber]], iron and beer, and the court library acquired [[e:manuscript|manuscript]] C of the Nibelungenlied. It stayed Catholic.
principality-of-furstenberg.e: In 1806 Fürstenberg was mediatised and divided mainly between Baden, Württemberg and [[s:principality-of-hohenzollern-sigmaringen|Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen]]. The princely family kept its estates, brewery and palace at Donaueschingen, where the park spring is still presented as the source of the [[e:danube|Danube]].

pictones.t: Gallic people of Poitou who built ships for Caesar against the Veneti and gave their name to Poitiers and Poitou.
pictones.o: The Pictones held the land south of the lower Loire, around Lemonum (Poitiers), with a coastline on the Atlantic. They were among the larger peoples of western Gaul.
pictones.r: Caesar used their shipyards in 56 BCE for the fleet that defeated the [[s:veneti|Veneti]]. Their leader Duratius remained loyal to [[e:rome|Rome]], which split the people during the revolts.
pictones.e: In 51 BCE Duratius was besieged in Lemonum by Dumnacus of the [[s:andecavi|Andecavi]] until Roman forces relieved him. Under [[e:rome|Rome]] Lemonum, later called Pictavi, became Poitiers, a major city and bishopric, and the region kept the name [[s:county-of-poitou|Poitou]].

principality-of-arbanon.t: The first Albanian state, a principality around Krujë ruled by the Progon family under Byzantine, Serbian and Epirote overlords.
principality-of-arbanon.o: Arbanon, in the mountains around Krujë in central [[s:albania|Albania]], gained autonomy in the late 12th century as Byzantine power declined. Its first known ruler was the archon Progon, around 1190, followed by his sons Gjin and Dhimitër.
principality-of-arbanon.r: The archons ruled a Catholic and [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] Albanian population from Krujë, balancing [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]], [[s:serbia|Serbia]], [[e:venice|Venice]] and the [[e:papacy|papacy]]. Dhimitër Progoni, who styled himself panhypersebastos, married Komnena, daughter of the Serbian ruler Stefan the First-Crowned, and corresponded with Pope Innocent III. After his death around 1215, the Greek lord Gregory Kamonas and then Golem ruled.
principality-of-arbanon.e: From the 1230s Arbanon fell under the [[s:despotate-of-epirus|Despotate of Epirus]] and then the [[s:empire-of-nicaea|Empire of Nicaea]], which took over Krujë around 1255. The area later formed part of the [[s:kingdom-of-albania-medieval|Kingdom of Albania (medieval)]].

province-of-quebec.t: Britain's first government of conquered French Canada, whose Quebec Act of 1774 protected Catholic religion and French civil law.
province-of-quebec.o: After the British conquest of [[s:new-france|New France]] in 1759 to 1760, the Treaty of [[e:paris|Paris]] of 1763 ceded [[s:province-of-canada|Canada]] to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]], and the Royal Proclamation of that year organised the St Lawrence settlements as the Province of [[e:quebec|Quebec]]. Its first civil governor, James Murray, soon found that plans to anglicise the French-speaking Catholic population were impractical.
province-of-quebec.r: The [[e:quebec|Quebec]] Act of 1774 extended the province into the Ohio country, allowed Catholics to hold office, kept the seigneurial system and French [[e:civil-law|civil law]], and recognised the Church's right to collect tithes. Government lay with a governor and appointed council, with no elected assembly. The economy rested on farming and the [[e:fur-trade|fur trade]] out of Montreal. American forces invaded in 1775 but failed to take Quebec City.
province-of-quebec.e: The arrival of thousands of Loyalists after 1783 created pressure for English law and representative government. The Constitutional Act of 1791 divided the province into [[s:lower-canada|Lower Canada]] and [[s:upper-canada|Upper Canada]], each with an elected assembly.

palanpur-state.t: A Pashtun-ruled state of northern Gujarat whose Lohani Nawabs held power for centuries, and whose Jain merchants later came to dominate the diamond trade.
palanpur-state.o: The ruling Lohani family, of Afghan origin, served the sultans of the region and by tradition held Jalore before establishing themselves at Palanpur. The register's start date follows family tradition; the dynasty was firmly settled at Palanpur by the 17th century.
palanpur-state.r: Palanpur was a largely agricultural state on the border of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] and Rajasthan, under Mughal and then [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] influence before coming under British protection in 1817. Its Muslim Nawabs ruled a mainly [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] and Jain population. The Palanpuri Jain merchant community later became leading diamond traders in Bombay and [[e:antwerp|Antwerp]].
palanpur-state.e: Nawab Taley Muhammad Khan acceded to [[e:india|India]], and Palanpur merged into Bombay State in 1949. It is now in Banaskantha district, [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]].

principality-of-turov-and-pinsk.t: A principality of the Pripyat marshes in southern Belarus, known for the preacher Cyril of Turov.
principality-of-turov-and-pinsk.o: Turov on the Pripyat had been an early seat of Rus' princes, ruled by Sviatopolk, son of Vladimir I, in the late 10th century. It was long attached to Kiev, but in the late 1150s Yuri Yaroslavich, a grandson of Sviatopolk II, made it independent, founding a local dynasty.
principality-of-turov-and-pinsk.r: The principality covered the wet, wooded lands of the [[s:dregovichs|Dregovichs]] and lived from farming, fishing and river trade. Its [[e:bishop|bishop]] Cyril of Turov, who died around 1182, was one of the finest preachers and writers of early Rus'. Over time it split into smaller [[e:appanage|appanages]] based on Turov, Pinsk and other towns, and its princes became minor players.
principality-of-turov-and-pinsk.e: After the Mongol invasion its lands weakened further, and in the early 14th century they were absorbed by the [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Grand Duchy of Lithuania]] under Gediminas. Pinsk later became a Lithuanian [[e:appanage|appanage]] duchy.

cr.a: Goran tek-en, following request by and knowledge from Veverve

principality-of-arches-charleville.t: A sovereign principality on the Meuse where Charles of Gonzaga founded the planned city of Charleville in 1606.
principality-of-arches-charleville.o: Charles of Gonzaga, duke of [[s:county-of-nevers|Nevers]] and Rethel, held the land of Arches on the Meuse, which claimed to lie outside both [[e:france|France]] and the Empire. In 1606 he founded a new town there, Charleville, named after himself, and ruled it as a sovereign principality.
principality-of-arches-charleville.r: Charleville was laid out on a regular plan around the Place Ducale, modelled on the Place des Vosges in [[e:paris|Paris]]. The principality minted its own coins and attracted craftsmen with tax exemptions. Charles later became duke of [[s:duchy-of-mantua|Mantua]] in 1627, and his Gonzaga heirs ruled the principality from [[e:italy|Italy]].
principality-of-arches-charleville.e: The last Gonzaga duke, Ferdinando Carlo, died in 1708 after siding with [[e:france|France]] in the [[e:war-of-the-spanish-succession|War of the Spanish Succession]]. [[e:louis-xiv|Louis XIV]] then took the principality into the [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]], though the Condé family claimed it.

portuguese-congo.t: The Portuguese protectorate of Cabinda, an enclave north of the Congo River whose oil and separatism shape Angolan politics.
portuguese-congo.o: Portugal had traded on the [[s:kingdom-of-loango|Loango]] coast for centuries. To secure its claim against [[e:france|France]] and [[e:leopold-ii|Leopold II]], it signed the Treaty of Simulambuco with the princes and chiefs of Cabinda on 1 February 1885, establishing a [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] over territory once ruled by the [[s:kingdom-of-ngoyo|Kingdom of Ngoyo]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-kakongo|Kingdom of Kakongo]].
portuguese-congo.r: The Berlin Conference left Cabinda separated from [[s:portuguese-angola|Portuguese Angola]] by a strip of land given to the [[s:congo-free-state|Congo Free State]]. It was governed from Cabinda town, at first separately and from the 1920s increasingly as a district of [[e:angola|Angola]]. [[e:timber|Timber]], cocoa and [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]] were exported, and from the 1960s offshore oil discovered by Cabinda Gulf Oil became the enclave's main resource.
portuguese-congo.e: Separatists of the Front for the Liberation of the Enclave of Cabinda claimed independence, but the 1975 Alvor Agreement made Cabinda part of independent [[s:portuguese-angola|Angola]], where it remains a province with a low-level separatist conflict.

prince-bishopric-of-brandenburg.t: An Ottonian missionary bishopric on the Havel that, after a long exile, became a small church territory absorbed by the Hohenzollern electors.
prince-bishopric-of-brandenburg.o: [[e:otto-i|Otto I]] founded the bishopric of [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]] in 948 at the captured [[s:principality-of-the-hevelli|Hevelli]] stronghold of Brenna, as part of his eastern mission, placing it under Magdeburg in 968. In the Great Slav Rising of 983 the [[e:slavs|Slavs]] destroyed the see, and its [[e:bishop|bishops]] lived as titular exiles until the 12th century.
prince-bishopric-of-brandenburg.r: After Albert the Bear took [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]] in 1157, the Premonstratensian cathedral chapter was re-established, and the cathedral on the island in Brandenburg an der Havel was begun in 1165. The [[e:bishop|bishops]] held a small territory around Ziesar, where they built their residence, but the margraves dominated them and claimed the right to nominate bishops.
prince-bishopric-of-brandenburg.e: [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]] became Lutheran under Elector Joachim II from 1539, and the last Catholic [[e:bishop|bishop]], Matthias von Jagow, accepted the change. The prince-bishopric was secularised and fully incorporated into the [[s:margraviate-of-brandenburg|Margraviate of Brandenburg]] by 1571. The cathedral chapter continued as a Protestant institution.

principality-of-piombino.t: A small Tuscan coastal state with the iron mines of Elba, ruled by the Appiani and later the Ludovisi and Boncompagni.
principality-of-piombino.o: In 1399 Gherardo Appiani, lord of Pisa, sold the city to Gian Galeazzo Visconti but kept Piombino, Elba and nearby islands as his own lordship. His family ruled it as lords and, from 1594, as imperial princes.
principality-of-piombino.r: Piombino controlled the iron mines of Elba and the channel between Elba and the mainland, a strategic route for [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]] shipping. Its small size made it dependent on stronger powers: Cosimo I de' Medici built Portoferraio on Elba in 1548, and [[e:spain|Spain]] later held Porto Longone. After the Appiani died out, the principality passed to the Ludovisi in 1634 and then to the Boncompagni-Ludovisi.
principality-of-piombino.e: In 1805 [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]] gave Piombino to his sister Elisa, merging it into the [[s:principality-of-lucca-and-piombino|Principality of Lucca and Piombino]]. In 1815 the [[e:congress-of-vienna|Congress of Vienna]] gave it to the [[s:grand-duchy-of-tuscany|Grand Duchy of Tuscany]].

potidaea.t: Corinthian colony on the isthmus of Pallene in Chalcidice whose revolt against Athens in 432 BCE helped trigger the Peloponnesian War.
potidaea.o: Potidaea was founded around 600 BCE by [[s:corinth|Corinth]] under the tyrant Periander, whose son Evagoras is named as founder. It stood on the narrow neck of the Pallene peninsula, controlling the way into it, and remained unusually close to its mother city, which still sent it annual magistrates in the 5th century BCE.
potidaea.r: A walled port city with an assembly and magistrates, Potidaea lived from trade in the northern [[e:aegean|Aegean]], Macedonian [[e:timber|timber]] and the produce of Pallene. It held out against the Persian commander Artabazus in 480-479 BCE and fought at [[s:plataea|Plataea]]. As a tribute-paying member of the [[s:delian-league|Delian League]] it was caught between loyalty to [[s:athens|Athens]] and its Corinthian ties.
potidaea.e: Ordered by [[s:athens|Athens]] to pull down its walls and expel the Corinthian magistrates, Potidaea revolted in 432 BCE and surrendered after a costly siege in 430 BCE; Athenian settlers replaced its people. It later joined the [[s:chalcidian-league|Chalcidian League]], was retaken by [[e:athens|Athens]] in 364 BCE and was captured by Philip II in 356 BCE. [[e:cassander|Cassander]] refounded it as Cassandreia.

principality-of-novgorod-seversky.t: A frontier principality of the Chernigov lands, home of Prince Igor, whose failed campaign against the Cumans inspired a great epic.
principality-of-novgorod-seversky.o: Novgorod-Seversky on the Desna was an old Severian town. At the Lyubech conference of 1097 it was assigned to the sons of [[e:sviatoslav-i-of-kiev|Sviatoslav]] II of [[e:chernigov|Chernigov]], and it became the seat of a junior branch of the Olgovichi, second only to Chernigov itself in their lands.
principality-of-novgorod-seversky.r: Its princes held a frontier zone exposed to the steppe and fought the Cumans as often as they allied with them. In 1185 Prince Igor Sviatoslavich led a raid against the Cumans that ended in his defeat and capture, the subject of the Lay of Igor's Campaign. Later princes included Dmitry Koribut, a son of Algirdas.
principality-of-novgorod-seversky.e: After the Mongol invasion the land passed to the [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Grand Duchy of Lithuania]] in the 14th century. In 1500 Vasily Shemyachich transferred his allegiance to the [[s:grand-duchy-of-moscow|Grand Duchy of Moscow]], which kept the territory by the truce of 1503. Vasily III arrested Shemyachich in 1523 and abolished the principality.

pattani-kingdom.t: A Malay sultanate on the east coast of the peninsula, famous for its 17th-century queens and annexed by Siam in 1902.
pattani-kingdom.o: Pattani grew as the successor to the old [[s:langkasuka|Langkasuka]] trading region. According to the Hikayat Patani, its ruler Phaya Tu Nakpa accepted [[e:islam|Islam]] in the mid-15th century, taking the name [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Ismail Shah, and the port rose as [[e:malacca|Malacca's]] trade expanded. It was nominally a tributary of [[s:ayutthaya-kingdom|Ayutthaya]].
pattani-kingdom.r: From 1584 Pattani was ruled for a century by four queens, Raja Hijau, Raja Biru, Raja Ungu and Raja Kuning. Chinese, Japanese, Portuguese and [[e:dutch|Dutch]] merchants traded there; the [[s:dutch-east-india-company-territories|Dutch East India Company]] opened a factory in 1602 and the English in 1612. Pattani was also a centre of Islamic learning, producing scholars such as Daud al-Fatani.
pattani-kingdom.e: Siam conquered Pattani in 1786 and split it into seven provinces in the early 19th century. In 1902 it annexed the area fully and deposed Raja Abdul Kadir Kamaruddin, a settlement [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] accepted in the Anglo-Siamese Treaty of 1909. The legacy shapes the Malay Muslim provinces of southern [[s:thailand|Thailand]].

peureulak-sultanate.t: A port on the east coast of Aceh claimed by tradition as the first Muslim sultanate in Southeast Asia, and seen as Muslim by Marco Polo in 1292.
peureulak-sultanate.o: Local tradition, recorded in late [[e:manuscript|manuscripts]] whose authenticity is disputed, says a sultanate was founded at Perlak in 840 by a ruler of Arab descent. Historians treat this date with caution. Perlak lay on the [[e:strait-of-malacca|Strait of Malacca]] and attracted Muslim merchants from [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]], [[e:persia|Persia]] and [[e:arabia|Arabia]].
peureulak-sultanate.r: The port exported [[e:pepper|pepper]] and forest products and was a meeting place for Muslim traders. When [[e:marco-polo|Marco Polo]] stopped at Ferlec in 1292 he reported that its townspeople had been converted to [[e:islam|Islam]] by Saracen merchants, while the people of the hills were not.
peureulak-sultanate.e: Perlak declined in the late 13th century and was absorbed by the neighbouring [[s:samudera-pasai-sultanate|Samudera Pasai Sultanate]], tradition says through a royal marriage. Today the region is part of East Aceh, and Indonesians often cite Perlak as the place where [[e:islam|Islam]] first took hold in the archipelago.

puerto-rico-united-states.t: Former Spanish colony ruled by the United States since 1898, a Commonwealth since 1952 whose people are US citizens without a vote in Congress.
puerto-rico-united-states.o: American troops landed at Guánica in July 1898 during the [[e:spanish-american-war|Spanish-American War]], months after [[e:spain|Spain]] had granted [[e:puerto-rico|Puerto Rico]] an autonomous charter. The Treaty of [[e:paris|Paris]] ceded the island to the [[s:united-states|United States]], and military rule gave way to civil government under the Foraker Act of 1900, with an appointed governor.
puerto-rico-united-states.r: The Jones Act of 1917 made Puerto Ricans US citizens. American [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] companies dominated the economy until the 1940s. The Nationalist Party of Pedro Albizu Campos demanded independence, and police killed protesters at Ponce in 1937. Luis Muñoz Marín became the first elected governor in 1948, and in 1952 the island became the Estado Libre Asociado, or Commonwealth, with its own constitution. Operation Bootstrap industrialised it, while hundreds of thousands migrated to [[e:new-york|New York]].
puerto-rico-united-states.e: [[e:puerto-rico|Puerto Rico]] remains an unincorporated US territory. Repeated referendums have shown divisions between statehood, Commonwealth and independence. A debt crisis led Congress to impose a fiscal oversight board in 2016, and Hurricane Maria devastated the island in 2017.

prince-bishopric-of-augsburg.t: Swabian church state of the bishops of Augsburg, who were forced out of their own cathedral city and governed instead from Dillingen on the Danube.
prince-bishopric-of-augsburg.o: The diocese of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-augsburg|Augsburg]] dates from late Roman times and was led in the 10th century by Saint Ulrich, who defended the city at the Lechfeld in 955. From the late 12th century the [[e:bishop|bishops]] assembled a secular territory along the Lech and [[e:danube|Danube]]. As the city itself won independence as the Free Imperial City of [[e:augsburg|Augsburg]], they moved their residence to Dillingen.
prince-bishopric-of-augsburg.r: The cathedral chapter elected the prince-[[e:bishop|bishop]], who ruled scattered lands including Dillingen, Füssen and parts of the Allgäu. Cardinal Otto [[s:county-of-waldburg|Truchsess von Waldburg]] founded the University of Dillingen in 1551, run by the [[e:jesuits|Jesuits]] from 1563, which made the territory a Counter-[[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] stronghold. Its estates were rural, with farms, forests and small market towns.
prince-bishopric-of-augsburg.e: The territory was secularised in 1802 and annexed by the [[s:electorate-of-bavaria|Electorate of Bavaria]], ending the [[e:bishop|bishops]]' secular rule; the last prince-bishop, Clemens Wenceslaus of Saxony, was also Elector of [[e:trier|Trier]]. The Catholic diocese of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-augsburg|Augsburg]] continues today.

principality-of-thessaly.t: Greek principality in Thessaly ruled by an offshoot of the Epirote dynasty, independent of Byzantium until the Catalans and Byzantines divided it.
principality-of-thessaly.o: On the death of Michael II of the [[s:despotate-of-epirus|Despotate of Epirus]] around 1268, his illegitimate son John I Doukas received Thessaly, with its capital at Neopatras. Byzantine writers called the region Great Vlachia, after its many Vlach inhabitants. John resisted [[e:michael-viii-palaiologos|Michael VIII Palaiologos]], defeating a Byzantine army at Neopatras around 1275.
principality-of-thessaly.r: John I held the Byzantine title of sebastokrator and ruled a mixed Greek and Vlach population of farmers and herders through local [[e:magnates|magnates]]. He allied with the [[e:latin|Latin]] [[s:duchy-of-athens|Duchy of Athens]] and the [[s:principality-of-achaea|Principality of Achaea]] against the restored [[s:byzantine-empire|Byzantine Empire]]. His sons Constantine and John II continued his policies, John II marrying a daughter of Andronikos II.
principality-of-thessaly.e: When John II died without heirs in 1318, Thessaly broke apart. The Catalan Company, ruling the [[s:duchy-of-athens|Duchy of Athens]], seized the south and created the [[s:duchy-of-neopatras|Duchy of Neopatras]], while local lords and the [[e:byzantine-empire|Byzantines]] took the north.

principality-of-abasgia.t: A Byzantine-aligned principality on the Black Sea coast of Abkhazia that grew into the Kingdom of Abkhazia in the late 8th century.
principality-of-abasgia.o: The Abasgoi lived on the coast north-west of [[s:kingdom-of-lazica|Lazica]]. In the mid-6th century the [[s:byzantine-empire|Byzantine Empire]] under [[e:justinian-i|Justinian I]] extended control over them, ended a local practice of selling [[e:eunuch|eunuchs]] to [[e:constantinople|Constantinople]], and sponsored their conversion to [[e:christianity|Christianity]], with a church built for them.
principality-of-abasgia.r: Local princes, called archons by the [[e:greeks|Greeks]], ruled as Byzantine clients from the hill fortress of Anacopia, near New Athos. The economy rested on farming, livestock and coastal trade. Anacopia withstood an Arab siege in 737, and the victory brought Leon I recognition as hereditary ruler from [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]].
principality-of-abasgia.e: His nephew Leon II, whose mother was a [[e:khazar-khaganate|Khazar]] princess, used Khazar support around 778 to throw off Byzantine authority, unite Abasgia with [[s:kingdom-of-lazica|Egrisi]] and take the title king, founding the [[s:kingdom-of-abkhazia|Kingdom of Abkhazia]].

principality-of-taranto.t: A great southern Italian fief created for the crusader Bohemond, later held by princes so powerful they rivalled the kings of Naples.
principality-of-taranto.o: After Robert Guiscard's death the Norman inheritance was divided, and in 1088 his eldest son Bohemond received Taranto and much of the heel of [[e:italy|Italy]] as compensation for losing the [[s:duchy-of-apulia-and-calabria|Duchy of Apulia and Calabria]] to his half-brother Roger Borsa. Bohemond soon left on the [[e:first-crusade|First Crusade]] and founded the [[s:principality-of-antioch|Principality of Antioch]].
principality-of-taranto.r: Taranto became a fief within the [[s:kingdom-of-sicily|Kingdom of Sicily]] and then the [[s:kingdom-of-naples|Kingdom of Naples]], often granted to royal relatives, such as the Angevin Philip I of Taranto from 1294. Its princes controlled the ports and olive and grain lands of Apulia and could field large armies. Under the Orsini del Balzo in the 15th century it covered much of southern Apulia.
principality-of-taranto.e: Prince Giovanni Antonio Orsini del Balzo, who rebelled against King Ferrante, died in 1463 without legitimate heirs. Ferrante seized his lands, and the principality was absorbed into the royal domain of the [[s:kingdom-of-naples|Kingdom of Naples]].

cr.a: My own edits, upon original work by MapMapster

principality-of-anhalt.t: Ascanian principality between the Harz and the Elbe that adopted the Reformation early and was repeatedly divided among branches of its ruling house.
principality-of-anhalt.o: Henry I, son of Duke Bernhard of Saxony of the Ascanian house, received the family's ancestral lands around the Harz and middle Elbe when his father's possessions were divided in 1212. He took the title Count, then Prince, of Anhalt, after the castle of that name near Harzgerode, founding a principality separate from Saxony.
principality-of-anhalt.r: Anhalt was repeatedly split among branches, such as Aschersleben, Bernburg, Köthen and Zerbst, each ruling small towns and farmland along the Elbe and Saale. Prince Wolfgang of [[s:principality-of-anhalt-kothen|Anhalt-Köthen]] signed the [[s:free-imperial-city-of-augsburg|Augsburg]] Confession in 1530, making Anhalt an early Lutheran land, and it later turned Reformed. Joachim Ernst reunited the territories in 1570 and issued a [[e:common-law|common law]] code.
principality-of-anhalt.e: After Joachim Ernst's death, his sons divided Anhalt in 1603 into [[s:principality-of-anhalt-dessau|Anhalt-Dessau]], [[s:principality-of-anhalt-bernburg|Anhalt-Bernburg]], [[s:principality-of-anhalt-kothen|Anhalt-Köthen]], [[s:principality-of-anhalt-zerbst|Anhalt-Zerbst]] and [[s:principality-of-anhalt-plotzkau|Anhalt-Plötzkau]]. These lines were reunited as the [[s:duchy-of-anhalt|Duchy of Anhalt]] in 1863, which became a free state in 1918 and is now part of Saxony-Anhalt.
principality-of-anhalt.re: Catholicism, then Lutheranism and Reformed Protestantism

persarmenia.t: The Persian-ruled part of Armenia after the end of its monarchy, where Armenians fought to keep their Christian faith and their church took its independent path.
persarmenia.o: When the [[s:kingdom-of-armenia-arsacid|Kingdom of Armenia (Arsacid)]] was abolished in 428, the larger eastern part of the country, assigned to [[e:persia|Persia]] by the partition of 387, became a province of the [[s:sasanian-empire|Sasanian Empire]]. It was governed by a marzpan, often an Armenian noble, from the city of Dvin.
persarmenia.r: Armenian noble houses kept their lands and armies, and the church remained central to society. When Yazdegerd II tried to impose [[e:zoroastrianism|Zoroastrianism]], Vardan Mamikonian led a revolt that was crushed at Avarayr in 451 but secured toleration, confirmed by the Treaty of Nvarsak in 484. Councils at Dvin rejected [[s:chalcedon|Chalcedon]], separating the Armenian church from [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]].
persarmenia.e: In 591 most of the province was ceded to [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]], and later wars returned it to contest. Arab armies took Dvin in 640, and by the 650s the region had become the [[s:principality-of-armenia|Principality of Armenia]] under the [[e:caliphate|caliphate]].

principality-of-kastrioti.t: Central Albanian lordship of the Kastrioti family, the base from which Gjergj Kastrioti, Skanderbeg, launched his revolt against the Ottomans.
principality-of-kastrioti.o: The Kastrioti family appears in the late 14th century, when Pal Kastrioti held two villages including Sinë, in the Dibër region. His son Gjon Kastrioti built a lordship stretching from the Mat valley towards the Adriatic coast near Lezhë, accepting Ottoman overlordship after the 1380s while trading with [[e:venice|Venice]] and [[s:republic-of-ragusa|Ragusa]].
principality-of-kastrioti.r: Gjon ruled as a regional lord, balancing Ottoman [[e:vassal|vassalage]] with Venetian and Ragusan ties; he was made a citizen of [[e:venice|Venice]] and granted trading rights. As the price of submission he sent his sons to the Ottoman court as hostages, among them Gjergj, who was raised a Muslim and served the sultan as a commander.
principality-of-kastrioti.e: After Gjon's death in 1437 the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] absorbed his lands. In 1443 Gjergj, now called Skanderbeg, deserted the Ottoman army after the battle of Niš, seized Krujë and returned to [[e:christianity|Christianity]]. In 1444 he gathered the Albanian nobles in the [[s:league-of-lezhe|League of Lezhë]], which inherited the Kastrioti lordship.

pate-sultanate.t: The leading city-state of the northern Swahili coast in the 17th and 18th centuries, ruled by the Nabhani dynasty and a cradle of Swahili poetry.
pate-sultanate.o: The Pate Chronicle claims that the Nabhani family, once rulers in [[e:oman|Oman]], arrived on Pate island in the 13th century and took power by marriage. Archaeology shows the town flourishing by the 14th century, though the chronicle's early dates are doubted. From Pate the sultans gradually extended their influence over the [[s:lamu|Lamu]] archipelago and the mainland coast.
pate-sultanate.r: Pate was a merchant city ruled by a sultan and leading families, trading [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]], cloth and slaves. It submitted to the Portuguese for a time but backed [[e:oman|Oman]] against them. In the 18th century Pate reached its peak, and its scholars produced some of the earliest [[e:swahili|Swahili]] written poetry, such as the Utendi wa Tambuka, composed in 1728.
pate-sultanate.e: Succession quarrels, defeat by [[s:lamu|Lamu]] at the Battle of Shela around 1812 and the rise of [[s:sultanate-of-zanzibar|Zanzibar]] brought decline, and Pate came under the [[s:omani-empire|Omani Empire]]. In 1858 the Nabhani leader Ahmad Simba moved to the mainland and founded the [[s:witu-sultanate|Witu Sultanate]].

principality-of-antioch.t: A Norman-founded Crusader principality in northern Syria that lasted 170 years until Baybars destroyed its capital in 1268.
principality-of-antioch.o: The [[e:first-crusade|First Crusade]] besieged [[e:antioch|Antioch]] from October 1097 and took it in June 1098, then defeated Kerbogha's relief army. Bohemond of [[s:principality-of-taranto|Taranto]], a Norman from southern [[e:italy|Italy]], kept the city for himself despite promises to return it to [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]], founding the principality.
principality-of-antioch.r: [[e:antioch|Antioch's]] princes ruled a population of Greek [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]], [[e:armenians|Armenians]], [[e:syriac|Syriac]] Christians and Muslims, with Italian merchants in Latakia and the port of Saint Symeon. The Assizes of Antioch codified its law. Its army was crushed at the Field of Blood in 1119, and in 1137 Raymond of Poitiers had to accept Byzantine overlordship. In the 13th century it was united with the [[s:county-of-tripoli|County of Tripoli]], and Bohemond VI submitted to the [[e:mongols|Mongols]] in 1260.
principality-of-antioch.e: The [[e:mamluk|Mamluk]] sultan [[e:baybars|Baybars]] stormed [[e:antioch|Antioch]] in May 1268, killing or enslaving much of its population; the city never regained its former importance. The title Prince of Antioch survived in the house of [[s:county-of-tripoli|Tripoli]] and later [[e:cyprus|Cyprus]].

principality-of-vereya.t: The last surviving appanage of the Moscow princes, bequeathed to Ivan III after its heir fled to Lithuania.
principality-of-vereya.o: Vereya, south-west of [[e:moscow|Moscow]], belonged to the lands of Andrei of Mozhaysk. In 1432 his younger son Mikhail Andreyevich began to rule Vereya together with Beloozero as his own [[e:appanage|appanage]].
principality-of-vereya.r: Unlike his brother Ivan of Mozhaysk, Mikhail stayed loyal to Vasily II during [[e:moscow|Moscow's]] civil war, and he was allowed to keep his lands after Mozhaysk was taken in 1454. He ruled a small principality of farmland and forest, dependent on the grand prince for protection and politics.
principality-of-vereya.e: In 1483 Mikhail's son Vasily, nicknamed the Daring, quarrelled with [[e:ivan-iii|Ivan III]] and fled to the [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Grand Duchy of Lithuania]]. Mikhail was forced to leave his lands to Ivan III, and on his death in 1486 Vereya was absorbed into the [[s:grand-duchy-of-moscow|Grand Duchy of Moscow]].

provisional-government-of-assiniboia.t: The Métis-led government formed by Louis Riel at Red River in 1869, whose negotiations with Ottawa created the province of Manitoba.
provisional-government-of-assiniboia.o: In 1869 the Hudson's Bay Company agreed to sell [[s:ruperts-land|Rupert's Land]] to [[s:canada|Canada]] without consulting the people of the [[s:red-river-colony|Red River Colony]]. Alarmed by Canadian surveyors, the Métis formed a National Committee, turned back the incoming lieutenant governor, William McDougall, and in November seized Upper Fort Garry. A provisional government followed in December, with Louis Riel as president from late that month.
provisional-government-of-assiniboia.r: Riel's government drew in English-speaking delegates through a convention that drafted a List of Rights, including provincial status, bilingual institutions and protection of land. It held prisoners from the Canadian party, and in March 1870 executed one of them, Thomas Scott, an act that inflamed Protestant Ontario. Delegates sent to Ottawa negotiated the terms that became the Manitoba Act.
provisional-government-of-assiniboia.e: The Manitoba Act of May 1870 created the province. When the Wolseley Expedition arrived in August, Riel fled. Promised land for the Métis was largely lost, but Riel is now honoured in Manitoba as its founder.

principality-of-smolensk.t: A wealthy Rus' principality on the upper Dnieper, long fought over by Lithuania and Moscow.
principality-of-smolensk.o: [[e:smolensk|Smolensk]], the old centre of the [[s:krivichs|Krivichs]], stood where goods were portaged between the [[e:dnieper|Dnieper]], the Dvina and the [[e:volga|Volga]]. Rostislav Mstislavich, grandson of Vladimir Monomakh, became its prince in 1127 and made it independent of Kiev, setting up a bishopric in 1136. His descendants, the Rostislavichi, ruled it for almost three centuries.
principality-of-smolensk.r: [[e:smolensk|Smolensk]] grew rich from trade with the Baltic, and in 1229 its prince Mstislav Davydovich made a treaty with Riga and [[s:gotland|Gotland]] that set rules for German merchants. Its princes were strong enough to compete for Kiev and Novgorod. The town built many stone churches, including the surviving Church of Saints Peter and Paul.
principality-of-smolensk.e: [[e:smolensk|Smolensk]] largely escaped the Mongol sack but became a tributary of the [[s:golden-horde|Golden Horde]]. Squeezed between the [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Grand Duchy of Lithuania]] and [[e:moscow|Moscow]], it was taken by Vytautas in 1395, and after a last revolt under Yury Sviatoslavich it was annexed outright in 1404. Moscow captured it in 1514.

cr.a: Goran tek-en, following request by and knowledge from Veverve

principality-of-temirgoy.t: A princely Circassian tribe on the Laba and Belaya rivers, whose dialect became the basis of the modern Adyghe literary language.
principality-of-temirgoy.o: The Temirgoy, or Kemirgoy, were one of the aristocratic Adyghe tribes of [[s:circassia|Circassia]], living along the Laba and Belaya rivers. Their princely house, the Bolotoko, rose to prominence among the western Circassians by the 16th and 17th centuries. Earlier history is not recorded separately.
principality-of-temirgoy.r: Society was ranked into princes, nobles, free peasants and serfs, bound by the Adyghe code of honour. The Temirgoy were among the strongest western tribes and often led coalitions against the [[s:crimean-khanate|Crimean Khanate]] and later [[e:russia|Russia]]. Prince Jambulat Bolotoko led raids and negotiations with Russia in the early 19th century.
principality-of-temirgoy.e: [[e:russia|Russia]] gradually forced the Temirgoy princes into submission, and the [[s:russian-empire|Russian Empire]] completed its conquest of their land in 1864. Many emigrated to the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]], but some remained in what became Adygea, and their dialect underlies literary Adyghe.

paulician-state.t: A fortified refuge of the dualist Paulician Christians on the upper Euphrates, which fought Byzantium alongside the Arab emirs.
paulician-state.o: The Paulicians, a Christian sect that rejected the church hierarchy and the veneration of icons and saw the material world as the work of an evil power, had been persecuted by [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] for generations. After Empress Theodora ordered a massacre of them around 843, the officer Karbeas fled with thousands of followers to the emir of Melitene and founded the stronghold of Tephrike (modern Divrigi).
paulician-state.r: From Tephrike and the forts of Argaous and Amara the Paulicians formed a militarised community that raided Byzantine [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]] in alliance with Umar al-Aqta of the [[s:emirate-of-melitene|Emirate of Melitene]]. After Karbeas died in 863 his nephew Chrysocheir led even bolder raids, reaching Nicaea and [[s:ephesus|Ephesus]] around 869, where his men stabled horses in the church of Saint John.
paulician-state.e: Basil I's forces defeated and killed Chrysocheir at Bathys Ryax in the early 870s, and Tephrike was taken around 878. The Paulicians were scattered; many were resettled in the [[e:balkans|Balkans]] around Philippopolis, where their ideas fed the later Bogomil movement.

principality-of-dukagjini.t: Northern Albanian lordship of the Dukagjini family, whose name survives in the customary law code known as the Kanun of Lekë Dukagjini.
principality-of-dukagjini.o: The Dukagjini were a noble family of the northern Albanian highlands who emerged as regional lords in the late 14th century. Around 1387 they held the port of Lezhë and its hinterland, between the territories of the Balšić lords of Zeta and the Kastrioti. Pressed by the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]], they handed Lezhë to [[e:venice|Venice]] in 1393.
principality-of-dukagjini.r: Power rested on control of mountain clans between the Drin river and the plains of Kosovo, with the family dividing lands among branches. The lords switched between Ottoman [[e:vassal|vassalage]] and Venetian protection, and were Catholic Christians linked to the bishoprics of the region. Highland society was governed by unwritten custom, later codified under the name of Lekë Dukagjini.
principality-of-dukagjini.e: In 1444 Pal and Lekë Dukagjini joined Skanderbeg's [[s:league-of-lezhe|League of Lezhë]], folding the lordship into the wider Albanian resistance. Lekë Dukagjini fought on after Skanderbeg's death until the Ottoman conquest of the late 1470s. The Dukagjini plateau and the [[e:kanun|Kanun]] still bear the family's name.

prince-bishopric-of-naumburg.t: An Ottonian bishopric on the Saale famed for its cathedral's lifelike founder statues, absorbed into Saxony after the Reformation.
prince-bishopric-of-naumburg.o: The bishopric was founded at Zeitz in 968 under Magdeburg. In 1028, with the approval of [[e:papacy|Pope]] John XIX and Emperor Conrad II, it moved to Naumburg, a new seat founded by the Ekkehardine margraves of Meissen. The [[e:bishop|bishops]] ruled lands around Naumburg and Zeitz.
prince-bishopric-of-naumburg.r: Naumburg Cathedral's west choir, made around 1250 by the anonymous Naumburg Master, holds twelve statues of the cathedral's founders, including the margravine Uta, among the finest works of Gothic sculpture. The [[e:bishop|bishops]] were imperial princes but leaned heavily on the Wettin rulers of Meissen.
prince-bishopric-of-naumburg.e: In 1542 the Elector of Saxony installed the Lutheran Nicholas of Amsdorf as [[e:bishop|bishop]] against the chapter's choice. After the last Catholic bishop, Julius von Pflug, died in 1564, the see came under [[e:saxons|Saxon]] administrators. From 1656 to 1718 it formed Saxe-Zeitz, and in 1815 it passed to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]].

pitcairn-islands.t: Britain's smallest and most remote overseas territory, settled by the Bounty mutineers and their Tahitian companions in 1790.
pitcairn-islands.o: Fletcher Christian and eight other mutineers from HMS Bounty, with Tahitian men and women, landed on uninhabited Pitcairn in 1790 and burned the ship. Violence killed most of the men, and the survivors were discovered in 1808. In 1838 Captain Russell Elliott of HMS Fly drew up laws that made the island a British possession and gave women the vote.
pitcairn-islands.r: The tiny community of mixed English and Tahitian descent was governed by an elected magistrate and council under British oversight, latterly through the High Commissioner in [[s:new-zealand|New Zealand]]. The islanders converted to Seventh-day Adventism in the 1890s. They live by fishing, gardening, selling handicrafts and stamps to passing ships, and they speak Pitkern, a [[e:criollo-people|creole]] of English and Tahitian.
pitcairn-islands.e: The whole population moved to Norfolk Island in 1856, but some families returned from 1858. Pitcairn remains a British Overseas Territory with about 40 to 50 residents, shaken in 2004 by trials for historical sexual abuse.

prince-bishopric-of-lebus.t: Frontier bishopric on the Oder that passed from Polish to Brandenburg control and was absorbed by the Hohenzollern electors after the Reformation.
prince-bishopric-of-lebus.o: The bishopric of Lebus was founded in the early 12th century by the Polish dukes, under the archdiocese of Gniezno. When the margraves of [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]] seized the Land of Lebus around 1249 to 1252, the [[e:bishop|bishops]] came under their influence while keeping estates on both banks of the Oder. They moved their seat to Fürstenwalde in the late 14th century.
prince-bishopric-of-lebus.r: The territory was small and its [[e:bishop|bishops]] weak, caught between [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]], [[e:poland|Poland]] and [[s:duchy-of-silesia|Silesia]]. They held lands around Fürstenwalde, Lebus and Storkow and depended on the Brandenburg [[e:prince-elector|electors]], who effectively nominated them. During the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] the electors installed Hohenzollern administrators, and the see became Lutheran.
prince-bishopric-of-lebus.e: After the last administrator, the bishopric was dissolved and absorbed into the [[s:margraviate-of-brandenburg|Margraviate of Brandenburg]] in 1598. Its lands west of the Oder remain in [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]], those east of it in [[e:poland|Poland]].

pachana-kaabu.t: One of the three royal provinces of the Kaabu Empire in present-day Guinea-Bissau, which took turns supplying the Mansaba of Kaabu.
pachana-kaabu.o: Pachana was a province of the [[e:mandinka|Mandinka]] [[s:kaabu-empire|Kaabu Empire]], which grew from a westward extension of the [[s:mali-empire|Mali Empire]] and became independent in the 16th century. Like other [[e:kaabu-empire|Kaabu]] provinces, it is known mainly through oral tradition and occasional Portuguese reports.
pachana-kaabu.r: Pachana, Sama and [[s:jimara-kaabu|Jimara]] were the royal provinces whose Nyancho warrior nobility, reckoned through the female line, provided the supreme king of [[e:kaabu-empire|Kaabu]] in rotation. Its own [[e:mansa|mansa]] governed with lineage heads, and the Nyancho lived largely from war, [[e:slave-raiding|slave raiding]] and trade with the Portuguese.
pachana-kaabu.e: Pachana declined with [[e:kaabu-empire|Kaabu]] under [[e:fula|Fulani]] pressure in the 19th century. After the fall of [[e:kansala|Kansala]] to the forces of the [[s:imamate-of-futa-jallon|Imamate of Futa Jallon]] in 1867, its lands came under Fula rule and later [[s:portuguese-guinea|Portuguese Guinea]].

principality-of-waldeck.t: Small north Hessian state of the counts and princes of Waldeck, known for hiring out soldiers and for surviving as a German state until 1918.
principality-of-waldeck.o: The counts of Schwalenberg acquired Waldeck castle above the Eder in the 12th century and took its name, emerging as counts of Waldeck by about 1180. They built up a county in the uplands between Hesse and [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Westphalia]], often under Hessian pressure, and adopted the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] in the 16th century. In 1625 they inherited the [[s:county-of-pyrmont|County of Pyrmont]].
principality-of-waldeck.r: The counts, raised to princes in 1712, ruled a poor, rural land of small towns from Arolsen, where they built a baroque palace. Revenue came partly from hiring out regiments to the [[s:dutch-republic|Dutch Republic]] and to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]], including troops used in the American Revolutionary War. George Frederick of Waldeck served as a [[e:dutch|Dutch]] field marshal under William III.
principality-of-waldeck.e: Waldeck joined the [[s:north-german-confederation|North German Confederation]] and in 1868 handed its administration to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] while keeping its prince. The last prince abdicated in 1918; the [[s:free-state-of-waldeck|Free State of Waldeck]] lost [[s:county-of-pyrmont|Pyrmont]] in 1922 and merged into Prussia in 1929. The area is now part of Hesse.

pervaneids.t: The Sinop beylik of the family of Mu'in al-Din Suleyman Pervane, the vizier who ruled Seljuk Anatolia under the Mongols.
pervaneids.o: Mu'in al-Din Suleyman, known by his title Pervane, was the most powerful man in the [[s:sultanate-of-rum|Sultanate of Rum]] in the 1260s and 1270s and conquered the [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]] port of [[s:sinope|Sinop]] in the early 1260s. After the [[e:mongols|Mongols]] executed him in 1277 for suspected collusion with the [[e:mamluk|Mamluk]] sultan [[e:baybars|Baybars]], his descendants kept Sinop as a hereditary domain.
pervaneids.r: The Pervane had built a [[e:madrasa|madrasa]] in [[s:sinope|Sinop]]. His son and grandsons ruled the port and its hinterland as Ilkhanid [[e:vassal|vassals]]. The last of them, [[e:ghazi|Ghazi]] Chelebi, was famed for naval raids against the Genoese of [[s:genoese-gazaria|Caffa]] and the [[s:empire-of-trebizond|Empire of Trebizond]].
pervaneids.e: After [[e:ghazi|Ghazi]] Chelebi's death around 1322, [[s:sinope|Sinop]] passed to the [[s:candarids|Candarids]].

populonia.t: The only major Etruscan city on the sea, and the iron-smelting centre of ancient Italy, working ore shipped from the island of Elba.
populonia.o: Populonia, Etruscan Pupluna or Fufluna, stood on the [[s:principality-of-piombino|Piombino]] promontory facing Elba. Villanovan settlements appeared there in the 9th century BCE, and by the 7th century princely tumulus tombs in the San Cerbone necropolis show a powerful elite. Ancient writers disagreed over whether it was founded by Corsicans or by [[s:volaterrae|Volaterrae]].
populonia.r: Populonia's economy rested on metals: [[e:copper|copper]] and [[e:tin|tin]] from the Campigliese and, from the 6th century BCE, iron ore from Elba smelted in furnaces around the Gulf of Baratti, whose slag heaps later buried the tombs. It was among the first Etruscan cities to mint coins, in the 5th century BCE, often showing the smith god Sethlans or a Gorgon head, and its port linked Etruria to [[s:corsican-republic|Corsica]] and [[s:massalia|Massalia]].
populonia.e: Populonia became a Roman ally in the 3rd century BCE and in 205 BCE supplied iron for Scipio's fleet against [[e:carthage|Carthage]]. Sacked by Sulla during the civil wars of the 80s BCE, it declined; Strabo found it largely deserted. The slag heaps were mined again for iron in the 20th century, uncovering the necropolis.

purushanda.t: Purushanda, an Anatolian city whose ruler bore the title great king in the age of the Assyrian merchants, later humbled by Anitta of Kussara.
purushanda.o: Burushattum appears in Old Assyrian trade letters of the 20th and 19th centuries BCE as a wealthy city in south-central [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]], probably at Acemhöyük near Aksaray, though the identification is debated. Assyrian merchants bought [[e:silver|silver]] and wool there and kept a trading house.
purushanda.r: Its ruler was the only Anatolian king the merchants called great king, suggesting overlordship over neighbouring cities. Later Mesopotamian legend made it the target of a campaign by [[e:sargon-of-akkad|Sargon]] of the [[s:akkadian-empire|Akkadian Empire]] to protect merchants, a story told in the text known as the King of Battle.
purushanda.e: In the 18th century BCE the king of Purushanda submitted to Anitta of [[s:kussara|Kussara]], offering him an iron throne and iron sceptre. The city then lost its independence and fades from the record by c. 1700 BCE.

province-of-new-hampshire.t: The small northern New England colony around Portsmouth, a source of masts for the Royal Navy, and the first colony to adopt its own constitution in 1776.
province-of-new-hampshire.o: Fishing settlements at Dover and Portsmouth, then called Strawbery Banke, appeared on the Piscataqua River from 1623. In 1629 John Mason received a grant of the land between the Merrimack and the Piscataqua and named it after his home county of Hampshire. Exeter was founded in 1638 by the dissenting minister John Wheelwright.
province-of-new-hampshire.r: [[s:massachusetts-bay-colony|Massachusetts Bay Colony]] governed the towns from 1641 until the Crown made New Hampshire a royal province in 1679. It shared a governor with the [[s:province-of-massachusetts-bay|Province of Massachusetts Bay]] from 1698 to 1741. Under Benning Wentworth, governor from 1741 to 1766, it issued the New Hampshire Grants west of the Connecticut River. Its economy rested on lumber, white-pine masts reserved for the navy, shipbuilding and fishing.
province-of-new-hampshire.e: Royal governor John Wentworth fled in 1775. In January 1776 New Hampshire adopted a temporary constitution, the first of any colony, and joined the Declaration of Independence as a state of the [[s:united-states|United States]].

powys-wenwynwyn.t: The southern half of Powys, ruled from Welshpool by princes who often sided with England against Gwynedd.
powys-wenwynwyn.o: After Madog ap Maredudd's death in 1160, his nephew Owain Cyfeiliog took the southern part of [[s:kingdom-of-powys|Powys]]. It was named after Owain's son Gwenwynwyn ab Owain, who ruled from 1195 and tried to lead the Welsh princes himself.
powys-wenwynwyn.r: Gwenwynwyn's rivalry with Llywelyn the Great of [[s:kingdom-of-gwynedd|Gwynedd]] cost him his lands for long periods. His son Gruffydd ap Gwenwynwyn fought and allied with Llywelyn ap Gruffudd in turn, and plotted against him in 1274. Owain Cyfeiliog was a noted poet and founded Strata Marcella Abbey. Welshpool and Powis Castle were its centres.
powys-wenwynwyn.e: Gruffydd supported Edward I in the conquest of 1282 to 1283, and his son Owain surrendered the princely title, holding the lands as an English barony. The heiress married John Charlton, and the lordship of Powis passed to his family.

peoples-republic-of-bulgaria.t: Communist Bulgaria, the Soviet Union's most loyal ally in Eastern Europe, ruled for 35 years by Todor Zhivkov.
peoples-republic-of-bulgaria.o: The Soviet army entered [[s:bulgaria|Bulgaria]] in September 1944, and the communist-led Fatherland Front took power. Opponents were tried by People's Courts, and a referendum in September 1946 abolished the monarchy of the [[s:kingdom-of-bulgaria|Kingdom of Bulgaria]]. The People's Republic was proclaimed on 15 September 1946, with Georgi Dimitrov becoming prime minister in November, and the Dimitrov Constitution followed in 1947.
peoples-republic-of-bulgaria.r: The Communist Party nationalised industry, collectivised agriculture and crushed opposition, executing the Agrarian leader Nikola Petkov in 1947. Under Todor Zhivkov, party leader from 1954, [[s:bulgaria|Bulgaria]] became the most faithful Soviet ally, industrialising rapidly with Soviet energy and markets. The 1984 to 1989 'Revival Process' forced Bulgarian Turks to take Slavic names, and in 1989 some 300,000 fled to [[e:turkey|Turkey]].
peoples-republic-of-bulgaria.e: On 10 November 1989, the day after the Berlin Wall opened, Zhivkov was ousted by reformers in his own party. Round Table talks led to free elections in 1990, and in November 1990 the country was renamed the [[s:bulgaria|Republic of Bulgaria]].

porbandar-state.t: The Jethwa Rajput coastal state of Saurashtra, birthplace of Mahatma Gandhi, whose father and grandfather served as its chief ministers.
porbandar-state.o: The Jethwa [[e:rajputs|Rajputs]] are among the oldest ruling clans of Saurashtra, and tradition gives their rule an early date. Their seat moved between Ghumli, [[s:ranpur-state|Ranpur]] and Chhaya before settling at the port of Porbandar in the late 18th century.
porbandar-state.r: Porbandar lived on sea trade with [[e:arabia|Arabia]] and [[e:east-africa|East Africa]] and on its fine building stone. Mohandas [[e:mahatma-gandhi|Gandhi]] was born there in 1869; his grandfather Uttamchand and father Karamchand served as [[e:diwan|diwans]] of the state. The last ruler, Natwarsinhji, captained [[e:india|India's]] first Test cricket side in [[e:england|England]] in 1932.
porbandar-state.e: Porbandar joined the [[s:saurashtra-state|United State of Saurashtra]] in 1948, which merged into Bombay State in 1956 and was divided in 1960, leaving Porbandar in [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]]. [[e:mahatma-gandhi|Gandhi's]] birthplace, Kirti Mandir, is a national memorial.
