prince-bishopric-of-utrecht.t: The Sticht, a church principality covering much of the northern Netherlands, whose bishops fought Holland and Guelders for five centuries.
prince-bishopric-of-utrecht.o: [[s:lordship-of-utrecht|Utrecht]] had been the seat of Willibrord's mission to the [[s:frisii|Frisians]] since the late 7th century. In the early 11th century the German kings granted [[e:bishop|Bishop]] Adalbold and his successors counties and secular rights, including lands in Drenthe and along the IJssel, turning the see into a principality of the [[s:holy-roman-empire|Holy Roman Empire]].
prince-bishopric-of-utrecht.r: The territory had two parts: the Nedersticht around [[s:lordship-of-utrecht|Utrecht]] and the [[s:lordship-of-overijssel|Oversticht]], today Overijssel and Drenthe. Utrecht was an imperial favourite, where Conrad II and Henry V died. The [[e:bishop|bishops]] were elected by chapters but often imposed by neighbours: David of [[s:duchy-of-burgundy|Burgundy]], son of Philip the Good, held the see from 1456. Towns such as Deventer and Kampen grew rich in the Hanseatic trade.
prince-bishopric-of-utrecht.e: Weakened by wars with Holland and the [[s:duchy-of-guelders|Duchy of Guelders]], [[e:bishop|Bishop]] Henry of Bavaria transferred his temporal power to [[e:charles-v-holy-roman-emperor|Charles V]] in 1528. The lands became the [[s:lordship-of-utrecht|Lordship of Utrecht]] and [[s:lordship-of-overijssel|Lordship of Overijssel]] in the [[s:habsburg-netherlands|Habsburg Netherlands]].

portuguese-bahrain.t: Bahrain under Portuguese overlordship, ruled through Hormuz from a rebuilt fort, until Safavid Persia took the island in 1602.
portuguese-bahrain.o: In 1521 a Portuguese and Hormuzi force under Antonio Correia attacked [[s:sheikhdom-of-bahrain|Bahrain]], defeating and fatally wounding the Jabrid ruler Muqrin ibn Zamil. The islands passed to the [[s:kingdom-of-ormus|Kingdom of Ormus]], a [[e:vassal|vassal]] of the [[s:portuguese-empire|Portuguese Empire]].
portuguese-bahrain.r: [[s:sheikhdom-of-bahrain|Bahrain]] was governed by Hormuzi governors, while the Portuguese kept a garrison and rebuilt the fort at Qal'at al-[[e:bahrain|Bahrain]]. The islands' value lay in their pearls and dates and in their position. Local revolts broke out, notably in 1529, and an Ottoman attempt to take the island in 1559 failed. The Portuguese presence itself was small for most of the period.
portuguese-bahrain.e: In 1602 the local governor was overthrown and the Safavid governor of [[e:fars|Fars]] took [[s:sheikhdom-of-bahrain|Bahrain]] for the [[s:safavid-empire|Safavid Empire]], which held it for most of the next 120 years. The fort, now part of a World Heritage Site, is the main relic.

principality-of-neuchatel.t: A small principality on Lake Neuchâtel ruled for 150 years by the kings of Prussia while also allied to, and later part of, the Swiss Confederacy.
principality-of-neuchatel.o: Neuchâtel ('new castle') appears in 1011 when King Rudolf III of [[s:duchy-of-burgundy|Burgundy]] gave the castle to his wife; in 1034 it passed with [[e:burgundy|Burgundy]] to the Empire. Counts of Neuchâtel ruled from the 12th century, and the county passed to the [[s:margraviate-of-hachberg|Hochberg]] family and in 1504 to the French house of Orléans-Longueville.
principality-of-neuchatel.r: The county became Protestant under Guillaume Farel in 1530 and was closely allied with Bern and other Swiss cantons. Its estates and towns enjoyed liberties. When the Longueville line ended in 1707, the estates chose King Frederick I of [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] as prince. Watchmaking in the Jura valleys, at La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle, became the chief industry.
principality-of-neuchatel.e: [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]] gave Neuchâtel to Marshal Berthier from 1806 to 1814. In 1815 it became a Swiss canton while remaining a Prussian principality, an anomaly ended by the republican revolution of 1848. [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] renounced its claims in 1857.

principality-of-monaco.t: A rock on the Riviera seized by the Grimaldis in 1297 and still ruled by them, now one of the world's smallest and richest sovereign states.
principality-of-monaco.o: In January 1297 François Grimaldi, a Genoese Guelph exile, took the fortress of Monaco disguised as a Franciscan friar, an event recalled in the monk on the family arms. The Grimaldis lost and regained the rock several times before establishing lasting control in the 15th century.
principality-of-monaco.r: The Grimaldis governed as lords, later princes, balancing between [[s:republic-of-genoa|Genoa]], [[e:spain|Spain]], [[e:france|France]] and [[s:duchy-of-savoy|Savoy]]. Honoré II placed Monaco under French protection in 1641 and adopted the title of prince. Revenues came from tolls, [[e:olive-oil|olive oil]] and citrus from [[s:free-cities-of-menton-and-roquebrune|Menton and Roquebrune]], until Charles III founded the Monte Carlo casino in 1863.
principality-of-monaco.e: Monaco was annexed by [[e:france|France]] in 1793 and restored in 1814 under Sardinian protection. [[s:free-cities-of-menton-and-roquebrune|Menton and Roquebrune]] broke away in 1848 and were sold to France in 1861. Constitutions of 1911 and 1962 limited princely power; under Rainier III and Albert II it became a banking and tourism centre.

principality-of-yaroslavl.t: A Volga principality around the city founded by Yaroslav the Wise, ruled by its own princes until it passed to Moscow in 1463.
principality-of-yaroslavl.o: Yaroslavl was founded in the early 11th century by Yaroslav the Wise at the meeting of the [[e:volga|Volga]] and the Kotorosl; a legend has him killing a bear there. In 1218 Konstantin Vsevolodovich of Rostov gave it to his son Vsevolod, who founded a separate princely line.
principality-of-yaroslavl.r: Its position on the [[e:volga|Volga]] made Yaroslavl a trading town. Vsevolod was killed fighting the [[e:mongols|Mongols]] on the Sit in 1238. Fyodor the Black, who ruled from the 1260s, spent years at the court of the [[s:golden-horde|Golden Horde]], married a daughter of the khan and was later venerated as a saint. The principality later split into many small [[e:appanage|appanages]].
principality-of-yaroslavl.e: Its princes increasingly served the [[s:grand-duchy-of-moscow|Grand Duchy of Moscow]], and in 1463 [[e:ivan-iii|Ivan III]] annexed the principality. The Yaroslavl princes survived as noble families such as the Shakhovskoy and Kurbsky. The city became one of [[e:russia|Russia's]] richest commercial centres in the 17th century.

pingnan-guo.t: The Muslim-led state of Du Wenxiu in western Yunnan, born of the Panthay rebellion against the Qing, which ruled from Dali for sixteen years.
pingnan-guo.o: Tension between Hui Muslims and [[e:han-chinese|Han Chinese]] over the mines of Yunnan led to massacres of Muslims, including at Kunming in 1856. In the uprising that followed, the Hui leader Du Wenxiu took Dali in 1856 and established a state, taking the title [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Suleiman as well as the Chinese title of generalissimo.
pingnan-guo.r: Pingnan Guo ('the state that pacifies the south') was multi-ethnic, including Bai, Yi and Han officials as well as Hui. Du Wenxiu revived Ming-style dress, promoted the jade, [[e:cotton|cotton]] and opium trade with [[s:myanmar|Burma]], and kept mosques and markets open. In 1872 he sent his adopted son Hassan to [[e:london|London]] to seek British recognition, without success.
pingnan-guo.e: Qing forces under Cen Yuying retook eastern Yunnan and besieged Dali in 1872. Du Wenxiu took poison and surrendered at the end of that year, hoping to save the people; he was beheaded, and the city's Muslim population was massacred.

principality-of-kashin.t: An appanage of the Tver lands on the upper Volga, linked with Saint Anna of Kashin and reabsorbed by Tver in 1426.
principality-of-kashin.o: Kashin, north-east of Tver, was part of the [[s:grand-principality-of-tver|Grand Principality of Tver]]. After Mikhail Yaroslavich was executed at the [[s:golden-horde|Golden Horde]] in 1318, his youngest son Vasily received Kashin as his [[e:appanage|appanage]], founding a separate line of princes.
principality-of-kashin.r: The principality was small, with an economy based on farming and local trade. Mikhail's widow Anna lived her last years in Kashin as a nun and was later venerated as Saint Anna of Kashin. Its princes repeatedly quarrelled with their Tver cousins and sometimes sought the support of [[e:moscow|Moscow]] against them.
principality-of-kashin.e: After several periods of union and separation, Kashin was finally merged back into the [[s:grand-principality-of-tver|Grand Principality of Tver]] in 1426. Together with Tver, it was annexed by the [[s:grand-duchy-of-moscow|Grand Duchy of Moscow]] in 1485.

pagan-kingdom.t: The first kingdom to unite the Irrawaddy valley, whose rulers built over 10,000 Buddhist monuments on the plain of Bagan and laid the foundations of Burmese culture.
pagan-kingdom.o: Burman settlers from the north occupied the Kyaukse plain and the middle Irrawaddy in the 9th century, and chronicles date the walls of Pagan to 849. The town became a regional power under Anawrahta, who took the throne in 1044, conquered the [[s:thaton-kingdom|Thaton Kingdom]] in 1057 and brought much of present-day [[s:myanmar|Myanmar]] under his rule.
pagan-kingdom.r: Pagan's kings ruled a core of irrigated [[e:rice|rice]] lands around Kyaukse and Minbu, with tributary regions beyond. Royal and private donors gave land and labour to the Buddhist sangha on a vast scale, building temples such as the Shwezigon, Ananda and Dhammayangyi. Old Burmese emerged as a written language, recorded in the Myazedi inscription of 1113 alongside Pyu, Mon and Pali.
pagan-kingdom.e: The flow of tax-free land to monasteries weakened royal revenues, and Mongol invasions under the [[e:yuan-dynasty|Yuan dynasty]] in the 1280s led to Pagan's fall in 1287. Real power passed to the [[s:myinsaing-kingdom|Myinsaing]] brothers, who deposed the last puppet king in 1297. Bagan became a World Heritage Site in 2019.

prince-of-wales-island.t: British East India Company settlement on Penang, founded by Francis Light, the first British foothold in the Malay world.
prince-of-wales-island.o: Seeking a naval and trading base on the eastern side of the Bay of [[e:bengal|Bengal]], the [[e:east-india-company|East India Company]] trader Francis Light negotiated with the [[e:sultan|Sultan]] of [[s:kedah-sultanate|Kedah]], who hoped for protection against Siam. Light landed on [[e:penang|Penang]] in August 1786, renamed it Prince of Wales Island and founded George Town.
prince-of-wales-island.r: The settlement was a free port that drew Chinese, Indian, Malay, Acehnese and Eurasian traders, and [[e:spice-trade|spices]] and [[e:pepper|pepper]] were planted. In 1800 [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] added the mainland strip of Province Wellesley. In 1805 it was raised to the status of a presidency of [[s:british-raj|British India]], with Thomas Stamford Raffles serving as assistant secretary.
prince-of-wales-island.e: Hopes of a naval dockyard faded and the rise of [[s:singapore|Singapore]] overshadowed [[e:penang|Penang]]. In 1826 it was merged with [[e:singapore|Singapore]] and [[e:malacca|Malacca]] to form the [[s:straits-settlements|Straits Settlements]], and George Town later became the capital of the Malaysian state of Penang.
prince-of-wales-island.re: Sunni Islam, Chinese folk religion, Christianity

principality-of-besleney.t: An eastern Circassian princely tribe on the upper Kuban and Laba, closely related to the Kabardians, whose descendants are the Cherkess of Karachay-Cherkessia.
principality-of-besleney.o: The Besleney lived on the upper Kuban, Laba and Urup rivers, between [[s:principality-of-kabarda|Kabarda]] and the western Circassians. Tradition links their princely house to the Kabardian aristocracy, and their speech is close to Kabardian. They appear as a distinct community from the 16th and 17th centuries; earlier history is not separately recorded.
principality-of-besleney.r: Princes and nobles ruled over free peasants and serfs according to the Adyghe code of conduct. The Besleney were horse breeders and herders, and their princes alternately allied with [[s:principality-of-kabarda|Kabarda]], the [[s:crimean-khanate|Crimean Khanate]] and [[e:russia|Russia]]. Their position on the routes between east and west [[s:circassia|Circassia]] gave them influence beyond their size.
principality-of-besleney.e: The [[s:russian-empire|Russian Empire]] brought them under its control in the course of the Russo-Circassian War, completed in 1864. Many emigrated to the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]], but part remained, and their descendants form much of the Cherkess people of Karachay-Cherkessia.

prome-kingdom.t: A small Burmese kingdom based at Prome on the lower Irrawaddy that broke from Ava in 1482 and fell to the rising Toungoo in 1542.
prome-kingdom.o: In 1482 Thado Minsaw, the governor of Prome and a son of King Narapati of the [[s:ava-kingdom|Ava Kingdom]], rebelled during a succession crisis and made his town, on the Irrawaddy near the old Pyu city of [[s:sri-ksetra-kingdom|Sri Ksetra]], the seat of an independent kingdom.
prome-kingdom.r: Prome controlled the river trade between Upper [[s:myanmar|Burma]] and the Mon coast and played Ava, the [[s:hanthawaddy-kingdom|Hanthawaddy Kingdom]] and Toungoo against each other. Its kings at times allied with the Shan rulers who took Ava in 1527, receiving support from the [[s:confederation-of-shan-states|Confederation of Shan States]].
prome-kingdom.e: Tabinshwehti of the [[s:first-toungoo-empire|First Toungoo Empire]] besieged Prome after taking Pegu, and in 1542 the city fell despite help from the Shan confederation and [[s:mrauk-u-kingdom|Arakan]]. Prome was absorbed into the Toungoo realm and later served as a provincial centre; it is the modern city of Pyay.

phaistos.t: Greek city-state built on the ruins of the Minoan palace in southern Crete, rival of Gortyn until destroyed by it c. 150 BCE.
phaistos.o: After the [[e:bronze-age|Bronze Age]] palace fell, [[s:palace-state-of-phaistos|Phaistos]] survived as a settlement on its ridge above the Mesara plain. In the early Iron Age Dorian-speaking [[e:greeks|Greeks]] dominated it, and by the Archaic period it was an independent polis, one of many on [[e:crete|Crete]], with Greek temples built over parts of the old palace.
phaistos.r: [[s:palace-state-of-phaistos|Phaistos]] controlled the western Mesara and the harbour of Matala. It minted coins from the 4th century BCE showing Talos, the bronze giant of myth, and Heracles. Like other Cretan cities it had an aristocratic constitution with [[e:kosmoi|kosmoi]] magistrates and men's messes. Its great rival was [[s:gortyn|Gortyn]], a few kilometres east.
phaistos.e: [[s:palace-state-of-phaistos|Phaistos]] was destroyed by [[s:gortyn|Gortyn]] in the mid-2nd century BCE and its territory absorbed. The site was later known chiefly for its Minoan palace, described separately as the Palace State of Phaistos.

prince-bishopric-of-toul.t: The smallest of the Three Bishoprics of Lorraine, an ecclesiastical principality of the Empire that produced a reforming pope and was absorbed by France.
prince-bishopric-of-toul.o: Toul had been a bishopric since late Roman times. In the 10th century, as the German kings sought loyal counterweights to the [[s:duchy-of-lorraine|Lorraine]] nobility, the [[e:bishop|bishops]] received comital rights over the city and its surroundings, traditionally dated to 928 under Henry the Fowler, making them princes of the [[s:holy-roman-empire|Holy Roman Empire]].
prince-bishopric-of-toul.r: The [[e:bishop|bishops]] ruled a small territory on the upper Moselle, often clashing with the dukes of [[s:duchy-of-lorraine|Lorraine]] and with the citizens of Toul, who won considerable self-government. Bishop Bruno of Egisheim became [[e:papacy|Pope]] Leo IX in 1049 and drove the Gregorian reform. The diocese itself was far larger than the temporal principality.
prince-bishopric-of-toul.e: In 1552 Henry II of [[e:france|France]] occupied Toul, Metz and Verdun as 'protector' during his war with [[e:charles-v-holy-roman-emperor|Charles V]]. French control of the Three Bishoprics was confirmed by the [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] in 1648, and Toul became part of the [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]].

principality-of-gottingen.t: Guelph principality on the upper Leine whose turbulent dukes, including Otto the Bad, struggled with their own town of Göttingen until 1463.
principality-of-gottingen.o: After the death of Albert I of Brunswick in 1279, his sons divided the [[s:principality-of-wolfenbuttel|Principality of Wolfenbüttel]], and around 1291 Albert II the Fat received the southern lands around Göttingen, Münden and Uslar, founding a separate Guelph principality on the upper Leine and Weser.
principality-of-gottingen.r: The dukes ruled a land of hills, forests and small towns, with Göttingen the main town. The town grew increasingly independent, joined the [[s:hanseatic-league|Hanseatic League]] and expelled Duke Otto the Bad, whose feuds and debts weakened the principality in the late 14th century. His son Otto Cocles, the One-Eyed, was nearly blind and handed government to the estates in 1435.
principality-of-gottingen.e: When Otto Cocles died in 1463, the principality passed to the Wolfenbüttel branch and was later joined to the [[s:principality-of-calenberg|Principality of Calenberg]]. Göttingen became part of the [[s:electorate-of-hanover|Electorate of Hanover]], where its university was founded in 1734.

principality-of-minden.t: Secularised Westphalian bishopric on the Weser that became a Prussian principality and gave its name to a famous battle of 1759.
principality-of-minden.o: The Bishopric of Minden, founded by [[e:charlemagne|Charlemagne]] around 800, had turned Protestant in the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]]. At the [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] in 1648 it was secularised and assigned to the [[s:margraviate-of-brandenburg|Margraviate of Brandenburg]] as part of its compensation for ceding [[e:pomerania|Western Pomerania]] to [[e:sweden|Sweden]].
principality-of-minden.r: Brandenburg-[[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] governed Minden through a provincial administration, later combined with the [[s:county-of-ravensberg|County of Ravensberg]] in a single chamber of war and domains. The town was fortified and garrisoned, and the region produced grain and linen. During the [[e:seven-years-war|Seven Years' War]] an Anglo-German army under Ferdinand of Brunswick defeated the French nearby at the Battle of Minden on 1 August 1759.
principality-of-minden.e: After [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia's]] collapse in 1806, Minden was divided between the [[s:kingdom-of-westphalia|Kingdom of Westphalia]] and, from 1810, [[e:france|France]]. In 1815 it returned to Prussia as part of the Province of [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Westphalia]]; the area is now in North Rhine-Westphalia.

principality-of-prosek.t: Short-lived lordship of the adventurer Dobromir Chrysos in the Vardar gorge, carved out during the Bulgarian revolt against Byzantium.
principality-of-prosek.o: Dobromir Chrysos, a Vlach or Bulgarian commander who had served in the Byzantine army, broke away during the Asen revolt that founded the [[s:second-bulgarian-empire|Second Bulgarian Empire]]. Around 1197 he seized the fortress of Prosek, in the Demir Kapija gorge of the Vardar, and nearby Strumica.
principality-of-prosek.r: Known mainly from the Byzantine historian Niketas Choniates, his realm rested on the near-impregnable fortress of Prosek and on several hundred warriors. The emperor Alexios III failed to take it and recognised him, marrying him to a relative.
principality-of-prosek.e: Chrysos rebelled again, and around 1201–1202 Alexios III defeated him and recovered his lands; Prosek soon passed to Kaloyan of [[s:bulgaria|Bulgaria]].

provisional-government-of-the-republic-o.t: The Korean government-in-exile founded in Shanghai after the March First Movement of 1919, which kept the cause of independence alive until 1945.
provisional-government-of-the-republic-o.o: In the wake of the March First Movement, independence activists met in Shanghai's French Concession and in April 1919 proclaimed the Republic of [[e:korea|Korea]] with a provisional constitution and assembly. Rival groups in Seoul and Vladivostok merged with it later that year, and Syngman Rhee was chosen as president.
provisional-government-of-the-republic-o.r: The government drew funds from Koreans abroad and ran diplomacy and propaganda, but it was weakened by factional disputes; Rhee was impeached in 1925. Under Kim Gu it organised attacks on Japanese leaders, including Yun Bong-gil's bombing in Shanghai in 1932, then moved through several Chinese cities before settling in Chongqing in 1940, where it formed the Korean Liberation Army and declared war on [[e:japan|Japan]] in 1941.
provisional-government-of-the-republic-o.e: The [[e:allies|Allies]] never recognised it, and its leaders returned to [[e:korea|Korea]] in late 1945 only as private individuals. The Republic of Korea's constitution claims descent from it, and it ceased to exist when that state was founded in 1948.

phagmodrupa-dynasty.t: The dynasty that replaced the Mongol-backed Sakya and restored native rule over central Tibet, patrons of the rising Gelug school.
phagmodrupa-dynasty.o: Changchub Gyaltsen, myriarch of Phagmodru, a domain linked to the Kagyu monastery of Densatil, fought the [[s:sakya-regime|Sakya regime]]'s administrators from the 1340s. By 1354 he controlled most of central [[s:tibet-1912-1951|Tibet]] and ruled from Nedong in the Yarlung valley.
phagmodrupa-dynasty.r: Changchub Gyaltsen reorganised the country into districts governed by appointed officials from fortresses (dzong), issued a law code inspired by the age of the [[s:tibetan-empire|Tibetan Empire]], and encouraged a revival of imperial traditions. His successors, called gongma, received titles from the [[s:ming-empire|Ming Empire]]. Drakpa Gyaltsen supported Tsongkhapa, who founded Ganden monastery in 1409, the start of the Gelug school.
phagmodrupa-dynasty.e: After a succession crisis in 1434, real power passed to the [[s:rinpungpa|Rinpungpa]] ministers and later to the [[s:tsangpa-dynasty|Tsangpa dynasty]]. The Phagmodrupa rulers survived as nominal kings at Nedong until the early 17th century.

principality-of-reuss-lobenstein.t: Tiny Thuringian lordship of the Reuss family, where every male ruler was named Heinrich.
principality-of-reuss-lobenstein.o: The Younger Line of the House of Reuss divided its lands in 1647 into Gera, Schleiz, Lobenstein and Saalburg. Heinrich X received Lobenstein in the Thuringian Highlands, and his descendants later split off Ebersdorf and Hirschberg as further sub-lines.
principality-of-reuss-lobenstein.r: Lobenstein was small, hilly and poor, with some mining and [[e:timber|timber]]. Like all Reuss branches, its counts named every son Heinrich, distinguished by numbers counted across the century. The rulers were Lutheran and governed through a modest court in Lobenstein. They were raised to princely rank in 1790.
principality-of-reuss-lobenstein.e: The Lobenstein line died out in 1824, and its lands passed to the [[s:principality-of-reuss-ebersdorf|Principality of Reuss-Ebersdorf]], which became Reuss-Lobenstein-Ebersdorf. In 1848 all these lands joined the [[s:principality-of-reuss-schleiz|Principality of Reuss-Schleiz]] to form the Principality of [[s:principality-of-reuss-gera|Reuss Younger Line]].

pedir.t: A pepper port on the north coast of Sumatra that flourished in the 15th century before falling to Aceh in 1524.
pedir.o: Pedir, the modern district of Pidie in Aceh, grew as a port on the [[e:strait-of-malacca|Strait of Malacca]] in the 15th century. It is mentioned in Chinese records and by early Portuguese writers. Its rulers were Muslim, following the example of nearby [[s:samudera-pasai-sultanate|Samudera]] Pasai.
pedir.r: Tome Pires, writing around 1515, described Pedir as one of the leading [[e:pepper|pepper]] exporters of [[e:sumatra|Sumatra]], rivalling [[s:samudera-pasai-sultanate|Pasai]], with merchants from [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]], [[e:bengal|Bengal]] and the Malay ports. It also exported [[e:silk|silk]] and [[e:benzoin-resin|benzoin]], and was a stopping place on the route from [[e:india|India]] to [[e:malacca|Malacca]].
pedir.e: In the early 16th century Pedir was drawn into the struggle between the Portuguese and the rising [[s:aceh-sultanate|Aceh Sultanate]]. [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Ali Mughayat Syah of Aceh conquered it around 1524, and it became one of Aceh's districts.

piploda-state.t: A small Rajput chiefship of western Malwa, long a dependency of the Nawabs of Jaora.
piploda-state.o: Piploda was held by a [[e:rajputs|Rajput]] Thakur family in western [[e:malwa|Malwa]] from the late 18th century. When the British settled Malwa after 1818, it was placed under the Nawab of [[s:jaora-state|Jaora]] as a tributary holding.
piploda-state.r: The Thakurs governed a few dozen villages and paid tribute to [[s:jaora-state|Jaora State]]. In the 20th century Piploda was separated from Jaora and placed directly under the [[e:malwa|Malwa]] Agency. Little else is recorded.
piploda-state.e: After accession to [[e:india|India]] Piploda was merged into [[s:madhya-bharat|Madhya Bharat]] in 1948 and joined Madhya Pradesh in 1956; it lies in [[s:ratlam-state|Ratlam]] district.

principality-of-guria.t: A small principality on Georgia's Black Sea coast, ruled by the Gurieli family between the Kingdom of Imereti and the Ottoman Empire.
principality-of-guria.o: Guria, the land south of the Rioni along the [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]] coast, was governed by a branch of the Vardanidze family, later called Gurieli, as eristavis of the [[s:kingdom-of-georgia|Kingdom of Georgia]]. As the kingdom broke apart in the 1460s, the Gurieli became effectively independent princes, nominally owing allegiance to the [[s:kingdom-of-imereti|Kingdom of Imereti]].
principality-of-guria.r: The princes ruled from Ozurgeti over a land of [[e:maize|maize]], vineyards and forested hills. Guria lay on the frontier with the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]], which seized its coastal fortresses and drew tribute; the [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trade]] through Ottoman ports was a persistent evil. The Gurieli took part in Imereti's dynastic wars, sometimes ruling it themselves, as Mamia I did.
principality-of-guria.e: In 1810 Mamia V accepted a Russian [[e:protectorate|protectorate]]. After the death of Mamia V's young heir, a revolt in 1828 was crushed, and in 1829 the [[s:russian-empire|Russian Empire]] annexed Guria.

paemani.t: One of the Germani Cisrhenani of the Belgian Ardennes, remembered in the name of the Famenne region.
paemani.o: Caesar lists the Paemani with the [[s:condrusi|Condrusi]], [[s:eburones|Eburones]] and [[s:caeroesi|Caeroesi]] as Germani living west of the [[e:rhine|Rhine]]. Their name is usually linked to the Famenne, in the modern Belgian provinces of [[s:county-of-namur|Namur]] and [[s:county-of-luxembourg|Luxembourg]].
paemani.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or settlements.
paemani.e: They joined the Belgic coalition against Caesar in 57 BCE. After the conquest they disappear from the sources, their land absorbed into the civitas of the [[s:tungri|Tungri]].

prince-bishopric-of-speyer.t: A prince-bishopric on the Rhine whose cathedral holds the tombs of Salian emperors, its bishops ruling from Bruchsal until 1803.
prince-bishopric-of-speyer.o: [[s:free-imperial-city-of-speyer|Speyer]] had been a bishopric since the 7th century, and Salian kings made it their family church; Conrad II began the great cathedral around 1030. In 1111 Emperor Henry V granted the citizens of Speyer privileges, and the [[e:bishop|bishops]]' secular rule over their territory developed in the 11th and 12th centuries.
prince-bishopric-of-speyer.r: The [[e:bishop|bishops]] ruled a territory on both banks of the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] but not the city of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-speyer|Speyer]], which became a free imperial city; they moved their residence to Udenheim, renamed Philippsburg, and in 1720 to Bruchsal, where Cardinal Damian Hugo von Schönborn built a baroque palace. The cathedral, burial place of eight emperors and kings, is a World Heritage Site.
prince-bishopric-of-speyer.e: [[e:france|France]] annexed the left-bank lands during the Revolutionary Wars, and in 1803 the right-bank territory, including Bruchsal, was secularised and given to Baden. The diocese of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-speyer|Speyer]] was re-founded in 1817 under Bavaria.

principality-of-kakheti.t: An eastern Georgian principality ruled by chorepiscopi, leaders with a churchly title, that resisted the Arab emirs of Tbilisi and the Bagratid kings.
principality-of-kakheti.o: [[s:kingdom-of-kakheti|Kakheti]], the land east of Tbilisi, broke away from the [[s:principality-of-iberia|Principality of Iberia]] in 786, when the nobleman Grigol took the title chorepiscopus and united its mountain communities. The weakening of central power under Arab rule allowed it to become a separate state.
principality-of-kakheti.r: Its rulers, whose title meant rural [[e:bishop|bishop]] although they were lay princes, ruled from Ujarma and later Telavi with the support of the mountain peoples of Tusheti and Pshavi. They fought the [[s:emirate-of-tbilisi|Emirate of Tbilisi]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-abkhazia|Kingdom of Abkhazia]], and in the 10th century absorbed the [[s:principality-of-hereti|Principality of Hereti]]. Viticulture and farming in the Alazani valley sustained it.
principality-of-kakheti.e: Around 1010 Kvirike III took the title king, forming the [[s:kingdom-of-kakheti-hereti|Kingdom of Kakheti-Hereti]], which held out against the united Georgian monarchy until 1104. [[s:kingdom-of-kakheti|Kakheti]] later re-emerged as a separate Georgian kingdom in the 15th century.

pskov-republic.t: A fortified city-republic on Russia's western frontier, which governed itself through its veche until Moscow annexed it in 1510.
pskov-republic.o: Pskov was long a dependency of the [[s:novgorod-republic|Novgorod Republic]], though it already had its own princes, among them the Lithuanian exile Daumantas, who defended it in the late 13th century. In 1348 the Treaty of Bolotovo recognised Pskov's self-government, and it became an independent republic.
pskov-republic.r: Power lay with the veche, which met by the Trinity Cathedral in the stone citadel known as the Krom, and with elected posadniks. Pskov hired princes to command its troops, often from [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Lithuania]] or [[e:moscow|Moscow]]. Its Judicial Charter is one of the most important legal texts of medieval [[e:russia|Russia]]. A frontier fortress, it repeatedly fought the [[s:livonian-order|Livonian Order]].
pskov-republic.e: In the 15th century Pskov relied increasingly on [[e:moscow|Moscow]] for protection. In 1510 Vasily III ended its independence, removed the veche bell and deported hundreds of leading families. The city became a Muscovite fortress and withstood the siege of Stefan Batory in 1581.

prince-archbishopric-of-bremen.t: Archbishopric of the North Sea coast, heir to Ansgar's mission to Scandinavia, which ruled the land between the Weser and Elbe until Sweden took it in 1648.
prince-archbishopric-of-bremen.o: The archdiocese of [[s:free-and-hanseatic-city-of-hamburg|Hamburg]] was founded in 831 for Ansgar, apostle of the North, and joined to [[s:free-hanseatic-city-of-bremen|Bremen]] after [[e:vikings|Vikings]] sacked [[e:hamburg|Hamburg]] in 845. Under Archbishop Adalbert in the 11th century it claimed authority over all of [[e:scandinavia|Scandinavia]]. After Henry the Lion fell in 1180 the archbishops built a secular principality between the lower Weser and Elbe.
prince-archbishopric-of-bremen.r: The archbishops governed marshland and moor from Stade and Bremervörde, while the wealthy city of [[s:free-hanseatic-city-of-bremen|Bremen]] slipped from their control. Free peasant communities in the marshes resisted lordship. The estates, including the cathedral chapter, nobles and towns, shared power. In the 16th century the land became Lutheran, and administrators came from princely houses such as [[s:duchy-of-holstein-gottorp|Holstein-Gottorp]] and [[e:denmark|Denmark]].
prince-archbishopric-of-bremen.e: The [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] in 1648 secularised it as the Duchy of [[s:free-hanseatic-city-of-bremen|Bremen]] under [[e:sweden|Sweden]], which ruled it with [[e:verden|Verden]]. [[e:denmark|Denmark]] took it in 1712 and sold it to the [[s:electorate-of-hanover|Electorate of Hanover]] in 1715. The land is now in Lower Saxony.

protectorate-of-southern-nigeria.t: The British protectorate over south-eastern Nigeria, later joined with Lagos, that formed the southern half of Nigeria before amalgamation in 1914.
protectorate-of-southern-nigeria.o: On 1 January 1900 [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] combined the [[s:niger-coast-protectorate|Niger Coast Protectorate]] with the southern lands of the [[s:royal-niger-company-territories|Royal Niger Company]] to form the [[e:protectorate|Protectorate]] of Southern [[e:nigeria|Nigeria]], under the high commissioner Ralph Moor, with headquarters at [[s:old-calabar|Old Calabar]]. It took over the delta trading states, the lands of the Igbo and Ibibio, and the remains of the [[s:benin-empire|Benin Empire]].
protectorate-of-southern-nigeria.r: The new administration conquered the interior by force, most notably in the Anglo-Aro War of 1901-1902, which destroyed the [[s:aro-confederacy|Aro Confederacy]] and its oracle. It built roads and courts, recruited labour and promoted the export of [[e:palm-oil|palm oil]] and palm kernels. Christian missions expanded rapidly, spreading schools among the Igbo and other peoples. In 1906 it merged with the [[s:lagos-colony|Lagos Colony]], and [[s:kingdom-of-lagos|Lagos]] became its capital under Governor Walter Egerton.
protectorate-of-southern-nigeria.e: On 1 January 1914 the Southern [[e:protectorate|Protectorate]] was amalgamated with the [[s:protectorate-of-northern-nigeria|Protectorate of Northern Nigeria]] to form [[s:colonial-nigeria|Colonial Nigeria]], while remaining a separate group of provinces. The southern provinces later became the Western and Eastern Regions of the Nigerian federation.

principality-of-herat.t: The last outpost of Sadozai rule, a frontier city-state whose sieges by Persia drew Britain and Russia into the Great Game.
principality-of-herat.o: When the [[e:barakzai-dynasty|Barakzai]] brothers took over most of the [[s:durrani-empire|Durrani Empire]] around 1818, the Sadozai prince Mahmud Shah and his son Kamran Shah held on to [[e:herat|Herat]], ruling it as an independent principality.
principality-of-herat.r: Kamran Shah's [[e:vizier|vizier]] Yar Muhammad Khan Alakozai became the real power and in 1842 killed Kamran, ruling himself until 1851. [[e:herat|Herat]] was a walled city on the route between [[e:persia|Persia]], [[e:central-asia|Central Asia]] and [[e:india|India]], and its strategic value made it central to the [[e:the-great-game|Great Game]]. Persia besieged it in 1837 to 1838, with a young British officer, Eldred Pottinger, helping the defence, and again in 1856, when [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] went to war with Persia to force its withdrawal.
principality-of-herat.e: By the Treaty of [[e:paris|Paris]] in 1857 [[e:persia|Persia]] renounced its claims. Dost Mohammad Khan took [[e:herat|Herat]] in 1863 after a ten-month siege, dying there days later, and Herat joined the [[s:emirate-of-afghanistan|Emirate of Afghanistan]].

peoples-state-of-hesse.t: Republican successor of the Grand Duchy of Hesse, a Social Democratic state on both sides of the Rhine.
peoples-state-of-hesse.o: Grand Duke Ernest Louis was deposed in November 1918, and [[s:grand-duchy-of-hesse|Hesse-Darmstadt]] became the People's State of Hesse, with a democratic constitution adopted in December 1919. It kept the grand duchy's three provinces: Starkenburg, Upper Hesse around Giessen, and Rhenish Hesse with [[e:mainz|Mainz]] and [[s:free-imperial-city-of-worms|Worms]].
peoples-state-of-hesse.r: Social Democrats led the state for most of the Weimar years under Carl Ulrich. Rhenish Hesse and [[e:mainz|Mainz]] were under French occupation until 1930. Darmstadt had a technical university and the Merck chemical company. The Nazis took power in March 1933 under Reich governor Jakob Sprenger, and the Jewish communities of Mainz and [[s:free-imperial-city-of-worms|Worms]], among the oldest in [[e:germany|Germany]], were destroyed.
peoples-state-of-hesse.e: In 1945 the parts east of the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] were combined with Prussian territories into Greater Hesse in the American zone, now the state of Hesse. Rhenish Hesse went to the French zone and later to Rhineland-Palatinate.

pal-state.t: A minor Rajput chiefship of the Mahi Kantha country in northern Gujarat.
pal-state.o: Pal was one of the many petty holdings of the Mahi Kantha region, held by a [[e:rajputs|Rajput]] family from around 1700. Its founding is not well documented.
pal-state.r: Its ruler held a few villages in the hilly country near the Rajasthan border, paid tribute through the [[e:gaekwads|Gaekwads]] of [[s:baroda-state|Baroda]] and was supervised by the British Mahi Kantha Agency. Little else is recorded.
pal-state.e: Pal merged into [[s:bombay-presidency|Bombay Province]] in 1948 and became part of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] in 1960, in Sabarkantha district.

paduspanid-dynasty.t: A dynasty of mountain princes in Ruyan and Rustamdar that lasted over nine centuries, from the fall of the Sasanians to the reign of Shah Abbas.
paduspanid-dynasty.o: According to Ibn Isfandiyar, Paduspan, a son of Gil Gavbara and brother of Dabuya, founder of the [[s:dabuyid-dynasty|Dabuyid dynasty]], received the mountain region of Ruyan in western Tabaristan around 665. His descendants ruled this upland between [[e:gilan|Gilan]] and Amol as hereditary ostandars.
paduspanid-dynasty.r: The Paduspanids survived by submitting in turn to the [[s:abbasid-caliphate|Abbasid Caliphate]], the [[s:alavid-dynasty|Alavid dynasty]], the [[s:buyid-dynasty|Buyids]], the [[s:seljuk-empire|Seljuk Empire]], the [[s:ilkhanate|Ilkhanate]] and the [[s:timurid-empire|Timurid Empire]], while keeping local power in fortresses such as Nur and Kojur. They converted from [[e:zoroastrianism|Zoroastrianism]] to [[e:islam|Islam]] and later to [[e:shia-islam|Shia Islam]]. In 1453 the dynasty split into two branches, at Nur and at Kojur, which often quarrelled. The region's economy rested on forests, [[e:rice|rice]] and livestock.
paduspanid-dynasty.e: [[e:abbas-i-of-persia|Shah Abbas I]] of the [[s:safavid-empire|Safavid Empire]] annexed [[e:mazandaran|Mazandaran]] and its principalities in the 1590s, deposing the last Paduspanid rulers by 1598 and ending their rule.

prince-bishopric-of-cammin.t: Pomeranian church state founded as the bishopric of the newly converted Pomeranians and secularised into a Brandenburg principality in 1650.
prince-bishopric-of-cammin.o: The bishopric of [[s:duchy-of-pomerania|Pomerania]] was founded in 1140 at Wolin after the mission of Otto of Bamberg, with Adalbert as first [[e:bishop|bishop]], and moved to Cammin by 1176. Exempt from any archbishop, it answered directly to the pope. In 1248 the bishops acquired the land of Kolberg, forming their secular territory with Köslin and Bublitz.
prince-bishopric-of-cammin.r: The [[e:bishop|bishops]] ruled a small but distinct territory, with Köslin and Kolberg its main towns and residences. They claimed imperial immediacy, which the dukes of [[s:duchy-of-pomerania|Pomerania]] contested, and the Pomeranian estates drew the bishopric into ducal politics. After the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] in the 1530s the see became Lutheran and was administered by members of the Pomeranian ducal house.
prince-bishopric-of-cammin.e: The last administrator, Ernst Bogislaw of Croÿ, handed it over after the [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] gave Cammin to [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]], which took possession in 1650 as the Principality of Cammin. The region has been part of [[e:poland|Poland]] since 1945.

paracas.t: A culture of Peru's southern desert coast celebrated for the finest embroidered textiles of the ancient Andes, preserved in hundreds of mummy bundles at the Paracas peninsula.
paracas.o: The Paracas culture developed on the south coast of [[e:peru|Peru]], around the Paracas peninsula and the Ica and Pisco valleys, from about 800 BCE. Early phases show the influence of the [[s:chavin|Chavín]] style in pottery and imagery before local traditions took over.
paracas.r: Paracas society was organised in chiefdoms supported by irrigation farming and rich fishing grounds. It is best known from its cemeteries: the necropolis of Wari Kayan, excavated by Julio C. Tello in 1927, held more than 400 mummy bundles wrapped in brilliantly coloured embroidered mantles of [[e:cotton|cotton]] and camelid wool. Paracas people practised cranial deformation and trepanation of the skull. Their pottery was painted with resin-based colours after firing.
paracas.e: Around 100 BCE the late Paracas tradition, known as Necropolis, merged gradually into the [[s:nazca|Nazca culture]], which inherited its iconography and textile techniques. The large Paracas Candelabra geoglyph is sometimes attributed to it, though its date is uncertain.

principality-of-anhalt-plotzkau.t: Short-lived Anhalt principality, a minor appanage whose line went on to rule Anhalt-Köthen.
principality-of-anhalt-plotzkau.o: Plötzkau, a small castle district on the Saale, was assigned in the 1603 partition of [[s:principality-of-anhalt|Anhalt]] to August, a younger son of Joachim Ernst. It began as an [[e:appanage|appanage]] of limited territory rather than a full share, and was formally set up as a principality in 1611.
principality-of-anhalt-plotzkau.r: Little distinguishes its government from the other [[s:principality-of-anhalt|Anhalt]] states: it was a small Calvinist territory administered from Plötzkau castle, with revenues from farming along the Saale. Its prince August acted as regent for the young princes of [[s:principality-of-anhalt-kothen|Anhalt-Köthen]] and served the joint interests of the Anhalt house during the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years' War]].
principality-of-anhalt-plotzkau.e: In 1665 the Köthen line died out and Lebrecht and Emanuel of Anhalt-Plötzkau inherited [[s:principality-of-anhalt-kothen|Anhalt-Köthen]], giving up Plötzkau, which returned to [[s:principality-of-anhalt-bernburg|Anhalt-Bernburg]]. The Plötzkau branch thus continued as the ruling house of Köthen until 1847.

province-of-maryland.t: The proprietary colony of the Calvert family on Chesapeake Bay, founded as a refuge for English Catholics and known for its 1649 Toleration Act.
province-of-maryland.o: George Calvert, first Baron Baltimore, sought a colony where Catholics could live freely, and in 1632 Charles I granted the charter to his son Cecil Calvert. In 1634 the ships Ark and Dove brought the first settlers, led by Leonard Calvert, to St Mary's City on the lower Potomac.
province-of-maryland.r: The Calverts held the colony as a proprietary palatinate with wide powers, though an elected assembly met from 1635. Catholics remained a minority, and the Toleration Act of 1649 protected Trinitarian Christians. Tobacco grown by servants and enslaved Africans was the mainstay. After the Protestant revolt of 1689 the Crown took over, the Church of [[e:england|England]] was established, and the capital moved to Annapolis in 1694. The Protestant Calverts regained the province in 1715.
province-of-maryland.e: The Mason-Dixon line, surveyed from 1763, settled the long border dispute with the [[s:province-of-pennsylvania|Province of Pennsylvania]]. Governor Robert Eden left in 1776, and Maryland declared independence as a state of the [[s:united-states|United States]].

palatinate-birkenfeld.t: A Wittelsbach line in the Hunsrück, from whose descendants came the kings of Bavaria and the dukes in Bavaria.
palatinate-birkenfeld.o: In 1569 Duke Wolfgang of [[s:palatinate-zweibrucken|Palatinate-Zweibrücken]] divided his lands among his sons, and Charles I received Birkenfeld, part of the old [[s:county-of-sponheim|County of Sponheim]] in the Hunsrück, founding the line of Palatinate-Birkenfeld.
palatinate-birkenfeld.r: The dukes ruled a small, scattered territory from Birkenfeld, sharing the [[s:county-of-sponheim|Sponheim]] lands with Baden, and kept a modest Lutheran court. Branches formed at Bischweiler and [[s:free-imperial-city-of-gelnhausen|Gelnhausen]]. Christian II acquired the lordship of Rappoltstein (Ribeaupierre) in Alsace by marriage in 1673.
palatinate-birkenfeld.e: In 1731 Christian III inherited [[s:palatinate-zweibrucken|Palatinate-Zweibrücken]], and the line moved there as Zweibrücken-Birkenfeld. His grandson Maximilian Joseph became the first king of the [[s:kingdom-of-bavaria|Kingdom of Bavaria]] in 1806, while the [[s:free-imperial-city-of-gelnhausen|Gelnhausen]] branch became the dukes in Bavaria, family of Empress Elisabeth of [[e:austria|Austria]].

palace-state-of-knossos.t: The largest Minoan palace centre and later a Mycenaean-ruled capital whose Linear B tablets are the earliest written Greek from Crete.
palace-state-of-knossos.o: [[s:knossos|Knossos]], near modern Heraklion, was occupied from the Neolithic and became [[e:crete|Crete's]] largest settlement. Around 1950 BCE the first palace was built around a central court. Rebuilt after an earthquake c. 1700 BCE, it grew into a complex of more than a thousand rooms, with a town of perhaps several thousand people around it.
palace-state-of-knossos.r: [[s:knossos|Knossos]] was the centre of Minoan civilisation, with frescoes such as the bull-leaping scene, light [[e:well|wells]], storerooms of pithoi and a theatral area. Administration used Linear A. After c. 1450 BCE Greek-speaking rulers took control and kept records in Linear B, listing sheep, wool, textiles and offerings to gods such as Potnia. The palace then dominated much of central and western [[e:crete|Crete]].
palace-state-of-knossos.e: The palace was destroyed by fire, traditionally c. 1375 BCE, though the date is debated and some scholars place the final destruction later. [[s:knossos|Knossos]] survived as a town and became the Greek city-state described separately as Knossos. Arthur Evans excavated and partly reconstructed the site from 1900.
palace-state-of-knossos.re: Minoan religion; later Mycenaean Greek religion

principality-of-samtskhe.t: A south-west Georgian principality ruled by the Jaqeli atabegs, which broke from the Georgian crown and was finally absorbed by the Ottoman Empire.
principality-of-samtskhe.o: Samtskhe, the upland borderland around Akhaltsikhe, was governed by the Jaqeli family as royal lieutenants. In 1268 Sargis I Jaqeli secured direct recognition from the Mongol [[s:ilkhanate|Ilkhanate]], making his lands effectively separate from the [[s:kingdom-of-georgia|Kingdom of Georgia]], and his heirs held the title of atabeg.
principality-of-samtskhe.r: The atabegs ruled from Akhaltsikhe over farming valleys, the cave monastery of Vardzia and routes to [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]]. Beka I Jaqeli issued a law code in the early 14th century. Samtskhe rejoined [[s:georgia|Georgia]] under George V but broke away again in the 15th century, becoming a battleground between the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] and [[e:safavid-empire|Safavids]] after 1500 and a [[e:vassal|vassal]] of the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]] from 1578.
principality-of-samtskhe.e: The Jaqeli rulers converted to [[e:islam|Islam]], and in 1628 the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] turned Samtskhe into the [[s:childir-eyalet|Childir Eyalet]], with Safar Pasha, a Jaqeli, as its first governor. Much of the population was gradually Islamised, and the region returned to Georgian rule only after the Russian conquest of 1829.

principality-of-hersfeld.t: A Benedictine abbey in Hesse founded by a disciple of Saint Boniface, whose abbots ruled a principality until it became part of Hesse-Kassel.
principality-of-hersfeld.o: Hersfeld began as a hermitage of Saint Sturmi around 736 and was refounded as a Benedictine monastery by Archbishop Lullus of [[e:mainz|Mainz]] around 769. [[e:charlemagne|Charlemagne]] granted it royal protection in 775, making it an imperial abbey. Its relics of Saint Wigbert made it an important pilgrimage centre.
principality-of-hersfeld.r: Hersfeld held lands across Hesse and Thuringia, recorded in the Breviarium Lulli. Its scholars included the chronicler Lambert of Hersfeld, who wrote a major account of the reign of Henry IV. The abbots were princes of the Empire, but rivalry with the town of Hersfeld and with the landgraves of Hesse slowly weakened them.
principality-of-hersfeld.e: The landgraves of Hesse became protectors of the abbey and, after the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]], effectively controlled it. In 1648 the [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] secularised Hersfeld as a principality granted to [[s:electorate-of-hesse|Hesse-Kassel]]. The ruins of its Romanesque abbey church are among the largest in [[e:germany|Germany]].

phaselis.t: Phaselis, a Rhodian colony with three harbours on the Lycian coast, a trading city later held by pirates and taken by Rome.
phaselis.o: Colonists from [[s:lindos|Lindos]] on [[s:rhodes|Rhodes]] founded Phaselis, traditionally in 690 BCE, on a peninsula at the border of [[s:lycian-dynasts|Lycia]] and Pamphylia. Its position on the coastal route between the [[e:aegean|Aegean]] and the eastern [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]] made it a natural port of call.
phaselis.r: Phaselis was a Greek city governed by its citizens and a member of the [[s:delian-league|Delian League]]. It traded [[e:timber|timber]], rose oil and other goods and had a share in the Hellenion at Naukratis in [[e:egypt|Egypt]]. Alexander of the [[s:macedonian-empire|Macedonian Empire]] stayed there in the winter of 334/333 BCE.
phaselis.e: In the 1st century BCE the pirate leader Zenicetes held Phaselis. The Roman general Publius Servilius Isauricus captured it in 77 BCE, and the city was then absorbed into the Roman world, later joining the [[s:lycian-league|Lycian League]].

protectorate-of-bohemia-and-moravia.t: Nazi-occupied Czech lands, nominally autonomous but ruled through terror, deportations and forced labour from 1939 to 1945.
protectorate-of-bohemia-and-moravia.o: After the Munich Agreement and the loss of the Sudetenland in 1938, [[e:germany|Germany]] occupied the rest of [[s:kingdom-of-bohemia|Bohemia]] and [[s:margraviate-of-moravia|Moravia]] on 15 March 1939, as Slovakia declared independence. The next day Hitler proclaimed the [[e:protectorate|Protectorate]] of [[e:bohemia|Bohemia]] and [[e:moravia|Moravia]] from [[e:prague|Prague]] Castle.
protectorate-of-bohemia-and-moravia.r: A Czech government under President Emil Hácha remained in place, but real power lay with the Reich Protector, first Konstantin von Neurath and then Reinhard Heydrich. Czech universities were closed in 1939, and Czech industry, such as the [[e:skoda|Škoda]] works, served the German war effort. Heydrich was assassinated by Czech parachutists in 1942, and the Nazis destroyed the villages of Lidice and Ležáky in reprisal. Most Czech [[e:jews|Jews]] were deported via Theresienstadt and murdered.
protectorate-of-bohemia-and-moravia.e: The [[e:prague|Prague]] uprising broke out on 5 May 1945, and the Red Army entered Prague on 9 May. The territory was restored to [[s:czechoslovakia|Czechoslovakia]], which expelled most of its German population in the following two years.

principality-of-kandahar.t: The principality ruled by the Barakzai 'Kandahar Sardars', half-brothers of Dost Mohammad Khan, between the fall of the Durranis and Afghan reunification.
principality-of-kandahar.o: As the [[s:durrani-empire|Durrani Empire]] fell apart after 1818, the powerful [[e:barakzai-dynasty|Barakzai]] brothers divided its lands. [[e:kandahar|Kandahar]] went to a group of brothers known as the Kandahar [[e:sardar|Sardars]], led by Purdil Khan and later Kohandil Khan, who were half-brothers of Dost Mohammad Khan of [[e:kabul|Kabul]].
principality-of-kandahar.r: The [[e:sardar|sardars]] ruled jointly over [[e:kandahar|Kandahar]] and its Pashtun tribes, relying on tribal levies and revenue from trade on the route to [[e:herat|Herat]] and [[e:india|India]]. They negotiated with [[e:persia|Persia]] and [[e:russia|Russia]] as well as with their relatives in [[e:kabul|Kabul]]. During the First Anglo-Afghan War the British occupied Kandahar from 1839 to 1842, and the sardars took refuge in Persia before returning.
principality-of-kandahar.e: After Kohandil Khan died in 1855, Dost Mohammad Khan seized [[e:kandahar|Kandahar]] and incorporated it into the [[s:emirate-of-afghanistan|Emirate of Afghanistan]], a key step towards reuniting the Afghan lands.

principality-of-kesh.t: A Sogdian principality south of Samarkand, centred on the city later called Shahrisabz, the birthplace of Timur.
principality-of-kesh.o: Kesh lay on the Qashqadarya River in southern [[s:principality-of-samarkand|Sogdiana]]. It became one of the Sogdian principalities in the 6th century, under the overlordship of the [[s:western-turkic-khaganate|Western Turkic Khaganate]], and was ruled by local lords who issued their own coins.
principality-of-kesh.r: Like its neighbours, Kesh was a town of farmers, craftsmen and merchants governed by a local dynasty and nobility. Chinese sources call it Shi, and it traded through [[e:samarkand|Samarkand]] and over the Iron Gate pass to Tokharistan. Very little detail survives about its rulers or institutions.
principality-of-kesh.e: Arab armies conquered Kesh during the campaigns of Qutayba ibn Muslim in the early 8th century, and it was absorbed into Umayyad and Abbasid [[e:transoxiana|Transoxiana]]. The city, renamed Shahrisabz, later became the home town of [[e:timur|Timur]].

portuguese-timor.t: Portugal's colony on the eastern half of Timor for nearly three centuries, whose sudden end in 1975 led to Indonesian invasion.
portuguese-timor.o: Dominican missionaries and traders from the Portuguese base on Solor had been active on Timor since the 16th century, buying sandalwood. In 1702 António Coelho Guerreiro arrived at Lifau as the first governor, but real power on the island was long contested by the Topasses, mixed-race Portuguese-speaking warlords.
portuguese-timor.r: Portugal ruled through alliances with local kings (liurai) and the Catholic Church. The capital moved to Dili in 1769. Sandalwood gave way to [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]] in the 19th century, and borders with the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] were settled in 1859 and 1914, leaving the Oecusse enclave. Governor José Celestino da Silva extended control by force, and the Manufahi revolt of 1912 was crushed.
portuguese-timor.e: Occupied by [[e:japan|Japan]] from 1942 to 1945 at great cost to its people, the colony returned to Portugal. After the [[e:carnation-revolution|Carnation Revolution]] of 1974 Fretilin declared independence in November 1975, but [[s:indonesia|Indonesia]] invaded in December. Independence finally came as [[s:east-timor|East Timor]] in 2002.

cr.a: Original: Columbano Bordalo Pinheiro Vector: Vítor Luís Rodrigues, António Martins-Tuválkin

pukara.t: The first major political and ceremonial centre of the Lake Titicaca basin, whose stone sculpture and sunken courts foreshadowed the later power of Tiwanaku.
pukara.o: Pukará grew from about 500 BCE on the northern side of the Titicaca basin in Puno, [[e:peru|Peru]]. A large terraced ceremonial complex was built against a red sandstone outcrop, with sunken rectangular courts at its summit. It became the dominant centre of the northern basin.
pukara.r: Pukará is thought to have been a chiefdom or early regional polity whose leaders controlled herding of llamas and alpacas, raised-field farming and trade in obsidian and other goods. It is known for carved stone stelae and statues, including figures holding trophy heads, and for polychrome incised pottery with feline and human images. Its sunken courts and stone sculpture tradition influenced later highland architecture.
pukara.e: The site declined after about 200 CE, and the centre of power in the basin shifted south to [[s:tiwanaku|Tiwanaku]], which absorbed elements of its art and ritual. The modern town of Pucará is known for its ceramic bulls, an unrelated colonial tradition.

poonch-state.t: A Dogra principality subordinate to Jammu and Kashmir, whose 1947 rebellion led to the creation of Azad Kashmir.
poonch-state.o: In 1850 Maharaja [[e:gulab-singh|Gulab Singh]] granted Poonch to his nephew Moti Singh, son of the [[e:lahore|Lahore]] minister [[e:dhian-singh|Dhian Singh]], as a [[e:jagir|jagir]] under [[s:jammu-and-kashmir-princely-state|Jammu and Kashmir]]. Its rulers held the title of Raja.
poonch-state.r: The Rajas governed a hilly region with a largely Muslim population, many of whom served in the British [[e:indian-army|Indian Army]]. The Maharajas of [[s:jammu-and-kashmir-princely-state|Jammu and Kashmir]] repeatedly sought to curtail Poonch's autonomy, and in 1936 its subordinate status was confirmed.
poonch-state.e: In 1947 Muslim ex-servicemen in Poonch rose against Maharaja Hari Singh's government, a rebellion that merged into the war over [[e:kashmir|Kashmir]]. The district was divided by the 1949 ceasefire line between Pakistani-administered Azad Kashmir and Indian [[s:jammu-and-kashmir-princely-state|Jammu and Kashmir]].

province-of-pennsylvania.t: William Penn's Quaker colony, a 'holy experiment' in religious freedom whose capital Philadelphia became the largest city in British America.
province-of-pennsylvania.o: In 1681 Charles II granted William Penn a vast tract west of the Delaware River to settle a debt owed to Penn's father. Penn planned a refuge for Quakers and other persecuted groups, issued a Frame of Government in 1682, laid out Philadelphia on a grid and, by tradition, made a treaty of friendship with the Lenape at Shackamaxon.
province-of-pennsylvania.r: The Charter of Privileges of 1701 created a single elected assembly and guaranteed freedom of worship to all who believed in God. Quakers, Germans, beginning with Germantown in 1683, and later Scots-Irish settlers poured in, and grain exports made Philadelphia prosperous. The Penn heirs remained proprietors, and the Walking Purchase of 1737 cheated the Lenape of land. Benjamin Franklin made Philadelphia a centre of [[e:printing-press|printing]], science and civic institutions.
province-of-pennsylvania.e: Philadelphia hosted the Continental Congress, which declared independence there in 1776. That year Pennsylvania adopted a radical democratic constitution, ending proprietary rule, and became a state of the [[s:united-states|United States]].

principality-of-reuss-greiz.t: The Elder Line of the house of Reuss, ruling from Greiz, one of the smallest states of the German Empire.
principality-of-reuss-greiz.o: In the division of the Reuss lands in 1564, the Elder Line received Greiz and the surrounding part of the [[s:lordship-of-plauen|Vogtland]]. After a split into Upper and Lower Greiz, the branches were reunited in 1768, and in 1778 Heinrich XI was raised to prince of the empire.
principality-of-reuss-greiz.r: Like their cousins, all male members were named Heinrich, but the Elder Line numbered them in a sequence that restarted at intervals. The principality was small, Lutheran and agrarian, later with textile mills in Greiz and Zeulenroda. Its upper and lower castles still dominate the town.
principality-of-reuss-greiz.e: Reuss Elder Line sided with [[e:austria|Austria]] in 1866 and was occupied by [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]], but joined the [[s:german-empire|German Empire]] in 1871, and Prince Heinrich XXII remained a noted opponent of Prussian policy. After the revolution of 1918 it merged with the Younger Line in 1919 into the [[s:peoples-state-of-reuss|People's State of Reuss]], part of Thuringia from 1920.

piedmontese-republic.t: The provisional republic set up in Piedmont after the French forced King Charles Emmanuel IV to abandon the mainland in 1798.
piedmontese-republic.o: In December 1798 French troops occupied Turin and forced Charles Emmanuel IV of the [[s:kingdom-of-sardinia|Kingdom of Sardinia]] to give up his mainland states and withdraw to the island of [[e:sardinia|Sardinia]]. A provisional government of Piedmontese patriots took over in Turin, proclaiming a republic.
piedmontese-republic.r: The provisional government abolished feudal rights and noble titles and held votes in which the Piedmontese communities asked to be annexed to [[e:france|France]]; the [[s:french-first-republic|French Directory]] approved the annexation in early 1799. Real power lay with French commissioners and generals, and French requisitions caused unrest in the countryside.
piedmontese-republic.e: In 1799 the Austro-Russian army under [[e:alexander-suvorov|Suvorov]] drove the French out of Piedmont, ending the regime. After [[e:napoleon|Napoleon's]] victory at Marengo in 1800, the French set up the [[s:subalpine-republic|Subalpine Republic]].

principality-of-mingrelia.t: A western Georgian principality ruled by the Dadiani princes, which under Levan II dominated western Georgia and kept autonomy until 1867.
principality-of-mingrelia.o: Mingrelia, or Odishi, the lowland between the Rioni and the Inguri, had been governed by the Dadiani family as eristavis since the Middle Ages. As the [[s:kingdom-of-imereti|Kingdom of Imereti]] weakened, the Dadiani became effectively independent, and from 1557 they ruled as sovereign princes, paying tribute to the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]].
principality-of-mingrelia.r: The princes ruled from Zugdidi and other residences over nobles and a largely enserfed peasantry. Levan II Dadiani, from 1611, made Mingrelia the leading power of western [[s:georgia|Georgia]], fighting [[s:kingdom-of-imereti|Imereti]] and [[s:principality-of-abkhazia|Abkhazia]]; Catholic missionaries such as Arcangelo Lamberti described his court. The [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trade]] with Ottoman ports was a lasting curse. The Mingrelian language was spoken alongside Georgian.
principality-of-mingrelia.e: Grigol Dadiani accepted a Russian [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] in 1803. After the [[e:crimean-war|Crimean War]] and a peasant revolt, [[e:russia|Russia]] took over the administration in 1857 and formally annexed the principality in 1867. Princess Ekaterine Dadiani was the last ruling figure.

principality-of-moldavia.t: Romanian principality between the Carpathians and the Dniester, celebrated for Stephen the Great and its painted monasteries, which merged with Wallachia in 1859.
principality-of-moldavia.o: Around 1346 the Hungarian king sent Dragoș, a Romanian noble from Maramureș, to set up a march east of the Carpathians against the [[s:golden-horde|Golden Horde]]. In 1359 another Maramureș noble, Bogdan I, drove out Dragoș's heirs and made Moldavia independent of [[e:hungary|Hungary]].
principality-of-moldavia.r: The voivode ruled with boyars and the [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox Church]] from Suceava and, after 1564, Iași. Alexander the Good gave the country stable institutions. Stephen the Great (1457–1504) defeated the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] at Vaslui in 1475 and built churches such as Putna and Voroneț; Voroneț and other Moldavian churches received their famous exterior frescoes in the 16th century. From the 16th century Moldavia paid tribute to the Ottomans, and from 1711 to 1821 it was ruled by Phanariot princes.
principality-of-moldavia.e: It lost [[s:duchy-of-bukovina|Bukovina]] to [[e:austria|Austria]] in 1775 and Bessarabia to [[e:russia|Russia]] in 1812. In 1859 it elected Alexandru Ioan Cuza, as did the [[s:principality-of-wallachia|Principality of Wallachia]], creating the union that became [[s:kingdom-of-romania|Romania]].

peloponnesian-league.t: Sparta's network of alliances, the leading military coalition of classical Greece and Athens' opponent in the Peloponnesian War.
peloponnesian-league.o: The league grew in the mid-6th century BCE when [[s:sparta|Sparta]], after defeating [[s:tegea|Tegea]] around 550 BCE, turned from conquest to alliance. City by city, Peloponnesian states such as Tegea, [[s:corinth|Corinth]], [[s:elis|Elis]] and later [[s:megara|Megara]] swore to have the same friends and enemies as the Lacedaemonians and to follow them wherever they led.
peloponnesian-league.r: There was no common treasury or capital beyond [[s:sparta|Sparta]]. Each ally was bound to [[e:sparta|Sparta]] by its own treaty; from the late 6th century a congress of allies voted on war, each city having one vote, and Sparta commanded the joint army. Sparta favoured friendly oligarchies in member cities. The league formed the core of Greek resistance to [[e:persia|Persia]] in 480-479 BCE.
peloponnesian-league.e: It fought and won the [[e:peloponnesian-war|Peloponnesian War]] against the [[s:delian-league|Delian League]] (431-404 BCE), but the Theban victory at Leuctra in 371 BCE and invasions of Laconia broke [[e:sparta|Sparta's]] hold. The liberation of [[s:messene|Messenia]] and separate peace deals by [[s:corinth|Corinth]] and others in 366-365 BCE ended the league.

perge.t: Perge, a Greek city of the Pamphylian plain, famous for its sanctuary of Artemis and the mathematician Apollonius.
perge.o: Greek tradition says Perge was founded after the Trojan War by heroes such as Mopsus and Calchas, and a city called Parha appears in a Hittite treaty. By the 7th century BCE it was a Greek-speaking city near the coast, inland on the Kestros river.
perge.r: Perge was a self-governing city whose patron was Artemis Pergaia, worshipped at a rich temple. It surrendered to Alexander of the [[s:macedonian-empire|Macedonian Empire]] in 333 BCE and later passed through Seleucid and Attalid rule. The mathematician Apollonius of Perga wrote his work on conic sections in the 3rd century BCE.
perge.e: Perge came under Roman control, and in 25 BCE it became part of the Roman province of [[s:galatia|Galatia]], later Pamphylia. Its finest monuments, including colonnaded streets and a [[e:theatre|theatre]], date from the Roman period.

pagania.t: Slavic principality of the Narentines between the Cetina and Neretva, whose pirate fleets challenged Venice for two centuries.
pagania.o: The Narentines were [[e:slavs|Slavs]] who settled the coast between the Cetina and Neretva rivers in the 7th century. By the 9th century they formed a principality, called Pagania by the [[e:byzantine-empire|Byzantines]] because they accepted [[e:christianity|Christianity]] late. Constantine VII lists its towns, including Mokro and Ostrog, and the islands of Brač, Hvar, Korčula and Mljet.
pagania.r: Ruled by its own princes and assembly of clans, Pagania lived largely from the sea, raiding and taxing Adriatic shipping. [[e:venice|Venice]] had to pay for safe passage, and in 887 the Narentines killed Doge Pietro I Candiano in battle. They accepted Byzantine missionaries in the late 9th century.
pagania.e: In 1000 Doge Pietro II Orseolo led a fleet that broke Narentine sea power. Pagania then came under the [[s:kingdom-of-croatia-925-1102|Kingdom of Croatia]] (925-1102) and later [[s:zachlumia|Zachlumia]], and the name fades by the 11th century.

principality-of-montenegro.t: Secular Montenegrin principality of the Petrović-Njegoš dynasty, which won international recognition of its independence at the Congress of Berlin.
principality-of-montenegro.o: In 1852 Danilo Petrović-Njegoš, heir of the [[s:prince-bishopric-of-montenegro|Prince-Bishopric of Montenegro]], declined to become a [[e:bishop|bishop]] and proclaimed himself secular prince with Russian backing. He issued a legal code in 1855, imposed taxes on the clans, and his brother Mirko Petrović defeated the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] at Grahovac in 1858, after which Montenegro's borders were first drawn.
principality-of-montenegro.r: After Danilo's assassination in 1860, his nephew Nikola ruled for over half a century as a patriarchal autocrat from Cetinje, where foreign legations were built. [[s:montenegro|Montenegro]] remained a poor land of clans and herders, heavily subsidised by [[e:russia|Russia]]. Nikola married his daughters into the royal houses of [[e:italy|Italy]], [[s:serbia|Serbia]] and Russia, and granted a constitution only in 1905.
principality-of-montenegro.e: War against the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] in 1876 to 1878 won recognition of independence at Berlin in 1878, nearly doubling the territory and gaining Nikšić, Podgorica, Bar and later Ulcinj. On his jubilee in 1910 Nikola proclaimed the [[s:kingdom-of-montenegro|Kingdom of Montenegro]].

palitana-state.t: A Gohil Rajput state in Saurashtra whose territory held Shatrunjaya, the hill of nearly a thousand Jain temples and one of Jainism's holiest sites.
palitana-state.o: Palitana was ruled by a branch of the Gohil [[e:rajputs|Rajputs]], the clan that also ruled [[s:bhavnagar-state|Bhavnagar State]]; the Gohils entered Saurashtra in the 13th century, and tradition gives Palitana's line an early date. Firm records are mainly from the 17th century onward.
palitana-state.r: The state's fame came from Shatrunjaya hill, covered with Jain temples built over many centuries by merchant patrons. The Thakore levied payments on pilgrims, which led to long disputes with the Jain community's trust, Anandji Kalyanji. British officials brokered a series of agreements in the 19th century fixing an annual sum paid by the Jains.
palitana-state.e: Palitana joined the [[s:saurashtra-state|United State of Saurashtra]] in 1948 and is now a town in [[s:bhavnagar-state|Bhavnagar]] district, [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]]. Shatrunjaya remains a major pilgrimage centre.

paros.t: Cycladic island famed for its fine white marble and its poet Archilochus, and coloniser of Thasos.
paros.o: Paros, in the central Cyclades, was settled by [[e:ionia|Ionian Greeks]] in the early Iron Age. Its translucent marble, quarried in underground galleries, became the prized stone of Greek sculptors. By the 7th century BCE Paros was strong enough to colonise [[s:thasos|Thasos]] c. 680 BCE and later Parion on the [[e:hellespont|Hellespont]].
paros.r: Archilochus, a pioneering lyric and iambic poet, was a Parian who joined the settlement of [[s:thasos|Thasos]]. Paros was a commercial and religious centre with a temple of Demeter. It supported [[e:persia|Persia]] in 490 BCE, and the Athenian Miltiades failed to take it in 489 BCE. In the [[s:delian-league|Delian League]] Paros paid one of the largest island tributes.
paros.e: Paros came under Hellenistic kings and later Roman control by 146 BCE. Its inscribed Parian Chronicle of 264 BCE, now in [[e:oxford|Oxford]], is a key source for Greek chronology, and Parian marble remained in demand.

petrocorii.t: Gallic people of the Dordogne whose name lives on in the Périgord and whose town Vesunna became Périgueux.
petrocorii.o: The Petrocorii lived in the valleys of the Isle and the Dordogne, in the modern Dordogne. Their name is usually read as the four armies, perhaps a league of four communities. Strabo notes their iron workings.
petrocorii.r: Little is known of their rulers. Their main oppidum stood at La Curade near Périgueux.
petrocorii.e: They sent five thousand men to relieve Alesia in 52 BCE. Under [[e:rome|Rome]] their capital was Vesunna, a well-preserved town whose temple tower, the Tour de Vésone, still stands. The city became Périgueux, and the medieval [[s:county-of-perigord|County of Périgord]] kept their name.

cr.a: Pétrocores (peuple celtique de Gaule). Autorité émettrice de monnaie

pinya-kingdom.t: A short-lived central Burmese kingdom founded by Thihathu in 1313, rival of Sagaing and forerunner of the Ava Kingdom.
pinya-kingdom.o: Thihathu, the last surviving of the three [[s:myinsaing-kingdom|Myinsaing]] brothers, founded a new capital at Pinya near the Kyaukse [[e:rice|rice]] lands in 1313 and proclaimed himself heir to the Pagan kings. His son Saw Yun soon broke away and set up a rival court at [[s:sagaing-kingdom|Sagaing]] in 1315.
pinya-kingdom.r: Pinya ruled the Kyaukse granary and parts of central [[s:myanmar|Myanmar]], but its kings struggled with rebellious [[e:vassal|vassals]], the breakaway [[s:sagaing-kingdom|Sagaing Kingdom]] and Shan raids from the north. Royal patronage of [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]] continued, and the court maintained Pagan-era titles and administration on a smaller scale. Uzana I and Kyawswa I were among its kings.
pinya-kingdom.e: In 1364 Shan forces from [[s:mong-mao|Mong Mao]] sacked both Pinya and [[s:sagaing-kingdom|Sagaing]]. Thado Minbya, a prince of the Sagaing line linked to the Pinya house, reunited the region and in 1365 founded the [[s:ava-kingdom|Ava Kingdom]] at a new capital nearby, which absorbed Pinya.

principality-of-reuss-ebersdorf.t: Tiny Reuss lordship in Thuringia that became a stronghold of Pietism and the Moravian Brethren.
principality-of-reuss-ebersdorf.o: Ebersdorf was separated from Reuss-Lobenstein in 1678 for Heinrich X, a younger son of the Lobenstein line, creating a small county within the Younger Line of the House of Reuss in the Thuringian Highlands.
principality-of-reuss-ebersdorf.r: The counts of Ebersdorf were devout Pietists who turned their small residence into a religious centre. Count Nikolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf, founder of the renewed Moravian Church at Herrnhut, married Erdmuthe Dorothea of Reuss-Ebersdorf in 1722, and a Moravian congregation settled in Ebersdorf. Queen Victoria's maternal grandmother came from the family. The rulers became princes in 1806.
principality-of-reuss-ebersdorf.e: Ebersdorf inherited Reuss-Lobenstein in 1824. Prince Heinrich LXXII, an eccentric absolutist, abdicated during the revolution of 1848, and his lands passed to Reuss-Schleiz, forming the Principality of [[s:principality-of-reuss-gera|Reuss Younger Line]].

perlis.t: Smallest state of Malaysia, separated from Kedah by Siam in 1843 and ruled by a dynasty of Arab descent.
perlis.o: After suppressing revolts in the [[s:kedah-sultanate|Kedah Sultanate]] in the 1830s, Siam divided the sultanate and in 1843 created Perlis as a separate dependency. Its first raja was Syed Hussain Jamalullail, a Kedah noble of Hadhrami Arab descent, whose family has ruled ever since with the title of raja rather than sultan.
perlis.r: Perlis was a small [[e:rice|rice]]-growing state on the Thai border, with limestone hills, [[e:tin|tin]] and a modest population of Malay farmers. It sent tribute to Bangkok and was governed by the raja with a small council. The royal seat was at Arau, and Islamic law and Malay custom shaped administration.
perlis.e: The Anglo-Siamese Treaty of 1909 transferred Perlis to British protection; it accepted a British adviser and became one of the [[s:unfederated-malay-states|Unfederated Malay States]]. It later joined the [[s:federation-of-malaya|Federation of Malaya]] and [[s:malaysia|Malaysia]], and Raja Tuanku Syed Sirajuddin served as king from 2001 to 2006.

province-of-santo-domingo-1861-1865.t: Spain's brief reannexation of the Dominican Republic, the only time a former Spanish American colony returned to Spanish rule, ended by the War of Restoration.
province-of-santo-domingo-1861-1865.o: Facing debt, political rivalry and the threat of invasion from [[s:republic-of-haiti|Haiti]], President Pedro Santana arranged for the [[s:first-dominican-republic|First Dominican Republic]] to be annexed by [[e:spain|Spain]], proclaimed on 18 March 1861. Spain, under Queen Isabella II and the government of Leopoldo O'Donnell, accepted, partly to strengthen its position in the [[e:caribbean|Caribbean]] while the [[s:united-states|United States]] was engulfed in civil war.
province-of-santo-domingo-1861-1865.r: Santana became captain general but resigned in 1862 as Spanish officials took over. The new regime offended Dominicans: it imposed Spanish officials and soldiers, new taxes and church rules, and treated mixed-race and black Dominicans with contempt, raising fears that [[e:slavery|slavery]] would return. Early revolts were suppressed with executions, including that of Francisco del Rosario Sánchez in 1861.
province-of-santo-domingo-1861-1865.e: In August 1863 rebels raised the flag at Capotillo, starting the War of Restoration, with [[s:spanish-jamaica|Santiago]] as their capital and Gregorio Luperón among the leaders. Disease and [[e:guerrilla-warfare|guerrilla]] warfare broke the Spanish army. [[e:spain|Spain]] repealed the annexation in March 1865 and left in July, creating the [[s:second-dominican-republic|Second Dominican Republic]].

palatinate-veldenz.t: A small Wittelsbach duchy on the Glan and in the northern Vosges, created in 1543 for a younger branch of the Zweibrücken line.
palatinate-veldenz.o: By the Treaty of Marburg in 1543, [[e:count-palatine|Count Palatine]] Rupert, uncle and former guardian of Duke Wolfgang of [[s:palatinate-zweibrucken|Palatinate-Zweibrücken]], received the old [[s:county-of-veldenz|County of Veldenz]] with Lauterecken and lands in the Vosges, founding the line of Palatinate-Veldenz.
palatinate-veldenz.r: The dukes ruled from Lauterecken and from Lützelstein (La Petite-Pierre) in the northern Vosges, a scattered and poor territory of farming villages. They were Lutheran, and Duke George John founded the town of Phalsbourg in 1570. The [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years' War]] and [[e:louis-xiv|Louis XIV's]] Reunions, which claimed the Vosges lands for [[e:france|France]] after 1680, devastated the little state.
palatinate-veldenz.e: When Duke Leopold Louis died without male heirs in 1694, a long inheritance dispute followed among the Palatine branches. It was settled only in 1733, when the lands were shared among the [[s:electoral-palatinate|Electoral Palatinate]] and other Wittelsbach lines.
